From her own Barbie doll to bench - how Ellie Kildunne slipped from Red Roses' XV

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:22:55 GMT

Kildunne has made 33 appearances for the Red Roses since the start of 2024, with 29 of those coming at full-back

She's the poster girl. She's the former World Player of the Year. She came second at BBC Sports Personality of the Year. She lit up the 2025 Rugby World Cup. She's even got her own Barbie doll.

So why isn't Ellie Kildunne starting for England against the USA on Friday night (21:15 kick-off)?

First of all she is human, let's not forget that.

We're all allowed ups and downs. It's just that Kildunne's dip comes with the large spotlight of her being the Red Roses' household name.

None of her team-mates come close to her popularity with fans both in and outside rugby union with her 239,000 Instagram followers. Her face and name are used for clicks by all the media, present company included.

However, if you follow the sport and watch her play, no-one is undroppable.

England suffered their first loss in four years to end their 41-Test unbeaten streak in Toronto against Canada. In that fixture and their previous match with the same opposition in Exeter, Kildunne, 27, was a target for the opposition. She was never given space, defenders stepped up, her arms were pulled and balls were spilt.

When England head coach John Mitchell benched her after England's loss in Toronto he was clear that "it isn't disputed that she adds huge value".

However, he went on to add: "She's just going through a difficult period at the moment, and it's important for us to help her through that.

"She wants to become consistent as well, and she'll get back. It's also important to create competition and to recognise that you have to become more consistent, especially when you're competing in the Red Roses.

"So it's really important to reinforce the behaviours that we think are necessary to our game, and that goes for everyone."

The key word we can take from that is "consistent" - mainly because Mitchell said it twice.

Kildunne remains one of the world's most phenomenal players when it comes to gainline success and metres gained.

Much of this is due to poor opposition defence, but her statistics show a decline over the past three seasons at international level.

It seems almost harsh to highlight as these are numbers other players could only dream of but she's also gone from beating an average of six defenders a game in 2024, to 4.2 in 2026.

Kildunne has also conceded more penalties in 2026 than either of the previous two years. Some of these statistics, althought not all, are mirrored in her PWR performances last season.

While Canada are not alone, it does appear they are one of the best teams at dealing with Kildunne's threats.

In their drawn match in Exeter, Kildunne made 17 carries for 47 metres, an average of 2.8m, which is well below her usual standards. In Toronto she had the ball turned over twice - that was her joint-most in any England game.

Emma Sing now appears to have some purchase on the England 15 shirt and it is well deserved. She is a different full-back to Kildunne, which is a bonus for the Red Roses.

Sing has three PWR titles with her club side Gloucester-Hartpury and has been one of their most reliable players throughout that period. She has got a monster boot round the park and off the tee and, while Sing might not score the same worldies we have seen from Kildunne, her highlights reel is none too shabby.

On Sing's starting selection in Ottawa, Mitchell was happy to explain the players' differences: "They play quite differently. So we're very fortunate to have two very good full-backs. But you know, Emma's been sitting in the in the wings in this particular phase of our campaign.

"She was intermittent through injury for a long period of time. So she's in a really good physical place, and she's worked really, really hard. So I think it's time to give her an opportunity."

Red Roses make six changes but Kildunne on bench again

How have Canada closed gap to world champions England?

No panic for England but Mitchell issues PWR warning

It is a bit crass, but if you only follow men's rugby, Kildunne is a bit more Marcus Smith, while Sing is a bit more Freddie Steward - they are just different players.

Add to that, Sing was brought up on a Devon sheep farm and is not a huge fan of the media spotlight. That is not to say that Kildunne has coveted it, but she is far more comfortable in the media space.

You also must tip your hat to Kildunne and how she has managed herself with her new-found fame. After England beat New Zealand at Allianz Stadium in September, she spent an hour signing autographs and doing selfies to an unrelenting, screaming chorus of "Ellie, Ellie, Ellie".

Managing your own needs as an athlete and the increasing demands of fans is not an easy circle to square.

So where does Kildunne go from here? That is actually the most exciting bit.

No-one with a spiral bomb like she produced in the 2025 Rugby World Cup final is going to fade into the shadows. She is an incredible athlete and rugby player, so the expectation is that, much like Doctor Who, she will just regenerate.

Kildunne 2.0 could end up spending more time on the wing for England initially, but you can only see her fighting for a shirt and getting better.

Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:49:25 GMT

Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been told.

In her closing speech at London's Southwark Crown Court on Friday, prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC said the women had "nothing to gain" from coming forward apart from "some closure".

Speaking for the defence, Polly Dyer told jurors Brand had pleaded guilty and been fined over possession of cannabis in 1995, but had no other "convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings".

Brand, 51, is on trial facing seven charges; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. He denies the charges.

Karmy-Jones KC told the court that this case brings together six different women, none of whom knows each other.

She said that while all the alleged victims have since moved on with their lives, due to this trial they have been forced to "relive what has happened to them".

None of the women involved has "sought the limelight" or "any kind of publicity", she said, adding there was "no benefit to them from perhaps some closure."

Referring to Brand's accusers' evidence the prosecutor said "how many said he was nice and then there was a like a personality change…

"His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty," Karmy-Jones KC said.

She added that the complainant's evidence had been that "he didn't listen when I said no, he didn't stop, he didn't care, pulling pushing… thrusting".

"In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim."

The prosecutor also dismissed the idea that a documentary had caused the women to "re-invent" what actually happened.

"There is no magic force in this documentary", she added.

"What in fact happened was these women have realised they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth."

She added: "Truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years."

She told the jury: "The experience of people raped may be something that looms a little bit larger in your mind rather than the intricacies of the outfit.

"The defendant couldn't really remember anything when he was interviewed, in stark contrast to now when he suddenly seems to remember all sorts of details about the week."

Addressing Brand's presented change in character, Karmy-Jones KC told the court "He may now be a completely different person to the man he was between 1999 and 2009."

She added: "He may well look back and not find some of his jokes funny".

"He may now treat women with kindness and consent".

Brand's wife Laura gave evidence yesterday, when she told the court her husband was a "kind and a wonderful father".

Karmy-Jones KC called her Russell Brand's "undoubtedly lovely wife", who "bravely" gave evidence.

However, she also noted that she was not with him at the time many of the alleged acts are said to have taken place.

"The reality is she wasn't there then, for the first five counts, she wasn't with him, nor was she with him for the final two counts."

"Any contact was, I believe, sparse."

In the final set of agreed facts in his trial, the court heard from Dyer about Brand's fine after he "pleaded guilty to one charge of possessing cannabis on 20 April 1995".

"He received a fine. He has no other convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings", she said.

The trial continues.

How a passenger's confession helped convict her cousin of murder

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:34:30 GMT

Warning: This article contains distressing content

One afternoon in April, a children's nursery worker approached her manager in what she described as an hysterical state.

Gabrielle Debotte said she had something serious to tell Nicola Goddard, adding: "You're going to hate me and I'm going to lose my job."

What the 27-year-old said next proved a turning point in the investigation into the death of popular head teacher Michael Mullins, who had been struck by a car the previous day and dragged under its wheels for more than a mile.

Debotte told the astonished Goddard she not only knew who was responsible for hitting the 56-year-old as he cycled home from work, but she witnessed what happened from the passenger seat.

That night, having initially been treated as a suspect, she sat in the interview suite at Stretford Police Station and named her cousin, 35-year-old former mechanic Simon Richardson, as the driver.

Thanks in part to the evidence provided by Debotte, Richardson was found guilty of murder after a two-week trial at Manchester's Minshull Street Crown Court.

The contrasts between the lives of the killer and his victim were stark.

Less than a month before he struck the head teacher, Richardson was freed from prison.

He had served 47 days on remand awaiting sentence for stalking, harassment, threats to damage property and assaulting an emergency worker, and was freed on 26 March after being sentenced to a non-custodial community order.

In the following weeks, he was "sofa-surfing" between various addresses - including the home Debotte shared with her father in Altrincham, Greater Manchester.

In contrast, the head teacher had spent the past 17 years leading Stretford Grammar School, where he was known as a man of "unshakeable principles and a compassionate leader".

To his family, he was a beloved husband, father and grandfather, who "truly excelled" in his "role as grandad".

He was a lover of sport and remained physically fit, regularly cycling the 19 miles between the school and his home in Northwich, Cheshire.

At 17:35 BST on 20 April, he changed into his cycling clothes, put on his helmet and set off as normal.

Detectives would later be able to plot his journey via his Apple watch, which monitored his speed, location and heart rate.

Not far from the cyclist's starting point, a black Volvo XC90 was already catching the attention of other drivers as it sped "erratically" along the semi-rural roads on the outskirts of Trafford and north-east Cheshire.

It was being driven by Richardson, who had agreed to give his cousin a lift from Altrincham to a beauty salon in Lymm to pick up some weight-loss jabs.

In court, Debotte told jurors Richardson had been driving very fast and when she told him to slow down, his only response was to "smirk" and claim he was "a professional driver".

At 18:07, the car reached a junction in Warburton, Trafford, which connected Dunham Road with Paddock Lane.

According to Debotte and other witnesses, the Volvo ignored stop signs and road markings on Dunham Road as it attempted to turn left.

Debotte told the court she shouted "bike" three times, but Richardson made no attempt to slow down or brake before the Volvo smashed into the left side of the cyclist.

Witnesses saw the head teacher being thrown into the air while his bike, phone, part of his helmet and a wireless earphone were scattered across the road.

Witness Leon Dalziel-Bush, who saw the crash from his own vehicle, said the Volvo was going at such speed that "by the time I processed what had happened, it had gone".

Dalziel-Bush and others got out to help, but after searching in ditches and grass verges, they realised the cyclist was nowhere to be seen.

Richardson, who according to Debotte, stopped for a "split-second" before accelerating away, was already guilty of very serious criminal offences.

What happened over the next four minutes or so, prosecutors argued in court, made him a murderer.

The prosecution case hinged on whether it could prove Richardson was aware the cyclist was trapped and suffering increasingly appalling injuries just inches from his feet.

Phil Barnes KC, prosecuting, told the jury that many of them would know what it feels like to drive "with a flat tyre, or with wheels that are slightly out of balance or misaligned".

"Now imagine driving your car, at north of 60mph, with a fully grown human being wedged in the suspension and steering assembly of one of your wheels," he said.

Barnes had suggested it "must have been obvious" to Richardson that the 56-year-old was there, but "he carried on regardless", knowing his actions "were in all likelihood killing the man beneath his feet".

But, thanks to Debotte's workplace revelation, the case was built on much more than that simple premise.

When she gave her statement to police, she described a scene of absolute shock and panic in the car, complete with "screaming and crying".

"I had never seen anything like that in my life," she said, adding: "I still have visions of it."

She also recalled how "moaning" could clearly be heard from beneath the Volvo as it sped away and that Richardson blurted out: "He's under the car."

Detectives would be able to prove, via watch and phone data, that his car had stopped on Wet Gate Lane in Lymm a short time after the collision.

The data showed the car had remained stationary on the rural country lane for about 90 seconds, as the cyclist was still clinging to life.

Debotte's account of those moments was absolutely crucial to proving Richardson was guilty of more than causing death by dangerous driving and failing to stop.

She said as she sat "frozen" in the passenger seat, he got out, walked around the front of the vehicle and tried to pull the head teacher free.

When the first attempt failed, he returned to the driver's seat and moved the steering wheel to try and free the wheels.

Debotte said Richardson got out again and crouched down to make another attempt to pull his victim free.

After failing again, he started the engine and drove further along Wet Gate Lane.

CCTV from a nearby farm showed the car swerving from side-to-side before the cyclist was finally thrown clear on to a grass verge.

From the position he was found, prosecutors were also able to say that the car must have driven over his body when it reversed and turned back towards the main road, all but ensuring his injuries were fatal.

The court was shown distressing evidence in support of Debotte's account, including images of a sharp-angled tyre mark left in a pool of blood where the car had stopped.

The jury heard the mark could only have been made by the wheels being turned while the car was stationary.

Nobody was around when the 56-year-old was thrown from the vehicle and left to his fate, but a few minutes later, motorcylist Andrew Beasant-Roberts found him after following a trail of blood from close to the crash site just over a mile away.

Beasant-Roberts made a 999 call and tried to perform CPR, but it was too late.

Detectives later found CCTV footage which showed Richardson and Debotte at Lymm Service Station minutes later, filling the car with petrol.

The pair then finished the errand they initially set out to do and picked up Debotte's jabs from the salon in Lymm.

She was dropped off at her Altrincham home at 18:45, where she stayed until she left for work again the following morning.

After dropping her off, Richardson quickly arranged to swap the Volvo for a silver Ford Transit work van with an associate.

He returned to Debotte's house in the van with a friend and the pair came and went from the house throughout the night.

Debotte said the men had been "laughing and joking" while listening to music and drinking her father's alcohol, but Richardson also lost his temper when she asked them to leave, punching a hole in plasterwork and kicking a chair.

She said there were no direct threats, but Richards outlined an account for her to give to police if they came knocking, which she wrote down in a note-taking app on her phone.

It included instructions to say she had lent Richardson her bank card on the day before and had not seen him again until late on the day of the crash.

However, Debotte said she already "knew she was going to talk to the police" and would be telling the truth.

In court, Debotte accepted she "absolutely" could have done more to alert the police to what had happened earlier, but her decision to seek them out before anyone else knew she had been in the vehicle allowed them to treat her as a witness.

Based on her description of the van, Greater Manchester Police officers found it the following day in Failsworth.

Despite knowing he was being tailed by a trained pursuit driver, Richardson tried to flee, first speeding through narrow residential streets and then making a final futile attempt to escape on foot.

He has never given a public account of his actions on 20 April.

The court heard he declined to answer police questions and on 22 October, at the conclusion of the prosecution case, the jury were told he would not be giving evidence in his own defence.

Jaime Hamilton KC, defending, explained while questioning witnesses that Richardson denied he knew the cyclist was under the car and denied he had got out of the vehicle on Wet Gate Lane.

However, the evidence and the testimony of Debotte meant the jury were sure he was guilty of more than a serious driving offence and fully convinced he had made the conscious decision to drag a helpless and well-respected family man to a most horrific death.

Richardson is due to be sentenced on Monday.

Driver guilty of dragging head teacher to his death

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:27:40 GMT

Warning: This article contains distressing content

A man has been found guilty of murdering a head teacher who was dragged to his death for more than a mile while trapped under the wheels of a car.

Simon Richardson crashed into 56-year-old Michael Mullins, who was cycling home from his job at Stretford Grammar School on the evening of 20 April in the village of Warburton in Trafford, Greater Manchester.

Prosecutors claimed Richardson, 35, fled the scene of the crash before stopping to try to dislodge the injured but still-living cyclist and then driving on with Mr Mullins still lodged underneath the vehicle.

Richardson was also convicted of dangerous driving and will return to Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court to be sentenced on Monday.

There were shouts of "Yes!" from the court's public gallery as the guilty murder verdict was announced.

Others could also be heard crying.

The judge, Mrs Justice Brunner KC, told Richardson that there was only one sentence for murder, namely life imprisonment.

In a statement released after the verdicts had been returned, Mr Mullins' family described him as "an anchor", "the perfect dad" and "our everything".

"My past, present and future have been brutally and callously torn apart," said his widow.

"My memories of being with Michael through the rough and the smooth are now permanently tainted with sadness."

Mr Mullins' son described his late father as "the type of Dad that would show up to everything".

He said: "Our last exchange of words together before he dropped me at the station was him reminding me of how proud he was of me."

Mr Mullins' daughter added: "I made a promise in those first days that I would live the rest of my life for my Dad and give myself the life he had started to see me grow into and wanted for me.

"I am here telling you all that my Dad was and always will be our everything."

The court heard Richardson, of no fixed address, had driven through "give way" markings at a junction in Warburton before colliding with the father-of-two, who went under the Volvo XC90.

Richardson then drove off before stopping in a country lane and twice getting out of the vehicle in attempts to pull Mr Mullins free, the jury was told.

He then mounted the grass verge in his Volvo and finally dislodged him before reversing over Mr Mullins, causing "crushing" chest injuries.

Richardson's cousin Gabrielle Debotte, who was a passenger in the front seat of the car, previously told the court that both of them had heard "moaning" shortly after the collision in Paddock Lane and that he had gone on to say: "He is under the car."

The prosecution claimed Mr Mullins' injuries were caused by "dragging and crushing" rather than the impact of the crash itself.

Prosecutor Phil Barnes KC told jurors: "Simon Richardson knew he was there and he inevitably knew what the consequences of driving on would be, and he did it anyway.

"For a split second after the collision, for a brief moment he possibly thought about doing the right thing and getting out and taking ownership of what he had just done and help the man he had just run down.

"But Simon Richardson did not get out. He did not do the right thing. He chose to drive away.

"The obvious reason is because he wanted to escape the consequences of what he had just done."

A motorcyclist followed a trail of blood and discovered Mr Mullins alone and barely breathing as he lay on a grass verge in a secluded country lane in Lymm, Cheshire.

The head teacher was pronounced dead at the scene shortly afterwards by emergency services.

Richardson was arrested the next day following a police chase.

He denied murder as he claimed he did not realise Mr Mullins was underneath his car and said he did not get out of his vehicle in a bid to free him.

But jurors did not believe him and found him guilty of murder.

Mrs Justice Brunner KC thanked members of the jury and acknowledged their job "cannot have been easy".

She discharged the jurors from taking jury service again for 10 years and told them: "This was, I know, an upsetting case and there was evidence which you may have found distressing."

Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:03:39 GMT

Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.

Óscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.

"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.

The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.

Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.

A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.

In January a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people in Adamuz in southern Spain.

Wednesday's tragedy was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.

Puente said on Wednesday a computer failure at about 08:30 that morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.

Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the crash.

Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.

Puente had said that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".

The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".

Meanwhile, Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.

On Friday Puente said he was "not going to use any worker as a shield".

But he said "many questions" arose as a result of the tragedy and he wanted to look at them "one by one".

"If the investigation shows there is human error we will act in consequence of that," he said.

The conservative People's Party joined calls for Puente's resignation after trade union CSIF called for the same earlier this week.

But Puente said on Friday he would not budge from his position.

"The easy thing for me would be to leave, but neither that fits with my character nor is it what the Prime Minister has asked me to do," he said.

"I feel immense pain and immense sadness for the victims and their relatives... I cannot let this pain paralyse me though. We have to find solutions to this problem."

The country is observing three days of mourning, as the families of victims and the survivors of the crash struggle to comprehend how it could have happened.

A 24-year-old athlete and a former government minister are among the victims of Wednesday's disaster, but many families are still waiting for information from authorities about their loved ones.

Esther San Emeterio, whose 54-year-old brother Pepe is still missing, told reporters in Toledo, near Urda, that officials were forcing families to wait in "uncertainty".

"We went to bed crying, outraged and full of shame," she said. "We are desperate and I want all of Spain to know. How can they keep us like this?"

Additional reporting by Sergi Forcada Freixas

Set up to fail? Where England's World Cup campaign went wrong

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:50:57 GMT

This video can not be played

Highlights: England 34-12 Papua New Guinea

As Mikey Lewis darted over for a late try in a desperate - and almost certainly fruitless - points chase against Papua New Guinea, the obituaries were already being written for England's Men's Rugby League World Cup campaign.

Much earlier on Friday, England's women had lacked the power and nous to overcome Samoa, losing 24-6 in a match that decided who went through to the semi-finals.

England's men actually won their game - 34-12 - but it was nowhere near the margin of victory required. Their elimination will be confirmed on Sunday unless Tonga beat Samoa by more than 46 points.

And so the likelihood is that for the first time in World Cup history, neither England's men nor their women will feature in the last four.

For the men, that ends a run that began with Great Britain at the first tournament in 1954.

The disappointment will only reinforce the idea that English rugby league needs a serious period of introspection - as well as significant investment to keep pace with the game in the southern hemisphere.

But there have been other factors to trouble England at this World Cup, hosted by Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea at short notice after France pulled out for financial reasons.

Even before a ball was kicked, the men were faced with a sense of impending doom - brought on by injuries, shambolic travel arrangements and a bizarre format that had England facing immediate jeopardy with a testing opener against Tonga.

England edge towards World Cup exit despite PNG win

Spirited England out of World Cup after Samoa loss

The northern hemisphere game has deep-rooted problems, and seems to be stuck in stasis when compared with the thriving NRL.

England had a record of being a major player at World Cups - having reached two finals and a further four semi-finals at the past six tournaments.

But when last autumn's 3-0 Ashes series defeat by Australia prompted the departure of head coach Shaun Wane, his successor was handed a near-impossible task.

Brian McDermott was appointed in April. Given just six months to prepare, the former Leeds Rhinos head coach had no mid-season international to work on a plan. Based in Australia because of his role as Gold Coast Titans assistant coach, he relied on virtual meetings to connect with his prospective squad and staff.

Four on-field sessions were planned in Australia before the World Cup. But only two were completed in full after his UK-based players were subjected to a 48-hour journey to Perth that left them exhausted - a situation McDermott compared to Planes, Trains and Automobiles, the 1987 road-trip comedy starring Steve Martin and John Candy.

It was a shambolic way to prepare for a pivotal opener against Tonga - one that always had the potential to consign the defeated team to an early elimination.

Following that 30-12 loss, McDermott said: "You give me another two or three weeks preparation or another couple of games of preparation leading into the tournament and I'd be really excited."

With the tournament organisers planning travel itineraries for the teams involved, any post-World Cup debrief ought to examine how that situation was allowed to occur.

It would have made more sense for England's opener to be against France - the only other team in the men's tournament made up largely of northern hemisphere-based players.

Wakefield Trinity's historic triumph may have delivered a wonderful sign-off story to the Super League season but it delivered another conundrum around England's squad selection.

Had McDermott known prior to 5 October that none of the Wakefield players in his thinking would be available, could arrangements have been made for his UK-based players to travel to Australia earlier?

In the end, only three of the 14 England-based players in the squad (George Williams, Matty Ashton and Ben Currie) participated in the Super League Grand Final on 3 October.

"If we come together next year as a group, we will be further down the track and we don't need to start from scratch," McDermott added.

"Bear in mind when we landed in Perth on the Friday [9 October], we are starting... like we didn't know each other.

"We were putting things in place about who we are as a group, what it means to us, how we are going to play, how we are going to attack and how we are going to defend. There's been a ton of work gone on."

While much of the pre-tournament noise centred on the omission of Jake Connor and England's long-running halves debate, very little focus was given to a decimated forward pack and other notable absentees.

Prior the first match, McDermott recounted Australia prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui's admiration for the strength of the English pack during last year's Ashes series.

England's ability to front up had also previously been talked up by Kangaroos boss Kevin Walters.

Yet McDermott had few of those same players at his disposal.

Matty Lees' season-ending injury in May was not only a blow for St Helens but also robbed England of a key enforcer, one who had previously shown he could stand up to the physicality of a powerhouse Tonga front row.

With second-rower Mike McMeeken and prop Caleb Hamlin-Uele unavailable, Morgan Smithies withdrawing from the squad injured and a calf complaint taking Morgan Knowles out of the equation for the encounter against Tonga, England were left short in that area.

That is before you even get to options such as Sydney Roosters' Billy Smith, Wigan's Jake Wardle and Leeds Rhinos duo Ash Handley and Mikolaj Oledzki, all absent through injury.

And when England had to chase the scoreboard after their defeat by Tonga - while hoping results elsewhere went in their favour - it left them in trouble.

They failed to get the numbers on the board they needed against Papua New Guinea. McDermott acknowledged that it left him and his players waiting for the inevitable.

"It feels like we lost the game," he said. "We won and, in any circumstances I would be really proud but I think something remarkable is going to have to happen now for us to go through.

"We've made massive strides together in such a short period of time, in difficult circumstances where the narrative of the last two weeks is that you've got to win by 70 and 60. You don't just need to win, you need to win by massive margins."

England's women were semi-finalists four years ago, but fell short this time

Whenever the Women's Rugby League World Cup has featured semi-finals previously, England or Great Britain have always been there. When it has not, they have always finished in the top four.

But this time, they approached the tournament with a different focus, as head coach Staurt Barrow opted for youth over experience.

His squad contained 11 players aged 23 or under, and was largely comprised of players who have full-time occupations away from rugby league.

And that told as England were humbled 78-0 by world champions Australia last Saturday, and found wanting by a Samoa side dominated by NRL Women's Premiership talent. While Australia's domestic league pays its players, money is much tighter in England's Women's Super League.

"Women's Super League has progressed to a certain level and we are bringing young players through so that creeps into the national team," said Barrow.

"It's good and refreshing - but at the same rate we are progressing, it's probably accelerating quicker on this side of the world if I am really honest.

"The investment into the NRLW is not only making the Jillaroos better but it's making all the Pacific nations better as well.

"I think nearly every player for Samoa has played NRLW at some stage and that competition is improving at a rate of knots. We'll have to go back and look at what we can do in our competition.

"We definitely need to do something because the acceleration of the game over here is phenomenal at the moment.

"Back home, we need to have more investment into the women's and girls game. It can't just be a token gesture at some clubs - and I'm not saying it is, but we need to put money into it."

This video can not be played

England out of World Cup after loss to Samoa

Barrow's other main problem relates to geography and an international calendar that leaves them ill-prepared to face the leading southern hemisphere nations.

Aside from a record 90-4 defeat by Australia in Las Vegas, England's women have been limited to six international fixtures since the previous World Cup, all against France and Wales - in which they have scored 348 points, while conceding four.

"We lost to the better side on the day. I am not going to deny that," Barrow added.

"It was a good game and a good game for England to be in because we have a problem at the moment where we play France or Wales. And no disrespect to those nations but we win them [games] - and we play the Jillaroos and lose heavily.

"This was a nice game to be in where it was competitive all the way. The more of those we can get will definitely help us as a nation."

Police watchdog to investigate Met over letter about Meghan's father

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:36:03 GMT

The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had decided an investigation was required into the force's "failure to pass on allegations of serious offending... to relevant overseas authorities at the time".

The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.

He has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".

On Thursday the Met said it had voluntarily referred itself to the IOPC.

The letter at the heart of the IOPC investigation was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.

The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".

Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason to not visit Thomas Markle and not allow him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.

Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".

The IOPC will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas.

The policing watchdog also said it had decided a further matter, relating to an alleged data breach in which information was passed on to a third party, "should be returned to the force to be appropriately dealt with". No details were provided about the circumstances of the alleged breach.

The Met said on Thursday that it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".

The letter was forwarded by officers to the Sussexes' royal office rather than to Meghan personally, while there have been reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to ask for one from the Sussexes.

The watchdog will have to consider how the contents of the letter were treated by the force at the time.

Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, previously told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".

"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken [and] why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies."

Reports of the Met's handling of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.

Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.

Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims. Police there have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.

However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they can examine the items.

Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha, who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

Britain's first £100m man facing defining moment

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 13:42:15 GMT

Jack Grealish was excluded from Everton's squad to face Newcastle United in the Carabao Cup for "a breach of club" discipline

When Jack Grealish breezed back into Everton in his white Lamborghini one hour before the end of this summer's transfer deadline, the excitement among supporters and the player himself was clearly evident.

Grealish's previous spell on loan from Manchester City had been cut short by a serious foot injury, but the 31-year-old had produced enough moments of excitement to make his return to the Finch Farm training base a rare moment of joy amid a miserable summer in the transfer market.

When Grealish finally left in the early hours - with the deal done, every autograph signed and every selfie posed for - it was a sort of homecoming for an everyman personality Everton fans had come to regard as one of their own.

This was a move with a lot riding on it - for Everton manager David Moyes, who had been left with only 18 senior players after a botched transfer window, and especially for Grealish, whose exile from City at the start of the final year of his contract confirmed his banishment.

Now, Grealish's future and Everton's faith in him, has reached a defining moment.

Grealish's exclusion from Everton's squad before the Carabao Cup tie at home to Newcastle was publicly described as "a breach of club discipline".

Specifically, it was a failure to turn up for training on Monday, leaving the talented maverick - who was Britain's first £100m footballer when he signed for City from Aston Villa in summer 2021 - facing another rebuild in his career.

Everton's decision to go public before the game with the reasons for Grealish's absence emphasised the seriousness of his transgression.

The fall-out means this now looks increasingly like Grealish's 'now or never' moment, because failure at Everton will surely mark a downward spiral from the top echelons of the Premier League.

Everton do not regard this week's misdemeanour as marking the proverbial 'Last Chance Saloon' for Grealish. Moyes does not have enough players at his disposal to make rapid outcasts of potential game-changers.

But it increases the pressure on the former England forward to win back the faith of fans who love his obvious enjoyment of life and the magic he has shown he can produce.

Moyes will hope it is a harsh lesson learned, because Everton now have even more to play for, given Wembley has suddenly come into view in the Carabao Cup.

BBC Sport believes there have been occasional time-keeping issues with Grealish in the past, but nothing on this scale from a personality regarded as a hard trainer who, in general, keeps himself in good condition.

Grealish has held talks with those in authority at Everton, where it is sure to have been made crystal clear there must be no repeat, certainly not under a strict disciplinarian such as Moyes, and he must now attempt to be rehabilitated back into the squad.

The inevitable decision to punish Grealish, taken at a high level within the club but with input and full support from Moyes, leaves him at the crossroads.

That is especially the case because Everton gave arguably their best performance of the season to beat Newcastle United 3-1 and set up a quarter-final at League Two Fleetwood Town, conquerors of Premier League champions Arsenal in the last round.

And it was done with the more dynamic style of 20-year-old Tyrique George playing on the left flank, which Grealish might have been expected to occupy.

Grealish dropped over 'breach of club discipline' - what now?

Everton cruise past Newcastle to reach EFL Cup quarter-finals

Everton manager David Moyes and Jack Grealish - pictured after victory at Aston Villa last season - had formed a close relationship

Moyes was guarded after the game and instead preferred to focus on a vital victory.

"You probably know I'm not going to give any details. It's a club decision and I support it. It's something I don't want to speak too much about," he said.

"The one thing about Everton is that they have got real good values. All the players stand behind it and accept the values, on the pitch and off the pitch, and I think the players did a good job.

"It is a small squad, but we are doing our best to keep challenging. We are not accepting any excuses for anything and I think the players are doing a great job. There was a humility about us."

The words were not specifically aimed at Grealish, but they might as well have been from a manager who will have been bitterly disappointed and angry about his transgression.

Moyes and Grealish formed a close relationship from virtually their first moment of contact in August 2025, the latter saying: "As soon as I spoke to the manager, I knew there was only one place that I wanted to go and that was Everton."

And Grealish, a key figure when Manchester City won the Treble of Premier League, FA Cup and Champions League in 2023, played his part until sustaining a foot fracture that ended his season in Everton's 1-0 win at his former club Aston Villa in January.

Grealish's happiness with life at Everton was illustrated when he decided against returning to City, continuing his rehabilitation at Finch Farm rather than going back to Etihad Stadium.

Everton weighed up a second loan deal to bring Grealish back carefully, with his injury, finances and - to a certain extent - his character all entering the equation before Moyes decided to move again for a player who insisted Merseyside was the only place he wanted to be.

Moyes was also juggling very limited options as owners The Friedkin Group appeared to back away from serious squad strengthening as they prepared to put the club up for sale.

Grealish's form this season has been underwhelming, failing to score or create an assist in eight appearances - two of those at City before returning to Everton - while his tendency to slow play down is at odds with the usual tempo Moyes requires from his team.

Moyes' fury will have increased because Grealish, who missed Saturday's loss at Arsenal through "illness", is part of a paper-thin squad that simply cannot carry passengers or have players ruling themselves out through needless ill-discipline.

There will be frustration too, as Grealish is a hugely popular within Everton's dressing room as well as with staff in every area of the club. He has been described as "a lad with a heart of gold, kind and charming, who actually loves being here".

This was illustrated when he recently made a £10,000 donation to a GoFundMe page for Everton fan Leon Skapars, 36, a father of three who has been diagnosed with cancer.

The family are raising money in a search for treatment options, and Skapars' wife Crystal said: "In that moment, Jack gave our whole family something we desperately needed, hope. What he has done for our family is something we will never forget. It makes us feel incredibly emotional."

Grealish also appeared to present awards at the Daily Mirror's 'Pride Of Britain' event recently, saying: "Footballers are classed as heroes - but these are the real heroes."

On Friday, Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca refused to discuss Grealish's actions at Everton, but did praise his character.

Maresca said: "It's not correct to talk about Jack in this moment, first of all because he is an Everton player and secondly because I don't have all the information.

"I still think he is a good guy and has a big heart."

In April, Grealish extended his role as principal ambassador to Special Olympics Great Britain for a further three years, having first joined in 2022.

Grealish marked the occasion by hosting five of the 10 Special Olympics GB athletes who completed the London Marathon at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium, surprising the athletes with a VIP experience, a stadium tour and spending time with them pitchside.

Those at Everton also regard Grealish as one of the first to engage with their community programme at Finch Farm, as well as meeting with the Everton in the Community Down Syndrome team.

Grealish often talks about the inspiration he takes from his sister Hollie, who has cerebral palsy.

He has, however, hit the headlines in less welcome circumstances over the years, and this latest incident ushered in more.

In April, Grealish was pictured asleep at a Manchester rooftop bar surrounded by drinks. It was a scene that is certainly not against the law but was at best unwise, especially with ever-present phone cameras around and the fact he was in rehabilitation from injury.

In March 2020, he was fined by his club Aston Villa and apologised publicly after breaking lockdown guidelines during the pandemic after leaving his house to visit a friend.

In November 2020, he admitted two counts of careless driving relating to two incidents in which a Citroen van and a Mercedes were damaged.

And yet, speak to most people in football - certainly at Everton - and the character references are unfailingly glowing about his outgoing personality and kind-hearted gestures, making his breach of discipline even more painful for his many admirers.

But after this latest setback, Grealish is running out of time and opportunities to justify that continued support.

Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 12:43:46 GMT

Sir Ian McKellen has led tributes to Sir Patrick Stewart following his death at the age of 86, calling him "the most respected and beloved actor of his generation".

Tributes to the renowned British actor have poured in since his death at his Los Angeles home after "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia was announced on Thursday.

"He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love," Sir Ian, Sir Patrick's X-Men co-star, said.

Famous for his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek, Sir Patrick was a versatile actor who won multiple awards, balancing Hollywood roles and a career in classical theatre.

William Shatner, who also helmed the USS Enterprise in Star Trek, said Sir Patrick brought "intelligence, grace and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did".

"Captain Picard stood for the best of us and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work," Shatner added.

Stewart depicted Picard in more than 170 episodes of the hit sci-fi TV series between 1987 and 1994, as well as in four feature films. He returned to the role for Star Trek: Picard in 2020.

Dame Judi Dench said she was "shocked" and "very sad" to hear of Sir Patrick's death, adding: "He's never been one of those actors who never felt like it that night, he was always very, very committed... He'll be much missed and he was much admired."

George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in Star Trek, said the actor "inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity".

Sir Patrick would later be celebrated for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier - most commonly known as Professor X - in the X-Men film franchise.

Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside him in the franchise, called him a "tremendous friend and man", saying: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."

Sir Ian, a longtime friend of his X-Men co-star, who officiated his wedding in 2013, said Sir Patrick was "defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire".

"You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues."

Sir Ian recalled first meeting Sir Patrick as young actors in the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and how he had expressed caution over him taking on the Star Trek role.

"He took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did," said Sir Ian, who appeared with Sir Patrick in a 2009 theatre production of Waiting for Godot.

He added that while the US had become Sir Patrick's "adopted home", he "never forsook his origins" growing up in Yorkshire, and said "the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as chancellor of Huddersfield University".

Sir Ian noted that Sir Patrick's final film appearance will be as Professor X in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday film. Marvel Studios described him as "a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman".

The Academy dubbed his voice "unmistakable", adding: "Whether commanding the bridge of the Enterprise or guiding a generation of young mutants, Sir Patrick Stewart brought a tenderness to his characters that made us feel we knew them."

Sir Patrick died on Wednesday "in the loving care of his wife", a statement from his family said. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," it added.

The veteran actor is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, as well as by his two adult children from his first marriage, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.

Born in the town of Mirfield in 1940, Sir Patrick's love of drama began at school where he was introduced to Shakespeare and his first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.

He threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."

When Sir Patrick was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010, he said he owed "literally everything" to his former English teacher who first encouraged him to perform.

His first foray into professional acting was when he joined the RSC in 1966, going on to play King John, Oberon in A Midsummer Night's Dream and Henry IV.

The RSC described him as a "colossus of both stage and screen", remembering him as "one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation" whose contribution to the company was "beyond measure".

Dame Harriet Walter, who first met Sir Patrick in his theatre days more than 40 years ago, said his passing was like a "huge giant tree has fallen in the forest".

"He had fire in his eyes and you were absolutely in the room with him," the Succession actress told BBC Newsnight. "I've never heard a bad word against him. And I think the world's going to be very poor without him."

Theatres in London's West End will dim their lights for two minutes on 3 November in his honour.

Hannah Essex, co-chief of the Society of London Theatre and UK Theatre, called him "one of the greatest stage actors this country has ever seen".

As well as having roles in films such as Safe House, Robin Hood: Men in Tights and the original Dune, Sir Patrick continued to appear on TV throughout his career, making guest appearances on Frasier, Futurama and the Simpsons.

US actor and animator Seth MacFarlane, who grew up as a fan of Sir Patrick, said he was "gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend" as they worked together on Family Guy, American Dad! and Ted.

MacFarlane described him as a "rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great and a great writer sound masterful".

Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".

Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."

Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft".

"Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.

Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.

The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."

The actor became a campaigner on domestic violence in later life, including becoming an ambassador for domestic abuse charity Refuge in 2007, after witnessing his mother suffer violence at the hands of his father.

Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge's board chair, said it had been a privilege to "watch his endless devotion" to the cause, adding that he "broke down barriers and taboos on the subject".

Andy Burnham considered Sir Patrick to be "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".

"He brought joy to millions," the prime minister's spokesman said on his behalf. "He always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.

Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 11:57:33 GMT

Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit by what is believed to be the largest crypto hack ever at $6.3bn (£4.7bn).

Crypto is a type of digital asset which does not exist physically like cash or coins. Instead, people use digital wallets on their smartphones or computers to access and manage it.

Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said it is working with the authorities to work out what has happened and it will cover all losses.

Here's what we know so far.

Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, where people can buy, sell and trade digital currencies, like Bitcoin, as well as deposit and withdraw them.

It was founded in China in 2017 and has hundreds of millions of registered users worldwide.

The exchange has come under scrutiny over the past few years - notably in 2023, when its then-chief executive, Changpeng Zhao, resigned after pleading guilty to money laundering violations.

Last year, a lawsuit in the US accused the company of helping send millions of dollars to US-designated terrorist organisations.

In 2024, the company said it has more than $160bn in assets.

The hack happened to Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance. com.

Binance. us, which provides trading services specifically for US residents, said it has not been affected by the issue.

In an initial announcement, Teng said: "Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop.

"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorised withdrawal transactions."

He said the hack "was not a simple 'one-click' action" but a "more complex attack process".

Raghu Nandakumara, vice president of industry strategy at cybersecurity platform Illumio, said this could mean an engineer was "talked into taking a test" and malware - malicious software – "landed on their laptop while they did it".

Because the laptop already had sufficient security privileges, Nandakumara said early reports suggest it became "the attacker's route straight into production, and from there to the wallets".

Teng has since said the hack was "not carried out by one person" and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".

"You can build a vault with mathematical firewalls, but if the individual holding the keys can be duped, the vault is opened," said Dr Clive Summerfield, head of FARx, a biometrics in AI security company.

It is not yet known who is behind the attack, but some analytics firms have pointed to North Korea - though this has not been confirmed.

AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report several elements of the Binance attack resembled earlier incidents linked to the territory, including a $1.5bn (£1.1bn) hack on the ByBit exchange in 2025.

These previous attacks have been linked to a cluster of cyber-criminals accused of working directly for the regime called the Lazarus Group - also known as TraderTraitor.

North Korean foreign policy expert Dr Edward Howell, from the University of Oxford, has told the BBC that Pyongyang "has a long history of using cyber warfare to extract cash".

Howell said North Korea "basically has a state-run cyber warfare agency", which it uses "to fund its weapons of mass destruction programmes" and as a "slush fund" for its leader Kim Jong Un's regime.

Howell added that as of the current day "about 40 – 50% of North Korea's weapons of mass destruction programmes are funded by cyber and crypto-currency warfare".

North Korea has always denied any involvement in these attacks; Binance has not directly responded to BBC queries about the incident's potential links to the area.

In his earlier statement, Teng said Binance users' funds are safe and, as a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals had been temporarily suspended.

He said the firm would cover all losses from its emergency reserve set up for such situations, and make up the rest with company funds.

Binance said it had been working with partners to freeze the affected assets, with around $3bn reportedly located so far.

Teng said concerned users can check funds on their Binance accounts. Experts suggest doing so through the official app and website, and to reach out to the company's customer service with any questions.

Users from other crypto platforms have also been warned to be wary of hackers seeking to exploit the situation.

Marijus Briedis, NordVPN's chief technology officer, said people should be on the lookout for things such as "an email claiming your funds are at risk", "a fake support account offering help" or "a message urging you to move your cryptocurrency to a 'safe' wallet".

"Check updates through the Binance app or a website address you already trust," he said.

"Avoid links in unsolicited messages, and never give anyone your password, verification codes or wallet recovery phrase."

Jennifer Craven, an international commercial fraud expert at the law firm Pinsent Masons, said the repercussions of the hack could "extend well beyond Binance".

"More broadly, the incident exposes the fragility of parts of the crypto ecosystem," she said.

"If a platform as sophisticated as Binance can suffer a serious attack, regulators will inevitably ask what that means for smaller, less mature platforms and currencies."

She said the attack would likely accelerate scrutiny of how the sector protects both its infrastructure and its customers.

Although there is no evidence yet that AI was used in this attack, it fits into a much wider concern in the financial industry of whether AI agents could potentially identify weaknesses in software and work out how to exploit them much faster than human hackers.

The Bank of England has warned this could leave institutions struggling to fix vulnerabilities before attackers take advantage of them.

Crypto has become an increasingly popular way of investing and transferring money online, partly because, unlike traditional currencies, it is not controlled by central banks or governments.

This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom.

But it also makes it extremely volatile, with it rising and falling in value at the whim of buyers and sellers.

According to Solcard, a crypto-funded prepaid payment and virtual card platform, somewhere between 560 million and 741 million people own crypto worldwide in 2026.

We went on holiday with our neighbours and swapped families - it tore us apart

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 06:21:28 GMT

Rachel Stone was five and her brother Ian was 10 when their mum and dad took them on a caravan holiday to Wales with the family next door.

They spent two fun-filled weeks together - but when they got home, each family split in half and swapped houses.

Rachel and her mother Kay moved in with the neighbour Eddie and his daughter Alison. Eddie's wife Irene and their daughter Dawn moved in with Rachel's dad Rex and her brother Ian.

Rachel tells Dr Sian Williams, host of Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, of the trauma of her family being torn apart, the chaos that unfolded and how she has come to forgive her parents.

Rachel and Ian had initially been delighted when a new family moved in next door. "We instantly hit it off, all four of us." They were thrilled to be going on holiday together.

Rachel remembers two caravans parked side-by-side and a trip up Mount Snowdon.

But when it was time to go home, everything was mixed up - people were getting in the wrong cars.

Rachel remembers her mum leaning back from the passenger seat, saying: "'We're going to have a new family. We're going to be living in number eight with Eddie and Alison. Alison's going to be your new sister.

"And your dad and brother are still going to live in number 10. And Auntie Irene and Dawn are going to live there. And Dawn's going to be your brother's new sister."

Rachel immediately felt "very panicked and afraid and upset" and says she started to cry.

As the car rumbled along, she felt "bewildered, but also a little bit excited". She liked Alison and had always wanted a sister.

That night, Alison let her sleep on her top bunk and the next morning the adults switched belongings between the houses in the Isle of Sheppey where they lived.

Rachel says she felt very confused. "You can't help but think that it's your fault."

Life at number 8, where Rachel now lived, was very different to number 10. Her old house had been clean, whereas this house had "dog hair, greasy things, car things".

She describes her mum as "firm but fair" and very practical.

Her stepdad Eddie "was never horrible to me, but I never called him dad. I wasn't his girl."

She also missed Ian desperately. "I was very proud of him. He was my big brother.

"I used to wait in the front garden for him to come home from school when I was a toddler."

Rachel was seven when the two couples went to court together and got divorced. They later married their new partners in separate low-key registry office ceremonies.

Rachel did not even know her dad had married Irene until she saw the wedding photo. Her visits to her old home tailed off when she was about 11 or 12. She says she found it difficult to go and visit her dad and did not get along with Irene.

Meanwhile, life with her mum Kay and Eddie was chaotic.

"[He] was quite possessive and controlling. By the time we got to 13, she [Mum] said, 'it's not sustainable, [we] can't live like this".

Rachel said school was her "escape". She got good grades and became a teacher. She got married and had two sons but is now separated and works as a business coach.

Throughout her life, Rachel's mother would never talk about the swap. "I asked a lot of questions. She told me it was complicated."

Decades later, on a family holiday with her own sons, Rachel asked again.

"I said to my mum, 'Oh, Joseph's 10 now... Ian was 10 when you let him go with Dad and Irene.'"

She says her mum was "beside herself with guilt and the shame... for her selfish decisions."

"Years later she actually said to me - the words I almost wanted to hear all my life - 'I'm so sorry I let you down and I want to try and make it up to you.'"

Rachel says it was the start of her rebuilding a "wonderful" relationship with her mum.

Rachel never had a close relationship with her dad. "He told me he had a choice between his wife and his children. Unfortunately for me, he chose his wife."

He and Irene stayed together until his death aged 81.

But when she spoke at her dad's funeral, Rachel said she felt she owed him an apology.

"I imagined a character of a perfect dad that had been taken away from me... I created this superhuman being that could be everything.

"And I wanted him to be like that. But I also think you have to accept people for who they are.

"I think that parents do the best they can... You can't hope for your parents to be something they're not."
