Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix

BBC News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 02:14:41 GMT

James Stevens calls himself a democratic socialist. The 24-year-old film student is the type of Democrat who recalls watching the provocative left-wing internet commentator Hasan Piker six years ago, "before he became relevant in politics". Last year, James flew up from his home in Georgia to New York City to canvass for Zohran Mamdani's mayoral campaign.

His mother, Tamara, 56, is a loyal Democrat too. But of a different ilk. She grew up Republican then switched to the Democratic Party after seeing Barack Obama on Oprah. These days, she's a loyal party woman, championing reproductive rights, attending campaign rallies and donating to local candidates.

Both mother and son want Democrats to win control of Congress at Tuesday's midterm elections, but they don't entirely agree on what they want their Democratic Party to be.

"I'm very sick of how compromising Democrats are to Republican policies that don't benefit a large group of people," James told me, as his mother looked on. "There needs to be a bold vision for the Democrats," he says, arguing that the party should adopt policies affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a left-wing splinter group. In his view, that means anti-Zionism, getting corporate money out of politics, and government-run free healthcare.

The conventional wisdom in Washington is that Democrats are well-positioned to take control of the House, and possibly even the Senate, after the vote next week.

Underlying conditions are in Democrats' favour – Republican US President Donald Trump's approval rating is at a record low for a president heading into a midterm, comparable to George W Bush in his final term in 2006; the Iran war still isn't over and it's proving unpopular with American voters; and this has led to higher gas prices, which are frustrating an electorate that is already worried about the cost of living. Traditionally, the midterms are a referendum on a sitting president. In 18 of the last 20 US midterm elections, the party in power has lost seats in the House.

And yet despite those circumstances, the Democratic Party is also unpopular nationwide. The Real Clear Politics polling average shows the American public sees the Democrats as only marginally better than the Republicans. Recent polls show the Democratic Party still has a net unfavourability rating among Americans. Political analysts say that if the Republicans manage to buck the trend and survive these midterms, one key reason is that the Democratic Party (or the Democratic brand) is disliked by a majority of American voters too.

Behind the headlines of which party or which candidates win this Tuesday, there's also a story this election season about Democratic identity. This is a fight between institutionalists and reformists, of people who want incremental change and those who demand root-and-branch transformation. The question is, who will win out in the long run?

I've covered every national US election in the past dozen years and this is an unusual one. When I was out interviewing voters ahead of the 2018 midterms during Donald Trump's first term, I was struck by how united many Democratic voters were in their opposition to the president. This time, I've noticed that under the facade of unity, there's a brewing fight.

There are persistent questions about what the Democratic Party stands for, and these divides erupted during the primaries this midterm cycle. "The identity of the party is pretty cloudy," said Ruy Teixeira, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a centre-right think tank. "It's all centred on reaction to the Trump administration and taking advantage of what is a thermostatic reaction against the administration... Beyond that, there's all these different factions in the party."

Part of the reason for this Democratic infighting is that the party never had a chance to have this fight during the 2024 presidential race, with the sudden departure of Joe Biden months before the election and nomination of Kamala Harris.

Analysts agree that if Democrats make big wins on election night, it still won't answer deeper, unresolved questions as they try to keep their big tent together to corral votes in Congress or eye the 2028 presidency.

In simplistic terms, the divide is between the centrist, more moderate wing of the party and its left flank. But operatives and analysts say it's also a divide between institutionalists and those who want to completely upend the existing institution. Both feel they have a better read on what voters genuinely want.

Usamah Andrabi, of the Justice Democrats, a prominent left-wing group, blames the Democratic establishment for ushering in a Republican Congress and president. "And so I think the people who led us into this mess are simply not gonna be the ones who lead us out of it," he told me.

"The affordability crisis… is a massive one, and it's not going to be resolved by tinkering at the margins," he added. Instead, he insists, it'll be solved through policies like universal healthcare and childcare, and redistributing money by cutting the Pentagon's budget to stop "endless wars". His organisation sprang up in 2017 to recruit and support the congressional members who became known as "the Squad", the furthest-left faction in the House, which includes members such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar.

Healthcare will be one of the main arenas in which this fight is likely to play out, says Carrie Dann, managing editor of the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan newsletter that forecasts the competitiveness of races.

"There is a lot of appetite for, at the very least, more transparency, more understanding of why healthcare costs are so high," said Dann. " Take a bad step, break your leg, and a huge swathe of Americans would see their worlds turned upside down by that because of the healthcare system as it is."

Several Democratic candidates this election cycle have outlined ideas to lower "out-of-pocket" costs for those who already have health insurance - being hit with additional costs on top of regular insurance payments is a common feature of the American healthcare system. But there's another flank of the party that is fed up with incremental changes and wants a national healthcare system that is free at the point of use - Medicare for All.

Recent polling suggests a majority of Democrats favour this kind of healthcare system, but a majority of Republicans oppose it.

But some Democrats say there's nuance in the issue.

"People want to have universal healthcare, and they also want to be able to keep their health insurance," says Neera Tanden, Joe Biden's former domestic policy adviser, now CEO of the Center for American Progress, a liberal think tank.

Mainstream establishment Democrats acknowledge that many people see healthcare as a right, but they insist that others strongly oppose a fully government-run programme, fearing lower standards of care, and insist on having the option of keeping their private health insurance.

Healthcare costs have gone up across the board - health insurance and out-of-pocket healthcare expenses, hospital expenses and prescription drug costs have all surged in recent years, rising faster than the rate of inflation. As medical expenses have increased, polls suggest the idea of universal healthcare isn't as outlandish as it once seemed, and this campaign cycle has shown that it's far less taboo for politicians to openly call for it.

Back in Georgia, it's an issue on which Tamara and James agree - they want universal healthcare.

But their most fundamental disagreement is over Israel. Tamara calls herself a Zionist. "My kids get mad at me for saying that," she said.

And they're hardly the only Democrats having this debate.

Dann, from the Cook Political Report, says one of the biggest lessons from this election cycle is that Democratic voters weren't just looking for candidates willing to fight Trump, but candidates willing to take on the establishment. Dann points to the key swing state of Michigan, where in the primary, Abdul El-Sayed - a fierce critic of Israel and its actions in Gaza - came out on top over the objections of the Democratic establishment.

"I think one reason for that was that he was not only talking about taking on Donald Trump, but taking on the Democratic establishment… the establishment in Washington writ large," she said. And part of that anti-establishment attitude is about US support for Israel.

Some who left the party in 2024 because they believe Biden was too supportive of Israel's actions in Gaza are now returning, energised by El-Sayed's tough tone.

"My red line has been Gaza," said Samraa Luqman, an Arab-American activist in Michigan who voted for Trump in the last presidential election, feeling betrayed by Democrats that year.

"2023 and 2024 have really taught this community a lesson that we are no longer going to be wishy-washy about the issue. It's Gaza or bust," she told me. "If you're not good on Gaza, on Israel, on Palestine, then we don't need you. We don't need you in office, and we don't need to vote for you, no matter what your party affiliation is."

But as El-Sayed has energised voters, he's also alienated others, particularly some who see support for Israel as connected to Jewish safety in the US and feel that antisemitism in their party has grown after the deadly Hamas attacks of October 7.

Zach Nessel is one of those Democrats. And he's increasingly worried about becoming politically homeless.

"We have people who don't think Zionists should have a place in our party, that they should be removed from the party," Nessel told me. "And as a proud Zionist, I don't want to be removed from the Democratic coalition just over this one issue in the Middle East."

Support for Israel became a litmus test in some Democratic primaries this season, leading to mounting resistance to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the longtime influential lobbying group.

But Dann tells me that it's not just Israel that's a litmus test, it's El-Sayed's race itself.

"Abdul El-Sayed's theory of the case is that he can run as an unabashed progressive in a purple state [a state that swings between the 'red' Republican party and 'blue' Democrats] and win because progressive ideas are not only popular if they're communicated correctly, but also activate voters who are not necessarily a normal part of the political process, particularly young people," she said.

If he wins, left-wing candidates will see it as a model, she adds. And if he loses, Democrats in the more centrist wing of the party will see it as evidence that left-wing ideas are out of touch with mainstream voters.

But there are others, like Jim Kessler with Third Way, a centrist think tank, who think Michigan shouldn't be the focus. He pointed out that if Democrats take control of the Senate it'll be because of more centrist candidates: Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Mary Peltola in Alaska, James Talarico in Texas, Josh Turek in Iowa, Adam Hamilton in Kansas. They, he said, are the ones expanding Democrats' odds this cycle. " So the bigger the Democratic victory, the more it seems like the centrist Democrats came through, not the DSA candidates," he said.

DSA-endorsed candidates made gains during the primaries this election cycle, but their ideas are still controversial to many.

" I don't think… the vast majority of working-class people in America are kind of mini socialists," Tanden told me, pointing to reporting that suggests the majority of people who support the DSA are college-educated voters.

" Working-class people are pretty moderate on issues like crime and immigration," she added.

Nonetheless, if Democrats gain the majority, their congressional leaders will have to navigate a group of Democrats in which there will likely be an increase in the loudest and most left-wing voices.

" The Democrats' biggest challenge is to figure out how to actually deliver on running the economy better and making things more affordable, because they've said over and over again and very loudly that's what they're going to do," said Teixeira.

In all likelihood, people will start thinking seriously about the next presidential candidate the day after the midterms.

So, who actually has the momentum: the left flank or the centre?

"I think after the election we'll see a lot of fighting between the factions to claim credit," Teixeira said. " And that will of course feed into the jostling for the presidential nomination for 2028."

Back in Georgia, Tamara and James may disagree on some things, but they both want Democrats to win big on Tuesday.

"I'm a very pragmatic person when it comes to progressive politics," James said. He wants to make it clear he doesn't agree with everything DSA members espouse.

So much of this midterm cycle has also come down to candidate quality - not just the message but the messenger. So I asked both mother and son who their "ideal" Democrat is.

Tamara instantly answered Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator running for re-election in Georgia.

It's a point of agreement. They both really like their Georgia senator.

Ossoff is seen by many as a rising star of his party. The seat he is contesting is characterised by the Cook Political Report as "likely Democratic" - considered by analysts to be an impressive achievement in a swing state that voted for Trump in 2024.

"He knows how to speak to moderate Republicans, moderate Democrats, and members of the DSA," Tamara said. "He's not afraid to pull any punches… I appreciate how much he talks about corruption."

On Wednesday night, she joined thousands of people just outside Atlanta for a rally to cheer on the senator as former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats.

And when Ossoff took the mic, he spoke at length about what he sees as "corruption" in the Trump administration and in American politics, healthcare and corporate money.

And I heard this concern from voters in Georgia this past week, not just at the campaign rally, but at early voting sites in both Republican and Democratic counties.

"We have a corruption crisis," said Richard Schosky as he walked out of the voting booth in north Atlanta, after casting his ballot early. It's an issue that seems to be resonating deeply with voters, although the White House has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing.

In fact, Dann with the Cook Political Report says "corruption has become one of the central issues of this election".

Still, she added, "Democrats would be foolish to believe that a very good night for them in November is a mandate for the Democratic Party," said Dann.

"They are as almost as unpopular as Republicans and the president."

Plant biology provides inspiration for PFAS replacement

New Scientist October 29, 2026

A plant-inspired waterproof coating could soon become a safer and more sustainable alternative to forever chemicals like the PTFE used in waterproof clothing.

Per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances, known as PFAS or forever chemicals, have proven both a blessing and a curse for modern society. Their manifold useful properties, which include having high heat resistance, while being both water- and greaseproof, inert and durable, have made them a staple of many consumer products, from cookware and clothing to medical tools and electrical insulation. More recently, concerns around their long-term persistence in the environment, and the resulting impacts on human health, have meant regulation has tightened substantially and scientists are now working to develop greener and cleaner alternatives.

But, as is often the case, nature may have already found the solution. “Plants transport water across very long distances using this structure called suberin,” says Joshua Yuan, a chemical engineer at Washington University in St Louis, Missouri. Composed of a mixture of greasy long-chain fatty acids, suberin combines with the plant polymer lignin to form a super-waterproof surface that lines the tiny vessels and tubes of the plant’s internal plumbing system.

Advertisement

The ‘forever chemicals’ toxic to your health – and how to avoid them

Drawing inspiration from these natural pipes, Yuan’s team recreated this waterproof coating from a combination of paper industry waste and animal fat. They spray-coated the suberin-like slurry onto glass, metal and cotton surfaces where the individual particles quickly self-assembled to form a continuous waterproof layer.

Unlike PFAS coatings, whose many carbon-fluorine bonds directly repel water molecules, the new coating operates by a completely different mechanism, says Han Zuilhof, an organic chemist at Wageningen University & Research in the Netherlands. The precisely nanostructured surface creates lots of tiny pockets of air, which effectively minimise direct contact between the coated material and water droplets on the surface – similar to the lotus effect seen on the leaves of many plants.

The new structure proved resistant to both contamination by limescale and mechanical wear, and showed a similar level of water resistance to state-of-the-art forever chemical coatings like PTFE. “It uses an interesting approach. Textiles will be one of the first sectors affected by PFAS restrictions, so it could be a good alternative,” says Carlo Antonini, a materials scientist at the University of Milano-Bicocca in Italy.

Scientists have found significant concentrations of a type of PFAS chemical in the air deep in the Amazon rainforest, suggesting it travelled over 100 kilometres from an industrial hub

The team is already exploring applications in food packaging, such as the internal linings of drinks cans, but the coating’s lower heat tolerance compared with PTFE means bakeware is currently off the table.

The versatile properties of such a material mean there is no shortage of potential uses. The real step forward though, is the completely bio-based nature of the coating, says Zuilhof. Suberin’s chemical structure is easily degraded under composting conditions and the team showed their nature-inspired material likewise broke down completely, without releasing harmful residues into the environment. “They’ve basically turned a waste product into something valuable, and that’s quite cool,” says Zuilhof. “I think this will be a source of inspiration to find other bio-based materials from different waste streams.”

Birds can get jet lag on long, fast flights and then fly off course

New Scientist October 29, 2026

You don’t need a jet plane to get jet lag – even feathers will do. At least one species of bird gets jet lag, in the sense that its body clock can diverge from local time by more than an hour on fast flights across the Atlantic, as revealed by navigational errors.

“We’ve slightly shied away from using the term jet lag itself, because people associate that with the health impacts of that clock shift, rather than the clock shift itself. But it’s exactly the same process that causes jet lag in people,” says Patrick Lewin at the University of Oxford. “It’s having these physiological and behavioural effects, where the birds are mistiming their behaviours.”

It is likely that other long-distance fliers, possibly including some insects and bats as well as birds, also get jet lag in the clock-shift sense, says Lewin.

Advertisement

Birds wearing tiny trackers reveal migration routes in amazing detail

Manx shearwaters are small seabirds that fly vast distances, using a technique called dynamic soaring to exploit wind gradients near the sea surface. “They’ve evolved this niche of being really amazing long-distance travellers,” says Lewin.

They breed on islands around the UK and Ireland. While parents are raising a chick, they may fly more than 1000 kilometres westwards to reach rich fishing grounds in the mid-Atlantic. Once they have food, they fly back in a fairly straight line, diverting only to skirt around landmasses such as Ireland.

How do they achieve these navigational feats? While some birds can sense Earth’s magnetic field, Manx shearwaters don’t appear to. Lewin’s team has confirmed this by attaching small magnets to the birds that should disrupt geomagnetic navigation. They had no effect.

Free newsletter

Instead, it appears that shearwaters rely on a sun compass – if you know what time it is, you can maintain a course by adjusting your orientation relative to the sun. Many animals, from insects and fish to turtles and birds, have been shown to do this. If their internal clocks are reset using artificial light and darkness, they head in the wrong direction.

“We realised that there might be a kind of natural experiment where the birds were manipulating their own clocks,” says Lewin.

For instance, at 6am, a Manx shearwater wanting to fly eastwards back to its nest needs to head sunwards. At noon, it needs to fly at right angles to the sun, which will be due south. But if a shearwater travels 15° of longitude eastwards, the local time will be 1pm, while its internal clock will still register the time as noon, so the sun will no longer be due south. This means birds flying rapidly east should veer slightly off course in a clockwise direction over the course of day, in the absence of other cues.

Australian moths use the stars as a compass on 1000-km migrations

Other researchers have been attaching GPS trackers to Manx shearwaters for decades, so the paths taken on nearly 4000 foraging trips are known. Sure enough, when Lewin and his colleagues analysed these flight tracks, they found birds on rapid return flights tended to deviate clockwise when out of sight of land.

The team considered other potential explanations, from the Coriolis effect to winds. “The one thing that best predicted the observed changes in shearwaters’ orientation was always this sun compass effect,” says Lewin.

The effect is small. After a 1000 km flight, a bird would have to fly only an extra 5 km to reach its colony, which, for such efficient long-distance fliers, is probably negligible, Lewin says. This might explain why Manx shearwaters haven’t evolved some mechanism for avoiding jet lag, he says.

Solving the mysteries of bird migration with technology not only unlocks unexpected secrets but is crucial to conservation efforts, says Rebecca Heisman in her fascinating first book

“What is good about the study is that they analyse a lot of tracks, making for robust data to test different models,” says Ken Cheng at Macquarie University in Sydney.

While other species may get this form of jet lag, too, long-distance flights by birds are typically done during migrations, and migrations usually involve mainly north-south travel, says Cheng, so jet lag won’t be much of a problem.

However, near the poles, the travel distance required to cross 15° or more of longitude becomes so short that many animals might be affected, says Lewin, perhaps even including polar bears or Arctic foxes travelling on sea ice.

“Near-polar species may be quite strongly affected,” he says. “Now, it all gets a bit complicated because you have 24-hour daylight and 24-hour darkness in parts of the year, so circadian rhythms break down generally in some species.”

Inhaling CO2 may rescue nerves’ ability to regrow

New Scientist October 29, 2026

Taking our first breaths marks the beginning of a new life, yet this may be the very act that limits our ability to grow and heal as adults. Studies in mice have pinned down newborns’ exhalation of carbon dioxide, immediately after birth, as the starting gun that switches off their cells’ intrinsic ability to regenerate.

“We were very surprised and excited by the CO2 effect,” says Zhigang He at Harvard Medical School, who led the research.

Your brain’s unexpected ability to regenerate and how to harness it

But when grown mice inhaled the gas, the regenerative pathways turned back on, a discovery He hopes could lead to targeted medical treatments. The results are “very tantalising”, says Nahum Sonenberg at McGill University in Montreal. “If correct, this is a groundbreaking discovery.”

Advertisement

Many species of fish, amphibians and reptiles can regenerate tissues, limbs and organs such as hearts following injury. Mammals also have some regenerative capacity before and shortly after birth, but lose this later in life. A protein master switch called mTOR is one reason they do so. It plays a central role in regulating cell growth in tissues such as the brain, heart and muscles, and its activity declines inside cells within minutes of birth. But the reasons for the drop were poorly understood, says Soroush Tahmasebi at the University of Illinois Chicago, who wasn’t involved in the latest research.

Zhigang He and his colleagues wondered if the shutdown could be related to the dramatic event of birth itself. To find out, they tracked mTOR activity in neurons in the retinas of mice delivered by caesarean section. As long as the newborns remained inside an intact amniotic sac, mTOR stayed high. But as soon as they were removed from the sac and the pups began to breathe air, mTOR activity dropped, even if the researchers kept the umbilical cord intact so that the nutrient supply from the mother was unchanged. This suggested the shutdown trigger was the transition from receiving oxygen through the blood of the umbilical cord to independently breathing air.

Free newsletter

The researchers also confirmed that temperature wasn’t a factor in the shutdown through separate tests in which newborn pups were kept at the same temperature – 37°C (99°F) – as they had experienced in the uterus.

Next, the team delivered pups in controlled gas environments, and found that mTOR activity still shut down even if they lowered oxygen levels in the air. But increasing CO2 levels to 10 per cent prevented the loss of mTOR activity.

Further experiments showed that exhaling CO2 triggers the mTOR shutdown by causing a rise in pH inside cells as levels of the gas fall.

We may finally know what kick-starts muscle contractions in childbirth

When adult mice inhaled air containing 10 per cent CO2, mTOR activity restarted across a range of tissues including brain, heart and muscle, and their neurons’ ability to regenerate after injury was restored. The work shows that the drop in CO2 when breathing starts is “the underlying mechanism driving regenerative failure, not only in neurons but potentially across multiple organs”, says Tahmasebi, “and importantly it is reversible”.

CO2 exhalation might not be the only factor governing the ability of cells to regrow, says He. “Other physiological changes associated with birth may also influence regenerative capacity.” But he hopes the discovery could lead to the development of simple, non-invasive therapies, perhaps based on inhaling CO2, for conditions such as spinal cord injury or traumatic brain injury.

A combination of widely available antibiotics may be able to treat heart failure after researchers found that the therapy regenerates heart cells in animals

Inhibiting mTOR with drugs such as rapamycin has previously been shown to have anti-ageing effects in many species including humans, whereas activating it rescues embryonic-like regenerative potential, at least in mice, but can cause cells to grow out of control, says Tahmasebi. The risk of cancer has deterred industry investment in drugs that activate mTOR, he says, but perhaps the role of CO2 could lead to ways to activate the cascade more safely, in a “temporary and tissue-specific” way.

Further research is still needed, however, to establish appropriate and safe CO2 levels and exposure times, as well as potential side effects. “We would not recommend attempting this without medical supervision,” says He.

The connection between air breathing and regenerative potential also has intriguing evolutionary implications. Vertebrates that acquire oxygen via gills and lose CO2 via their skin – some fish species, as well as amphibians during aquatic larval stages – tend to have high capacity for regeneration, whereas mammals and birds, dependent on air and lungs, are generally much more limited. Breathing could therefore be an underappreciated evolutionary factor shaping regenerative abilities across many forms of life, the researchers say.

Rusty crust made Mars warm and wet

New Scientist October 30, 2026

Mars once had a climate that kept it warm enough for water to flow on the surface. But scientists haven’t been able to agree on an atmospheric recipe with enough warming potential. A new proposal says that hot water circulating underground produced a missing ingredient.

Water reacting with iron in Mars’s crust may have delivered a steady supply of hydrogen to the atmosphere for millions of years, says Cin-Ty Lee at Rice University in Texas.

While not a greenhouse gas itself, hydrogen can have a planet-warming effect through its interactions with atmospheric carbon dioxide. Collisions between the H2 and CO2 molecules deform both of them, and this makes them absorb wavelengths of infrared radiation that CO2 by itself doesn’t block, so the molecule pairs enhance the greenhouse effect.

Advertisement

Did NASA’s Viking landers find life on Mars after all, asks new book

Depending on the total amount of CO2 in the Martian atmosphere, even a few per cent of hydrogen in the atmosphere could be enough to bring the average global temperature above freezing. “I think there’s enough CO2 even now to do it,” says Lee.

The underground hydrogen production plant that Lee proposes is the extremely thick crust, thought to extend as far as 80 kilometres below ground, that underlies Mars’s southern highlands. “Like an iceberg floating on water, the higher the mountain, the thicker the root,” he says.

Just as on Earth, the crust will contain radioactive elements, such as uranium, thorium and potassium, which produce heat as they decay. Thicker crust contains a greater total quantity of these elements, while the surface area available for cooling remains the same. In 2024, Lee published calculations showing that, with sufficiently thick crust, ice in its upper few kilometres would melt and create aquifers.

Free newsletter

Once those aquifers exist, Lee told the annual conference of the Geological Society of America in Denver, Colorado, earlier this month, the water will start shedding its heat by circulating up and down through the porous upper layers of the crust. These layers mostly consist of basalt, which is rich in iron. The water would make the iron rust, a process that frees up its constituent hydrogen molecules, which would then find their way up into the atmosphere.

The hydrothermal pump eventually died, leaving Mars the cold desert it is today, because it ran out of both water and power. “For the water, this was a one-way ticket,” says Lee. “And also the radioactivity diminished.”

Ramses Ramirez of the University of Central Florida, who has studied volcanoes as potential sources of hydrogen for the warming of Mars, says that until he has seen a full paper about the idea, he is sceptical the idea can explain Mars’s formerly warm surface “without invoking some extremely favourable circumstances”.

The Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft, set to launch on 20 October, will bring back samples that should solve a moon mystery that has been vexing scientists for more than a century

Ramirez also notes that the possibility of water releasing hydrogen from rocks was proposed over a decade ago. But, according to Lee, while earlier studies just supposed that water somehow would be involved, his work shows “how it’s almost inevitable that this has to happen” with a thick enough crust.

He says his idea is testable by looking deep into the Martian crust. “If we find that it is oxidised down to several kilometres, this is the only way it can happen.”

As scientific bycatch, this would then also provide an explanation for the redness of Mars. Meteoroid impacts or other processes would expose some of the rusted rock on the surface. “With the erosion by wind, you are going to generate a lot of dust and it coats everything,” says Lee.

How did the biggest crypto heist in history just happen?

New Scientist October 30, 2026

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange Binance has been hit with the biggest ever cryptocurrency heist, in which billions of dollars of reserves were drained in just 20 minutes.

From 8:05pm on 29 October, $6.36 billion in cryptocurrencies were shifted from wallets in a coordinated attack believed to have originated from a North Korean-linked hacking unit called TraderTraitor. This group was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit crypto exchange in February 2025.

The US Treasury has previously said that such stolen funds are used to finance North Korea’s nuclear missile programme.

Advertisement

Despite cryptocurrency’s founding idea of decentralisation, meaning no one has singular control over the money flowing through the network, there are some large single points of failure. It is thought one of these was the cause of the Binance hack, which gave access to a system the exchange uses to authorise transfers out of customers’ accounts.

Quantum computer quickly mines cryptocurrency while using less energy

In a statement, Binance said its early investigations indicate the security incident may stem from a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer. TRM Labs, a cybersecurity firm, suggests that preparations for the attack may have begun several days ago.

Binance claims it has found no evidence that the private cryptographic keys used to authorise transactions were stolen. Instead, the attackers appear to have gained access to the software that requests withdrawals, potentially allowing them to instruct Binance’s own systems to approve the transfers. However, the investigation is continuing and the firm has said in a subsequent statement there may have been “additional points of breach”.

“It shouldn’t be possible for a single [developer] PC to be compromised and somehow for that to allow the entire exchange to be compromised,” says Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey, UK. “I don’t understand how that can happen.”

If that is the case, it highlights how precarious major financial hubs in the crypto world can be to single points of failure.

Free newsletter

“You can build a vault with mathematical firewalls, but if the individual holding the keys can be duped, the vault is opened,” says Clive Summerfield at FARx, a cybersecurity company. “Most crypto platforms are as centralised as any bank, with a small number of privileged individuals controlling billions. The difference is that once crypto is transferred, it’s gone.”

That centralisation can be a blessing as well as a curse, though: cryptocurrencies Tether and Circle have been able to freeze billions of dollars of stolen coins, stymying the hackers in attempts to transfer about half the stolen funds any further.

Woodward says the Binance incident potentially strikes a distinction between crypto security and more traditional finance. “You would hope there’d be things like two-man rules [where two separate people have to approve a change] or things that banks have for changing critical systems, but it doesn’t look like those were in place.”

Scientists confirm fruit and vegetable skin really is good for you

New Scientist October 30, 2026

Some people are convinced that fruit and vegetable skin is particularly nutritious, and now scientists have confirmed the idea. They have discovered that these parts of fruits and vegetables often contain far more fibre than the flesh we normally consume.

The finding suggests cooks are unwittingly discarding fibre-rich food by chucking out the seeds, skins and stems of fruits and vegetables when preparing a meal.

Home cooks and caterers should adopt “root to tip” eating and start cooking with squash peel, watermelon rind and pepper stalks to improve the public’s intake of dietary fibre, the team says.

Advertisement

Our food system is vulnerable to El Niño, warns UK climate minister

“We’ve really got to shift our purchasing habits to buy whole fruits and vegetables, and then use all of the fruits and vegetables in dishes,” says Rachel Gibson at King’s College London.

Gibson and her colleagues tested the fibre content of 12 fruits and vegetables, including butternut squash, kiwi fruit, watermelon, broccoli and bell pepper. The team measured the fibre content both in the parts typically consumed and the parts that usually go to waste.

They found that, in 10 of the 12 produce types, the normally wasted components contain more fibre than the commonly consumed parts. Butternut squash seeds and skin, for example, contained 9.25 grams of fibre per 100 grams, compared with 2 g of fibre per 100 g of squash flesh. Meanwhile, the skin and core of a pineapple core contains 450 per cent more fibre than the flesh. These skin and core components are often tough to chew, but the researchers say they can be blended, grated or roasted to make them more palatable.

Free newsletter

Just 4 per cent of British adults meet the recommended minimum daily intake of 30 g of dietary fibre, with the average adult consuming around half that per day.

Gibson suggests caterers could use the findings to design fibre-rich meals using more produce that would otherwise go to waste. This could reduce food waste and cut costs for commercial kitchens, as well as increasing dietary fibre intake, she says.

King’s College London’s canteen piloted a “root to tip” menu in May 2025. Meals included a West African peanut stew made with all of a butternut squash, kale stalks and leek tops, and a watermelon salad featuring pickled watermelon rind.

Rejigging the meal choices on offer in a canteen can prompt people to make healthier, climate-friendlier decisions

Eating a larger proportion of harvested fruit and vegetables will also improve the resilience of the food system in the face of climate shocks, says Gibson. “Everything we pull out of the ground that we can eat, we should be eating.”

Christian Reynolds at City St George’s University of London says the research is an “exciting investigation”. But he points out that the most carbon-intensive food waste is meat and dairy products. Reducing fruit and vegetable waste is therefore “part of the solution, but it’s not the only thing we need to do”, he says.

In Dark Eden, I imagined how life might exist on a sunless planet

New Scientist October 30, 2026

I came up with the idea of the planet Eden in 1992 for a short story called The Circle of Stones. At that time, I had no idea that there really were such things as planets without suns, but it seemed likely to me. It also seemed possible to me that life might arise on such a planet, since, even here on Earth, whole ecologies thrive without sunlight around thermal vents in the deep ocean. Life on Earth may have even have begun in such places.

Quite often, if something seems likely, it does indeed happen. (In another book, I predicted that a US president would one day seek to take over Greenland and Canada.) Having written that story, I learned that free-floating planets did indeed exist. Being dark, they’re hard to spot, but a number have been detected using gravitational lensing. And I gather it’s not particularly controversial to think that some of them might support life (though not quite in the form that I chose to imagine it – but I’ll come to that).

When creating a world for a story, I don’t usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent. I didn’t build Eden by doing a lot of research, but I did put a lot of thought into how it might all work. This wasn’t so I could put it all in the book – no one in Eden knows this stuff and the story is told entirely by its characters! – but so that I had something to guide my imagination and make my invented world feel coherent.

Advertisement

Free newsletter

My idea was that Eden had once been covered in ice, but its hot core meant there was liquid water below the ice in which life could come into existence. One particular kind of life form appeared, somewhat resembling tree roots, that was able to obtain additional energy by pushing deep down into hot rocks, pumping its sap through them to heat it, and then pumping it back up again, like a geothermal power station. One of the ways these organisms used this heat was to push upwards into the planet’s shell of ice, melting parts of it, feeding on the nutrients it contained, and creating more living space – and they carried on doing so until much of the surface of Eden was ice-free, and had an atmosphere that would turn out to be breathable by humans.

Millions of years later, this thawed-out surface, now populated by a multitude of different life forms, became the stage on which my drama could unfold: first that early story, then another story and then the novel Dark Eden and its two sequels. In Dark Eden, a tiny community of humans, descended from stranded visitors from Earth, eke out a living using tools made of stone and wood, and try to make sense of their life as exiles from a sunlit world that lives on in folk memory, but which they can only very shakily imagine. (In the biblical story of Eden, humans are exiled from Eden – my Eden is the place of exile.) Their stories tell them that Earth people could fly through the air, that there was a thing there called leckytrickity, that Earth animals had eyes that you could look into and see their minds looking back out at you, not like the flat, blank eyes of Eden creatures.

Our writers pick their favourite science fiction books of all time

On the surface of Eden, those root-like life forms put up structures that Eden’s humans call “trees”. A whole ecosystem has evolved around them, including “starflowers” that parasitise their roots. (These, as it happens, turn out to be a rich source of Vitamin D. Phew! What a stroke of luck!) And there are many animals – or quote-unquote “animals”, strictly speaking, since they’re not related to the animal kingdom of Earth. There’s no sunlight in Eden (and therefore no alternation of day and night) but, like organisms that live in the ocean depths of Earth, Eden’s life has developed bioluminescence. The “trees” have luminous “lanternflowers”; the starflowers glitter. Imagine a leafless forest on a moonless night, lit by thousands of Chinese lanterns. Then add in twinkling fairy lights at ground level. With your eyes half-closed, the forests of Eden would look something like that.

Just as life on Earth depends on plants that turn sunlight into chemical energy, so the life of Eden depends on geothermal trees. They bring heat to the surface to power their metabolisms, they keep the air warm and, if you live on Eden, the steady “Hmmmph hmmmph hmmmph” of their constant pumping is the background of your waking and sleeping life, merging in the distance to a steady hum. All the trees are hot, and some of them are so hot that you’d burn yourself if you touched their trunks. If you cut down a tree, you have to watch out for the spurt of scalding liquid that bursts out.

When I read stories set on alien planets, I’m sometimes disappointed in the “animals” (I’ll drop the inverted commas now). Writers often seem to dream up a motley collection of bizarre creatures without much regard for how they might actually survive or how they are related to one another. I tried to design my animals on evolutionary principles, giving thought to how they were adapted to their environment, the role they played in the ecosystem and how they might plausibly have evolved. Animals on Earth fall into a large but finite number of basic body plans. For example, monkeys, cows, crocodiles and seagulls all have four limbs and, though some descendants of quadrupeds have lost their limbs (snakes, whales), there are no examples of quadrupeds developing extra ones. In the same way, large animals on Eden all have a six-limbed body plan. There are other animals that don’t conform to this, just as there are arthropods, et cetera on Earth, but the large animals are all based on this six-limbed pattern.

From drowned worlds to virtual utopias via deep space, wild ideas abound in Emily H. Wilson’s picks for her favourite sci-fi reads of the year

I’ve already mentioned how different Eden eyes are from the eyes of terrestrial animals. They have evolved alongside the evolution of bioluminescence, rather in the way that colourful flowers and nectar-eating insects have evolved alongside one another on Earth. Eden trees use luminous lanternflowers to attract the creatures that help them reproduce, just as flowering plants on Earth use colour and scent.

I gave a lot of thought to the biology of Eden, but I have to admit that, in strictly scientific terms, my imaginary world isn’t entirely viable. Free-floating planets with warm cores? Yes! Not just possible, but a certainty! But free-floating planets with warm surfaces? Sadly no. More than one astronomer has told me they just couldn’t happen. No matter how many radiator-like trees there might be, I’ve been told, it still wouldn’t be enough to maintain liquid water or a warm atmosphere.

Let’s call it “fiction science”, science made up for a story, which works in some places and in others allows itself poetic licence. Almost all science fiction uses fiction science and Dark Eden contains several other examples. I took some liberties with human genetics, for instance. And then there’s the question of how people got to Eden in the first place. (It’s many light years away from Earth.) Like the writers of pretty much all stories set in interstellar space, I pretended that faster-than-light travel was possible and went with that, although it most probably isn’t.

(I think that’s OK. It allows us to visit, in our imaginations at least, parts of the universe we could never otherwise hope to reach.)

What I wanted from Eden was for it to be a world that hung together well enough to be a satisfying setting for my story, one in which I and my readers could immerse ourselves. The story is about exile and loss. The perpetually dark sky, and the animals with their blank unreadable eyes, serve as reminders that Eden folk are exiles. At the beginning of Dark Eden, every human being in Eden lives around a circle of stones that marks the place where their ancestors first touched down. And this circle represents to Eden folk the hope for return and redemption, which is central to their whole world view.

The fact that I took some liberties when constructing Eden doesn’t mean it wouldn’t be interesting also to write about a real free-floating planet. And, as it happens, I’ve had the opportunity recently to do just that. In a project initiated by Comma Press, I was one of a number of writers who paired up with astronomers from Jodrell Bank to write stories for an anthology called Firmament. My astronomer collaborator, Ida Janiak, helped me build a scenario in which a free-floating planet called Lupus arrives in the solar system. Apart from being roughly Earth-sized, Lupus isn’t much like Eden, but somewhat like the Jovian moon Europa. Its surface is covered by a kilometres-thick shell of ice in no danger of melting, with a liquid ocean beneath and… well, read the story! The anthology will appear in November but there will also be a condensed version of mine and Ida’s story in the Christmas edition of New Scientist, out online on 16 December and in print on the 19th.

I hope, meanwhile, you will immerse yourself in the luminous forests of Eden with their pulsing trees. Possible or not, they are very beautiful, if I say so myself.

Dark Eden by Chris Beckett (Corvus) is the November read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here, and join the discussion on Discord here.

Read an extract from Dark Eden by Chris Beckett

New Scientist October 30, 2026

We went out by a path that led through a big clump of flickering starflowers and then into Batwing. A whole bunch of Batwing grownups and newhairs were in their clearing banging away at a giant redlantern tree with their blackglass axes, working in the pink light of its flowers.

We walked round the edge of their clearing to Family Fence, dragged away the branches at the opening, and went out into open forest. No more shelters and campfires ahead of us now: nothing but shining trees.

Hmmmph, hmmmph, hmmmph, went the trees. Hmmmmmm, went forest. We walked for a waking under the light of the treelanterns, slashing down whatever birds and bats and fruit we could get as we went along, and finally stopped to rest at the big lump of rock called Lava Blob. Old Roger handed us out a gritty little seedcake each, made of ground-up starflower seeds, so we could have something in our bellies, and then we settled down with our backs against the rock, so we didn’t have to worry about leopards sneaking up behind us. There were lots of yellowlantern trees round there, which we didn’t get so much back in Family, and also yellow animals called hoppers that came bouncing out of forest on their back legs and wrung their four hands together while they looked at us with their big flat eyes and went Peep peep peep. But hoppers were no good to eat and their skins were no use either, so we just chucked stones at them to make them go away and let us sleep in peace.

Advertisement

Free newsletter

When we woke up, Starry Swirl was still bright bright in sky. We ate a bit of dry cake and off we went again, under redlanterns and whitelanterns and spiketrees, with flutterbyes darting and glittering all round us and bats chasing the flutterbyes and trees going hmmph, hmmph, hmmph like always, until it all blurred together into that hmmmmmmmmm that was the background of our lives.

After a few miles we came to a small pool full of shiny wavyweed and all us newhairs took off our wraps and dived into the warm water for crabfish and oysters to eat. All the boys watched Tina Spiketree diving in, and they all thought how graceful she was with her long legs, and how smooth her skin was, and how much they wanted to slip with her. But when she came up she swam straight to me, and gave me a dying oyster with the bright pink light still shining out of it.

“You know what they say about oysters, don’t you, John?” she said.

Tom’s neck, she was pretty pretty, the prettiest in whole of Family. And she knew it well well.

In another couple of hours we reached the place where Peckham Hills began to rise up out of forest of Circle Valley, and started to climb up through them by Monkey Path, which isn’t really a path, but just a way we know through the trees. The trees carried on up the slopes – redlanterns and whitelanterns and scalding hot spiketrees – and there were flickering starflowers growing beneath them, just like in the rest of forest. Streams ran through them down from darkness and ice, heading towards Greatpool, still cold cold but already bright and glittering with life. And small creatures called monkeys jumped from tree to tree. They had little thin bodies, and six long arms with a hand on the end of each. Handsome Fox shot one with an arrow, and was pleased pleased with himself, even though they were all bones and sinews and only give a mouthful of meat, because they move fast and are hard to aim at with those big blotches on their skin that flash on and off as they swing among the lanternflowers.

As we climbed up it got colder. The starflowers disappeared, the trees became smaller, and there weren’t any monkeys any more, only the occasional smallbuck darting away through the trees. And then the trees stopped and we came out from the top edge of forest onto bare ground. Pretty soon, when we’d climbed above the height of those last few little trees, we could see whole of Circle Valley spread out below us – whole of Eden that we knew, with thousands and thousands of lanterns shining all the way from where we stood on Peckham Hills to Dark shadow of Blue Mountains away in the distance, and from Rockies over the left, with the red glow of Mount Snellins smouldering in middle, to the deep darkness over to our right that was Alps. And above all of it the huge spiral of Starry Swirl was still shining down.

Of course, with no trees to give off light with their lanternflowers or to warm the air with their trunks, it was dark dark up there – you could only just barely make things out in the starlight and the light from the edge of forest – and it was cold cold, specially on our feet. But us newhairs dared each other to run up as far as the snow. The ice felt like it was burning, it was so cold, and most kids took ten twenty steps, yelled and came running down again. But I took Gerry right up to the ridge of the hill and then, ignoring Old Roger yelling at us to come back, went far enough down the other side so that the others couldn’t see us.

“We’ve made our point now, haven’t we, John?” Gerry said, shivering. We only had waistwraps on, and buckskins round our shoulders, and our feet were hurting like they’d been skinned. “Shall we go back down to rest of them now?”

Our writers pick their favourite science fiction books of all time

My cousin Gerry was about a wombtime younger than me – his dad was giving his mum a slip, in other words, about the time that I was born – and he was devoted to me, he thought I was wonderful, he’d do just about anything I asked.

“No, wait a minute. Wait a minute. Be quiet and listen.”

“Listen to what?”

“To the silence, you idiot.”

There was no hmmmmmmmm of forest, no hmmph, hmmph, hmmph of pumping trees, no starbirds going hoom, hoom, hoom in the distance, no flutterbyes flapping and flicking, no whoosh of diving bats. There was no sound at all except a quiet little tinkle of water all around us coming out from under the snow in hundreds of little streams. And it was dark dark. No tree-light up there. The only light came from Starry Swirl.

We could barely make out each other’s faces. It made me think about that place called Earth where Tommy and Angela first came from, way back in the beginning with the Three Companions, and where one waking we would all return, if only we stayed in the right place and were good good good. There were no lanterntrees back there on Earth, no glittery flutterbyes or shiny flowers, but they had a big big light that we don’t have at all. It came from a giant star. And it was so bright that it would burn out your eyes if you stared at it.

“When people talk about Earth,” I said to Gerry, “they always talk about that huge bright star, don’t they, and all the lovely light it must have given? But Earth turned round and round, didn’t it, and half the time it wasn’t facing the star at all but was dark dark, without lanterns or anything, only the light the Earth people made for themselves.”

“What are you talking about, John?” Gerry said, with his teeth chattering. “And why can’t we go back down again if you just want to talk?”

“I was thinking about that darkness. They called it Night, didn’t they? I’m just thinking that it must have been like this. What you get up here on Snowy Dark: it’s what they would have called Night.”

‘Reverse physics’ could help bridge the classical and quantum worlds

New Scientist October 30, 2026

There’s a bit of an open secret in physics. Even when our theories work well – and some have been rigorously tested for centuries – we don’t always fully understand them. We start with experimental evidence, then build mathematical models and theories, test and update them with more experiments and hope that it all adds up. Often, it does. But were a mathematician to ask what a theory we built this way is – that is, what type of well-defined mathematical objects comprise it – that isn’t a question that researchers can always fully answer.

“The sense from a lot of physicists is these are maths details and that is not really physics, so it’s not their job to set them straight,” says Gabriele Carcassi at the University of Michigan. But if we are to tackle the biggest problems in physics, such as marrying quantum mechanics with general relativity to produce a theory of quantum gravity, we may have to take a different tack.

That’s where the “reverse physics” programme comes in. It is Carcassi’s passion project: he spends his days trying to put physics on accurate, rigorous and meaningful mathematical foundations. He is mapping out the bridge you must be able to walk to fully connect mathematics and physics. Carcassi puts it like this: “When the maths is derived from the right physical assumptions, the physical assumptions can be derived from the maths.”

Advertisement

Key oddity of quantum physics may run even deeper than anticipated

Like most physicists, I didn’t learn to think this way. All the concepts that were taught to me came from physics, such as fields or forces or even slices of space-time, then I’d learn just enough about what they are mathematically to know which equations predict their behaviour. If you asked me to define a mathematical object called a Lorentzian manifold, I am really not sure that I could, yet I have a fairly good mental image of the physical thing it is representing: space-time as the fabric of reality. Reverse-engineering a theory of a changing space-time, essentially the theory of general relativity, from ideas like Lorentzian manifolds and other mathematical ingredients certainly hadn’t been put on my radar throughout my education.

But Carcassi and his colleagues at the Assumptions of Physics project want to establish these equivalent, two-way definitions for nothing less than all of physics. It’s an enormous undertaking, to say the least.

Trained as an engineer, Carcassi fell into this line of work because he married a physicist, Christine Aidala at the University of Michigan, who had a lot of physics books lying around. Reading them puzzled him, particularly those on quantum mechanics. Whereas most people get hung up on the matter of which interpretation of quantum mechanics is correct – if and how a theory captures the objective physical reality of our world, or if there even is an objective reality – Carcassi found that every idea was missing something.

Why no one can agree on what quantum physics really means

“To me, all these [theories, such as quantum mechanics] are models, and I need to understand when they’re applicable and when not, essentially what they’re supposed to describe and under what assumptions,” he says. While he was grappling with this, the situation got worse. “I realised that we don’t really understand classical mechanics,” he says. This isn’t to say that classical mechanics doesn’t work, but that some of its theoretical ingredients are ill-defined, in Carcassi’s view.

As we talked, I was reminded of my advanced mechanics courses where I learned about objects called the “action” and “Hamiltonian”. They are incredibly useful, and I can define them loosely in English, saying something about an object’s preferred path through space or about its energy, but I’d be offering intuition that I got through homework problems more than mathematical rigor.

Carcassi says his experience was similar. “You know how to use them. You know their properties, but what exactly are they describing? You don’t know. I basically started reverse engineering a lot of these things.” This is just one example of the kind of definitional work reverse physics could offer.

“The tagline is to find a minimal set of physical assumptions from which we can rigorously re-derive the laws,” he says. Ideally, this would resolve many existing physics paradoxes and puzzles, such as the role of measurements in quantum physics where objects seem to acquire a fixed reality only after being observed. If we understood the maths underpinning those scenarios better, we could ascertain whether the world is fundamentally fuzzy or if a solid reality exists after all.

In the past 11 years, the Assumptions of Physics team, primarily consisting of Carcassi and Aidala, has broken down essentially all of classical physics into a set of mathematical equivalencies that allow the researchers to run over that bridge between maths and physics in either direction. Notably, entropy – which quantifies whether a physical system must assume one very precisely ordered state, or can find itself in many more equally likely states – has emerged as a key player in their effort.

For instance, they have shown that restricting any change in the entropy of a system is equivalent to previously known rules for how such a system can evolve over time. Reverse physics has already illuminated connections between quantum and classical physics – according to the team’s list of mathematical concepts and assumptions that undergird all of physics, it seems that classical physics is akin to quantum physics, but with entropy made high.

Quantum theory is challenging long-standing ideas about entropy

Carcassi is currently working on a slew of quantum problems, and candidly notes that it will be difficult to tackle various features of quantum field theory (QFT), where quantum fields extend through all of space and infinitely large numbers are known to crop up. One of the central objects that physicists use for QFT computations – for instance, to predict outcomes of particle accelerator experiments – is the “path integral”, which even professors who teach it often admit is an poorly defined headache for mathematicians. I’ve personally been fascinated by this enough to have devoted to a chapter to the path integral in my book.

But Carcassi’s quantum hopes soar higher: he thinks reverse physics could help researchers marry quantum physics and Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity by providing sufficient clarity on how both can be built from a shared mathematical base. “How can we even proceed and try to get new theories of physics, if we don’t even understand exactly what we have in the current one,” says Carcassi. The quest for a theory of quantum gravity has been one of physics’ biggest and least fruitful efforts for decades, which makes any new approach welcome.

Intriguingly, the way reverse physics could interweave these two pillars is indifferent to many of the common quantum fights among physicists. Carcassi and his collaborators aren’t interested in whether the equations of quantum theory imply that we live in the multiverse or that, for example, everything in the cosmos is inextricably connected with everything else. They are interested in the commonalities between every possible mathematical framework for quantum physics, and whether any resultant theory that encompasses them all makes sense with how we can measure and observe the universe.

Trying to redo all of physics from the ground up in this manner isn’t for the faint of heart. But what intimidates Carcassi is mostly the lack of funding and broad interest into this type of nitty-gritty work in physics’ very foundations. With appropriate funding and a big enough team, the reverse physics programme could be completed within a decade, he says. It brings to mind a story from my college years.

Once, during office hours, I told a physics professor about all the maths courses I was taking in the hope that they’d make me a better physicist. “I just know there will be a moment when all the maths and physics come together, and I finally get it all,” I said. The professor chuckled. He said he’d been waiting for that moment for his whole career. I hope the wait will soon be over.

The 12 strangest science stories we can’t stop thinking about

New Scientist October 30, 2026

There are some stories that stay with you forever, the big scientific moments that change the course of history. These are not those moments – but we can’t stop thinking about them anyway.

Surgeon Stuart Meloy was performing a pain-relief operation on a woman’s spine when she started exclaiming emphatically. “You’re going to have to teach my husband to do that,” the woman said. This inspired Meloy to invent an implant to help women who are unable to achieve orgasms in the usual way. New Scientist broke the news in 2001, sparking a frenzy of worldwide media excitement. But 13 years later, Meloy was still struggling to raise funds for a full clinical trial, and the “orgasmatron” never reached a climax.

We aren’t the only primates capable of coming up with creative ways to pleasure ourselves. In a study of long-tailed macaques (Macaca fascicularis) in Bali, Indonesia, Camilla Cenni at the University of Lethbridge in Alberta, Canada, and her colleagues filmed hundreds of examples of male and female monkeys using stone tools as sex toys, rubbing or tapping them on their genitals. According to Cyril Grueter at the University of Western Australia, the Balinese monkeys get plenty of food handouts from humans, and this frees up time for sexual experimentation. But some monkeys in other places have unusual kinks, too: another study reported a wild macaque in Japan rubbing its genitals on the back of a sika deer.

Advertisement

In 2015, surgeon Sergio Canavero announced plans to carry out the first human head transplant, intended to extend the lives of people with muscle and nerve degeneration or widespread cancer. He claimed his technique could overcome technical hurdles, including how to fuse the spinal cord and prevent the body’s immune system from rejecting the head. In the following two years, Canavero published animal experiments supposedly backing up his methods, but other surgeons remained highly sceptical. A human head transplant never did happen, but Canavero has reportedly moved on to an even bolder ambition: transplanting a brain into a non-sentient clone.

Have you ever wondered if a rat can drive a car? Kelly Lambert at the University of Richmond in Virginia has. She and her colleagues built a tiny car with three copper bars that would steer it left, forward or right. Sure enough, 18 rats learned to drive towards food rewards. They even found it relaxing, as measurements of their stress hormones indicated. Lambert proposed that driving challenges could replace traditional maze tests when using rat models to study neuropsychiatric conditions.

Humans are more similar to rats than we like to think. In a psychology experiment, Noam Sobel and his colleagues at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, surreptitiously filmed 153 volunteers. After shaking hands with someone of the same sex, people smelled their shaking hand more than twice as much as they did before the handshake. Puzzlingly, after shaking hands with someone of the opposite sex, people were more likely to sniff their non-shaking hand. The team suspected that humans use chemical signals all the time without being aware of it.

Communication through scent is, of course, widespread in mammals, but some never-before-seen behaviour in dolphins took biologists by surprise in 2025. While studying Amazon river dolphins (Inia geoffrensis), or botos, in Brazil, Claryana Araújo-Wang at CetAsia Research Group in Ontario, Canada, saw a male “flip his belly up out of the water, expose his penis and then proceed to urinate into the air”, she told New Scientist. They saw dolphins do this a total of 36 times, and most of the time another male was nearby and would pursue the stream of urine. The purpose of this behaviour hasn’t yet been established, but hormones in urine might signal a male’s social position or physical condition, said Araújo-Wang.

Orcas have begun wearing salmon hats again – and we may soon know why

As for human modes of communication, many of us struggle to put our smartphones down – so the last thing we’d want is for them to crawl across the table towards us. Nevertheless, Marc Teyssier at the University of Paris-Saclay in France and his colleagues gave phones this ability in 2018, with a robotic appendage dubbed the MobiLimb. It plugs into a device’s USB port and, for some reason, looks eerily like a human finger, giving it a spooky quality reminiscent of Thing from The Addams Family. The MobiLimb can stroke your wrist, wave, wag like a tail or, most disconcertingly, drag the phone around. Thankfully, the idea hasn’t taken off.

If you find the thought of a phone with a finger horrifying, wait until you hear about the nightmare-inducing hairy frog Trichobatrachus robustus. In 2008, researchers reported that these frogs can break their own bones to produce claws that burst through their skin. David Blackburn at Harvard University’s Museum of Comparative Zoology thought these weapons were for defence, but two years later, another team argued that they were used in fights between males – and that the frog’s unusual hairs were a kind of armour to protect its vulnerable parts from sharp claws.

In 1957, when New Scientist was 1 year old, we reported on a new method for shrinking an adult human body to the size of a baby. At an exhibition of inventors in Winnipeg, Canada, the unnamed inventor of this process claimed it would make disposing of dead bodies simpler, as they could be slid into underground tubes and take up less space. The method involved applying high pressure to the corpse and squeezing out fluids so its flesh could be compressed into a mould. “All this is, of course, highly ingenious but it is uncertain why the inventor thinks that his newly proposed form of burial is in any way better than the current and very popular method of cremation,” the writer mused.

The brain has its own microbiome. Here’s what it means for your health

We may take it for granted, but the anus, which allows food to pass through the body, was an evolutionary breakthrough, both figuratively and literally. The earliest animals, like jellyfish today, had only one gut opening, where food went in and waste came out. In 2019, scientists discovered that the warty comb jelly (Mnemiopsis leidyi, pictured top) forms an anal opening when it needs to defecate, but it vanishes straight afterwards. This, they suggested, could represent how the anus evolved in the first place.

Flatus – gas expelled from the anus – has been a topic of endless fascination for many readers (and journalists). In 2001, we featured the work of Michael Levitt at the Veterans Administration Medical Center in Minneapolis, a leading authority on the subject. He developed a “Toot Trapper” that reduces odours by trapping certain gases using activated charcoal. We also reported on a device for monitoring gas emissions from dogs, used to test dog snacks that were supposed to reduce flatulence. In 2016, researchers in Australia worked out which foods cause the smelliest farts by mixing faeces with different foods. They recommended eating less protein and more slow-release carbohydrates to minimise hydrogen sulphide production. In 2022, Nagarajan Kannan at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, and his colleagues worked out that some poos float because of gas from gut microbes, confirming a hypothesis first put forward by Levitt 50 years earlier.

Even stranger things go on inside some people’s intestines, as we found out in 2019. A 46-year-old man started experiencing unexplained mental fogginess, dizziness and memory loss, and had to give up his job. Later, doctors found high levels of alcohol in his blood when he hadn’t been drinking. Eventually, they realised his gut contained high levels of Saccharomyces cerevisiae – brewer’s yeast – which got him drunk any time he ate a lot of carbohydrates. This rare condition, known as auto brewery syndrome, had been triggered when the man took antibiotics for a thumb injury, which disrupted his gut microbiome. This year, a study reported that another man with this condition fully recovered after getting a transplant of faeces from a healthy donor. Both articles were written by Alice Klein, who we also have to thank for the monkey sex toys, car-driving rats, smelly farts and floating poos. Thanks, Alice!

Two fires in vegetation near the $48 million clifftop property of New Zealand’s second richest person have been referred to police.

A helicopter had to be called to help put out one of the fires, which occurred on a bush-clad cliff-face overlooking Gentlemans Bay near the large Riddell Rd estate of billionaire Graeme Hart in Auckland’s Glendowie.

No buildings were damaged, Fire and Emergency Northern Communications’ shift manager Josh Pennefather said.

The first fire was reported to emergency services by someone on a boat at 3.19pm yesterday, and was also spotted by a nearby police maritime unit, Pennefather said.

“Our crews … found a fire on the eastern side of the cliff face … the original size was approximately 50 metres by 100m with no access from the beach or cliff top.

“Our crews were doing a ground-based attack on the fire to prevent it spreading, but they couldn’t access the seat of the fire.”

A helicopter arrived around 5pm and the fire was out by 8.45pm, but a 111 caller told Fire and Emergency the area was again on fire just before 11pm.

Email us

About 25 firefighters responded and found the fire was “in the same area … but appeared to be further east than the one [in the] afternoon”, Pennefather said.

“We did request police to attend based on the information that it was further east, just because … it could be from an ember spread or it could be suspicious circumstances, but you’d have to check with police as to what information they have.”

Firefighters have since left the scene.

As far as he knew no police request had been made as of 6.45am for a fire investigator to go to the scene, Pennefather said.

Inquiries into the fires were “ongoing”, a police spokesman said this morning.

Hart, the private equity and packaging magnate, has an estimated fortune of $14.1 billion, according to this year’s NBR Rich List.

That put the 71-year-old in second place, after he was earlier overtaken by Zuru co-founders Nick and Mat Mowbray, with the toy entrepreneurs having an estimated combined wealth of $20b.

Hart owns 10 neighbouring sites on Riddell and Waitara roads, with combined rateable value in May 2024 of more than $91m, according to property records.

The highest value of these is a two-hectare site that’s home to an 878sq m Italian-style mansion and has a rateable value of $48m.

In 2013, the Herald reported Hart had completed a huge new three-level banquet hall with a domed glass atrium and its own swimming pool and wine cellar, set in a large flat area overlooking the Hauraki Gulf.

Hart and wife Robyn bought the land in 1995 for $2m and built the house over a number of years.

Cherie Howie joined the Herald in 2011. She has been a journalist for more than 20 years and specialises in general news and features.
