Apec 2026: Who will represent New Zealand at the Shenzhen summit? – Fran O’Sullivan

New Zealand Herald October 30, 2026

Outgoing Trade Minister Damien O'Connor went to Apec in 2023, but who will go this year? Photo / Getty Images

It’s a moot question just who will represent New Zealand at the upcoming Apec Economic Leaders’ two-day meeting in Shenzhen, China, which starts on November 18.

Will a declared Prime Minister go? Will it be an outgoing PM in a caretaker capacity? Or will an outgoing trade minister be subbed in (again in a caretaker capacity as happened in 2023 when Joe Biden hosted Apec), while political parties get on with coalition negotiations to form the next Government?

My view is that the two main contestants to be Prime Minister should sort this without too much politicking.

If the incumbent Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon, looks likely on election night to continue, it would be no hardship to fly to Hong Kong, cross the border to Shenzhen and return the next day after the leaders’ meeting.

There would be some toing and froing if the incumbent is reduced to caretaker status (in other words, loses the election), but either Luxon or the outgoing Trade Minister should go anyway, given the importance of New Zealand’s relationships with the leaders of the other 20 nations that make up Apec.

If it is Chris Hipkins in the box seat on election night, it could be difficult for him to be sworn in as Prime Minister within 10 days unless the result is clear-cut.

Sir John Key managed that feat in 2008, quickly negotiating confidence and supply agreements with the Act, Māori and United Future parties to form the fifth National Government.

Immediately after his first Cabinet meeting and swearing-in on November 19, 2008, Key flew to Peru to join international leaders addressing the unfolding global financial and economic crisis – the upshot of the Global Financial Crisis.

But the Greens are a much more significant player and want a seat at the table of a Labour-led Coalition. There is potentially Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori to contend with.

This is China’s third time hosting Apec. The first, in Shanghai in 2001, was just weeks after the September 11 attacks on the Twin Towers in New York.

A summit that had just welcomed China’s accession to the World Trade Organisation became dominated by security issues (although claims that China was manipulating its currency were also a point of contention from the US side, denied by the host).

China hosted again in 2014 in Beijing, with a focus on forming a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific.

I went to the CEO summits held during those two Chinese-hosted Apec meetings and will do so again this year for what promises to be a tense affair, given that Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin will be there.

On October 19, the Kremlin said that Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping could meet alongside the Apec meeting. According to the Wall Street Journal, Putin proposed the idea during a phone call with Trump on October 9.

It has been referred to in some quarters as the “New Yalta”. But Trump has suggested that such a gathering should focus primarily on nuclear disarmament rather than Ukraine.

The Hudson Institute opined that the significance of such a summit would extend well beyond its immediate agenda.

“It would reflect a broader transformation in international relations: the growing temptation to replace established institutions, alliances and multilateral frameworks with direct transactions among great powers,” the US think tank said.

New Zealand is a founding member of Apec, the world’s largest trade forum.

The 2026 summit builds on work that this country’s leaders and officials established in 2021, when New Zealand hosted Apec virtually during the Covid pandemic.

The theme, “Building an Asia-Pacific community to prosper together”, is ambitious given the recent history of the US-China relationship.

Back to who gets to go. The final voting day is November 7.

But the official results will not be declared until November 27. The last day for the return of the writ, which is subject to any electorate recounts, will be December 3.

Unless a clear result is obvious at next Saturday’s election (and the leader of one of the two major parties concedes), it may take some time to form a Government, particularly if Opportunity is in the mix and tries to play the established parties off against each other.

In 2023, coalition-making was a drawn-out affair.

Outgoing Prime Minister Hipkins, who had conceded an election loss, could have chosen to go to San Francisco in a caretaker capacity. He chose not to, and outgoing Trade Minister Damien O’Connor was subbed in, taking part in the full leaders’ meeting alongside all the big political guns.

The press gallery pulled their bookings and stayed home to cover the protracted coalition negotiations between Luxon, Winston Peters and David Seymour.

Just a senior business journalist from RNZ and I were present, although I was there for the CEO summit, which sported impressive speakers such as former US Trade Representative Mike Froman, former US Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, who got fired the next day … it was a mind fest.

O’Connor chaired a mini-ministerial discussion on the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP). He also engaged with the Biden-led Indo-Pacific Economic Framework talks, which Trump kicked to the kerb after winning the presidency again.

The prospect of Trump and Xi sitting down together at Apec is inevitably fuelling hopes that the world’s two most powerful economies can put their differences aside and strike a stronger trade truce.

Dr Zack Cooper, an American foreign policy specialist, has delivered a timely warning. The new buzzword surrounding the US-China relationship is “constructive strategic stability”, he says.

“If that were true, many Americans would be quite happy with that result,” he observed while delivering the Sir Howard Kippenberger lecture at Victoria University of Wellington. “The problem, of course, is that it’s not true.”

Cooper is one of the sharpest observers of US foreign policy, particularly as it involves Asia.

He has been in New Zealand this past fortnight as the 2026 Sir Howard Kippenberger visiting professor of strategic studies at Victoria.

He is a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, where he studies US strategy in Asia, including alliance dynamics and US-China competition.

His assessment goes to the heart of the uncertainty facing Asia-Pacific economies. The question is not whether Trump and Xi can produce a cordial encounter, announce a deal or give markets a temporary lift. It is whether the two powers are prepared to confront the underlying disputes that continue to shape their relationship.

Cooper’s argument is that they are not there yet.

“The US and China have actually not resolved any of the core problems that we have in our relationship,” he said, arguing that both were sidestepping the most difficult issues, including the economic relationship and cross-strait tensions involving Taiwan.

Cooper is also sceptical of the “New Yalta” analogy.

At the original Yalta Conference in Crimea in February 1945, Franklin Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin met to discuss the final stages of World War II and the post-war settlement.

Yalta subsequently became shorthand for great powers carving up the world into spheres of influence.

The Soviet Union’s expansion of control across Eastern Europe, and the failure to honour commitments on free elections, helped to cement Yalta’s darker historical reputation.

The analogy is therefore politically charged. It suggests that the destinies of countries could be settled over their heads by a handful of powerful leaders.

Yet today’s strategic environment is fundamentally different. The US and China are not negotiating a post-war settlement after defeating a common enemy.

They are managing a long-running competition between different political and economic systems, with interests that extend across trade, technology, military security and international institutions.

For countries such as New Zealand, that distinction matters. The language of a new Yalta can obscure the complexity of the choices facing smaller states.

That’s why it is important that small states like New Zealand should be represented in Shenzhen.

MDMA therapy and the Kiwi doctor helping dying strangers

New Zealand Herald October 30, 2026

The first MDMA-assisted therapy trial in New Zealand is happening inside a clinic in Auckland’s Parnell. Months on, Dr Will Evans spoke exclusively to the Weekend Herald about his peculiar job of guiding people through death.

Evans’ clinic sits inside a wooden villa surrounded by a wild, fragrant garden in Parnell.

Persian rugs and crystals decorate the therapy rooms at Mana Health and sunlight spills in through the open windows. Outside, Evans stands behind a cafe bar serving coffee and a botanical water to visitors.

The site is home to the business, Body, Breath and Mind, created by Evans and his wife, Naima Evans. It is a method they have developed from their contrasting careers that incorporates aspects of yoga, meditation, somatic awareness, and investigations into psychedelic therapy.

Inside the clinic, 15 people have been quietly receiving a dose of MDMA and sitting with Evans for up to eight hours as part of a landmark trial.

Two other participants in the study have also received the therapy in the South Island and at another Auckland site.

All the participants are facing a cancer diagnosis, and the results so far have shattered Evans’ expectations.

The study is now searching for more people with cancer to take part and for further donations to complete the trial by April next year.

At age 46, Evans is someone who has been surrounded by death for most of his medical career, but that doesn’t lighten the weight of responsibility he feels for this work.

He trained in neurology and pharmacology before being drawn into palliative care through work in the oncology ward at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in Sydney.

The hospital experience left him feeling dissatisfied that the focus of palliative care was on treating only the physical body in relation to a person’s deteriorating state, whereas he had observed many patients were often going through mental anguish that was integral to understanding their pain.

The problem niggled at him: it felt as if he was offering treatment to people but never solving the root cause of their suffering.

As Evans walks calmly through the clinic, the hallway smelling faintly of essential oils, he points out the room where he has carried out most of his lengthy discussions about death with people who have taken MDMA.

Doctors often end up being forced to ignore a person’s internal unwellness, he says, because of the pressure facing them within the health system.

Dying patients in particular were facing a flood of difficult feelings such as anger, a sense of unfairness or resentment, endless questioning and a deepening anxiety about what might come next.

“The focus was all on survival and fighting and treating the disease, and death, which was this elephant in the room, was treated as a medical failure,” he says.

“It seemed to me there was so much suffering not being addressed around this issue that it almost felt like this was my only option, there was this sense of responsibility to not continue to ignore that suffering.”

In Australia, the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) has permitted the use of MDMA for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder. But the cost of receiving this treatment is high, at about $20,000.

Evans says his patients have experienced a dramatic decrease in death anxiety and many have felt being pain-free or comfortable for the first time in years.

Naima Evans has studied different traditions of yoga therapy, somatic movement, and breathwork and has assisted people throughout the trial in learning mindfulness techniques.

“It [MDMA] kind of ripens the person and their state to bring up material that they can then process and liberate,” she says.

By learning breathwork or meditative practices, people could slow down their mind, come into their body, and rediscover the same peaceful feeling they had experienced in a session while taking MDMA.

Through working with people who were dying, Evans has a rare insight into the kind of questions and thought patterns people experience when they are facing the end of their life.

“Often, they would come to beautiful conclusions, and they weren’t complex things, they were simple, very clear,” he says.

“I always felt incredibly grateful to be sitting at the bedside of enlightenment, of people who were grappling with the fundamental question of being and not being.”

He says often people will discuss memories of pain or suffering inflicted upon them by loved ones, and through the sessions people will often seek to mend bridges with family members or to restore broken relationships.

The whole theory behind different types of psychedelic therapy such as MDMA and magic mushrooms is that these substances can increase plasticity in the brain, which could make the brain more open to change and developing new neural pathways.

MDMA therapy lowers a person’s fear response, Evans says, and enables them to access things they might find too painful to think about in their everyday consciousness, which could allow them to process difficult or deeply suppressed thoughts.

Early results from a study involving neuroscientists working with survivors following the October 7, 2023 attack in Israel revealed MDMA could provide some psychological protection against trauma.

During the NOVA music festival, where Hamas terrorists killed about 370 people and took dozens of hostages into Gaza, many of those attending the festival were on different forms of party drugs, such as LSD and magic mushrooms. Neuroscientists have found those people on MDMA appeared to cope better mentally with the traumatic event.

The outcomes Naima has witnessed of people in the trial is that they were able to find immense emotional relief and become more comfortable with the process of dying.

Evans says a session taking MDMA combined with therapeutic assistance allowed people to reach this feeling of complete and utter acceptance, a state of healing.

For Aaron Edgington, 51, who recently took part in the trial, the therapy helped him face head and neck cancer while being the solo parent of his 3-year-old daughter.

In handwritten notes made by Edgington following the experience, he talked about a deep sense of peacefulness that stayed with him and that he found he could return to in difficult moments following the session.

“I’ve felt, at times, like I’ve been searching for something, searching for answers ... it feels like I don’t have to necessarily search for that peace. I can actually find it within myself,” he wrote in his notes.

Edginton is looking after his young daughter in New Zealand as her mum currently lives in Vietnam, and says one of the hardest parts of the cancer diagnosis was worrying about her long-term welfare and her potential future without him.

“I suppose the initial thought is that it’s like a death sentence, so of course you’re reeling right. It’s pretty tough.

“I’m in a little bit of an uncertain space right now waiting on results. It obviously means so much to me being with my daughter, and I’d like to think I have longer, and maybe I do.

“But you don’t know, you just don’t know for sure.”

He said that when going through cancer treatment, you often feel physically strong and healthy outside of treatment windows but the diagnosis is still hanging over you all the time as this dark reality.

MDMA therapy made him feel more comfortable, aware of himself and connected to the present moment, something that allowed the painful knowledge of the diagnosis to not take up the forefront of his mind.

As a clinician, working with people facing death could be very emotionally heavy.

“I think it’s revealed to me how there is a complete blind spot in medicine, all forms of medicine where you’re dealing with death and dying, disease and suffering constantly, and there’s a lot of vicarious trauma that happens,” Evans says.

“I don’t know if it’s dealt with very well in medicine. We don’t have an inbuilt system of self-care for the carer, even not just for doctors but for family members caring for loved ones who are dying.

“There’s a need to look after yourself in the presence of that trauma ... it taught me to take extra time to make sure that your cup is full so it can overflow into other people’s lives, rather than just running on empty all the time.”

The trial so far has seen some unexpected outcomes.

Three patients the Weekend Herald spoke to in May who were involved in the MDMA trial have all seen marked improvements in their cancer after the completion of the therapy.

The significant joint pain Edginton was experiencing throughout his cycles of chemotherapy treatment reduced after receiving MDMA therapy.

In Evans’ view, some of these results may be linked to the easing of stress that some patients have experienced in the aftermath of the trial, and he wondered if this may have helped support their immune response.

However, it was too early to make any assumptions about its impact on cancer outcomes and it is an opportunity for further research.

He and Naima also say the intense reflection and processing carried out in the therapy sessions is not solely reliant on a psychedelic experience or drug.

“I guess this is one version of a self-inquiry or self-reflective process that can change your life, but there are so many, so that would be the other thing is not to get fixated on psychedelics as a substance you have to take in order to have these experiences.”

He says this is definitely not something that should be attempted alone without clinical support and the experience within recreational settings is entirely different.

Other services such as Hospice NZ also provide free palliative and end-of-life care to people which includes providing psychological and spiritual support to people who are dying and their families.

This can also mean home visits and inpatient stays with nurses.

The cost of MDMA therapy could be a prohibitive factor in its conceivable introduction into the health system because of the labour required, with an extensive number of hours needed for therapists to oversee patients.

Currently, the therapists doing the work involved with the trial are voluntary and not being paid for their time.

Evans says they are doing this out of goodwill and because they believe in the transformational effect it is having on people who are dying.

To finish the study by the desired date of April next year, Evans is hoping they will be able to raise a further $300,000 to support the work.

To take part in the trial, people have to be over the age of 18, living with a confirmed cancer diagnosis, and experiencing distress. Interested individuals and health professionals can find out about the study and make inquiries by contacting info@manahealth. co. nz or 0274907717.

Donations to support the work can be made through The Mana Foundation Trust website.

He also met several puppies, cuddling a 16-week-old cocker spaniel–French bulldog cross.

It's now just a week until election day.

Luxon was out late last night at the cricket at Eden Park for New Zealand v India.

This will be the last Weekend Herald politics column before election day.

Next Saturday, when many of you will head to the polls to cast your vote, this paper will have to abide by polling-day blackout rules, prohibiting me from writing more or less anything about the election taking place that day.

I'm trying to decide whether next week's column will be about Sidney Bechet, why Wellington should get over itself and fulsomely back Sir Peter Jackson's movie museum, or why the film La La Land actually has a happy ending.

The temptation for this week is to offer a breathtaking Cassandra-like insight into the election to come.

The truth is, despite having lived and breathed this election more or less since the votes were counted after the last one, I honestly haven't the faintest idea how it's going to go – and nor do you, nor does anyone. The election is impossible to predict. Tiny changes in likely voting, changes that would still fall within the margin of error for most polls, could have an enormous impact on who gets elected, how large parties are and, most importantly, who can form a Government.

In fact, the result of this election is so unclear that one of the most common things said about it – that the result will be "tight" – could be wrong as well.

"It's an orange colour and the actual nib of it is so big... The circles aren't that big," Lynn said.

Tam of the Mongrel Mob is now campaign history.

Mowbray's presence has been omnipresent as he seeks to engineer an overhang on the right of politics by trying to persuade people to give their party vote to Act or New Zealand First instead of National.

Horror polls, scare tactics and sleepwalking voters emerge this Halloween – Editorial

New Zealand Herald October 30, 2026

Christopher Luxon and the National Party must have been spooked by the RNZ-Reid Research poll this week. Photo / Annaleise Shortland

Was a trick played on the National Party this week? A rogue poll for Halloween perhaps?

Whatever the reality, the numbers from the latest RNZ-Reid Research poll this week would have sent a shiver up the spines of Christopher Luxon and the party faithful.

The poll showed National on 24.8%, which was below even its horror 25.6% result in 2020.

The poll recorded Labour on 30.6%, while the Green Party was on 14.5%, the Act Party 10.1%, New Zealand First on 9.9%, Opportunity Party on 7.2% and Te Pāti Māori on 1.9%.

Somewhat confusingly, the poll result was notably different to the 1News-Verian poll released on Tuesday. That poll had National on 29% and Labour on 27%, with Opportunity on 6%.

The two polls were conducted over almost the same period last week.

So, which one was more accurate? Now that we are only a week out from election day, we may only find out next Saturday night.

Luxon, however, was clearly spooked by the RNZ-Reid Research poll and he responded with some political scare tactics.

“If RNZ’s poll today becomes reality, there will be dire consequences for Kiwis,” he said.

“It would mean Labour winning, in coalition with the Greens with Chlöe Swarbrick as Finance Minister. Higher taxes for hard-working people. Prices rising and mortgages skyrocketing. There is only one way to stop that from happening: get out now and party-vote National.”

Luxon also warned, while campaigning in Auckland, voters against “sleepwalking into this election”.

He denied panic was setting in after the horror poll result but rather wanted to “highlight to New Zealanders what’s at risk”.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said Luxon had only “blame, excuses and fear” to offer New Zealand.

“Christopher Luxon just looks more and more diminished and more and more desperate by the day.

“My message to New Zealanders is: don’t go and vote based on fear, vote based on hope, vote based on the sort of future that you want for New Zealand.”

Swarbrick, and her desire to hold the purse strings and push for radical tax reform, has been a common attack line from the right-leaning parties.

But it has also followed the Labour Party around like a ghost.

Hipkins has repeatedly insisted a Labour-led Government would have Labour’s finance spokeswoman Barbara Edmonds as Finance Minister and the only tax they would introduce is their capital gains tax.

If the Greens receive 15% of the vote and have a significant influence in the direction for the next government, then the negotiations could prove to be a nightmare for Hipkins.

With a week to go this campaign is feeling tired, and the electorate is showing signs of fatigue. Several Herald readers have written letters to the editor with a common theme, are we there yet?

However, depending on your political persuasion, it may be that Halloween comes a week later this year.

Napier CBD shops respond to plans for major shopping centre with 30-plus stores: ‘Would kill us’

New Zealand Herald October 30, 2026

Napier CBD (left) could lose shoppers to the huge retail development (right) off Prebensen Drive. Photo / NZME

Napier CBD shop owners have concerns after plans were revealed for a huge shopping centre on the fringe of the city that will boast 30 to 40 shops.

Some shop owners in the city centre say the new development could “kill us” unless the CBD improves its parking and retains a clear point of difference.

Mana Ahuriri and partners TW Property revealed last week a plan to develop a large chunk of land off Prebensen Drive into a sprawling retail destination.

It will be built on the other side of Prebensen Drive from major retailers Kmart, Mitre 10, Chemist Warehouse, and JB Hi-Fi.

TW Property has since confirmed that, when completed, it will boast 30 to 40 shops across about 70,000sq m of retail space, complemented by 2000 free car parks.

It will take years to deliver across three stages, with the first stage anticipated for completion in 2028.

TW Property confirmed it would not be a mall as such because most of the shops won’t be interconnected.

The land is zoned “large format retail” meaning minimum shop sizes of 500sq m.

As such, the centre will feature mainly national brands and large-scale stores, rather than smaller shops or boutique brands.

The zoning also allows for cafes and fast-food restaurants, which are part of the plans.

Engagement with prospective tenants is underway, although it is too early to say which retailers and fast-food joints will go in.

TW Property commercial director Terry May said he was of the view the project wouldn’t take stores out of Emerson St, in central Napier, given the restrictions for large retail.

It plans to lodge its first resource consent applications for the project, through Napier City Council, in the coming weeks.

Maree Cooper, owner of Emerson St shop Handmade in the Bay, said she did not believe Napier had the population to cater for both shopping precincts.

She said the key to survival for Napier CBD shops would be having a point of difference, such as plenty of boutique shops.

She said the CBD was more of an experience, complemented by its art deco buildings.

“It has to be completely different.”

She said if the CBD and the new shopping precinct were directly competing, then “it would kill us”.

She said offering free parking in the CBD after 3pm on weekdays would help shops. It is currently free after 6pm on weekdays.

That would mean parents can pop into town after school pick-up, and that initiative had helped shops in parts of Tauranga city centre, where she used to work, she claimed.

Other shop owners Hawke’s Bay Today spoke to supported the parking idea.

Vinci’s Pizza owner Vincent Michaelsen said he did not like big-box shopping centres, as they felt rather heartless, but could see the appeal and convenience.

“You can’t deny that appears to be what the population wants.

“So, in that sense, it’s good that Napier is getting a development,” he said.

“I think the bigger concern will be the medium-box-sized stores.

“Businesses, I think, that could be in the CBD should be in the CBD.

“For example, it will be bad news for the CBD if, you know, Postie Plus, Kathmandu, Macpac, the likes of those sorts of stores, move on.”

He said Vinci’s Pizza offered its customers “a genuine, authentic sense of hospitality and vibrancy”, which was not available at a big-box shopping centre.

He said there would always be a market for that.

“But, naturally, when you take away the shopping [options] you definitely dwindle down the market of the CBD.”

Until recently, Michaelsen was the chairman of Napier City Business Inc, and said the council could have done better at notifying businesses of plans for the city’s retail offering.

Part of the land to be developed, 58 Severn St, was previously zoned main industrial and has been rezoned “large format retail” in Napier City Council’s new District Plan.

Giftware and Engravers owner Andrew Glenny said parking remained a big issue for the city centre, particularly given the new development would have plenty of free parking.

In his view, just having a point of difference was not enough to keep people coming into the CBD to shop.

“Really, it’s more parking spaces,” he said.

“It doesn’t have to be free parking, just more parking.

“It’s accessibility. There is not enough around here.

“For me, that is the main thing. When you look out there with Kmart and Mitre 10, they have a huge amount of car parks.”

If there was an exodus of major stores from the CBD moving to the new precinct, then “I think that would seriously kill this area”.

Adore Collection, on Emerson St, co-owner Steve Holyer said shopping in Napier CBD was an experience, and a different offering than a large-scale shopping centre.

He said he told his staff ahead of tourists or visitors arriving: “We are not a souvenir shop, we are part of their holiday, so deliver”.

He said the CBD needed to be clear on what it was offering customers and visitors, as visiting shops was just one reason people came into the city centre.

“I think it is a good opportunity for the CBD in terms of what our role is in the community going forward.”

He said Hamilton, for example, had the likes of The Base shopping centre, the centre city, and Chartwell shopping centre.

He said, in his view, they were all competing with each other with similar offerings, and needed more differentiation.

He said he would like to see more collaboration between the council and shop owners to form a clear vision for the CBD, and to keep shop owners better informed.

Napier Mayor Richard McGrath said the CBD had mixed parking options, with a focus on people coming and going.

“New Zealand is in a cost of living crisis, but if people wanted to see their CBDs thrive, they need to change their shopping habits and stop buying online,” McGrath said.

He said the council had received nothing official from developers and would work within the rules set out in the District Plan and the Resource Management Act (RMA).

Napier City Business general manager Pip Thompson said she believed there were enough parks in the CBD.

“People just have to park a little bit further away and walk to where they need to get to.”

She said that rather than focus on parking, Napier’s CBD needed to adapt to changing shopping habits and work together to attract people.

“I see it as a positive for Hawke’s Bay, Napier and the CBD. It’s a really good chance for us to look at what’s going to make us look a little different.”

She said the CBD had advantages the new shopping centre couldn’t offer, including its beautiful Art Deco buildings and seaside location, where people could enjoy food by the water.

School, church and homestead with historical links for sale in Central Hawke’s Bay

New Zealand Herald October 30, 2026

Wallingford School, in rural Central Hawke's Bay, has served as a family home and is now being sold by Property Brokers. Photo / Property Brokers

For 124 years, the Wallingford School was at the heart of its small rural community in Central Hawke’s Bay.

Established in January 1881, the school educated generations of children, many from families living and working on surrounding farms and stations, including historic Wallingford Station.

The school is now for sale, and Property Brokers listing agent Matt Oliver said it was one of the more unusual properties they had brought to market.

“After educating generations of local families, it’s now looking for someone with the imagination and vision to give it a new purpose.

“There’s plenty of work to be done, but equally plenty of potential, and it’ll be interesting to see what ideas buyers come forward with.”

The grounds are full of reminders of its old school days, including the tennis court, school swimming pool (as-is condition) and lawns, now paddocks.

The school was a gathering place, social hub and important part of everyday country life.

Changing times and declining rural populations eventually took their toll.

By the end of 2004, just six pupils remained, and the school officially closed its doors on April 15, 2005.

Since then, the 1.22ha site in two titles and former school buildings have served as a family home.

Some buildings need a little love and attention, and the property is being sold as is, where is.

A landmark in the Wanstead community is also being sold as is, where is.

The Wanstead Presbyterian Church, at 1747 Porangahau Rd, has been at the heart of countless celebrations and gatherings.

Rich in history and character, the building sits on an 879sq m section, just a 15-minute drive from Waipukurau.

Property Brokers residential sales consultant Molly Baldwin said the property has received a huge amount of interest.

“The church hasn’t been used as such for number of years, however, it is still looking in fabulous original condition thanks to the local community and neighbours who look after the grounds.

“The property is surplus to requirements so this opportunity allows locals who hold a special connection, church members or just those interested in a unique and special opportunity, to purchase this beautiful church.”

The church is in original condition with an about 60sq m footprint.

The building has double-door entry, stained glass windows and an impressive timber ceiling, and inside is set out as one large open space.

The property will be sold without any furniture, with no water, bathroom, bedrooms or septic connections and is a blank space to create, restore or transform.

The power has been disconnected, and the boundary is not fenced.

Further northwest a homestead at 45 Mill St, Ongaonga is for sale.

The story begins with two families, a sailing ship and a journey halfway around the world in 1877.

What followed was a remarkable chapter in the early history of Ongaonga.

Oliver said after admiring the homestead for many years, it’s a privilege to bring it to market.

“With only two families having owned the property since the late 1800s, it’s a remarkable piece of Ongaonga’s history.”

He said it could become a grand family home, boutique accommodation or something entirely different.

“I’m really looking forward to seeing what the next chapter holds for this very special property.”

The two-storey residence was built by George Coles, whose pioneering family established the famous Coles Brothers building and joinery business responsible for constructing much of early Ongaonga.

George was 8 years old when he arrived in New Zealand from Droxford, England in 1877 aboard the Columbus.

Travelling on the same ship was the Cantle family, also answering the call from Ongaonga founder Henry Bridge for skilled carpenters, with 5-year-old Adeline, whom George would marry in 1900.

Together, they made the property their family home.

After George’s death in 1941, Adeline lived there until she died in 1964.

Their son Maurice and his wife Vera also called the property home during the 1950s, before it eventually passed into the hands of the Simpson family.

Doug Simpson had worked in the Coles Brothers factory, and the property has remained in the Simpson family ever since.

Michaela Gower joined Hawke’s Bay Today in 2023 and is based out of the Hastings newsroom. She covers Dannevirke and Hawke’s Bay news and loves sharing stories about farming and rural communities.

Tauranga deputy mayor wrongly sworn in as JP, has applied through normal process

New Zealand Herald October 30, 2026

Tauranga City Council Deputy Mayor and Mount Maunganui ward councillor Jen Scoular. Photo / Kelly O'Hara

Tauranga’s deputy mayor was unlawfully sworn in as a Justice of the Peace last year and is reapplying for an appointment.

Jen Scoular, also the Mount Maunganui Ward councillor, was asked soon after her appointment to be sworn in as a Justice of the Peace (JP) for when she deputised for Mayor Mahé Drysdale’s in events such as citizenship ceremonies.

She and Drysdale were sworn in as JPs in the Tauranga District Court on January 20, 2025.

But inquiries from a concerned local JP revealed that, unlike a mayor, a deputy mayor could not automatically become a JP by virtue of office.

The Ministry of Justice confirmed Scoular was not legally entitled to be sworn in, and the Bay of Plenty Justices of the Peace Association and Tauranga City Council acknowledged the swearing-in ceremony should not have gone ahead for her.

Scoular said she was advised she had to undertake a JP swearing-in process within months of becoming deputy mayor.

“My understanding at the time was that this was connected to my role in deputising for the mayor, including citizenship ceremonies.

“I relied on that advice in good faith ... I have not exercised Justice of the Peace functions.”

She said her engagement with the JP association sparked her interest in becoming a JP in her personal capacity.

“I am therefore working through the usual appointment process, which I see as another way I could contribute to and serve the Tauranga community.”

The concerned JP, whom the Bay of Plenty Times agreed not to name, said he contacted the Bay of Plenty Justices of the Peace Association in October when he learned of Scoular’s swearing-in.

His inquiries revealed the ceremony was “not legally valid”. A mayor can automatically become a JP when they are elected and sworn in, but deputy mayors must follow general appointment and approval processes.

The JP said he asked the association to explain how the error happened and how it would be remedied.

Bay of Plenty Justices of the Peace Association president Glenn Williams’ response, seen by the Bay of Plenty Times, said the national Royal Federation of NZ Justices’ Associations found Scoular should not have been sworn in.

Williams told the concerned JP Scoular had since started the formal appointment process.

The JP said he was “dissatisfied” with Williams’ response and escalated the matter to the national body, and also contacted the Secretary for Justice.

“This was not a minor mistake or a generally held belief that a deputy mayor has automatic entitlement to become a JP. Ignorance of the law is not an excuse,” he said.

He contacted the association and the Ministry of Justice again 11 months later to see if Scoular had since been legally sworn in.

“I felt compelled to raise the matter publicly so it doesn’t happen again, and I feel there needs to be some accountability and transparency.”

Williams told the Bay of Plenty Times the association could not establish how the swearing-in request reached it.

“After consulting the Royal Federation, we concluded the swearing-in should not have gone ahead. Ms Scoular confirmed she had not undertaken JP functions and would not do so.

“An apology was made to the judge who conducted the swearing-in ceremony, and it was accepted.”

He confirmed Scoular has applied to be a JP “through the normal process”.

Williams said Scoular’s nomination had been processed, and the approval decision lies with the Associate Minister of Justice.

He said the association and the national body had taken steps to ensure the mistake was not repeated.

He acknowledged the error and thanked the concerned JP for raising it.

Royal Federation national manager Rae McPhee said it was not directly involved in Scoular’s swearing-in as JP.

McPhee said if Scoular’s nomination was approved, she would need to undergo induction training and be sworn in again.

The matter had been referred to the federation’s in-house ministerial adviser to consider whether changes could prevent a recurrence.

Wayne Newall, the Ministry of Justice’s appointments and specialist functions manager, said the ministry became aware of the issue last month.

“This appears to have been an isolated incident.”

Newall said Scoular’s application was expected to be considered by the associate minister after the election.

A council spokesperson said staff sought advice from the local JP association in 2024 about arrangements for the newly elected mayor and deputy mayor.

Based on that advice, Drysdale and Scoular attended swearing-in ceremonies. The council later discovered the advice was incorrect.

“The deputy mayor attended the ceremony in good faith based on information provided to her. She did not initiate the process.”

“[The] council is not aware of any other former Tauranga deputy mayors being appointed or sworn in as JPs by virtue of holding elected office.”

Drysdale said the matter was referred to the appropriate parties once the council learned of the error.

He said Scoular had not “exercised Justice of the Peace functions” since her wrongful swearing in.

Sandra Conchie is a senior journalist at the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post and has been a journalist for more than 26 years. She mainly covers police, court and other justice stories, as well as general news. She has been a Canon Media Awards regional/community reporter of the year.

The Holiday Grump: Enni Amanda’s book recommended on NBC’s TODAY

New Zealand Herald October 30, 2026

Hamilton author Enni Amanda has since signed eight-book deals with Finland’s Gummerus and Britain’s Atlantic Books. Photo / Tom Eley

Ignoring suspicious emails remains sound advice. Though for Hamilton author Enni Amanda, one such email contained a publishing breakthrough.

NBC’s Today wanted a copy of her self-published novel, The Holiday Grump.

“It sounded like spam.”

She showed her business partner the email. Neither was convinced it was authentic.

“It sounded too good to be true,” Amanda said.

Then her husband suggested looking at the sender’s domain.

“It checked out,” Amanda said.

She sent in a copy and on Christmas Eve morning, she woke to find her book was recommended on American television.

First came a sales spike.

Then came a newspaper feature in her native country, Finland, interest from publishers and a literary agency offering to organise an auction.

Amanda has since signed eight-book deals with Finland’s Gummerus and Britain’s Atlantic Books, alongside further international rights agreements.

After independently publishing 10 books, she recently celebrated her first launch at Rototuna Library.

But in an interview, the conversation moves easily from international publishing to the merits of a man who wears elbow patches.

Amanda’s romantic lead is a grumpy bookshop owner. She wanted someone well-read, a departure from the firefighters and action heroes who often get the girl.

Elbow patches, she said, deserve more appreciation.

The Christmas romantic comedy takes place in a fictional Maine town, with Finnish culture woven through it.

Amanda developed the setting with an author friend in Britain, then invited other writers to contribute stories.

They mapped the town before they began writing. Amanda said, closing her eyes, she could imagine the town and walking down its streets.

Then the characters moved in and made themselves comfortable.

“They’re like people you can hear talking in your head. Sometimes they don’t shut up,” Amanda said.

To her, that opportunity to step into somebody else’s life is part of writing’s appeal.

“I really enjoy living someone else’s life vicariously.”

She wrote her first book at 11 and wanted to become an author.

For a while, she added professor of literature to the ambition, thinking it sounded more substantial in her academic family.

Instead, her working life took her through graphic design, film school, acting and screenwriting.

She moved from Finland to New Zealand in early 2006 and later studied at Auckland’s South Seas Film and Television School.

Amanda fondly recalled her time at the school, including co-founder Gerben Cath and his familiar opening line “Believe you me”.

While she loved writing and directing, getting productions off the ground was difficult. Plenty of scripts went into a drawer.

In 2018, pregnant with her second child, she returned to novel-writing, treating the approaching birth as a deadline.

Then the baby arrived, the baby grew, and Amanda kept writing.

Hamilton entered the story unexpectedly.

After about a decade in Auckland, where she worked as a graphic designer, the prospect of commuting from West Auckland to the North Shore for work prompted a search for a life elsewhere.

Hamilton was not initially on the list, but a job brought her here. The city gradually grew on her.

She liked the river. The lifestyle suited her. The region eventually became material for a series, Hideaway Harbor, now being prepared for release through a publisher.

International deals have brought contracts, deadlines, and decisions she no longer makes alone.

Letting go of cover design for her own books is particularly difficult, Amanda said.

But she now illustrates covers for other authors through her design business.

Looking ahead, there are more manuscripts to deliver, including a Holiday Grump sequel and a Minnesota series drawing on Finnish cultural connections.

Amanda wanted to retain a Finnish flavour while appealing to American readers.

“They [Americans] do not read anything that’s not set on US soil.”

Between commitments, she also wrote a murder-mystery romantic comedy set in the Pacific.

She thought she might publish it independently, but her agent had other ideas.

For now, Amanda is happy to return to writing after her launches.

The Auckland event was on Sunday morning, October 18, which suited her. Nobody was too tired, and the light was good.

The film-maker in her still notices.

Having a publishing representative in person mattered, too. From New Zealand, so many professional relationships exist mostly through email.

But anyone hoping she can teach others how to reproduce her breakthrough may be disappointed.

“No, I’m not gonna go online and start selling a course.”

Tom Eley is a multimedia journalist at the Waikato Herald. Before he joined the Hamilton-based team, he worked for the Weekend Sun and Sunlive. He previously worked as a journalist at Black Press Media in Canada and won a fellowship with the Vancouver Sun.

Inside the crumbling marriage of a ‘love rat’ pilot accused of murder

Sydney Morning Herald October 31, 2026

In the cold night air outside his home, Robert Crawford looks up from the bottom of a retaining wall, the glow of a police officer’s torch illuminating his face.

His wife, Frances, lies lifeless in her floral pyjamas on the grass. Her hand rests on her chest, and her right ugg boot is close to her leg. Blood runs from her nose across her face.

An orange ride-on mower is next to her, overturned on its left side, its wheel turned hard to the right and stuck in reverse.

Footage from responding officers, filmed in the early hours of July 30, 2024 and played to a Supreme Court jury this week, shows the former Royal Australian Air Force pilot explaining the lead-up to his wife’s death.

He has pleaded not guilty to murder. His defence team says Frances died in a tragic accident.

Prosecutors say the 49-year-old staged the scene to look like she was killed when the mower she was riding rolled over the wall.

The RAAF pilot was a “love rat”, the prosecution says, whose wife discovered his double life. In admissions to the court, Crawford had a string of extramarital affairs with at least 10 women over a decade, including three air force colleagues.

He killed Frances, either through strangulation or with blunt force, so he would not lose millions of dollars in a divorce, the prosecution says.

Taking into account settlement finances and Frances’ life insurance policy, her untimely death would become very profitable for Crawford, at about $5.4 million, the jury heard.

“Robert Crawford loves money,” Crown prosecutor Chris Cook told the court earlier in the week, “… loved it so much that he killed for it.”

The footage shows Crawford climbing back up the retaining wall in his pyjama shorts and a jumper, on what paramedics would later tell his trial was an “incredibly cold night” in the Upper Lockyer, on the family’s sprawling 40-hectare property, estimated to be worth up to $2.6 million.

Crawford told a Triple Zero operator in a 3.37am call that he believed his wife was moving the mower because she was worried about sprinklers coming on.

By 4.27am, Crawford is at the kitchen table, a grey blanket draped over his shoulders. He starts to cry.

Sergeant Glen Thomas asks him: “What happened here tonight?”

Crawford is softly spoken, often inaudible in the footage, as he talks about how he discovered his wife. A paramedic prepares him a cup of tea as he rocks forward, his forehead almost touching the table.

He tells the officer he went to bed about 11.30pm after studying. He says he believed Frances was watching a Korean show on Netflix.

When he woke up and discovered his wife wasn’t in bed, he checked the house, calling “where are you”, he says.

“I checked the rooms, the guest rooms and stuff, couldn’t see anything there, couldn’t see anything out the front, couldn’t see anything,” he says.

He talks about taking the mower out to fix the battery, and Frances asking him to move it because their sprinklers were due to come on overnight. Text messages on the pair’s phones discussing the mower have been tendered to the court.

Crawford explains he went outside, aided by the torch on his phone, and saw the mower had fallen over the retaining wall.

“All I could see was her legs,” he sobs, gesturing with his hands.

He says he managed to pull his wife out from under it.

In the Triple Zero call, Crawford tells the operator “she is so cold”. A pump, pump, pump noise can be heard in the background as he attempts to resuscitate her.

Just a year before her alleged murder, Frances Crawford stood in her kitchen, a tissue in her hand, surrounded by concerned police.

Her husband lingered outside, dressed in a grey bath robe, his RAAF flight suit peeking out from underneath.

Frances was measured and articulate as she told officers what had happened early on July 20, 2023.

Though still married, the Crawfords had separated, and she had changed the locks. But her husband broke in that morning, pulling louvres off their patio window.

Frances became emotional as she told officers how her husband had cheated on her.

“I have forgiven and forgiven and forgiven, I cannot keep going,” she says in the body-worn footage shown to the jury.

“For me,” her voice breaks. “I can’t live with that any more. I don’t see that his personality is going to change, and I’ve spent 25 years trying to make peace, trying to make it work.”

The footage is a glimpse inside a disintegrating marriage, marred by Crawford’s extramarital affairs.

The recording is also some of the last words police have of Frances explaining her husband’s actions.

Dressed in a suit, Crawford this week sat within arm’s length of his wife’s family and friends, separated only by glass surrounding the courtroom dock.

Each day the pilot arrived flanked by lawyers, and left surrounded by cameras and journalists as he made his way to a waiting Mercedes-Benz.

And as one woman after another testified about his infidelity, he maintained his composure.

He’d messaged a RAAF colleague, Sarah Woodsell, with whom he had had an intimate relationship, about how he would “still shoot for reconciliation” and not divorce his wife because there was “more sport to be had. Just kidding. I hope this calms down soon”, the court heard.

In another message, he said: “It’s like a sport. It’ll be fun? Haha.”

When the Crawfords reconciled in the months before Frances’ death, he agreed to a set of boundaries. These included Crawford avoiding interactions with females, telling his wife his whereabouts, attending church with her, and not lying.

The jury was shown a scoresheet Frances had been keeping on her husband the week before her death. She would tick off daily activities, which included the days they had sex, as well as prayer, meditation and sharing feelings.

Around this time, their children expressed concern for their mother. Youngest son, Jake, who is now also in the RAAF, told the court: “I was distressed for her, scared for her safety. None of us kids wanted her in an environment with my dad.”

Frances also told loved ones she lived in fear, the court was told.

The weekend before her death, the pair travelled to Kingscliff, staying at the luxury Peppers Resort and Spa. Frances had rated her husband a “7” on the Saturday, when they had argued, and an “8” when they returned home.

Pages upon pages of messages displayed to the jury showed Crawford discussing his feelings with other women.

In some exchanges with Woodsell, the pair openly discussed Frances, including what they would do if Frances ended up contacting Woodsell. In one, Woodsell referred to Frances as a narcissist, and sent Crawford information about the condition.

Frances had been suspicious about her husband having affairs, and talked with friends and family about it. But when she discovered flights for two people had been booked to Queenstown in New Zealand, she suspected one of the tickets was for Woodsell.

“He did not let on that it was not me. He let her believe it was me,” Woodsell told the court.

In reality, Crawford had booked a flight for his new lover – another colleague, Antonia Guterres.

He had begun a relationship with the younger woman, who eventually fell under Crawford’s direct chain of command in mid-2023, about the time he was separating from Frances.

In a message to Woodsell, Crawford wrote: “I didn’t tell her about Toni [Guterres] because you know what she’d do … she’d start abusing Toni and calling work … She’s so psycho. But anyways.”

Woodsell told the court Crawford had gushed that he was “basically in love” with Guterres, and they had discussed having children. He also spoke of how he could reverse a vasectomy.

Guterres herself took to the stand, becoming emotional as she told the jury how her life became indelibly entwined with Crawford’s, while she battled other work issues within the RAAF.

Crawford had repeatedly offered her help, encouraging words, and asked her to catch up, including for coffee and to paint. At one point, Crawford had asked her if she wanted to move with him to Papua New Guinea, the court heard.

Over his time with Guterres, he told her he felt “trapped” at home, “broken and really struggling”. He told Guterres his wife was bipolar, and “off her meds”.

While Guterres’ and Crawford’s affair was brief, Crawford was still tearfully expressing feelings for her while at a work event on June 25, 2024.

Almost a month later, he sent a message to Guterres, saying: “Ant can you promise me something … Can you try to do one fun thing or something that you enjoy each day.”

Days later, his wife was dead.

Crawford’s relationship with Guterres came after he had a two-year relationship with another pilot, Emily Renshaw, which began in 2020, the court was told.

Renshaw said Crawford did not want to end his marriage out of fear from being exiled from the church, and a divorce would delay his retirement plans.

Two days before her death, on the weekend away at Kingscliff, Frances confronted her husband, saying “all the girls [were] to stroke your ego”, and calling him a “f---ing cheat” and “a miserable excuse for a human being”.

According to testimony this week, Crawford told paramedics of the great weekend he and Frances had just spent at Kingscliff in the minutes after they had found her dead.

Graphic images of her lying on the grass were shown to the jury.

One paramedic told the court the accused talked to his unresponsive wife in an endearing way, and about moving the mower. “Why did you shift it? I would’ve moved it for you,” he could be heard saying.

At one point, he tried to interlace his fingers with hers, the court heard.

Paramedics said the coldness of her body made it obvious she could not be revived. One said he touched the mower to see if it was still warm, but it was also cold.

Frances Crawford was declared dead at 4.05am.

The jury is expected to hear from medical experts next week, as the trial before Justice Lincoln Crowley continues.

Theatre is Michael Paynter’s ‘idea of hell’ but he’s making an exception for John Farnham

Sydney Morning Herald October 31, 2026

The acclaimed performer has a lot in common with the legendary Australian singer he plays in Whispering Jack. And it’s not just that they’ve both been Jesus.

One voice was better than the rest at this year’s AFL grand final, and it wasn’t Kylie Minogue’s. No shade on Kylie but the man who sang the national anthem a cappella had the best pipes on field.

That’s not a controversial statement: there’s a rocking power to Michael Paynter’s voice and those who’ve heard it tend to become fans. Anyone, for instance, who saw him in the 2024/25 stage production of Jesus Christ Superstar, for which he received rave reviews and industry awards in the titular role of Jesus. Those, too, who know him as a much-loved part of the Australian music scene, including as a member of the Jimmy Barnes and Icehouse touring bands.

And those who went to his The Great Australian Songbook concerts, which began in February as seven gigs and ended up as 30 concerts running right through to September, the venue sizes doubling as they went along. Barring the few songs for which a special guest joins him each night, it’s Paynter solo on stage, with a guitar and a piano, singing household hits such as Flame Trees, You’re the Voice, Even When I’m Sleeping and We Are Australian. So popular has it been that a return Songbook tour was recently announced for 2027, to include more than a dozen regional centres as well as every capital city.

Singer, guitarist, pianist – Paynter does the lot, along with being an accomplished songwriter and music producer. But for most at the Melbourne Cricket Ground that last Saturday in September, or watching it on TV, his was not a familiar name. Not like Kylie or even G Flip, her support act.

That’s changing fast, however, and will likely shift again when Paynter takes on the role of The Voice himself, John Farnham, in Whispering Jack: The John Farnham Musical. The Sydney Theatre Company will premiere the show on November 15 ahead of a likely national tour with commercial producer Michael Cassel Group and Gaynor Wheatley, the widow of Farnham’s late manager and best friend, Glenn Wheatley.

There’s a certain synchronicity to Paynter playing Farnham. Paynter was born in 1986, the year Whispering Jack came out. They’ve both been Jesus in Superstar (Farnham in 1992) and have both done versions of the great Australian songbook (Farnham released a Songbook album in 2005). It’s more than that, though. They both know what it’s like to be the next big thing – then not. And just as Farnham’s second wave came at the age of 37, so Paynter, at 40, appears to be moving from a career supporting others into one in which it’s finally him owning centre stage.

I’m meeting Michael Paynter at his favourite cafe in Oakleigh, in Melbourne’s south-east. He walks in punctually and I’m struck by three things I’d noticed at his Sydney Songbook concert back in April. The first: he’s ripped. Paynter is a gym junkie and it’s there in his physique, which he shows off on stage via tight black T-shirts and fitted pants that finish slightly above a set of clean white sneakers, typically worn with invisible socks. Second, he’s a friendly bloke, with more than a dash of the loveable dagginess Farnham was renowned for. Third, he’s a man of God, with a silver cross hanging on a chain around his neck. He wears it offstage and on.

The cross makes sense when Paynter tells me he’s the son of pastors, who left their jobs as an art teacher (mum) and bank manager (dad) to set up a non-denominational church on Victoria’s Mornington Peninsula. That was in 1986; he was christened at their first service. Music was a regular part of life for the family, which included daughter Bethany, who also works for the church. “Dad has a great voice and mum’s a great piano player,” Paynter says. He started piano lessons at the age of five and by 12 had also picked up the guitar, mainly to impress girls.

It was a happy upbringing, which he’s felt embarrassed about in the past. Not very rock ‘n’ roll, and he very much wanted to be rock ‘n’ roll. “I created a bunch of demons in my closet when I signed to a record label but they were of my own making, because I had a very normal, non-traumatic upbringing.”

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Paynter orders a cold brew, no milk, which I assume is to do with lactose being bad for the voice, which I’ve heard from singers before. “No,” he says with a laugh. “Where you eat and where you breathe are two different holes, so unless you’re lactose-intolerant and it causes problems … ” Most of the ritualistic things singers do “are up here”, he says, tapping his head. “It’s fine, I have them as well.” It’s simply that he really loves coffee. “It’s like whisky – if you have a good whisky don’t put it with coke or ice, just have a whisky.”

When Paynter finished school he enrolled in a double law/business degree at Victoria University. He’d won a statewide school music competition and was performing on the side, and when Mushroom Records founder Michael Gudinski asked him to play guitar for his teen daughter, who went by the stage name of Kate Alexa, he quit the degree to focus on music.

Gudinski wasn’t the only bigwig to notice Paynter’s talent. So too did then Sony boss Denis Handlin, who put him on the kind of development deal labels offered budding singer-songwriters back then. “They don’t exist any more but it was kind of like, here’s $5000, come back in five months with five songs, and if they’re good, we’ll sign you and turn them into something.” He came back; they signed him.

Paynter spent a decade with Sony, much of it living in Britain and the US, where he joined the songwriting teams for big names including the Black Eyed Peas and James Blunt, and toured with the likes of Seal and Miley Cyrus. “It didn’t make me arrogant – well actually that’s debatable – but it gave me an inner confidence to believe in what I do.” In 2010 he wrote the single Love the Fall, recording it with The Veronicas, who took it to number 19 on the ARIA charts. “Looking back [its success] was because it featured The Veronicas, I’m very aware of that,” he says. “But it was a great song and it opened a lot of doors for me.”

At a certain point the music industry changed, however, and in 2011 Paynter and Sony parted ways. “To invest in a singer or a band and hang in there for the long haul was gone,” he says. “It was the quick buck, TV every night, 10 million eyeballs. It makes complete sense. So they moved to that model and let a lot of singers and bands go.”

In his own version of “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em”, in 2013 Paynter auditioned for the second Australian season of The Voice, where he got as far as the top four before bombing out. “I sang horribly,” he says of his final performance. “TV can be nerve-wracking at the best of times. There was a lot riding on it for me and I wasn’t my best self.”

He was by now living back in Melbourne, in his late 20s, and keen to start a family with his wife, Keinzley, who he’s known since kindergarten. “That was the end of me wanting to be an artist,” he says. “I just didn’t want to do it any more. I lost the drive to be famous.”

Instead, he started a business with his friend Michael De Lorenzis to write, mix and record songs for other artists. MSquared ran for 15 years, snaring two ARIAs and three Golden Guitars, before the pair decided to close it last year. In tandem Paynter continued working as a session player – at weddings and pubs, for bands such as Bachelor Girl and Killing Heidi, and for a while, was tour manager for The Veronicas. In 2011 he started playing with Icehouse, then from 2020, with Jimmy Barnes’ band.

He and Keinzley had three young daughters and between family life, producing and gig work, he was fully occupied. The last thing he was thinking about was a musical.

Then, in 2024, Mahalia Barnes was cast as Mary in a new production of Jesus Christ Superstar. They couldn’t find their Jesus. She knew Paynter through her dad, Jimmy. She knew he dug Jesus. She suggested him and he got the part. “I got two standing ovations a night, in the middle of the show,” says Paynter with incredulity.

As Superstar was coming to an end, word started getting around that a Farnham musical was in the works. There’s always a tension in musicals: do you veer towards an actor who can sing or a singer who can act? With a character like Farnham it was a no-brainer: any musical would be stillborn if the lead didn’t have a knockout voice.

People started suggesting Paynter, but he initially wasn’t keen. “There’s a lot about theatre I don’t like,” he says bluntly. “You’re doing the same thing, in the same place, at the same time, with the same people, in the same clothes, the same way, for a year. That’s my idea of hell.” The world he was used to was much more free-flowing. “Every stage is new, you’re on a plane every second day. Writing songs you’re in a new studio, with a new person, every time. There’s a lot of movement and that keeps me interested.”

It didn’t help that he’d been working at MSquared while doing Jesus Christ Superstar, which meant 9am-5pm songwriting, recording and managing other artists, then jumping in the shower, scoffing down some food, and getting to the theatre for his evening shift.

But … he loved Farnham. His voice, his output, everything about him. And with the closure of MSquared, he wouldn’t have to work during the day then perform in the evening. “His music is among my favourite ever,” he says. “He’s always been the greatest singer this country has ever produced. And he’s the sort of man … you’d be lucky to have people speak about you the way people in this industry speak about John. He’s a hard worker who doesn’t give up, keeps coming back. He’s a larrikin but one who loves his wife and kids.”

Paynter is now pumped for his theatrical return and yes, can see the similarities between his story and Farnham’s. “You get dropped from the label, you miss out on a reality TV show … My whole career has been about trying to keep the flame flickering as the seasons change.”

Life experience means he’s not counting on the musical to change the trajectory of his life. “I’m in an incredible season now, with momentum and acclaim and public attention, which is lovely, but 12 months from now that might not be the case,” he says. “It’s just cool that people are digging me, but they’ll get over it and I’ll have to change again.” We shall see.

Whispering Jack is at Sydney’s Roslyn Packer Theatre, Nov 15 - Jan 3.

Death Cab for Cutie’s Ben Gibbard made another divorce album. This time, he wanted to get it right

Sydney Morning Herald October 31, 2026

The indie rock band’s new album takes fans back to the place they first fell in love with Death Cab.

Ben Gibbard isn’t famous. At least, that’s what he tells me on a call from his home in Seattle, at the tail end of a weeks-long media circuit, during which he’s hardly had a chance to catch his breath. But even if you haven’t heard of him, there’s a good chance you know Death Cab for Cutie, the band he’s fronted for close to three decades.

When we speak, Gibbard, who turned 50 in August, has been promoting Death Cab’s much-anticipated 11th album, I Built You a Tower. Releasing a record is tough, but Gibbard isn’t complaining. The positive reception to his latest work has been, he says, a pleasant reminder that the band’s egos have not degraded their taste.

“We were quietly confident when we were making it [the album] but there’s always that moment where you’re like, ‘Oh my god, did we actually make something good or are we just completely deluding ourselves?’” he says.

Gibbard, and bass guitarist Nicholas Harmer, are the two remaining original members of Death Cab, which formed in Bellingham, Washington in 1997 and became renowned for injecting heartfelt emotion into ’00s indie rock. I Built You a Tower – recorded in just three weeks and released in early June – marked the band’s return to an indie label, ANTI Records, after 20 years with Atlantic Records.

For the past four years, the band’s back catalogue has been getting a workout – not just on the playlists of decades-long fans, but on stages at sold-out shows around the world – as Gibbard celebrated 20 years of Transatlanticism and The Postal Service’s Give Up, the sole album borne out of a side project in which he and producer Jimmy Tamborello collaborated long-distance, mailing each other demos on CD. In 2025, the band also completed a small North American tour revisiting their 2005 Grammy-nominated album Plans.

While onstage Gibbard was steeped in the nostalgia of his own music, his personal life was collapsing in the background. In 2023, Gibbard and his wife – photographer Rachel Demy, who he married in 2016 – separated; the pair’s divorce was finalised in 2024. It was during this period that I Built You a Tower came to life.

“It’s a record about the compartmentalisation of grief, how we compartmentalise grief to get through our days,” says Gibbard. “In the story of my actual life, the precipitous moment was a divorce.”

Gibbard says that, with this album, he didn’t want to write a book report about the dissolution of a marriage. “It’s not a blow-by-blow account, it’s not a tell-all – it’s an investigation of the internal,” he says.

The divorce was Gibbard’s second. In 2015, following his split from New Girl actor and musician Zooey Deschanel, Death Cab released Kintsugi, an album well-known to be about their breakup.

Compared to I Built You a Tower, Kintsugi was scathing. The album’s opening track, No Room In Frame, is thought to be about the couple’s move to Los Angeles and Deschanel’s rising television success. Gibbard doesn’t mince words in the song’s chorus, asking: “Was I in your way? When the cameras turned to face you.”

“I wouldn’t change anything about that record – it was the record I felt I needed to write at the time,” says Gibbard. “When I was younger, I’d write songs that had a lot of finger-pointing or bitterness or anger. And I’m just not interested in writing from that place any more.”

On the new album’s title track, Gibbard describes building a metaphorical tower in his mind, to keep someone locked away out of his thoughts, only for it to spectacularly fail. On Pep Talk, he describes waking up at sunrise, needing to convince himself he can survive the day ahead.

What else has the man known for writing about lost loves learnt about relationships following his second divorce? “People make mistakes. People hurt each other. But at the end of the day, this relationship was eight great years and two kind of bad ones,” he says. “And I don’t think I would change anything about it.”

I Built You a Tower has earned critical raves. Pitchfork said the album showcases Gibbard’s “best musical impulses in a decade” and suggested it “evokes the band’s golden era”, rare acclaim for any band entering their third decade.

If you ask local Death Cab fans where they first heard the band, most (the Millennials among them, at least) will give you the same answer: on The O. C. According to Gibbard, before The O. C. premiered in 2003, bands like Death Cab, Modest Mouse, The Shins and Bright Eyes weren’t being played on the radio and “certainly weren’t getting airtime on MTV”. All of them found a new audience through the teen drama.

In the series, Death Cab became a character in its own right, consistently referenced as the favourite band of main character Seth Cohen – which fan hasn’t repeated his now-iconic “Hey, do not insult Death Cab” line? – and even made a live cameo. This exposure became a way of circumventing the traditional ways of finding new listeners outside college radio stations or the indie rock scene.

“I won’t lie, it went from ‘This is an interesting novelty’ to ‘Are we being exploited by the Fox Network?’” says Gibbard. But 19 years after the series wrapped, any concerns about the band losing credibility through their affiliation with it have been put to bed.

“However we might have felt at the time, or how snarky or dismissive people wanted to be, I think it’s very clear we got the better end of that stick,” he says.

With local fans still mourning missing out on both 20th anniversary tours, which didn’t travel to Australia, there are high expectations for Death Cab’s visit to Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane in November for their first tour in seven years.

For those looking to explore the band’s back catalogue, Gibbard says their past albums can be categorised into four distinct eras.

For the past 20 years, Gibbard has kept the set list for every single show the band has done. Before visiting a new city on tour, he looks back to the last time the band was there, checking what songs were played or missed. Except for the songs fans expect to hear at every show – he’s not looking to cause a riot by skipping I Will Follow You into the Dark – Gibbard curates a new set list, with the past one in mind, to make sure he’s giving people a new Death Cab experience.

“I love that we have what seems to be a really loyal fan base and yet, we’re not famous,” he says. “We make a good living and, you know, I think we’re still doing good work.”

Death Cab for Cutie’s I Built a Tower is out now. The band performs at Sydney’s Hordern Pavilion on November 12, Melbourne’s Margaret Court Arena on November 13, and Brisbane’s Fortitude Music Hall on November 15.

Arteta can take inspiration from George Graham to expunge painful Anfield memories

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 20:00:23 GMT

Arsenal have not won at Liverpool for 13 league games but Gunners’ win in 1989 remains one of club’s greatest nights

Mikel Arteta used a Spanish word to describe what it felt like to be helpless at Anfield while playing for Everton in 2011: bajar. “It’s when a cyclist is going up and looks amazing, then in one kilometre he goes ‘boom’ and he’s struggling again,” he said in Amazon’s All or Nothing documentary. “The game was going well and then suddenly I could only see red shirts flying around. The game is passing all over me and I cannot react. I only had that feeling in my career once, and it was at Anfield.”

Given Arteta’s record at Liverpool, Sunday’s showdown with his childhood friend Andoni Iraola – five days after Arsenal were dumped out of the Carabao Cup by Fleetwood – could be expected to fill him with dread. Arteta finally tasted victory there as a player with Arsenal in September 2012, after five failed attempts in the Merseyside derby, but ended up spending the night in hospital with concussion after colliding with Jordan Henderson in an incident he has described as “the biggest fear of my life”.

Arteta was part of the Arsenal side that won at Anfield again six months later thanks to goals from the new signings Lukas Podolski and Santi Cazorla. That was the last time the club triumphed there in the Premier League. They have not won at Anfield for 13 league matches, equalling the club’s worst run at Liverpool. Arsenal’s one victory at Liverpool in the interim came in the League Cup on penalties in 2020 on Arteta’s second visit as a manager.

The Spaniard tried to prepare his players for a trip to Anfield in November 2021 by playing You’ll Never Walk Alone over the training ground speakers but that ended in a 4-0 defeat. He was criticised after last season’s loss in late August, when Dominik Szoboszlai’s late free-kick ended a sequence of three Arsenal draws at Liverpool, for a perceived failure to take off the handbrake, having started Mikel Merino as his No 10. Gary Neville went as far as to say Arsenal lacked “the mentality to go and win big matches at big away grounds”, an assertion that will have hurt Arteta but does have credence: they have not beaten Manchester City in the Premier League at the Etihad since 2015 under Arsène Wenger.

Arteta will be keen to disprove such perceptions, especially after Arsenal struggled so badly against a team 84 places below them in the pyramid in a stadium that holds fewer than 6,000 people. The strikers Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyökeres surprisingly started in tandem at Fleetwood, presumably in an attempt to lighten the load on Martin Ødegaard, although both look badly out of form. Bukayo Saka is out with a thigh injury, there are concerns over Noni Madueke’s ankle and Arsenal’s failed appeal over Max Dowman’s red card rules out the teenager for three matches.

With that in mind, Arteta’s best chance of beating Liverpool is probably by taking the cautious approach that has served him so well and was the cornerstone of last season’s Premier League title triumph. He can take inspiration from one of the most famous nights in Arsenal’s history 37 years ago when George Graham’s side arrived at Anfield needing a 2-0 victory to be champions.

“I told my players to keep things tight in the first half – it was imperative we did not concede,” said Graham in an interview to mark the 20th anniversary of that dramatic finale to the 1988-89 season, when Michael Thomas scored in stoppage time to end Arsenal’s 18-year wait for the title. “The papers were saying we’d have to attack from the off, but I was adamant that was wrong. If Liverpool had scored an early goal it would have been over. But they did very little attacking and played into our hands.”

Before the 1989 game, Arsenal’s players ran to all four corners of the ground to hand flowers to Liverpool fans as a show of sympathy after the Hillsborough disaster the previous month – an idea proposed by their longstanding director Ken Friar, who died this month.

Graham and Arteta were 44 when they won their first league titles and the similarities do not end there. The former Scotland midfielder, who scored almost 80 goals for Arsenal and helped them win the Double in 1971, was known for his emphasis on defending as a manager and “1-0 to the Arsenal” became synonymous with Graham, especially towards the end of his reign. Arteta has revived that tradition since he took over in December 2019, recording 1-0 victories 32 times in the Premier League, more than any club apart from Everton.
