Arsenal scored their first set-piece goal of the season in a routine 2-0 win at home to Everton last Saturday and targeting Liverpool’s weakness from set plays while keeping things tight at the other end could be the most effective tactic against a team who have been finding their feet under Iraola in recent weeks.

“Collectively, we acknowledge the importance of defending,” said Arteta last year when asked about comparisons between his team and Graham’s. “We know that if we excel in that part of the game, the chances and the probabilities to win more matches is going to be very, very high.”

Arsenal flew back to London after losing to Fleetwood on penalties in a shootout that will have revived bad memories of May’s Champions League final defeat by Paris Saint-Germain.

The Carabao Cup has stretched Arteta’s squad in the past two seasons, when they reached first the semi-finals then the final, so that is one potential positive from their elimination – not that the ultra-competitive Spaniard would agree. For him, the only way to respond to the most embarrassing night of his managerial career will be to follow in Graham’s footsteps on Sunday.

Fiesta awaits in Mexico City as Kimi Antonelli speeds towards F1 history

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 20:00:22 GMT

Italian 20-year-old is on the verge of becoming the youngest world champion with the Mexican Grand Prix ready for a carnival coronation atmosphere

An undeniable highlight of this Formula One season, marked by discontent at the new regulations, has been getting swept along by the sheer joy that the world champion-in-waiting, Kimi Antonelli, has displayed on his way to a title he will almost surely secure this weekend at the Mexican Grand Prix.

Antonelli was still a teenager for the first half of the year and it seemed fitting to describe him as such. His exuberant embrace of competing for Mercedes at the sharp end of F1 in just his second season was that of any 19-year-old. Like discovering a life-changing new band or how much fun can be had with a cold beer, a wide grin was barely off his face.

He is 20 now, still but a stripling and on Sunday at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez if he finishes in ninth place or better he will be F1’s youngest world champion, and the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

Antonelli has confessed that as a four-year-old he did not recall when Sebastian Vettel became the previous youngest title winner in 2010. “I remember I was playing with Hot Wheels, but I don’t remember him clinching it,” he said.

This weekend he will likely embrace an unforgettable moment. Antonelli has shone on track, at home with the complex requirements of the new energy-managed cars, extracting a pace and control such that even his more experienced Mercedes teammate George Russell has been left flailing in his wake. To which traits he has allied a sharp and incisive driving style that has been extraordinary at times and a judgment that has belied his years.

That he has done so with such alacrity, especially after a difficult rookie season last year, has surprised many. Not least those team principal Toto Wolff pointedly observed had been questioning whether Antonelli should even be in F1 after his debut season. Doubts now assuredly consigned to the dustbin of history, in the city where Leon Trotsky, who coined the phrase, was killed in 1940.

It has been clear how much the Italian loves what he does and how that has informed his performances. At his shoulder through the trials of last season and the triumphs of this, has been Peter Bonnington. Bono, as he is known, was Lewis Hamilton’s engineer across the British driver’s six titles with Mercedes. He and Antonelli have established a close relationship, a friendship, with the Italian taking on board his colleague’s experience and cool head, often referencing him and the importance of their interaction.

During Antonelli’s run of five successive victories in the opening period of the season, the last of them was a striking performance in Monaco. Taking an exceptional pole position to deny Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, who was in fearsome form on the streets of the principality, he then delivered a remarkable race win, including seeing off two restarts.

After this, Bono, who often has the avuncular air of an older brother with his young charge, gave an almost disarmingly straightforward explanation of what made his driver so quick.

“As soon as he’s happy in the car: happy driver, fast lap time,” he said. The team have adopted an approach to allow Antonelli the opportunity to ensure he could drive in a way that allowed him to truly embrace being himself and in so doing, taking the pressure off.

Bonningham described this as “giving him the freedom to do what he enjoys, giving him the freedom to enjoy driving the car, that’s a real big thing and not stressing too much. He’s just a joy to work with.”

To trust the youngster’s instincts and talent, when the temptation to micromanage him must have been overwhelming, has worked brilliantly. Even as the opposition caught and at times surpassed Mercedes, Antonelli was able to deliver when a win was off the table. When it was, as at the last round in Austin, he stepped up to sweep it away with a nonchalance that typified why he is world champion elect.

This makes the atmosphere in Mexico City all the more febrile in what is already one of the most vibrant venues on the calendar. Antonelli could barely have chosen a better location to enjoy the celebration of his childhood dream. The fans here embrace F1 with the same passion the Italian has for his trade.

With the race coinciding with Mexico’s Day of the Dead, the city and the paddock are adorned with the bright orange Mexican marigolds, the “flor de muerto”. Skulls and skeletons, candles and colour are plentiful to welcome the return of the departed in a joyful, festival lending the weekend an already celebratory air.

The F1 faithful are also in good cheer in welcoming home hero Sergio Pérez back to the grid, with Cadillac and his image everywhere in Mexico City. On occasion he appears as a lifesize cardboard cut-out, rather incongruously in a line of fabulously-dressed skeletons. Yet fans will also doubtless revel in having this marvellous venue celebrate F1’s youngest champion in the heady atmosphere of the stadium section of Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Hamilton has experienced it twice, when he sealed the title here in 2017 and 2018, and the seven-time champion’s assessment of Antonelli’s season was as telling as that of his former race engineer.

“You never know how anyone’s going to do under pressure until you see them,” he said. “I could assume that he was going to be fine with the weight you have on you. When you have to do all these appearances and all these things, pulled left, right and centre. But he’s taken it in his stride. He’s a relatively old soul in that young body.”

Antonelli was withdrawn from his media duties on Thursday, with Mercedes saying he was unwell and needing to recover properly, but the Italian has stated he would like to finish the job in style and be able to relax for the remaining four races. There is no reason to believe he will suffer from any yips, certainly. He has demonstrated no such weakness thus far, even under the most intense pressure, with team principal Wolff sharing a further insight into why the 20-year-old stands ready to make history.

“In Austin, he came to my office sat down on the sofa and said: ‘I’m going to enjoy this one. Isn’t it funny? I’m not thinking at all about the championship,’” Wolff recalled. “I said: ‘Stick to that attitude. You have the best job in the world. Don’t forget that.’ He has the right mindset.”

The best job in the world and one he has, admirably, embraced with that irrepressible joy. The right mindset indeed. A deserved champion awaiting his coronation. On this form, not for the last time.

How can playing for Manchester City fit into Marc Guéhi’s moral universe?

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 20:00:22 GMT

Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League

I felt unbelievably ponderous. My head was made of Aztec stone. I realised I didn’t want to be with all these people. Somebody came at me, a huge individual in silver and blue. I fell at his feet and grabbed one shoe. I started untying the lace. He kicked away from me. I got up and walked off. I was exceedingly hungry.

Not my words. Also not the words of the Manchester City centre-back Marc Guéhi, despite what you were thinking there. This is instead a condensed quote from the mind of Gary Harkness, existentially curious college running-back and the narrator of Don DeLillo’s great American football novel End Zone.

This passage describes a moment where Gary plays a game having been urged by his friends to smoke pot beforehand to discover whether it improves his understanding of time and space, or just makes him want to lie down and untie someone’s laces. It marks a turning point for Gary. To this point football has been a comforting world. He sees clarity in its militaristic rituals, finds in sport “the illusion that order is possible”, hears hidden truths in the coaches’ shouted instructions. Button up. Get fetal. Get fetal. Get fetal. Run with reckless abandon.

Now the illusion has collapsed. Gary walks off the football field and begins instead to fixate on cold war fears and nuclear apocalypse. Death and political power have entered the chat.

Now, I’m not saying Marc Guéhi is Gary Harkness. You might be saying that. That’s your choice. But Guéhi has seemed a bit distracted in the last few weeks. Oddly for an agile and technically sound centre-back, he has seemed brittle and absent, vulnerable to being pressed.

There have been a couple of things said about City’s players in this regard. The first is that their minds might not be wholly on the game, that in the middle of a game against Croatia, for example, concerned only with manoeuvring through tiny pockets of space, Nico O’Reilly is also thinking” “Hmm, but how is it possible even by omission to honestly contravene rules E.3 and E.4 which state clearly that …oh. Wait, no. Oh dear.”

Football doesn’t work like this. The physical game is a place of total focus. But still, nothing is watertight. And this speaks to the second thing people have said, repeated like an absolute truth, that the players are entirely separate from all this. They cannot be questioned here, or indeed expected to ask questions of their own. The players are simply avatars, employees, free from any kind of agency. Players don’t have access to Google. They cannot make moral judgments. And yes, this may not be true of any other human in any other field. It may be the case that elite footballers are in fact unusually empowered, free to do whatever they want. But the consensus is clear. It is not a footballer’s business to have opinions on their employers, or what happens out of their line of vision.

This does help to avoid some tricky conundrums. Guéhi, for example, is a man of absolute public principle. Fair enough. I respect his willingness to resist popular pressure and personalise his support for the rainbow armband by writing things about Jesus on top of it. This is living your values. It’s free speech, figuring out your own moral universe. Doing so by following the absolute tenets of his religion. Go for it.

At the same time, Guéhi is playing for a club that has been convicted of cheating and lying. People are free to disagree with the rules. But if others are sticking to them, this amounts to deceit, stolen win bonuses, stolen glory. And the Bible is very clear on this. Thessalonians 4:6: “No one should transgress and defraud his brother.” Proverbs 20:17: “Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.” Now, I don’t believe these words to be divinely ordained. They’re great words. Totally dig the vibe. But Guéhi does believe these things to be an absolute instruction. How does this fit together in his head? How does that gravel (pending appeal) taste right now?

Again, fine if you can square it. It’s a personal journey. Park the apparent moral dilemma. See if your legal team can come up with a better final outcome. But things have changed in one significant way since the verdict dropped, an element that is now unchallenged, and which has been largely unremarked in the middle of the chaos. Understandably so. This stuff is gruelling. Everyone just wants to watch some football in the brief lull between legal rage events. But there are two points worth making in the interim. The second of which is an admission that affects many other things.

The first issue is: do you actually understand the basis of the Manchester City appeal? That evidence has seemingly been leaked. The irrefutable body of evidence, Body Of Evidence 2, the long-awaited tribunal-based Madonna erotic thriller vehicle, contains a vital detail: the additional money in City’s coffers, almost a billion, did not come from the owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group, which is owned, like City, by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan. This would be against the rules. It came instead from the Abu Dhabi government, which is essentially the Abu Dhabi royal family, of which Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan is a member; as he is also, wearing a different hat, of the Abu Dhabi government.

And maybe this means it’s fine. It seems the government often tops up the sponsor companies like a benevolent uncle. In the period the charges relate to there was no need for sponsor deals to be of market value, as there is now. So if we accept all this, if we can establish a binding principle of wearing different hats in different rooms, this may be a way out. Maybe.

This is a familiar concept in the high court, in an age of shell companies and tricky fiscal flows. Mega-million cases hang on whether ownership really is separate, or whether this is, to echo a phrase, a sham process. The person on the Clapham omnibus might not buy any of this. Do these really seem like separate entities? Or a bit like adopting a French accent when the bailiffs ring up and maintaining that, no, Monsieur Ronay is not here, and he definitely doesn’t run this dry cleaners. That, instead, is me.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

If you make the case you win the case. This is all in the end about the application of rules, and that is a good thing. But the key point here is the secondary issue derived from this. City’s leaked defence, in making their case, is also saying, without pretence or mucking about, that the club is indeed funded by the Abu Dhabi government. This is something City’s fans have at times weirdly denied. But we have it in plain sight now, not just admitted but insisted on. The ultimate source of the dizzying success of the club that has defined a Premier League era is the government. Guéhi is, in effect, an Abu Dhabi civil servant. Perhaps the United Arab Emirates national team should have six stars on their jersey, one for each Premier League won. But there is no way of covering your ears now. City actively want us to accept this.

What are the consequences of this new fact? It comes with two urgent questions. The first is the moral one. Back again to Guéhi as the best example. This is what he is promoting here. And Guéhi is a man entirely guided by the principles of his faith. A private matter perhaps, except that it’s not, because Guéhi’s church explicitly orders its members to go out and proselytise. Guéhi is a member of Ballers in God, which actively tries to awaken Christian faith in the dressing room. He plays with Christian messages on his matchday kit intended to make you, the reader, think yes, maybe I too should follow this evangelical church.

And here is the key thing. This is a criminal offence in Abu Dhabi. Under UAE penal code, giving out Christian leaflets will get you arrested. A Christian pastor in the UAE was sentenced to a year in prison for giving a Muslim a Bible. Some Americans were deported for giving out Christian literature in the Dubai shopping district. Spreading the gospel, which Guéhi is morally bound to do, is illegal in the place that pays his direct employers.

Are players just avatars, empty shells? How much do you really believe in this? These are, more than ever, very interesting questions. And they don’t just apply to issues of personal principle.

The regulator now has this information, too. Abu Dhabi funded the purchase of Nolito. Abu Dhabi dictated the flow of English football finance. The same pocket that paid for this is also funding at arm’s length the civil war in Sudan, the hospital massacres, the piles of bodies so high they can be seen from satellite imaging. Abu Dhabi, which criminalises homosexuality, which crushes dissent, is openly identifying itself as the mega-funder of a Premier League club. Is this a fit and proper influence?

There are very obvious reasons why this is not desirable. Governments spy and wage war and break rules. They have a sacred trust to promote their own interests by any means necessary. It is hard to see how this kind of owner fits the regulatory framework. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had to twirl through semantic hoops when buying Newcastle to establish it was an entity at one remove from a government, as opposed to a government entity. In making the opposite case for their funding City have not only exposed their own live-your-values central defender, they have put themselves in a place where, even if you win on one front, you’ve started to look like a very strange presence.

This deserves to be unravelled in all its wider implications. It may be the biggest issue here, whatever the final verdict. How can this be the right thing? How can City’s fans look their own autocratic government-funded club in the eye? The quiet thing has been said out loud. And its implications are bigger than the game, bigger than legal opinion. Enough, perhaps to make you question the existential point of this thing, where the best course of action really might be to walk off and look for the nearest cheeseburger.

Canada and EU announce new alliance open to like-minded countries

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 19:42:15 GMT

Alliance for the Future, unveiled at Montreal summit and open to other countries, conceived for world ‘shaken by new storms’

Canada and Europe have announced a new alliance of like-minded nations to serve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a powerful hedge against the unpredictable nature of geopolitics, while welcoming other countries to join.

Speaking to reporters on Friday from Montreal, the prime minister, Mark Carney, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, called the new partnership the Alliance for the Future and said the “deepest possible partnership between Canada and the 27-member bloc had the potential to offer unprecedented stability and opportunity”.

“Our societies have been shaken by new storms,” Carney told reporters, referring to the damaging effects of the climate emergency but also the “erosion of democratic norms” and “the weaponization of trade”.

As they concluded their two-day summit, Canada agreed to contribute to a €90bn support loan for Ukraine. Leaders also said future discussions would lead to a more integrated market worth tens of billions of dollars, reduced trade and travel restrictions, and new educational opportunities for both sides.

While a trade war between Canada and the United States has seen Carney go hunting for new geopolitical partners, an over-reliance on American companies – especially for defence – has also given Canada pause.

Last week, Elon Musk throttled the speeds of Starlink and Starshield over Ukraine in mid-October, severely disrupting Ukrainian military and defense operations.

Carney has repeatedly raised the concern that Canada’s defense technologies could be at the whim of political actors or companies with opposing interests. Musk, a dual Canadian citizen, is a critic of Canada’s governing Liberal party and has advocated for provinces to separate.

Carney pointed to a planned merger between the Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc and Germany’s Aleph Alpha GmbH as a step to lessening reliance on American AI giants. The tie-up will see the newly formed company have dual headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, and Canada’s federal government has announced a stake in Cohere worth up to C$1.6bn.

“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know, or by whom we don’t trust,” Carney said on Thursday.

Brussels and Ottawa also announced an agreement on Friday that would bringing Canada into Europe’s supercomputing network, giving Canadian access to European machines to train AI models.

In addition to lofty promises of helping to reshape the global order, or giving safe harbour to like-minded nations looking to weather uncertainty, Canadian and EU leaders also pitched their new, deeper relationship as one that addressed key sources of anxiety for residents, including the cost of living.

“When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it’s the families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” Von der Leyen said, noting that previously trusted trusted suppliers of energy, critical minerals or semiconductors “are increasingly turned into instruments of pressure”.

“More competition, more choice,” Carney said earlier in the day, suggesting the alliance could find ways to build certainty around supply chains and “withstand shocks, together”.

The leaders once again brought up the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member. The designation is uncharted territory, said Von der Leyen, who added: “We have the ambition, trust, and creativity to shape it together.

“This [associate membership] is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”

While the leaders committed to the idea of associate membership, they said a clearer scope of the role would come at a 2027 summit. Some EU members had bristled at the idea of Canada being given a legally meaningless designation that they fear confuses other nations looking for membership. Germany and other states had worked behind the scenes to remove the phrase from a draft of the summit statement. But Von der Leyen, who first floated the term, and Carney both again referred to “associate membership” at the summit.

European Council president Antonio Costa, meanwhile, said earlier that Canada was “by far the most European of the non-European countries”, a sentiment that reflected a belief that despite geography, there was a collective sense of shared values.

Costa said the two sides would pursue “the most closer, the most deepest, the most stronger association ever between European Union and a non-European country”.

Still, the mere fact of the summit has caused friction in the province of Quebec, where the separatist Parti Québécois was recently elected to a minority government. The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, skipped the event after Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak publicly at it.

“The federal government would have us believe that the premier of Quebec being granted permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence for representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote in a social media post earlier in the week.

He said an invitation to sit at the head table was the federal government asking Quebec “to get back in line, with the vassalization and invisibilization of Quebec which that implies, in exchange for obtaining better seats to watch the party”.

Man accused of sexually assaulting woman drugged by husband says he thought it was ‘their kink’

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 18:06:32 GMT

Two of four men on trial say they met couple via online ads and swinging website and had no idea wife had been drugged

Men accused of sexually assaulting a woman whose then husband drugged her for years and allowed her to be abused have described being invited to the couple’s home via online adverts and a swinging website.

One of those accused of assaulting Joanne Young, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, as she lay restrained and blindfolded said he was a young man “trying out things” and had no idea she was drugged.

A second said there was a large “cuckold community” of men who watched their wives having sex, claiming his encounter was “just a sex meet” and she seemed “fine”.

Philip Young, 50, has pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and sexually abusing his former wife, 49, at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire, over a number of years. The prosecution has said he advertised his wife online and “loaned” her out to other men.

Four other men are on trial at Winchester crown court, including Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, of Swindon, who denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching in June 2016.

In police interviews read out to the jury, Sanderson-Doyle said he contacted Philip Young via Craigslist after seeing an ad in its adult section for a woman tied and blindfolded. He said he thought he had met a couple “trying to live out whatever their kink is”.

He said he went to the Youngs’ house on his motorcycle. He asked if he should take his shoes off when he arrived, but kept his balaclava on throughout. He saw there were toys in the house so assumed the couple had children.

Sanderson-Doyle, then 21, said he found Joanne Young “tied up and blindfolded” as she had been pictured in the online ad. She did not say anything but seemed awake.

The defendant said that at one point he heard her say “No” but he thought she wanted him to do something different rather than stop completely.

Sanderson-Doyle told police he started to get a “vibe she wasn’t enjoying it or was not comfortable” and left soon afterwards.

He continued: “I thought I had her consent. I didn’t know she was drugged,” adding: “I was just a young guy trying out things.” He called the encounter a “non event”.

A second man, Norman Macksoni, 48, of Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, denies one count of rape in February 2017. He told police he worked as an MC and went by the username “dark stranger” on the swingers’ site where he made contact with Philip Young.

Six women who have been “haunted” by their encounters with Russell Brand came forward to give evidence against him with nothing to gain and no appetite for fame, a court has heard.

The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, said the women, who do not know one another, had not been compelled to make police complaints by the “magic force” of media reporting on Brand’s alleged misconduct.

In her closing speech, she told jurors at Southwark crown court that the women had “vivid recollections” and had “bravely” come forward to the tell “the truth” after realising they were not alone.

Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.

Karmy-Jones denied that a 2023 Dispatches documentary about Brand had had “such a subliminal hold on the minds of six perfectly rational women” to make them “invent, reimagine, recharacterise, recast” their encounters with the comedian.

She said the complainants had described a similar pattern of behaviour, saying: “Six women who have nothing to gain, who have not sought the limelight, who have not looked out for some form of publicity, who have not taken part in a documentary, not made claims for compensation.

“There is no benefit to them, apart from perhaps some closure by coming before you and telling you their accounts of what happened to them so long ago.”

She said the women described how Brand’s “demeanour changed” before he assaulted them. “Listen to their accounts,” the prosecutor told the jury. “Many said he was nice and then it was like there was a personality change. A pivot. His eyes changed, he snapped from charming to frightening and nasty.

“He didn’t listen when they said no, he didn’t stop, he didn’t care, he kept pulling, pushing, tugging, thrusting. In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim.”

She said the women had given the court “specific details” about Brand’s conduct. “What’s happened, we suggest, is these women have realised they’re not alone and they’ve bravely come before you to tell you the truth. The truth of what happened to them so many years ago.

“The truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years,” she said.

The prosecutor also accused Brand of using “gaslighting” to “good effect” by asking some of his accusers for their telephone numbers or emails after the alleged assaults.

She said women were a “disposable commodity” to Brand and later added: “He was a defendant who was rampant in his desire to have sexual contact whenever her wished, whenever he pleased.”

Karmy-Jones described the account of the youngest witness, a fan then in her early 20s who accused the TV personality of anally raping her at his London townhouse after meeting her at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.

He cared only about his “birthright orgasm” and ignored her pleas for him to stop, the prosecutor said, adding that she was “just another number to add to his 5,000 notches which he was marking up”.

The court heard Brand had a “flavour of disdain” towards the allegations, which the prosecution suggested was “a reflection” of his “whole approach to the female species at that time”.

“Women as a whole were disposable, they didn’t matter to him. He didn’t even need to know their names. They were just a means to an end.

“As he said in a 2017 interview, they were the amusements in what he described as his playground of orgasms,” Karmy-Jones continued.

Earlier on Friday the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, gave legal directions to the jury in which he pointed out that they would have “rival arguments” to consider.

Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

His barrister, Ian Winter KC, is due to deliver his closing speech on Monday.

The trial continues.

The Guardian view on Labour’s fiscal devolution: the future of Burnhamism will play out in municipal England

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 17:56:11 GMT

Replacing government grants with revenue streams from taxation will not in itself reduce regional inequalities. But the political implications are radical

Following Wednesday’s budget, the Treasury minister, Torsten Bell, was challenged by the BBC’s Evan Davis on whether its modest series of “breathing space” measures could truly be said to have ended “40 years of neoliberalism”. This line of questioning is becoming a familiar one. Andy Burnham’s ringing declaration of long-term intent is now being regularly deployed by commentators to suggest an emerging gulf between rhetoric and action.

Mr Bell’s response was a good one. Recalling how “Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s hugely hollowed out local government [and] tried to emasculate our big cities”, he called the fiscal devolution roadmap unveiled in the budget a step change and a really big deal. From 2028, mayoral strategic authorities will for the first time receive a share of income tax receipts, and from next year they will be allocated 20% of business rates revenue. That figure will potentially rise to 100% by the end of the decade, while a new overnight visitors levy will add another local income stream.

These are structural changes that will transform the relationship between local government and a notoriously overly centralised state. They have so far failed to generate anything like the coverage that accompanied the Conservatives’ levelling-up programme, which degenerated into a tawdry pork barrel exercise for “red wall” Tory MPs. But it is on this municipal terrain that Mr Burnham’s aspiration to rebalance the country, reduce regional inequality and “roll back” the 80s will be played out.

Replacing government grants with guaranteed income streams will give strategic authorities more certainty over future revenue – against which they will be able to borrow – and the ability to plan flexibly according to locally set priorities. The devil will be in details to be announced in next year’s spending review, in particular regarding mechanisms to ensure poorer areas with a smaller tax base do not lose out. But the roadmap is a first move towards restoring proper agency to local authorities struggling to cope with the disastrous twin legacy of deindustrialisation and austerity.

Further steps will need to be taken if, as the prime minister intends, local government is to drive “good growth” that improves general living standards and prospects throughout communities. As the Local Government Association pointed out, cash-strapped councils on the frontline face a £7bn funding gap by 2028-29, and are in a perennial struggle merely to meet their statutory obligations on social care. Strategic authorities need to be given the capacity to gradually reassume control of priorities in sectors such as care, housing and the utilities. That will take time and investment at scale in forms of community provision that can offer an alternative to a model in which services have been outsourced and profits offshored.

Devolution will not of itself reduce inequalities or restore a degraded public realm. But this week’s budget measures began the necessary process of rewiring British politics. Mr Burnham’s core conviction is that radical devolution can redistribute power to those who know their own community best, and allow councils to rebalance the relationship between the public and the private sector. After decades in which the latter has profited hugely from calling nearly all the shots, that is very much the right direction of travel. The starting gun has been fired in a process that can lead to a genuine renaissance of municipal England.

The Guardian view on 50 years of The Selfish Gene: flawed, outdated, yet still a model of truly popular science writing

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 17:56:07 GMT

Richard Dawkins’ first work has thrilled fans and frustrated critics for five decades. The science has moved on, but any writer looking to supplant its place must learn its lessons

Richard Dawkins’ The Selfish Gene was not predicted to be a success. Its initial print run, published this week in 1976, was just 5,000. It went on to sell millions, and is perhaps the most influential work of pop-science ever. For 50 years, it has been the go-to resource for the layperson seeking to understand evolution.

What accounts for its enduring power? Prof Dawkins’ central claim, that “we are survival machines – robot vehicles blindly programmed to preserve the selfish molecules known as genes” was provocative, stripping the messy stuff of human and other life down to a simple law. And yet the book is primarily concerned with proving that complex, selfless behaviour such as altruism in animals can emerge from these basic “selfish” drives, satisfyingly resolving an apparent paradox. Prof Dawkins – a zoologist by training – also succeeded in conjuring entertaining, vividly drawn vignettes of the lives of animals, from lions and ants to hawks and honeybees, to make his points.

Nevertheless, 50th anniversary celebrations have been somewhat muted. In an essay in the journal Nature, the historian of science Nathaniel Comfort suggests there is something almost malign about The Selfish Gene’s commitment to a simple kind of determinism.

There is certainly that and more to take issue with. Prof Dawkins fought publicly with eminent biologists such as Stephen Jay Gould about whether genes were the primary target of natural selection, rather than the individual organism or group – a legitimate clash between differing theories that was mirrored in the scientific literature. More quietly and damningly, many biologists bemoan the way the book seems to assume every trait is some kind of adaptation – hardly the textbook view, which has long recognised the role of randomness and chance in evolution. It also focuses almost exclusively on animals. And it is hard to read Prof Dawkins fresh, without the knowledge that the later books are repetitive and that his comments outside his field – including on feminism, disability and describing Islam as “the greatest force for evil in the world today” in 2013 – don’t suggest a great or sensitive thinker.

Perhaps the best way to read The Selfish Gene is alongside its critics. Prof Dawkins’ Oxford tutor Arthur Cain called it a young man’s book, pointedly suggesting that the author would come to regret or recant his most bombastic claims. Prof Dawkins never really did, but his intransigence brought out the best in his critics, from Prof Gould to Richard Lewontin or Hilary and Steven Rose. Read all together, it makes for a full and rollicking picture of modern evolutionary debate

It also remains a model of style. The philosopher John Dupré, no fan of Prof Dawkins’ scientific thought, nonetheless calls it a paradigmatic example of successful popular science writing. The book works on this level because it takes a point of view in a live scientific debate, and argues its side with engaging dash and zeal. Prof Dawkins is often too polemical, but most science writing tends to be heavily didactic, with little argument or rhetorical flourish. And it is possible to both inform and persuade: Sean Carroll’s Endless Forms Most Beautiful and Nick Lane’s The Vital Question take a similarly clear, provocative line.

The science has moved on, and The Selfish Gene has flaws. But any writer looking to supplant its place in the public imagination with a more capacious vision of evolution must reckon with the reasons for its long-running success. For all its problems, it remains a model of its genre.

On Friday, the IOPC decided to use its formal powers to launch an investigation into the Met. The police watchdog views the claims in the 2019 letter as potentially alleging serious offending.

Its investigation will look at who in the Met made decisions such as not to pass on the claims to police forces in countries where wrongdoing by Markle was alleged, and whether police policies and procedures were followed.

An IOPC spokesperson said: “Following a voluntary conduct referral from the Met police, we have decided an independent investigation is required into its failure to pass on allegations of serious offending, contained in a letter it received in 2019, to relevant overseas authorities at the time.”

Why M&S director Kathryn Turner is the ultimate ‘Gay Halloween’ costume idea

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 17:18:49 GMT

Product development boss at Marks & Spencer inspires niche outfits after unexpected success on social media

She is not the most likely viral star. But with 310,000 followers on TikTok and 270,000 on Instagram, Marks & Spencer Food’s director of product development, Kathryn Turner, has suddenly become one of the year’s big hits on social media. Her videos take the viewer with her as she goes in-store to look at new dessert launches, including its banana, caramel and pecan pudding, or taste test its latest products, such as its cherry and chocolate cookies.

Turner is part of Marks & Spencer’s wider social media strategy implemented in 2020 as a way of attracting younger shoppers. Instead of using traditional influencers, M&S now champions 100 of its own employees on TikTok.

Turner, who launched her account in May, now regularly receives more than 1m likes on her videos, with celebrities including Nigella Lawson and Stormzy among her followers. Part of the appeal is Turner’s insider knowledge and expertise: she has worked at M&S since 1995.

This weekend, she will gain another prestigious accolade as fans spurn ghosts, witches and vampires and instead dress up as her for Halloween. The formula is simple. Some Turner-esque glasses, a blond wig and a packet of M&S cookies.

The content creator Liam Gleed has been posting videos of himself as Turner in the run-up to Halloween and plans to wear the costume this weekend. “To be very real, I love a sweet treat and I work close to an M&S so I follow her socials to find out what snacks I’ll be getting every Friday at work,” he says. “The more niche you go for Halloween, the better. Why go as basic characters when you can dress as your current fixation or icons of the internet?”

Gleed says it is the “real person” element that appeals to him. “I think it’s quite hilarious that someone who works as a product developer at M&S can become this on social media,” he says. “That’s what made the content work so well – it is so random that she is this popular figure from quite a normal job.”

Dressing like someone such as Turner – an improbable online star – rather than a spooky character or a movie star fits into the idea of Gay Halloween. This is a way of approaching the dress-up holiday that utilises an online pop culture reference – the more specific the better. It taps into “if you know, you know” culture.

This year, that could be anything from an iced coffee at a job interview, based on a viral story about whether or not it is acceptable, to Chappell Roan’s security guard, who allegedly made a fan cry, or the prenup papers for Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s marriage.

According to the website Know Your Meme, the term Gay Halloween dates to 2023 but had a precursor in “jokes about ‘Gay Halloween’ costumes being absurdly niche” on X. The idea has now spread to everyone online, however. “I don’t think that gay people are exclusively culpable for this,” says James Greig, features editor of Dazed. “I can remember around 2016 finding it really annoying when straight guys were going [to Halloween parties] as very, very niche memes.”

It is well documented that Halloween has been embraced by queer people owing to the holiday providing the freedom to dress up without judgment – it is sometimes called “gay Christmas” – and Gleed argues that its origins remain here. “Personally, as a gay man, I think it’s just another way for us to express ourselves,” he says. “We aren’t afraid to be our authentic selves after coming out, and to dress as someone so niche makes it comedic gold. I think the gays are doing it best because we don’t feel that shame of getting judged because we have been anyway.”

As for which Gay Halloween costumes may be popular this year, José Criales-Unzueta, style correspondent at Vanity Fair, wrote about the trend recently. They have a few predictions beyond Turner, including references to Heated Rivalry and Drake’s recent viral poncho.

The internet is also championing a New York pothole filled by the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and the foliage during Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl performance. “But the best ones are the ones you cannot foresee,” says Criales-Unzueta. “Part of the magic of Gay Halloween is the unexpected.”

Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 17:13:48 GMT

Humanitarian convoy brings food and medicine to Russian-held city where people have suffered severe shortages

People living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine were evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.

The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River, opposite Kherson, has suffered months of serious food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including about 50 children.

The humanitarian convoy, including 25 buses and ambulances, had arrived in the city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine.

The localised ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region allowed for the roads out of Oleshky to be de-mined, making evacuation possible.

While Ukrainian territory lies just 3 miles (5km) from Oleshky, evacuees will need to travel to the southern Russian city of Anapa and on to Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.

Davyd Arakhamia, a lawmaker with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party – who was part of the delegation to Oleshky – confirmed the evacuation of some people who were travelling to Anapa.

“From there, they will fly by plane to Belarus, and then travel by bus to their homes,” he said.

Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an online post: “At this moment, the humanitarian operation is under way in Oleshky.” Budanov is not part of the delegation in Oleshky.

While earlier reports had suggested more than 500 people wanted to move to Ukrainian territory, it was unclear how many people travelled in the convoy.

Kyiv’s delegation reached the city late on Friday morning to prepare for the evacuation, with footage on social media showing tearful residents embracing delegation members as they gathered in heavy rain to wait for the main evacuation convoy to arrive. Several hundred people, mainly older people, have chosen to stay.

Asked if she was packed and ready to leave by a member of the Ukrainian delegation, a woman who identified herself as “Anna” was shown on video saying: “Yes, we are on bus 20, my son is on bus 17. To Ukraine.”

Oleshky’s population has declined to about 2,000 since the star of the war, according to authorities and volunteers, and many of those who stayed have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads to get food and water.

Some say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild plants added.

“We’ve been through so much here in these five years,” one woman said in a report broadcast on Ukrainian TV. Another older woman, preparing to evacuate, said: “If we had our health, maybe we’d stay there a bit longer, but that’s it. We just want to be with our children.”

Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with people there, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city.

“They are currently checking empty houses and, in some cases, moving into them,” she told the Associated Press. “They are also pressuring local residents to evacuate to Russia, rather than to Ukraine,” she added.

The convoy arrived under a ceasefire in the area, which the US first lady, Melania Trump, claimed to have helped broker – a rare example of cooperation between the warring sides.

On Friday, the Kremlin, however, described it as a special case that was “difficult to extrapolate” to the wider search for a peace settlement.

Oleshky was seized by Russian troops during the first days of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

It has suffered extensive damage and was badly flooded after the destruction of the huge upriver Kakhovka dam in June 2023.

“The problem is that a lot of people are staying,” one woman told Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who was on the ground to coordinate the operation with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.

“I’ve been told that ‌it’s their own choice,” Lubinets replied. “At the very least, we’ll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through.”

He added: “This is the first time since 2022 that a ceasefire has been established across such an extensive stretch of the frontline and has been maintained for ​such a significant duration.”

Aditya Chakrabortty was spot-on in his analysis of John Healey’s budget (Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget, 28 October). It was a drop in the ocean of what is needed to bring about the scale of change this country needs and, importantly, was promised by Andy Burnham.

As the affordability crisis rages on, people may feel some relief at the small cost of living measures announced for households and businesses. But when we’ve been told we’ll get a wholesale reset and an end to neoliberalism, 4p off the price of gherkins and a temporary tiny bank tax isn’t going to cut it.

So, what’s the solution? The government must fairly tax the vast fortunes of the richest people and corporations, left mostly untouched. Recouping the massive wealth and profits siphoned off to shady tax havens each year, equalising how the tax system treats income from wealth and work, and building HMRC’s capacity to properly measure and collect tax from the very richest would raise tens of billions to help pay for targeted, meaningful cost of living support and Burnham’s ambitious plans to fix the housing crisis, fund social care and devolve power and wealth to every region.

Reforming capital gains tax – a proposal supported by members of his own party – would make things fairer and raise around £19.7bn a year, enough to build 90,000 new council homes (the number needed each year to end the housing crisis) and train 128,000 new NHS nurses.

This government cannot survive much longer on vibes alone, and Labour is already on its last chance. Burnham must use his 10-year plan and spending review to lay out a proper roadmap to genuinely improve lives and transform the country, otherwise he risks being remembered for gherkins, which isn’t much better than Liz Truss’s lettuce. Perhaps it could be followed by another to ban school uniforms altogether. The reasons for having them are specious and outdated. There is an idea that it makes class differences invisible. Pedestrianisation won’t save Oxford Street

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 17:10:19 GMT

Oliver Schick writes that there is a limit to how much footfall is beneficial. Plus letters from Iain Nelson and Tom Hardy

The real causes of the problems seen in Oxford Street (The long read, 22 October) are high rents, the chaotic system of business rates and the replacement of many smaller footprints with larger ones; these are the main factors that have made the street less viable. The large flagship shops depend on being surrounded by good-quality small businesses to attract customers.

Much of what the mayor of London is doing here is a de facto part-privatisation – stopping up a very important public highway for a large number of users of “unwelcome” modes of transport, to benefit private landowners.

Rather than buses being a main culprit here, it is much more likely that the gradual downgrading of bus services along Oxford Street has contributed significantly to its decline.

The strategic mistake of routing Crossrail along Oxford Street – long after this plan lost its part-justification (dating from when it was conceived decades ago) of stimulating the West End – has caused the dangerously high footfall levels that have become a main motivation for pedestrianisation.

The Crossrail route should have been changed to connect Heathrow and Stratford through centres in south London, but we have to live with it now. There is a natural limit to how much footfall is beneficial for urban centres, and disadvantaging everyone who doesn’t want to get there by underground railway isn’t going to change this.

The factors at play that have weakened Oxford Street are not unique to it, and none of them will be affected by these actions from the mayor of London, who is largely powerless to address them without central government taking corrective action. Oliver Schick London

I like to see Sadiq Khan contributing to the Guardian, but on this occasion I have to quibble with his description of Oxford Street as “our nation’s high street” (We’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music too, 26 October). I live on the border of Wales, and whether a street in London is pedestrianised or not is entirely irrelevant to me. It’s not my high street and never will be. Iain Nelson Selattyn, Shropshire

Credit where credit is due. Contrary to accusations at the time that businesses had suffered, footfall on Oxford Street actually increased by 13.5% as visitors were drawn to the utopia that was Extinction Rebellion’s blockade in April 2019 – a harbinger, in microcosm, of what a greener, less polluted world might look like. Tom Hardy London

One man’s war on the scourge of sodcasting

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 17:10:14 GMT

Readers respond to an article about learning from Japan on curbing ‘loudcasting’ and antisocial behaviour

Emily Bratt missed out one way of addressing antisocial behaviour – on buses or elsewhere – which is to address the problem oneself rather than waiting for official enforcement (Fine ‘headphone dodgers’ if you will, but to really tackle antisocial behaviour, Britain should look to Japan, 24 October). I give sodcasters on the bus a minute or so and then ask them to use headphones or turn off the sound. It doesn’t always work, but the offenders don’t like it, and the less they like the response they get, the less they will do it. Donald Smith Haddington, East Lothian

I’m all for banning “loudcasting” – because I’m a retired bus driver and I will not be the one charged with enforcing it. Heaven help the poor sods who will. Jenny Eldershaw Buxton, Derbyshire

It’s not only in Japan that children are taught to be socially responsible. When my eight-year-old daughter visited her new UK primary school on return from her early school years in rural Zimbabwe, she didn’t understand when the teacher apologised for the state of the classroom because the cleaners were on strike. She also asked: “Which day does our class clean the toilets?” Anne Spargo Upper Colwall, Herefordshire

Re Emily Bratt’s suggestion that schoolchildren should help with “caring” for their school, when I was at Dartington Hall – a progressive co-educational boarding school – in the 1960s we did what was called “useful work” before classes. It involved us in the processes of running the school. Among other things, I tidied the library, thus learning the Dewey classification system; was printer’s devil to the bookbinder, Eric McNally, producing play programmes and the school prospectus; spent two terms in my O-level year setting up chemistry lab equipment for A-level classes; and was filing clerk for the careers advice department.

Responsibility was a key word at Dartington, it being well understood that freedom is not free – it comes at a price – and that consideration for others and support for the community are essential. Ruth Gilbert Marsden, West Yorkshire

How do you bounce back from Liz Truss-level public failure? Don’t be shameless; do show remorse

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:55:53 GMT

From surgeons to senior civil servants, even the most decent people can make disastrous mistakes. But these gaffes require honesty

Gabriel Weston made a mistake at work this summer. It doesn’t define her – she was and is a well-regarded NHS surgeon and author – but it was serious enough, as she explained in an extraordinarily candid series of Instagram and Substack posts this month, to prompt an investigation that left her feeling “ashamed and alone and really quite nervous”. Whatever went wrong in the operating theatre was bad enough to be classed a “never event” (something that should never be able to happen if the process is working properly) and triggered a nagging anxiety that she might somehow do it again, unless she figured out where she had unexpectedly gone wrong.

It’s a fascinating insight into a process that most people never have the courage to talk about openly. But it also highlights why it’s so hard in practice for doctors and other professionals to acknowledge and learn from mistakes – as every public inquiry into every public scandal ends up recommending, only to repeat it all over again after the next one – rather than close ranks and cover up. Weston says she only spoke up out of frustration with what she saw as her employers’ failure to support her (she had asked to reduce what she considered an overloaded operating list to take some pressure off, which she says has now happened, leaving her full of praise for the hospital’s ultimate response). Judging by the responses to her posts, she’s not alone.

I thought of Weston this week when Liz Truss published Bank Job, the second book she has written in two years circling the drain of her career. This one seems if anything even less self-aware, blaming the Bank of England, not herself, for the spectacular failure of her mini-budget (even her old cheerleaders at the Telegraph called it deranged). But it’s also oddly sad. There’s something near-pathological about the inability to engage with an excruciatingly public failure, as if the truth would shatter her. She can’t seem to leave the whole episode alone – can’t withdraw, as Keir Starmer has, into stony silence about his own prematurely curtailed time in Downing Street – yet can’t really face it head-on either.

How does anyone learn from cataclysmic failure? I don’t mean the frothy, early-career kind that seemed the end of the world at the time, but which you can laugh about now from the security of knowing that eventually everything turned out fine. Those aren’t the kind of failures the state really cares about avoiding. Nor do I mean the kind whose authors somehow manage to fail upwards anyway – or at least onwards, like Truss, into some strange reincarnation on YouTube. The failures that most haunt their authors, but which often hold the most useful lessons for preventing such a thing ever happening again, are often of the “there but for the grace of God go you and I” kind, involving formerly blameless and conscientious people who make one inexplicably dumb mistake, often under pressure or when exhausted.

Richard Jackson was a high-flying civil servant working on counter-terrorism, who one night accidentally scooped up two classified documents that should never have left the building along with some routine papers he was taking home. Realising his error that night, he fatally compounded it by deciding to sneak the files back before their absence was noticed, only to accidentally leave them on the train – where they were found and handed into a BBC reporter, resulting in a security scandal that cost Jackson his job and left him close to suicide. The advice on coping he shared in a recent episode of BBC Radio 4’s Life Changing series – get dark thoughts out of your head by writing them down or telling someone; keep a note of all the nice things people have ever said to you; don’t let your life be defined by one mistake – seems useful for individuals in the eye of the storm. But so perhaps is what Weston calls a degree of professional “care and acceptance” for good people who have failed, and want help working out why.

Shamelessness has a deservedly terrible reputation in public life, and for some mistakes forgiveness can be too much to ask.

But it’s shame that prevents thoughtful people learning from failure; shame that drives the cover-up; shame that ruins, and sometimes even ends, lives. People willing to honestly examine their own mistakes for others’ benefit deserve some grace in return. The true shame lies with those refusing to offer it.

Sky-high ratings – for a lacklustre series: The Celebrity Traitors has become too nice for its own good

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:52:28 GMT

Too many recruitments, frustrating confessions and an underwhelming murder in plain sight … this series has failed to take off

This article contains spoilers for the episode of The Celebrity Traitors on 29 October. Do not read on if you have not seen it.

What happens when a game that revolves around secrets and lies gets derailed by the truth? That’s what played out last night in the penultimate episode of The Celebrity Traitors, when – spoilers ahead! – James Acaster was dramatically confronted at the round table about his role in murdering Ross Kemp. After being grilled by Michael Sheen in a soliloquy that felt borderline Shakespearean, Acaster did something we have never seen before on this show: he fessed up to the entire thing, falling on his sword and revealing his true identity.

Acaster’s reveal is one of the defining scenes in a series that has broken the show’s sky-high ratings records. Yet watching the episode – and this celebrity series as a whole – I can’t shake the feeling that it’s been underwhelming. The grand finale could provide some big twists, but the show so far has felt tentative and lacked a certain spark. If Acaster’s confession had happened last year, it would have been merely a blip. But here, it feels emblematic of a series that, no matter what happens in the final, hasn’t quite lived up to the hype.

The selection of the Traitors is one of the most important parts of the game because these players have an outsized influence on its direction and, as a result, often take up more airtime. They also become the unofficial narrators of the show as they are the only ones who know what is really going on.

Part of the reason this series has felt lacklustre is because most of the Traitors were selected by the Traitors themselves, rather than producers who make a living from creating addictive TV. It all started with Richard E Grant’s epic blunder in episode one, when he told Joe Lycett that he was a Traitor and was quickly banished from the game. Not only did this deprive the audience of watching Grant and fellow Traitor Maya Jama scheming in the turret, but it set in motion a chain of events in which most of the Traitors were recruitments.

The problem here is that some of the recruited Traitors didn’t seem up to the task of murder and betrayal. Acaster made no secret of the fact that he didn’t want to be a Traitor, and Hannah Fry didn’t seem fully comfortable in the role, either. I have no problem with these players being authentically themselves, but it’s more fun to watch characters such as Alan Carr (from the 2025 series) gleefully plotting in the shadows – to witness supposedly “nice” celebrities mastering the dark side. That’s what the game is about.

The number of recruitments has also made the show feel stilted. Being a Faithful is a tricky task at the best of times, but it’s borderline impossible to have consistent theories or a sense of momentum when someone is being recruited every few episodes, rendering many events from earlier in the game null and void. The “original” Traitors making it deep into the game isn’t just satisfying for the audience; it’s also important for how the game functions. Too many recruitments can erode narrative cohesion.

As a format, The Traitors is close to being the perfect gameshow, which is why it has become a smash hit in almost all its international versions. But one flaw that’s baked into the game is that the biggest characters are often murdered or banished first, because they are seen as a threat to either the Traitors or the Faithful.

This has an even greater impact on the celebrity version because we already know the players. For the audience, there is a sense of disappointment when a celebrity they really like gets eliminated early on. (Myha’la, I will avenge you!) This doesn’t exist in the same way on the civilian version, because we don’t necessarily know what we’re missing out on.

I can’t shake the feeling that the celebrities are just a little too nice to each other. Perhaps this is because they have been on TV before and are wary of how they will be perceived, or don’t want to fall out with someone they might see again in a professional setting. As someone who watches many international versions of The Traitors, I prefer the charm of the British show to the American version: the latter is far more conflict-filled and glitzy. But with this series, we’ve gone too far in the opposite direction. It’s become too nice and Acaster falling on his sword encapsulates that.

On social media, there is a lot of anger towards Acaster, with some accusing him of making a mockery of the game. That was my initial reaction, too – and his confession has somewhat taken the wind out of the show’s sails ahead of the finale. But nobody watching at home can know how they would react in such a high-pressure situation.

The backlash against the comedian is really misplaced frustration that this series hasn’t delivered many of those “OMG!” moments we have been accustomed to. Even the murder in plain sight – usually a box-office highlight – felt underwhelming. You can fill a castle with celebrities and engineer all kinds of twists, but sometimes it just doesn’t pan out the way you would hope. That’s reality TV for you.

The Celebrity Traitors finale airs on BBC One at 8pm on 30 October

Grealish could have been Everton’s poster boy of a new era. Now his career is in limbo

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:50:09 GMT

After being dropped for ‘a breach of club discipline’, the winger must face the same questions about respect and self-awareness

For the biggest game in Manchester City’s history, Jack Grealish was given a starting berth while Phil Foden, Julián Alvarez and Riyad Mahrez were on the bench. Grealish played the full 90 minutes of the Champions League triumph against Inter because Pep Guardiola had the greatest faith in the attacking midfielder, but three years on he is at risk of being yesterday’s man.

That trust dwindled, not helped by injuries, and Grealish made only 17 Premier League starts over the next two seasons under Guardiola. City wanted him to leave in the summer of 2025, and Everton provided the solution, taking him on loan and borrowing him again for this season. Six Everton appearances into this campaign he was left out of the squad for Thursday’s Carabao Cup win against Newcastle after missing training on Monday. Everton went public with the fact that there had been “a breach of club discipline”.

Grealish is 31 and has 39 England caps. He is supposed to be a senior player but his career has involved far too many indiscretions. Breaking lockdown rules, a driving ban and more than once becoming a viral sensation for being pictured inebriated out and about have painted an unwanted picture. Learning from mistakes is part of life but Grealish’s indiscipline is apparently not dwindling with age. Guardiola warned him over his behaviour, dropping him in 2021 for a match against Newcastle after he and Foden arrived for training worse for wear.

Grealish is aware of his flaws, which is a starting point, but dealing with them is a separate matter. “People go: ‘He likes to go out, he likes to party,’ and I do,” Grealish told Sky Sports last year. “I want to be able to live my life and enjoy myself but obviously there’s a time and a place to do that. Sometimes, I’ll be honest with you, I probably haven’t picked the right times.”

Initially at Everton it seemed Grealish could be the poster boy of a new era. There were winners against Crystal Palace and Bournemouth by early December of last year and he had accumulated six assists in 20 Premier League appearances before his season was ended in mid-January by a foot injury. Grealish had been inconsistent, though. He has not played more than 28 league games in a season since 2019-20 at Aston Villa, which should concern him.

There were reservations at Everton about taking Grealish back this summer but Iliman Ndiaye’s sale to City made it a pragmatic move to fill the void. Grealish had carried out pre-season under Enzo Maresca, who gave him chances in the Community Shield and on the opening day against Bournemouth. The Italian had time for him but the unlikely redemption arc at City was soon quashed. Maresca showed affection for Grealish on Friday, saying: “I still think that he’s a good boy, big heart.”

At his best, Grealish is a wonderful player, a carefree spirit when dribbling with his socks around his ankles. In full flow, he gets fans up off their seats, makes and takes goalscoring chances and forces opponents to foul him, but those moments have been fleeting for far too long. The next seven months are crucial to Grealish’s career; he is at an age where he could play at the top for years but his status is declining rapidly. He is a £100m City signing and treble winner but those are past glories. Grealish needs to prove he has the respect for himself and for Everton to want more.

Grealish’s contract at City concludes at the end of the season, so there is plenty of incentive for him to show he is capable of shining in the Premier League and inspiring Everton to the cup win they crave. Instead, his career is in limbo. David Moyes was terse on the subject of Grealish on Thursday and seems unlikely to recommend keeping him beyond his loan. The Everton manager is working with a very small squad, so losing a senior player for avoidable reasons will surely frustrate and irritate him.

In an industry where the public is kept at arm’s length, Grealish is very approachable, happy to sign autographs for longer than his peers, eager to do the charity elements that come with playing for major clubs and known for his personal touch when others are businesslike. When entering and leaving Hill Dickinson Stadium, Grealish is mobbed, such is his popularity. He embraces it, posing for selfies with anyone who demands one, channelling a lot of positive energy into others, but he needs to find the self-awareness to do the same for himself.

“With me, I’m a big confidence player – I want to feel loved,” Grealish once said. He will not be feeling that from Moyes any time soon without radical change.

Australia set 288 to win on final day after South African centurions turn tide

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:40:33 GMT

Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder hit hundreds for hosts

Australia face last-day chase to clinch Test and the series

It would be unfair to say that Australia let a winning position slip on the fourth day of the third Test at Cape Town, only because that would undersell how Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder prised it away. Australia’s vaunted four bowlers, owners of 1,674 wickets at day’s beginning, could only raise that to 1,678 by day’s end. In the process, a lead of 40 became 287. South Africa had been 40 for four in the first innings at Gqeberha and bounced back to win; they were effectively 40 for four in the third innings here, and now have a great chance to do the same.

The unlikely basis was Rickelton, a franchise circuiteer who spends most of his year smiting runs or keeping wicket in 20-over blocks. In this series he was monstered in Durban by Josh Hazlewood, out for none and two while pinch-hitting as an opener, then made scant impression down the order with 31 in Gqeberha. He looked like a modern cricketer become anachronism in this ancient form.

Yet, while Rickelton strikes at 150 runs per hundred balls across his T20 career, his first-class rate is one third of that speed. There are strings to his bow that are not dyed royal blue by the global Mumbai Indians conglomerate. That was the particular set of skills he employed here, disavowing the lead of his top order the day before in assuming that a placid surface was made for rollicking shots. Instead, he and fellow white-ball dasher Matthew Breetzke absorbed everything that Australia’s freshly rested bowlers could hurl at them.

On a pitch without lateral movement, there was still good bounce for the short ball, and increasingly marked turn for Nathan Lyon out of the footmarks. The pair dealt with both, while Rickelton showed a facility to punctuate defence with a single in most overs, keeping the innings at least rolling in first gear. The first session added 62 runs, the lead 102.

Still, the lunchtime wicket of Breetzke looked to have turned things Australia’s way, finally impulsive as he pulled to long leg. That ended a streak for Pat Cummins of 372 balls without a wicket, unprecedented in his career, despite some good spells along the way. But Rickelton was now set like cement, and Mulder joined him in that durability, to lunch and beyond.

Lyon kept ripping his off-breaks, with an inside edge from Rickelton into Alex Carey’s shin behind the stumps, and umpteen balls that landed safely after deflecting off body or bat, but reward never came. Mulder took the occasional chance attacking spin. Rickelton kept picking off rare bad balls from the quicks, driving down the ground when overpitched, backing himself on the up once the new ball showed no signs of seam. The pair tormented the Australians until well into the final session, Rickelton’s century coming after a slow march through the 90s, the partnership reaching 154 and South Africa’s lead an increasingly daunting 235 on that rapidly wearing pitch, before his departure set off a late burst of activity. Much of it involved the livewire Marnus Labuschagne, out of runs but still a red-cordial kindergarten class in the field, getting vast turn with his leg-breaks as Mulder kept sweeping him outside leg stump, where the only risk was a gloved catch.

Yet when Mulder changed tack, repeatedly reverse-sweeping that same line while aiming for the exposed off-side fence, a full toss that would normally disappear over square leg was instead hit to the only fielder in an acre, Inglis at backward point, who spotted Rickelton running and Mulder standing still. Labuschagne at the bowler’s end was quick enough to gather the throw: Rickelton run out for 101.

With tired Aussies and 70 minutes to go, things were set up for a Marco Jansen blitz, but he followed the team trend of holing out on the pull, hitting Starc to Lyon for nought. Lyon finally got his first wicket for the day when the opposing off-spinner Simon Harmer shouldered arms on one, big turn doing the trick, then Gerald Coetzee ran himself out for the same score, Labuschagne bobbing up again with a sizzling direct hit from the cordon to the non-striker’s end.

Nine down and 251 ahead, South Africa’s lead suddenly looked light. But Mulder fixed that with Kagiso Rabada as support, also taking care of the small personal matter of moving his score from 82 to 115, farming strike for long periods between targeting boundaries. He was finally caught down the ground from a cross-bat shot at Cummins in the last over of the day, trying to hit a fifth six.

A neatly apportioned match that already had one full innings occupy the entire first day will now have another full innings occupy the fifth. A target of 288 is perfectly balanced for a match that has been so even. At the last, it must tilt one way or the other, and with it the series.

North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:35:44 GMT

Binance exchange says it will cover customer losses as it scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far

Q&A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?

Tell us: have you been affected by the Binance hack?

Business live – latest updates

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.

Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets.

Analysts said the exchange had been subjected to an unprecedented attack with “never-seen-before” laundering patterns as the hackers made off with assets worth billions of dollars.

Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.

Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in the previous record crypto heist.

TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been “additional points of breach” in a sophisticated attack.

Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report.

Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.” Teng said Binance had set aside $6.34bn to cover stolen assets.

The company was founded by the Chinese-born entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao, now a Canadian and United Arab Emirates citizen, who was jailed for four months in 2024 after pleading guilty to money laundering violations. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

The company said: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.”

Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.

Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.

In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.”

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.

North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered. The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.

Binance ⁠is working on the aftermath of the hack with law enforcement ⁠around ⁠the world, ​including the FBI and the US Secret Service.
