Tether, an issuer of stablecoins, which trade at a value fixed to a conventional currency like the US dollar, said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m. The largest losses related to the Ethereum cryptocurrency, with $3.8bn-worth affected, according to Elliptic.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.

The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across almost 150 attacks, according to TRM. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget ‌said roughly $350m in crypto had ​been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability ​to hackers.

Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.

Binance. US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.

The UK’s financial watchdogs are monitoring the hack for any potential fallout. While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system.

Poundland in peril: how rampant inflation and price wars left £1 stores exposed

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:20:41 GMT

With the chain on the brink of administration, its low-profile US owners face questions about their conduct

‘It was a very successful and simple proposition,” laments one former Poundland boss. With every product in the shop sold at £1, and the price in its name, its proposition to shoppers was the clearest of any UK high street chain.

Now the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer could disappear amid heavy competition and inflation that has eaten into its ability to offer bargains.

Its potential collapse has brought distress for its up to 12,000 staff in the run-up to Christmas, and as shoppers head to the chain for Halloween costumes and treats.

Meanwhile, its low-profile owners are facing questions from the prime minister over their behaviour in the week his government’s budget attempted to offer support to the high street.

Poundland’s future hangs in the balance – and not for the first time – after the 36-year-old retailer filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process.

The legal measure protects Poundland, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland, from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. However, the prospect of it avoiding mass store closures and job losses diminishes by the day as suppliers hold back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade.

The chain’s potential demise comes after Gordon Brothers, the American restructuring specialist which bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner in June last year, rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the whole chain by Martin Property Group.

While the Northern Irish firm is still in talks about taking on Poundland, it is understood its offer amounts to about £15m. That would pay off only half the £30m shareholder loan, the majority of which was taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the company. The deal would also include taking on a further, asset-backed loan worth about £90m, it is understood.

This deal has been rejected by Gordon Brothers despite Pepco, Poundland’s former owner, which holds the other £7.5m of the debt, being prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business, as first reported by Sky News.

One source who knows Poundland well said that Gordon Brothers had already taken about £10m in fees and interest out of the chain in the last year and that wanting another £30m was “egregious”. Gordon Brothers did not respond to a request for comment and has not confirmed this figure.

Gordon Brothers said earlier this week that options for the whole and parts of the business “are being thoroughly and objectively evaluated, with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland’s people and all relevant stakeholders”.

Sources close to the process said Gordon Brothers was unwilling to accept the Martin deal as the latest offer includes only about £7.5m up front and the rest over the next two years, leaving uncertainty for creditors, staff and suppliers.

One source said Gordon Brothers had sought bidders for the whole of Poundland but “the market had spoken” and only one little-known financial bidder with no history of running a large retail chain in the UK had come forward who might only go on to break up Poundland itself.

Instead, the restructuring specialist is understood to believe that suppliers and staff would be safer with the “trusted established retail operators” who have already put forward firm offers for parcels of outlets that amount to about half of Poundland’s stores, which could be converted to their formats.

A deal may yet be agreed with Martin over the next 10 days, especially with political pressure from Andy Burnham. On Friday, he told the Telegraph: “We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn’t been accepted, then the business secretary and I want to know why that is the case.”

For now, Gordon Brothers appears more keen on a break-up after losing faith in the likelihood of Poundland finding a route to long-term profitability amid tough times on the high street and heavy competition.

Rapid inflation on the cost of goods and labour, energy and business rates in recent years has forced Poundland to take a hit on profits and sell products for more than £1, including items for £5 or more.

In the past, Poundland removed products if it could not sell them profitably for a pound, but its choices have become more limited. High inflation – triggered first by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and then the Middle East conflict – has exposed a business model which always appeared to have a shelf life.

In most supermarkets a two-litre bottle of milk costs over £2, a pack of KitKats is at least £1.50 and a tin of Heinz baked beans is about £1.40, according to the price comparison site Trolley. Cutting the size of Poundland has, meanwhile, reduced its scale, making it harder to get good deals from suppliers to protect margins.

Poundland has also admitted that it made mistakes in recent years, including putting its Pepco clothing ranges into stores, which proved unpopular with UK shoppers.

The expansion of cut-price chains such as Savers, The Range, B&M, The Works and Home Bargains alongside budget online rivals such as Temu, Shein and Amazon means the cheaper end of the UK retail market is now very crowded.

Meanwhile, the low-wage shoppers that make up the core of Poundland’s clientele have little spare cash for non-essentials amid rising household bills. Those with more to spare have more options in their supermarket shop, where they are increasingly locked in by loyalty-card-linked discounts.

Poundland’s pre-tax losses widened to £85.3m in the year to September 2025, from a loss of £45.4m in 2024, as sales at its outlets in the UK, Republic of Ireland and Isle of Man slid almost 12% to £1.55bn, according to accounts filed at Companies House.

In September Poundland said its revenues had returned to growth, up 3.3% at established stores in the latest three-month period, but sources said the business was not generating enough cash to pay off its loans.

US-headquartered Gordon Brothers has a long history of involvement in selling off the assets of UK high street businesses, including offloading the stock and and fittings of failed retailers such as Toys R Us.

It previously owned the British fashion brands Laura Ashley and Ben Sherman, where it oversaw the closure of their stores, and it recently bought LK Bennett, which has also closed its stores this year.

One advisory expert said Poundland’s owners had intended the buyout to be a rescue operation rather than a break-up but ultimately: “Gordon Brothers has ended up doing what Gordon Brothers do. Leopards do not change their spots.”

He said Gordon Brothers was likely to “come out looking like the worst version” of a restructuring firm. The number of stores likely not to find an immediate buyer “might not be as catastrophic as half” but it was unlikely buyers would be found for all, he added.

Poundland’s possible demise is part of a wave of consolidation of similar outlets over the past decade.

Poundworld closed its 350 stores in 2018, and Poundland bought its rival 99p Stores in 2015. Poundland then closed about 200 of its then 800 UK stores in a restructuring last year.

Poundstretcher was bought by Majestic Wine’s owner, Fortress, in 2024.

Poundland itself has a rocky history during which it has passed in and out of the hands of investment firms. Founded with one store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, the company was listed on the London Stock Exchange in 2014 at a value of about £750m by its then owner, the buyout firm Warburg Pincus.

Just two years later, Poundland agreed to a £597m takeover by Steinhoff, the South African retail conglomerate, after the British chain struggled to digest the takeover of 99p stores.

By 2018, Poundland had to seek new investment after an accounting scandal at Steinhoff and was hived off into Pepco, a company formed from Steinhoff’s European retail business. Poundland was then preparing to rejoin the London stock market when the Covid pandemic hit in 2020, scotching those plans as high streets across the UK closed down for months.

Last year, with costs rising, Pepco was looking to sell. Gordon Brothers stepped in, snapping up the struggling chain with its £1 deal. It remains unclear whether someone new will flip another coin to bet on turning Poundland around.

Putellas provides mindset change as London City bid to upstage champions

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:16:24 GMT

Ballon d’Or winner’s move to WSL has transformed the Lionesses on and off the pitch with belief soaring ahead of Manchester City clash

As Martin Semmens, the London City Lionesses chief executive, sits down is his office he looks like the cat that got the cream. He says he has just learned that the club’s Instagram page has generated 34m hits since Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d’Or on Monday evening, and it is only Thursday afternoon. On Sunday, two clubs with seven of the top 30 players in the Ballon d’Or rankings will go head-to-head when Manchester City visit Hayes Lane, Bromley. It is, Semmens, says, “awesome for the WSL”.

From the outside, it can feel slightly surreal. The independent women’s club, owned by the businesswoman Michele Kang, are third in the top flight, two‑and‑a‑half years after finishing eighth in tier two, and Semmens believes signing the world’s best player has helped change the mindset of everyone at the club.

“Her impact on our commercial business is extraordinary,” he says. “From a leadership point of view, she allows us to start thinking about really winning. The environment today feels like it can beat Man City on Sunday and that’s a lot down to her.”

He acknowledges that Putellas, a World Cup winner with Spain and four-time European champion with Barcelona, and her brand – she has more Instagram followers (3.7m) than a men’s club the size of Porto, for example – were pivotal in helping the club secure what they claim is the largest front-of-shirt sponsorship deal in the women’s game, with Nike. The club say it is worth more than the new NWSL franchise Atlanta’s sponsorship of $4m (£3m) a year.

“It’s insanely big,” Semmens says. “Our view on how to run this business, rightly or wrongly, was to invest first, invest in the everything to make it awesome, and then the commercial deal will be big. The other way, of: ‘Let’s sit back, let’s grow a fanbase, let’s wait for the money to come’ – we don’t have the patience for that. Michele’s vision was: ‘I’m going to invest now to prove that we can bring these deals in.’ That deal allows us to kick forward, it allows us to keep investing in players and infrastructure, because without it, we’re just burning Michele’s money, which is not the plan.”

Even with Kang’s money, signing a player who had been loyal to Barcelona for 14 years was never going to be straightforward. Semmens, the former Southampton chief executive, says: “The conversation went: ‘Wait until I’ve finished winning a Champions League with Barcelona and then we’ll have a conversation,’ which we loved and we respected, but we always had a feeling she would come.

“I think she had bought into four or five significant things. One, that we are independent, we’re a women’s-first environment. [Two] there’s a lot of power in coming to London, as a city. The WSL is important – people see WSL as the growth brand. And, after that, Michele had an unbelievably massive impact [on Putellas’s decision]. Alexia said to me: ‘Well, she said she was going to do all this stuff and she’s done it. So I want to be part of that.’ And then also, it allows her to have a legacy in the future – she will grow this club to a point where she’s creating a pathway for the next young players to come through in London.”

There are questions facing the club in relation to how much they have been spending and eyebrows were raised – to put it mildly – around the rest of the league when London City recorded an operating loss of more than 10 times their revenue for the 2024-25 season, when they won promotion as second-tier champions. Since then salary cap rules have been introduced in the WSL, stating no club’s player wage bill can exceed the following figures combined: 80% of revenue, plus up to £4m or a further 25% of revenue (whichever is higher).

Last season, when London City finished sixth, the league’s handbook said no punishments would be dished out for any breaches of that cap for that campaign only. From this term, points deductions could apply, which is one reason why it was imperative to increase commercial revenues. But were they within the rules last term?

after newsletter promotion

“We are 100% within the rules, we will always be,” Semmens says. “It’s so important to Michele.” He says the “goal of the business” is to be profitable within five years and likens last year’s investments to a “start-up fund”: “The [salary cap] rules were set up with a clear understanding that they wouldn’t come until this year. The handbook is 100% clear. We want to see investment coming into the women’s game. Anything that kind of restricts positive and good investment obviously worries [me] but there is a need for rules and we’re 100% fine with that. We are super-transparent. We can reassure the fans that we are financially viable, sustainable, and we’ve made serious investments over the last two years to be profitable and successful in the future.”

Another question facing the club, particularly given their league position, is whether they would be eligible to compete in the Women’s Champions League, given Kang also owns the record eight-time European champions OL Lyonnes in France. Semmens says in reference to Uefa’s multi-club ownership rules: “One hundred per cent, it can be resolved. We will continue to argue the case that you should be able to [invest into multiple clubs] to see the women’s game accelerated.“It’s not about exchanging players like the men’s game. It’s not about one club dominating and the other being a feeder club. It’s a different model but we fully understand and respect the rules. Therefore, we will set ourselves up in a way where we’re allowed to and can compete in Europe together. There are clear rules, clear precedents in the men’s game and clear things you can do to allow both teams to flourish. We’re fully aware of that and we’ll comply with the rules.”

London City are three points off Chelsea and Manchester City, and Semmens says the aim is to “build a squad that is consistently in the top three”. He is looking forward to Sunday. “This is probably the No 1 game in the women’s game in the world this weekend,” he says. “That’s what we want to be: on the map.”

I wrote a book about death. Here’s what people really think about dying

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:00:17 GMT

In the eight years since my graphic novel on death published, I’ve learned readers of all ages want to talk about loss and preserve their family’s stories

Becoming an author in my late 50s was unexpected, the result of my daughter Hallie’s own existential anxiety in her early 20s.

Fearing my untimely demise, she begged me to write down advice that would cover all of life’s bases going forward. I agreed, but put the project off for years; it wasn’t until she cornered me with a laptop on vacation that I gave in. She asked countless questions, and I found, to my surprise, that I had plenty to say. Hallie helped shape the manuscript, and then spent a year painting its warmly emotional gouache illustrations.

Our graphic novel, What to Do When I’m Gone: A Mother’s Wisdom to Her Daughter, was published in 2018. Though marketed for mothers and daughters, it holds my advice to all three of my children on moving forward after I die. Included are notes on grief and loss and life, plus a few recipes – not because I’m a great cook, but because food is so integral to family heritage. The book is a lighthearted, emotional and highly illustrated ode to moving forward and living life fully while grieving the loss of a parent or, really, anyone you love.

What we’ve learned in the eight years since its release is that readers of all ages have a deep hunger to know more about their parents’ backgrounds, beliefs and values, including around grief and loss.

They want to talk about all of it.

Gone wasn’t exactly a hot property. All but one publisher rejected it, uncertain who would buy a book on death and grief. But Bloomsbury editor Nancy Miller saw potential for broad readership. Eight years later, it has been published in seven languages and continues to find new readers.

The book has brought us comments from around the world. The most common:

I lost a parent (or other loved one, including spouse or beloved pet) and your book helped me through.

I gave the book to my kids and wrote my own notes in the margins.

I can’t bear the thought of my mom or dad dying, but they don’t want to talk about it. I’m hoping that sharing the book with them will start some conversations.

But the most frequent sentiment we hear is: My mom or dad died, and I wish they had left me something like this.

In book events in New York and on the west coast, invariably, someone in the audience was crying. Sometimes, it was because of the person’s fractured relationship with their mother, and grieving the loss that represents. Most often, it was because they missed their mom or dad, and did not have a record of their unique voice and wisdom to lean on.

There is science behind this hunger to know more, to deepen this vital connection between the generations. Studies have shown that knowing more about family history, including weathering hard times, is good for mental health and identity formation.

I understand that hunger to know more, both as a longtime journalist and as a daughter. Years before Hallie coaxed me into doing our book, I wanted to capture my own mother’s story and did a series of interviews with her. Two decades after her death at 85, the slim memoir that resulted preserves her voice, wit and love for family.

At the moment she died, I was at her bedside holding her frail hand when, suddenly, I was swept into an invisible cyclone of memories and feelings that lasted for several minutes – and left me stunned.

Years later, that otherworldly experience helped me pen the closing pages of our book.

But this isn’t an ad for Gone. You, like some readers, might even hate it: “It just rambles on about recipes and driving a car off a cliff and being trampled in a Black Friday sale and replacing your mother with someone else,” wrote one Amazon customer called Christine. “Is there even a point to the book?”

Yes, Christine, there is a point. Two, actually:

Love endures long after the person we love dies.

Talk about your beliefs, history and values with the people you love while you’re alive; share the stories that are yours, and in turn, theirs.

Thankfully most readers seemed to understand, given all the feedback we’ve received. Some found themselves “ugly crying” in bookstores (though the book is funnier than it sounds) and many sent notes or wrote emotional reactions online.

“As someone who has lost their mom, it’s something I reach for often when I need a hug from her,” Dara wrote. Natsu shared the book with her mother, who then wrote her own book – each section named after a favorite song – which Natsu spent a year illustrating. Some readers acknowledged that their parents would have very different advice from mine, but echoed that universal desire for help finding their way forward.

My twin grandchildren may need such help.

At two and a half, they are little human yardsticks by which I measure my remaining years. I may be around for their high school and perhaps college graduations, but clearly, the first decades of their lives will be the last decades of mine. And the older I get, the more I appreciate simple days, simple problems: hangry toddlers, high grass that needs mowing.

I can fix these, unlike the world’s larger problems: the climate crisis, injustice, greed, the othering and abuse and killing of entire populations.

These children, and their children, will need help making their way through chaos we cannot yet fully imagine.

But there is a book.

In it, they will see the sense of humor and worldview Hallie and I share, and perhaps better understand their own. When they hit hard times, I hope they will find comfort in its pages.

So, Christine, the underlying message is this: Think about what you will leave behind.

Hallie and I always intended that Gone would encourage other families to have these deeper conversations: why you chose the paths you did, what you truly care about and why, how you think about death and grief and what’s beyond. The only real requirement is willingness to examine what you believe.

Each person’s life leaves an imprint, and that imprint most affects the people we love – those who are here and those yet to come. Tell them what really matters.

Because, as many people around the world have told us, it all matters more than you will ever know.

Suzy Hopkins, a former newspaper reporter and magazine editor, is the author of What to Do When I’m Gone and What to Do When You Get Dumped. She lives in Cincinnati, Ohio. She previously wrote about the unique grief of divorce for the Guardian.

‘It really was the idiots in charge’: inside the TV sketch show that launched a generation of stars

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:33:19 GMT

It influenced The Simpsons and sparked the careers of Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, John Candy and many others. Now this extraordinary Canadian series is finally getting its due

SCTV – short for Second City Television – is one of most influential comedy shows ever created. In the 1970s and 80s, while North American comedy fans worshipped at the altar of Saturday Night Live, the comedy nerds loved SCTV. The Canadian sketch show was weird. It was dark. It was multilayered and years ahead of its time.

Dave Thomas, head writer and an original cast member, was there from the start. “Conan O’Brien said that he used to watch and he thought, ‘This show is being written specifically for me,’” Thomas tells me. “There were references in it that he was absolutely sure only he got. We wrote at the top of our reference level. And the idea was to see if the audience would meet us there.”

Thomas was part of an astonishingly talented cast that included John Candy, Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, Rick Moranis, Joe Flaherty, Martin Short, Harold Ramis and Andrea Martin. They wrote and starred in the series, which ran intermittently in Canada from 1976 to 1984. At a time when American shows dominated the airwaves, and homegrown content tended to be earnest factual programmes along the lines of Hinterland Who’s Who, Canadian audiences were delighted to see a show that reflected their culture while being – to everyone’s surprise – actually funny. It even went on to find a late-night audience in the US.

To celebrate its legacy, Netflix has just added 134 episodes of SCTV to coincide with its release of a new documentary – SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of. Like many of the show’s fans, Thomas isn’t exactly enamoured with the title.

“Yeah, the title is kind of insulting in a way,” he says.

That’s not the only problem. While it’s a decent primer for revisiting the show, featuring new interviews with the surviving cast members, including Thomas, the documentary could have been so much more. Many things are skipped over, such as the musical acts, including bands like the Boomtown Rats and the Plasmatics, who didn’t just perform but also appeared in sketches. And while the cast took care of the writing in the show’s early days, they were later joined by talented staff. These omissions rankle with Thomas.

“Tom Hanks and Bob Odenkirk doing the narrative on how it was written? I thought, what the fuck? Why don’t you ask some of the people who wrote it? We had some really good writers on that show.”

There is a cracking story to be told. For the uninitiated: the cast of Chicago’s legendary Second City improv theatre had already been plundered by producer Lorne Michaels to create Saturday Night Live in 1975. It seemed to make perfect sense to use Second City’s Toronto outpost to create a Canadian version of SNL. Gilda Radner and Dan Aykroyd had already been poached by Michaels, so the remaining cast members were asked to make a television sketch show without knowing the first thing about it.

“For the first two seasons, SCTV was a failure,” Thomas remembers. “It was the poor brother of SNL. Our greatest weakness was that our show looked cheap as shit. So we made it about a small television station, and that’s why it looks so cheap.”

Each episode of SCTV covered one broadcast day for a run-down TV station in the fictional rural Canadian town of Melonville. As well as parodying the film and TV of the time, the backstage dramas of the station also played a part.

“We were learning,” Thomas tells me. “We were being paid to learn how to produce television while doing it. It really was the idiots running the asylum for the first two years. There are a lot of things we got credit for that were just horrible mistakes.”

The naivety of the cast and the low budget, paradoxically, freed up the sketch-writers: without shiny sets and special effects, they focused on characters. There was the overbearing station manager Guy Caballero, the cheapskate’s cheapskate; the garrulous variety star Johnny LaRue, who was an extension of John Candy’s party-loving nature; Catherine O’Hara’s showgirl Lola Heatherton; Eugene Levy’s appalling standup, Bobby Bittman; and Harry, the Guy With a Snake on his Face. Sketches were smart, sharp and featured startlingly accurate impressions (Thomas’s Bob Hope was a standout).

As time went on, the show found its feet, started gaining an audience, increased its budget and grew more sophisticated.

“I was particularly proud of the evolution of the comedy,” Thomas remembers. “Like the parody of the television show Fantasy Island, which was also a parody of Casablanca, and also a parody of Road to Morocco, and also a parody of The Wizard of Oz, all weaved in and out. A lot of the Simpsons writers said that’s what they loved about SCTV, that it brought in a kind of a multilayered writing. And they said: that’s the way we write The Simpsons.”

But as the money came in, the creators’ freedom dwindled. Used to having everything their own way, the cast and writers baulked when threatened with any outside interference.

“I remember one of the producers that NBC had sent up was in the cafeteria one morning, crying,” recalls Thomas. “I said, ‘What’s the matter?’ He goes, ‘The goddamn cast, they shut me out. They stonewall me. I’ve got a good mind to quit.’ And I said, ‘Well, you probably should quit because you’re here in the cafeteria, crying. Is that what you had in mind when you got into showbiz?’”

Being produced in isolation gave SCTV a distinct personality and a legion of devoted fans. But the team were still very much on the outside.

“We went to New York for a press conference,” Thomas says. “There were only three people there and two of them were student journalists. But we thought, well, screw this press conference, let’s go to Studio 54. We’re on television. We should be able to get in. They wouldn’t let us in.”

Thomas and Rick Moranis (later to star in Ghostbusters, with Harold Ramis, and Honey, I Shrunk the Kids) were part of SCTV’s most surprising breakout success. Asked to include more specifically Canadian content in the series, they improvised two-minute pieces to camera featuring two dim-witted, beer-swilling, hockey-watching Canucks, Bob and Doug McKenzie. The characters caught on: Canadians, so used to watching American stereotypes played for laughs on TV, loved seeing two of their own get the same treatment. The documentary shows Beatles-like levels of hysteria at McKenzie brother appearances. They went on to record albums and make a film.

Not everyone in the cast was delighted by all this, as Thomas admits. “There’s no question that the success of the McKenzie brothers was a divisive factor and played a role in Rick and I leaving. There were little things like that which definitely sowed some seeds of division, but we were still family.”

The show shifted networks, time slots and cast members until it eventually fizzled out in 1984. But the SCTV family went on to greater heights. John Candy became a Hollywood star. Eugene Levy and Catherine O’Hara featured in many of Christopher Guest’s comedies (including Best in Show and A Mighty Wind), as well as starring in Schitt’s Creek together. Martin Short is, well, Martin Short.

And Thomas has a wildly varied career: he starred in the sitcom Grace Under Fire, wrote Spies Like Us with Dan Aykroyd, started an animation company and is now developing an Amazon show with his son. But Thomas will always be fiercely proud of his SCTV achievements.

“I loved that show because, I thought, nobody’s doing this. Nobody is doing a show like this. There was a network tendency to dumb everything down to the stupidest person in the room. And we didn’t do that.”

SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of streams on Netflix from 30 October

This is the hard lesson from Israel’s election: to stop nationalist populists, you can’t play by gentlemen’s rules

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:12:57 GMT

The opposition can’t win unless they join forces with Arab parties. Benjamin Netanyahu knows this, and will use every ruse to stay in power

It’s less an election result than a philosophical puzzle: what happens when a win contains a loss, a loss contains a win and the two collide? That’s the question posed by the confused and confusing outcome of this week’s Israeli election, one that, despite its murky uncertainty, offers clear, sharp lessons – both for that country and for those locked in combat with nationalist populists across the globe.

Start with the result that has simultaneously handed Benjamin Netanyahu a devastating defeat and a strong chance of staying on as prime minister, extending a run that has seen him lead Israel, on and off, for more than 19 of the past 30 years. The defeat is clear enough. At a stroke, his parliamentary majority was wiped out. Before Tuesday, the parties that together comprised his ruling coalition controlled 68 of the Knesset’s 120 seats: that tally has now shrunk to just 53, far short of the 61 seats needed for power. That’s a loss in anybody’s language.

And yet, Netanyahu does not look or sound like a man defeated. That’s because he knows that while the parties arrayed against him won many more seats than he did – 67 to his 53 – their chances of forming a government are slim. If they fail, one or two of them might peel away and enter a so-called national-unity government – under Netanyahu as PM – or there will have to be fresh elections, ones from which, most analysts agree, Netanyahu would emerge stronger.

The opposition’s problem is not arithmetical. It goes much deeper. Put simply, a big chunk of the anti-Netanyahu seats were won by parties that chiefly represent the one in five Israeli citizens who are Palestinian. This was the big twist of Tuesday’s election, a huge surge in turnout for what Israelis refer to as the Arab parties. Usually, far more Jewish than Arab Israelis participate in the country’s elections, but this year that pattern was flipped: turnout in Palestinian communities inside Israel hit 80%. The result is a record total of 19 seats for Arab-led parties. The anti-Netanyahu bloc cannot form a government without them. In today’s Israel, Palestinian politicians are the kingmakers.

On paper, the next step might look straightforward enough. All Netanyahu’s Jewish opponents need do is team up with their Arab colleagues and they can send the PM packing. But such an alliance would mark a watershed in Israeli history. It would mean breaking a taboo that has endured, with only fleeting exceptions, since the founding of the state, a taboo rooted in mutual suspicion.

On the one hand, Israel’s Jewish-led parties have long shunned the mainly Arab parties because the latter identify as anti- or non-Zionist, meaning they reject Israel’s self-definition as a Jewish state. For that same reason, Arab-led parties have maintained a boycott, refusing to legitimate the Israeli state by participating in its government.

In 2021, a short-lived “government of change” broke the taboo by including in its ranks Ra’am, an Islamist party regarded, improbably enough, as the most moderate of the Arab groupings. But after the Hamas massacres of 7 October 2023, the taboo was restored – and hardened. Netanyahu cast Palestinian-Israeli politicians as an enemy within, as tacit allies of the Hamas killers, a framing buttressed by a crude anti-Arab racism voiced most explicitly by his coalition allies – the likes of Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich – and which sought to delegitimise Israel’s entire Arab minority.

This was Netanyahu’s core message throughout the campaign: you can’t trust my opponents because, when the moment comes, they will sit with “the Arabs”. In recent days, he and his allies have doubled down on that message, claiming high Palestinian turnout means that “the Arabs are stealing the election” – rather than merely exercising their democratic rights – and, on Thursday, alleging that Qatar paid Palestinian-Israeli citizens to vote, thereby rendering the entire result void.

Instead of challenging Netanyahu’s framing, and insisting that the vote of every citizen, Arab or Jewish, is of equal worth, most of the main opposition parties – Yair Golan’s Democrats were the exception – bowed to it, pledging that they would not forge a coalition with the largely Arab parties, and certainly not with any group more radical than Ra’am. Now they find themselves in a bind. On their own, the Jewish-led opposition cannot form a government. Unless they somehow manage to lure defectors from Netanyahu’s bloc – perhaps one or both of the ultra-Orthodox parties – even Ra’am’s support won’t be enough to reach the magic number of 61. They need Arab partners – and probably several of them.

This, then, is the big lesson for Israel. That group that has long opposed Netanyahu – Jewish-Israelis who despise a PM on trial for corruption, who has mounted serial assaults on Israel’s institutions, including the supreme court, and brought isolation, if not pariah status, upon the country – are now confronted with a fact that has long been true but which they have preferred not to see: that they are a minority in the land they once dominated. As Aluf Benn, editor of the liberal daily Haaretz, told me: “The Jewish vote is predominantly rightwing in Israel and has been for decades.”

That means the Jewish Israeli opposition cannot win alone. This week stands as proof, because this was their perfect opportunity. Netanyahu was at his lowest ebb, the leader on whose watch the most calamitous day in Israeli history took place, the leader who promised to destroy Hamas in Gaza, but who succeeded only in turning that place into a ruin, killing tens of thousands and, in the process, destroying Israel’s standing in the world. He faced in Gadi Eisenkot, his lead challenger, a decorated former general rooted in the Mizrahi working class, a man universally regarded as honest and decent, a bereaved father whose own son fell in the Gaza war – a man, in other words, who might have been designed to appeal to the very voters who for so long have been beyond the opposition’s reach. And yet none of that was enough to win.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The only way the opposition can succeed is by making common cause with their Palestinian fellow citizens, just as Democrats in the US – who have not won a majority of the white vote since 1964 – could never win the presidency without the support of Black Americans. No one should underestimate the scale of the task, which requires a deep cultural shift as much as a political one. It should have been the work of decades, rather than a panicked scramble in a few rushed weeks of coalition horse-trading. It demands a reshaping of Israeli society, breaking a pattern of systemic discrimination and inequality within the country that has existed since the founding of the state (to say nothing of the post-1967 occupied territories where, of course, millions of Palestinians have no vote at all in Israeli elections). That task was always essential, but this week has confirmed that, if the right’s lock on power is ever to be broken, it can be delayed no longer.

Much of this is peculiar to the unique political terrain of Israel. But there are broader lessons for all those fighting nationalist populism, whether that be Donald Trump in next week’s US midterms, Marine Le Pen in France or Nigel Farage in Britain. First, don’t accept the terms laid down by the other side: that was the cardinal error made by Netanyahu’s challengers. Second, mere opposition and criticism is not enough. The nationalist populists will always tell a compelling story; you have to tell an equally compelling one of your own. And, last, you need to be every bit as determined as they are. Too often you play by gentlemen’s rules, when those you are fighting are anything but gentlemen. Netanyahu is without shame and will do anything – cross every line, cut any deal – to keep power. The opponents of such a man will prevail only if they show an equal resolve in seizing it.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:06:39 GMT

Archaeologists uncover jewellery, cosmetics and coins in cabinet sealed since eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79

Fragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to coins and a child’s necklace, have been found tucked away in a wooden wardrobe sealed off for almost 2,000 years in the ruins of Pompeii.

The artifacts provide an intimate glimpse of daily life in the ancient Roman city before it was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The wardrobe was discovered in a room of a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, which was one of the most bustling streets in Pompeii.

The items inside included tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner and a bronze lantern.

But the most intriguing relic was a necklace featuring more than 20 small charms crafted from various materials and representing several deities, including depictions of the gods Bes and Mercury.

The type of necklace, known as a crepundia, was traditionally worn by children. Its decorative charms rattled to help parents keep track of their children and could also help them be identified.

“A crepundia had a very special function,” said Gabriel Zuchtriegel, the director of Pompeii archaeological park.

“It was a reminder of their parents who perhaps lived far away … it was very typical of this society of people, who were often displaced. Many people moved around in the Mediterranean area and tended to carry personal objects with them.”

The wardrobe contained other items including 38 bronze coins, cooking pots and a wooden box with lead weights, suggesting that someone who lived in the home was a tradesperson.

The fact that money and personal objects were left behind could point to the owners having to flee the eruption at short notice, Zuchtriegel said.

Archaeologists also found the fragmented skeletons of two mice inside an amphora that had been kept in a storage area of the home.

The home had previously been associated with a person called Cornelius Maximus owing to the discovery of inscriptions, which are no longer visible. Its ​facade was first excavated ​in 1912, but experts are only now delving into some of its rooms as part of a wider restoration project.

There are also excavations under way at the Villa of the Mysteries in a suburb of Pompeii, which also first came to light in the early 20th century.

“It’s never been completely excavated, so we kind of want to finish the job,” said Zuchtriegel. “What’s interesting is that we’re not excavating in the part where the owners lived and where great frescoes are to be expected, but in the servants’ quarters.

“So what we hope to find there is more insight into the daily life and economy of those who were somehow in the shadow of history. The majority of the inhabitants in the Villa of the Mysteries were actually servants.”

Excavations at Pompeii regularly yield discoveries from the ruins of the ancient city. In 2025, a large and sophisticated thermal bath complex, which was thought to have been used by its owner to woo well-heeled guests, was found during excavations of a home on Via di Nola in Regio IX, a wealthy district of the city.

A home containing a cramped bakery, where enslaved people were believed to have been imprisoned and made to produce bread, was found in the same district in 2023.

Buy a wind-up radio – and don’t forget the chocolate: survival experts on how to prepare for an emergency

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:00:17 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

UK government guidance says we should be ready for the unexpected, but what’s actually helpful to have at home? We ask the specialists

The best power banks – tested

How prepared are you for an emergency? Do you have a few extra tins of beans in the cupboard, or a full-on preppers’ kit in the cellar? While no one likes to think about worst-case scenarios, you can’t have failed to notice the growing noise around being sensibly, practically ready for floods, power cuts, cyber-attacks and other events.

The government launched its Be Ready campaign in October with guidance on how to prepare for emergencies, including a list of suggested items to have at home.

To help you understand what to buy, and where to buy it from, we asked survival, medical and nutritional experts for their advice. “There’s lots of panic about upcoming floods, El Niño and AI attacks, but this emergency preparedness is something we all should be doing anyway. It’s just a good idea to look after yourself and your family like this,” says Hannah Cloke, regius professor of meteorology and climate science at the University of Reading. And if you are in a position to do so, consider donating to a charity like Trussell to help support one of the almost one in 10 UK households already experiencing food insecurity.

From wind-up radios to water filters, here’s what the experts recommend adding to your list.

Are you stocking up on essential items at home? What products have you found useful for past events such as power cuts or being without water? Please let us know how you’re following government advice at thefilter@theguardian. com.

“Top of my list is a good first aid kit with sterile dressings that you can cut to size, not just little plasters, and some kind of tape to secure it with,” says John Hudson, chief survival instructor to the UK military and author of How to Survive: Lessons for Everyday Life from the Extreme World. “Zinc oxide tape is good because it’s super sticky and can be used for blisters. Other basics include crepe or elastic roller bandages, sterile eye pads, blunt-ended scissors, tweezers, safety pins or clips, alcohol-free antiseptic wipes and gloves for if you’re helping someone else. Lifeventure makes good travel-sized first aid kits.”

Will Duffin, an NHS GP working in urgent care who runs the Extreme Medic Instagram account, also stresses the importance of a good first aid kit. “I recommend buying an off-the-shelf first aid kit, and then you can add bits into that,” he says. “One of the main things for families is a thermometer and some Calpol.” Duffin also suggests having supplies of basic, over-the-counter medication that might come in handy, such as paracetamol, ibuprofen, antihistamines, Imodium and rehydration sachets.

“The other day-to-day one is wound care – cuts, aches and sprains. So have some antiseptic, sterile gauze, basic dressings such as plasters and medical tape,” he says. As well as getting the gear, you need to have some idea of what to do with it, which is why Duffin recommends going on a basic first aid course. Organisations such as St John Ambulance and British Red Cross offer various options.

Traveller first aid kit

Braun ThermoScan 7 ear thermometer

Tommee Tippee 2-in-1 thermometer

In case channels of communication go down, the government has advised buying a battery or wind-up radio, some of which also have a torch and a USB slot to charge your phone. “It’s such a simple piece of kit. The wind-up versions are great because in an emergency, you can use the power of your own arm to power the battery,” says Cloke.

Immver wind-up radio with 10,000mAh battery and LED torch

“If you haven’t already got some kind of woolly throw or blanket in the house, get one. It doesn’t have to be expensive merino wool or anything like that; it just needs to be wool,” says Hudson. The same goes for woolly jumpers, too. “People have probably got enough clothes in their house, but make sure you have something that’s got a lot of wool in it. A jumper is brilliant because if it’s chucking it down with rain and you get caught out, wool will keep you warm even when it’s wet,” he says. Both are helpful if you have no way to heat your home, and are one of the best ways to keep you warm even if it’s damp.

Recycled wool blanket

“[Many of us] are in our cars all the time, and what happens if you get stuck? Put some blankets and warm clothes into it, have a torch, some batteries, jump leads, a small shovel, a hi-vis jacket so you can safely ask for help at night, some basic water and long-life food, and a first aid kit. A mini version of what’s in your house,” says Cloke. It’s also a good idea to have a sleeping bag in the boot of your car, so that if you’re driving and you get stuck or your car breaks down, you can stay warm in the car, says Hudson. “The sleeping bag can help stop you from becoming hypothermic. You want a hollow-fibre one because it will still keep you warm if it gets damp. Snugpak does great stuff, and several of its products are used by the military. You can also get secondhand sleeping bags from military surplus stores,” he says.

Snugpak the sleeping bag

AA winter car kit with folding snow shovel

“Most of us have got torches on our phones, but in an emergency you will want to save the battery for contacting people and other things. A basic torch and some spare batteries are a very useful thing during a power cut,” says Cloke. You can also buy wind-up torches, which save on batteries.

Energizer 1,000-lumen metal torch

Duracell Plus AA alkaline batteries (30 pack)

“Some of the cheap space blankets take up no space, but they’re like wrapping yourself in something thinner than a crisp packet, so they will rip if there are any sharp edges or wind. Reinforced ones are really robust. They’re a big sheet that’s silver on one side and brightly coloured on the other, with rivets in the corner, so you can do all sorts with them,” says Hudson. “Space blankets are lined with very thin, highly reflective aluminium so any radiated body heat is reflected back to you rather than being lost to your surroundings. Plus, the orange colour is a great way to get spotted by any potential rescuers if you’re outdoors.”

Redcamp heavy-duty emergency blanket

“Head torches are great because you’re still able to use both hands while being able to see in the dark,” says Hudson. “You can spend a fortune on them, but you don’t have to. I bought an Energizer one recently, and it’s all that you really need. That one needs batteries, but you can get rechargeable ones too – I have one from Everbeam.”

Energizer Vision 400-lumen head torch

Everbeam 650-lumen head torch

For more, read the Filter’s guide to the best head torches

“Having water stored is really important for a whole range of emergencies. The [mains] water might go off or get contaminated in some way. The key thing is to make sure you’ve got enough for the number of people in your household. My advice is to have 10 litres per person per day for hygiene, cooking and drinking,” says Cloke. The government guidance suggests having enough bottled water for three days. It says you should have “three litres per person per day for drinking. More would be needed for other tasks such as cooking and washing”.

Sign up to The Filter

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

after newsletter promotion

Hudson recommends a water filter bottle such as Pure Hydration’s Aquapure Traveller, which has a clever purifier cap to reduce harmful substances and microorganisms in water. You put in any fresh water, screw the cap on, and drink the water you squeeze through the purifier. “They’re amazing,” Hudson says. “The filter takes out a lot of the things in water that can harm you, from large things such as pathogens – worms and snail eggs – through to bacteria and tiny viruses, so you can more safely drink from any fresh water source you can find, such as rivers or rainwater. We’ve used them for 20 years in all sorts of environments with the military.” It’s a good idea to buy extra filters, too, although Hudson says they’re “good for 350 litres, so enough water at least 10 days if you’re not somewhere super hot and/or humid”.

Aquapure Traveller

“I think a power bank is more useful than batteries,” says Hudson. “You can buy big ones [he recommends the size below] that will also jump-start a car, which is quite handy, and also charge things such as head torches and phones. These days the bigger, the better if you don’t have to carry it; so many items need juice.”

Portable car battery jump-starter power pack

For more, read the Filter’s guide to the best power banks and battery packs in the UK for reliable charging on the go

“Basic alcohol hand gel is important. If the water supply goes out, things like coughs and colds can spread within the family. Having a supply of hand sanitiser is good preparedness,” says Duffin. Cloke also recommends stocking up on “packets of wet wipes for basic hygiene, particularly if you’ve got babies”.

Cuticura antibacterial hand gel

Wet Ones Be Fresh Original antibacterial wipes

“Candles provide light without burning through your power supply. Go for stocky, fat ones because they’ll fall over less easily and last longer. Tea lights are also good – they don’t burn for ages, but you can buy sackfuls of them for not much money. You need matches too, like the big chunky boxes of Cook’s matches. Don’t leave unattended, and make sure you’ve got a fire extinguisher or a fire blanket,” says Hudson.

Votive pillar candles, four pack

“Tinned beans, chickpeas and lentils all have a long shelf life and are rich in fibre, nutrients and protein,” says Dr Federica Amati, head nutritionist at Zoe, nutrition lead at Imperial College London’s school of medicine and author of The Appetite Reset and Every Body Should Know This. “Getting a variety is good for flavour reasons, but also for micronutrient content. Dried lentils are easy to cook, but if there’s a power cut or a shortage, tinned and jarred lentils will serve you better.” Oh, and don’t forget a tin opener.

Oxo Good Grips soft-handled tin opener

“Microwaveable pouches are fantastic. If you’ve got a few ready to go, then if for whatever reason you don’t have enough water or can’t use the hob but you have a microwave, you can have these. Some of them you don’t even need to microwave, and you can just eat them out of the packet,” says Amati.

Merchant Gourmet brown, red and wild rice, 250g x 6

“Get a variety of tinned fish, like mackerel, sardines, anchovies and sprats. Tinned mackerel is one of the easiest to integrate, and you can get them tinned with tomatoes, which a lot of people prefer if they don’t like fish. Find something you like, and then buy a couple more of those in your next shop, so you can build up a supply,” says Amati.

“Buy frozen fruit and vegetables, if you have the space. Frozen veg is picked ripe and blanched within hours. Have some frozen berries and veg – broccoli, cauliflower and peas. You can get jars and tins of vegetables too, like roasted peppers, sweetcorn, carrots or beetroot,” says Amati. It’s also worth noting that, in the case of a power outage, food should stay frozen for up to 48 hours in a full freezer, or 24 hours if it’s half full, provided you keep the door closed.

“UHT milk is worth getting, and make sure you have enough teabags, because you might be able to have a cup of tea, and those things are still important. Dark chocolate is also awesome – it keeps for months, needs no cooking or power, and offers plenty of energy in a small square, mostly from cocoa butter fats that sustain you rather than causing a rapid rise and crash in energy,” says Amati. She suggests opting for 70% cocoa or above so that “you also get more fibre, magnesium, iron and cocoa flavanols, plant compounds that support healthy blood vessels”.

For more, read the Filter’s guide to the best supermarket dark chocolate

“Oats are fantastic,” says Amati. “You can just add hot water, mix them up, and then you’ve got something to eat. And you can eat them raw, mixed into yoghurt or milk.”

“If you can’t buy fresh bread and you can’t freeze it, unopened vacuum-packed rye bread can last about six months, and it’s super nutritious,” says Amati.

Biona organic rye bread, 500g

“If there’s been some kind of tech outage and things are slowly coming back up, you might not be able to use your cards or phone to pay for stuff, so it’s worth having a little bit of cash,” says Hudson.

“Everyone’s got people’s numbers in their phones, but what if the phone’s broken? Have some numbers written on a piece of paper, like people that you care about that you want to check in with and a number for a local medical centre in case you need to get your prescription,” Hudson says.

“If you’ve got some extra regular medication, that’s great. Sometimes people struggle to get that prescribed for them. But if you can stay a few days ahead, that will really help in case of emergency. I like to suggest having enough for a week or a month if you can, or at least two days if you’re struggling,” says Cloke.

Duffin suggests having “at least seven to 14 days of your vital repeat medications in hand”, and that this is a useful thing to do anyway. “Request your script early, not just because of a severe weather event or a nuclear attack. If supply chains become more volatile, the medicine you need may not be in stock and might need to be ordered in.” The government guidance says that “it’s important to request prescriptions up to five working days before you need your medicine”. The NHS also has an online form you can use to request emergency supplies of prescription medicine if you have run out, but note that they advise against ordering more than needed.

Christa Pike makes first public comments since failed execution: ‘There is pain in my mind and in my soul’

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:15:48 GMT

Pike is facing death penalty for 1995 murder of classmate, despite surviving a botched execution last month

Christa Pike has marked a month since her failed execution by Tennessee and released a statement in which she laments the “incompetence” that has led to this moment, adding that despite ongoing healing she remains in constant physical pain and mental anguish.

In comments released by her legal team on Friday, the prisoner said that there had not been a moment since she was injected with a massive dose of the sedative pentobarbital that she had not been in pain. “My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” she said.

Though she does not mention the state authorities who tried to kill her a month ago by injecting a full 5g of pentobarbital into her arms, she does make a pointed criticism clearly targeted at them. “I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” she said.

Pike was strapped to a gurney in the Tennessee execution chamber on 30 September, facing death for the 1995 murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18. Members of the execution team spent almost an hour trying to establish an intravenous line through which to pump the sedative, but the procedure was botched and the prisoner survived.

Medical experts told the Guardian they were shocked by the apparent level of incompetence displayed in the execution chamber, after a blow-by-blow account of events was released by Pike’s lawyer, who was present in the room.

Pike is being held in the infirmary at the Debra Johnson rehabilitation center in Nashville, where she was returned after 10 days of intensive hospital treatment. She is being kept largely in solitary confinement, she said, “away from other people and the human connections that mean so much to me”.

Such isolation was its own form of pain, she said, given that she spent the first 28 years on death row in solitary confinement.

The events of 30 September have roiled Tennessee and sent shock waves across the US. The Republican governor of the state, Bill Lee, has ordered a pause on further executions until an outside review is conducted.

It is not clear what Tennessee intends to do with Pike. Earlier this week, Lee said he expected her death sentence to remain the same unless the courts determine otherwise.

Pike, dictating her statement to her lawyers, said that she had been prepared to die that night. “I had made my peace.”

Since she awoke, “alone in a hospital confused and in pain”, she has been searching for meaning about what happened to her. “I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time.”

She said in her slow road to recovery she drew sustenance from the “extraordinary love and support I have received from people around the world. To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is humbling.”

She thanked the first responders, doctors and nurses who cared for her in hospital, as well as her attorneys and those who “fought for me, stood beside me and refused to give up on me”.

She added: “I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone.”

Spain’s trust in high-speed rail ‘broken’ after second deadly crash this year, says PM

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:13:52 GMT

Pedro Sánchez vows to investigate crash that killed 69 people – and rebuild public confidence

Europe live – latest updates

Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has admitted “trust in high-speed rail has been broken” after Wednesday’s train collision that killed at least 69 people, injured more than 100 and prompted a national debate on the safety of the country’s rail network.

Sánchez said Spain was “working tirelessly” to provide information as quickly as possible to the families of the victims – who include people from at least 23 different foreign countries – adding his government was committed to finding what had caused the country’s second deadly train collision this year.

Two trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other train slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near Urda, in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.

The crash came nine months after 46 people were killed and dozens injured when two trains – again one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz, in Andalucía.

“It’s unacceptable for a country like Spain – which has such a powerful high-speed rail system – to experience two accidents of this nature and magnitude within a single year,” the prime minister said on Friday.

“Therefore, our task isn’t merely to investigate the causes of what occurred, but also to provide solutions to further strengthen our nation’s high-speed rail system. Public trust in the high-speed system has been broken; the government’s responsibility goes beyond diagnosing the causes – it must also offer solutions to ensure that a tragedy of this scale doesn’t happen again.”

Shortly after Sánchez spoke, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, who is under growing pressure to resign, gave a press conference in which he dismissed calls to step down, promising instead to focus on “providing the Spanish people with solutions” to restore trust.

“My duty now isn’t to talk about whether or not I carry on with my job; it’s to solve the problems, clarify what happened and offer clear explanations,” he said. “The most important thing I can do is offer solutions as best I can. If the investigation shows there were failures of organisation or control, we will act accordingly. And if individuals are found to be responsible, action will be taken.”

Puente once again suggested that responsibility for Wednesday’s crash appeared to lie within the Madrid control centre of Spain’s state infrastructure operator, Adif. He said that in the run-up to the crash, the LZB signalling system – which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied – had gone down, but emphasised that such incidents were not uncommon. Once the system was down, he said, control and decision-making powers reverted to humans, as was the case in other transport sectors.

The minister added that the crash had occurred after an Adif operator ordered the Renfe train to move off at “normal” speed, rather than following the protocols, which stipulate a top speed of 40kph (25mph) so that drivers can see any dangers ahead in good time. According to a preliminary investigation report released on Thursday, the Renfe train was travelling at between 160kph and 200kph when it hit the Iryo train.

The report concluded: “The sequence of malfunctions, instructions, and actions eventually led to the collision, in the absence of the necessary mitigating barriers.”

Puente said the operator in question was a 48-year-old man, with all the relevant up-to-date training and two years of experience in control centres, who had been managing this specific area since February this year. “So, it was a sector he knew well,” the minister added.

Transport unions have pushed back at the government, arguing that current workloads are too demanding to handle safely and asking for more personnel.

“We believe [the minister] is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions,” Raquel Ayllón, a spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers union, told the Associated Press. “Human error isn’t incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing.”

Spain’s conservative People’s party (PP), which is forecast to topple Sánchez’ socialist-led minority coalition government in next month’s snap general election, has repeatedly called for Puente to step down.

The PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said his party was holding Puente and Sánchez “politically responsible” for both rail crashes. “Whoever has failed in their duty to run the transport ministry properly must bear the consequences,” he said. “And the person who appointed them – and kept them in their post – even more so. If they do not resign, we will remove them at the ballot box.”

Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor who now leads the leftwing Frente Amplio coalition that is running in the election, also said Puente needed to go. “We’re not going to engage in the triviality of debating whether that resignation should take place today, tomorrow, or the day after,” she said. “It must happen as soon as possible.”

Puente, asked about the possible effect of the latest crash on the election, said he had given the matter “zero thought”.

“I don’t believe anyone would expect me to be thinking about the election campaign at a moment like this,” he told reporters.

‘Amateur morons’: Flávio Bolsonaro’s short-lived ‘president-elect’ claim met with mockery

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:08:41 GMT

Brazilian media ridicule defeated candidate over ‘shameful’ absconsion to US and bizarre letter with wrong coat of arms

Flávio Bolsonaro had hoped that by Sunday night people would be calling him the next president of Brazil.

Instead, the far-right politician’s decision to flee to the US after losing the election and – for 58 minutes – to declare himself “Brazil’s true president-elect”, has made him a laughing stock, with Brazilian newspapers and commentators raining a barrage of scornful adjectives down on the conquered candidate.

“If it served any purpose at all, Flávio’s foolishness liberated the democratic right from a family of coup-mongers, which for far too long held it hostage to their reckless folly and irremediable disdain for Brazil,” the conservative Estado de São Paulo newspaper thundered on Friday.

Bolsonaro fled to Miami on Tuesday night, 48 hours after being beaten by his leftwing adversary, the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, by 4.4m votes. Lula’s victory has been recognised by rightwing leaders from around the world, including El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, not to mention Bolsonaro’s own party and many key allies.

But on Wednesday after landing in the US, Bolsonaro published an outlandish letter – reportedly produced with the help of ChatGPT – in which he declared himself “the true president-elect of Brazil” and made phoney claims about election fraud.

Perhaps most bizarrely, he claimed he would continue to lead Brazil’s opposition from abroad, comparing himself to Charles de Gaulle, who in the 1940s led a French government-in-exile against the Nazis from London, and the 19th-century Cuban independence hero José Martí, who challenged the Spanish empire from New York.

“They were all treated as criminals by the regimes they confronted. History called them something else,” Bolsonaro said, also likening himself to Venezuela’s Nobel laureate María Corina Machado and Rui Barbosa, a Brazilian politician who went into exile in London in the late 19th century after challenging an authoritarian president known as “the Iron Marshal”.

Just under an hour after Bolsonaro’s proclamation was first published on social media, a corrected version was issued, altering his claimed status to “leader of Brazil” – reportedly after he was upbraided by Trump administration officials keen to avoid a full-blown diplomatic split with Brazil’s actual leaders.

The amended letter also updated the out-of-date Brazilian coat of arms that had been used erroneously in the letterhead of the first version referring to the “United States of Brazil” – a name the South American country has not used since 1967.

Bolsonaro’s flight – and his brief but bogus claim to be “president-elect” of one of the world’s largest democracies – prompted an outpouring of opprobrium and ridicule.

“[This letter] seems to have been written by a foolhardy, loony halfwit,” Flávia Oliveira, a prominent political commentator, told the network GloboNews.

The Estado de São Paulo’s leader writers said: “Flávio’s letter isn’t worth the ink of this newspaper, but there’s no way the embarrassment can be ignored,” before savaging a man they called “a con artist of the highest order”.

The Rio broadsheet O Globo said Bolsonaro’s “shameful and sneaky” decision to abscond laid bare the “pathetic” nature of his political movement, Bolsonarismo, while the Folha de São Paulo said it exposed the true nature of the “authoritarian, ignorant, incompetent” Bolsonaro family.

José Casado, a columnist for the conservative magazine Veja, wrote: “The comedy storyline has already guaranteed him a spot in the pages of political satire.”

Merval Pereira, a conservative columnist for O Globo, called Bolsonaro “a madhouse Napoleon”.

Even Silas Malafaia, a pugnacious televangelist who is close to Bolsonaro’s jailed father, Jair Bolsonaro, had harsh words. “Bolsonaro’s kids are jackasses … A bunch of amateur morons,” Malafaia was quoted as saying by O Globo.

Some observers see Bolsonaro’s post-defeat getaway as proof that his dispirited movement is dead. “I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, said this week, calling the result “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying right wing”.

The Estado de São Paulo’s editorial board agreed. “Flávio belongs to the past and will soon vanish into the basement of political irrelevance from which he should never have emerged,” they predicted, urging conservatives to ditch Bolsonaro and throw their weight behind his ally Tarcísio de Freitas, the São Paulo governor.

Others warned Bolsonarismo would remain a powerful political force, even if the Bolsonaro family’s leadership of the far-right movement was now in doubt.

Social media users were also merciless in their reaction to Bolsonaro’s short-lived claim to be “president-elect”. One meme invited supporters to attend his January inauguration – at Cinderella Castle in Walt Disney World, Orlando. Another parodied his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan “God, homeland and family”, which became “Goodbye, homeland and family”.

Donald Trump has declined to publicly recognise the result of an election he has called “a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil”. But a US diplomatic cable obtained by the Folha de São Paulo called Lula’s victory “surprising but definitive”.

Asked if he saw Bolsonaro as Brazil’s “rightful” leader, the US president replied: “I won’t get involved.”

‘His honesty gave courage to survivors’: domestic abuse charities praise Patrick Stewart’s legacy

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:00:18 GMT

Actor first shared his childhood experiences as part of Amnesty International campaign and became Refuge ambassador

When Patrick Stewart was growing up in the 1940s, he witnessed how, after his father beat his mother, home doctors and ambulance workers would tell her: “You must have done something to provoke him.”

Stewart knew the violence was never warranted, a conviction that became the spark for a lasting commitment to campaigning for greater understanding of domestic abuse.

As news emerged of his death, aged 86, domestic abuse campaigners praised his legacy and said his contributions had helped raise awareness of domestic abuse and its impact on children.

Kerry Moscogiuri, Amnesty International UK’s chief executive, said that although Stewart, as Capt Jean-Luc Picard in the sci-fi TV series Star Trek, was “best known for playing heroes on screen … one of his bravest acts was telling the truth about his own childhood”.

“For many years, he stood with Amnesty. He spoke openly about the violence his mother suffered at home to support our campaign to stop violence against women. His honesty gave courage to survivors around the world,” she said.

“Our thoughts are with his wife, family and friends. The best way to honour him is to carry on the fight he believed in. It should appal us all that the scourge of violence against women and girls continues and governments must do far more to end it.”

Stewart shared his story for the first time in 2004 as part of Amnesty International’s global campaign to cut violence against women.

At the time, he recalled: “I saw the self-loathing of my father, due to his inability to control his violent outbursts. I saw society, police, doctors and neighbours conspire to hide the abuse with comments like: ‘She must have provoked him’, and: ‘It takes two to make an argument’.”

He was moved to speak out about his childhood in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, after his 79-year-old brother said that “what happened had blighted his life”, and was spurred by a conviction that “violence must be controlled. If you fail to raise your hand in protest, you are part of the problem.”

The most recent government figures show almost one in 10 adults in England and Wales experienced domestic abuse in the last year, prompting domestic abuse charities to warn that the government was “not on track to fulfil its pledge” to halve violence against women and girls in a decade.

In 2007, Stewart became an ambassador for the charity Refuge, a role he continued in for the rest of his life. His work included attending events and fundraising, as well as contributing his lived experience to policy discussions, with the result that children were recognised as victims of domestic abuse in their own right in the Domestic Abuse Act 2021.

Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge’s chair of trustees, said the charity was “deeply saddened” to hear of his passing.

She added: “I was privileged to watch his endless devotion and passion to the cause. He told me he did the work in honour of his mother, and in lending his voice he raised much-needed awareness of the cause and broke down barriers and taboos on the subject.

“He empowered other survivors to come forward to speak out about the domestic abuse they had experienced and raised vital awareness of the longstanding impact domestic abuse has on children. He was very proud of the work he did with us and leaves an important legacy behind. He will be sorely missed by Refuge colleagues past and present.”

Cherie Blair KC, who is also a Refuge ambassador, said she recalled being “profoundly moved” when she first heard Stewart’s account of his father’s violence towards his mother, and the “devastating impact it had on him as a child”.

Describing him as a “powerful advocate”, she added: “At that time, it was unusual for a man, particularly someone as famous and respected as Patrick, to speak so openly about domestic abuse. His courage in sharing such painful personal experiences helped to break the silence surrounding domestic violence and reminded us that its consequences extend far beyond the immediate victim to the children who witness it.

“Patrick understood how important it was for men to speak out against violence towards women. His support for Refuge was not simply lending his famous name to a worthy cause. It was a deeply personal commitment, sustained over many years.”

The domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, Nicole Jacobs, said: “Patrick was a powerful advocate for women’s rights, using every opportunity to courageously share his experience and give a voice to survivors and child victims of domestic abuse. His loss will be deeply felt by all of us working towards a world free from domestic abuse. My thoughts are with his family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”

The chief executive of Women’s Aid, Farah Nazeer, described Stewart as a “true ally” for speaking out.

She said: “Eradicating domestic abuse, and wider violence against women and girls, requires a whole-society approach and champions like Sir Patrick were instrumental in raising awareness of domestic abuse and its long-lasting impact on women and children alike.”

In the UK, the national domestic abuse helpline is 0808 2000 247, or you can visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www. befrienders. org.
