‘Ceilidh renaissance’ lures gen Z offline in search of real-life joy

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 13:00:54 GMT

Young dancers at the Ivy House in south-east London join the older crowd amid a renewed appetite for authentic, community events

The Ivy House pub in Nunhead, south-east London, has long been associated with raucous music, with the rock legends Ian Dury and Elvis Costello gracing its stage in the 70s, and indie favourites caroline and Kiran Leonard pulling in crowds today. But last Friday, it was a traditional Scottish ceilidh dance rather than a grassroots gig luring London’s cool kids to its sticky dancefloor.

The event is emblematic of a renewed appetite for analogue, in-person experiences among a younger generation plagued by a loneliness epidemic and fatigued by meeting people on dating apps.

“We spend a lot of time looking at screens,” said Matt, who saw the event as a refreshing way to spend time offline. “It’s really lovely to come together in spaces with lots of different people.”

The popularity of the ceilidh is evidenced by the launch of Ceilidh the Musical, which promises a “heart-warming party” with no experience required and started its tour at Shoreditch town hall, east London, last week.

According to the ticketing platform Eventbrite, from 2024-25 ticket sales for ceilidh events in the UK grew by 16%, while there was 15% growth globally. Page Dudley, a spokesperson for the platform, said young people were looking for events that were “communal and a lot less polished”.

“It’s my first time at a proper ceilidh,” said George, 35, at the Ivy House. “I just like how silly it can be. It just makes you feel alive.”

His partner, Louise, 32, was also a ceilidh first-timer. She said she liked how nobody was judging other people’s dance abilities. “It’s nice that it’s all ages,” she said. “When you strip away the ego, everyone just becomes their childlike selves.”

Jamie, 19, is a seasoned ceilidh attender and said they were becoming much more popular among his peers. He has even bumped into schoolfriends unexpectedly at ceilidhs. “Everyone is just laughing at the same stuff, especially when people get confused [with the dance moves],” he said.

Anna Spree, the communications, events and fundraising assistant at Link Age Southwark, which raised money from ticket sales at the Ivy House dance, said the “ceilidh renaissance” had allowed the local anti-loneliness charity to reach new people.

“[The dances] were accessible enough that anyone could join in, but also slightly complex, which made them a lot more fun,” she added.

Ceilidh, which comes from the Gaelic word for “visit” or “gathering”, originated in Scotland and Ireland in the 19th century.

“I’ve noticed the ceilidhs we’ve been putting on have been attended by a lot of under-30s,” said Alison Craig, a guitarist in the South East London Folk Orchestra (SELFolk), which provided the music on Friday.

The ceilidh was organised after a successful dance in the same pub last year, which Craig recalls was bustling with young ceilidh newcomers. “The last time I saw the Ivy House bouncing like that was in about 1975,” she said.

Although this particular ceilidh took place in a bar, Craig maintained that ceilidhs could be good for dry nights out, too: “You think, bloody hell, I’ve just had a Saturday night out and not had a drink.”

Ed McCabe, the founder of London Ceilidh Club, has also noticed the shift. “Ever since Covid, it’s really boomed,” he said. “People just want to be in a room together.” He believes ceilidhs have “low barriers to entry” and are a great place to meet new people – or even find love.

“There’s a whole aspect that you can’t look cool while you’re doing it,” he said. “You’re sweaty, you can’t stop smiling … it’s a great place to meet someone.”

Craig echoed this: “It’s not about trying to look sexy or really cool,” she said. “Not to say ceilidhs aren’t sexy or cool, because they can be. You just need to get into it and enjoy it.”

Richard Jones, who plays the accordion in SELFolk, suggested another great thing about ceilidhs was that they weren’t heteronormative. “It’s non-gender, if you like,” he said.

His bandmate Neil McLean, who plays the flute, agreed. “We don’t really do men and women, we do ones and twos,” he said. “It’s the opposite of not being picked for sports at school.”

SELFolk hosts regular ceilidhs which attract a crowd across all ages, according to Jones. “[People] know it’s safe, they know they can have a good time, and they don’t need to come in groups,” he said. “Very quickly the group becomes its own community.”

‘I felt bad for my exes’: Awkwafina on making deeply personal TV – with her grandma

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 13:00:54 GMT

The star takes on her biggest challenge yet: resurrecting her family’s Cantonese restaurant. She discusses the stress of rewatching her sitcom, nearly becoming a meat inspector … and her beloved matriarch, who passed away after filming

I’m embarrassed I didn’t bring anything. It’s 10-something in the morning, and I’m meeting Nora Lum, 38 – best known as rapper, comic actor and writer Awkwafina – the morning after the Bafta TV awards. I feel that I should have brought her a pastry pick-me-up. Yet here I am empty-handed. “It could have been Chinese buns,” she playfully suggests.

Yes, it could have been. Especially because we are meeting to discuss her new series on Apple TV, Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook. It sees the star of box-office hits Crazy Rich Asians and Marvel’s Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings travel across the US to learn from a new generation of Asian American chefs, in the hope that she might revive her own family’s long-closed Cantonese restaurant. But there’s one problem: she can’t cook.

Or so she says. “Unlikely” cook? There’s nothing unlikely about it, I wager. Sure, in the first episode, Lum looks genuinely alarmed by the triple threat of hot oil, high heat and sharp knives in wok cooking. But she does very well. She clearly has a knack for food.

“Well, I think it was the easiest knack to develop, because all it really takes is to eat at a ton of restaurants and order food constantly,” she pushes back.

“But look, I was raised by immigrant Chinese people – I did eat all the weird Chinese stuff,” she says, understating her family’s impressive culinary credentials. The full story is thus: back in the 50s, Lum’s great-grandfather Jimmy opened one of New York’s first Chinese-American restaurants in Flushing, Queens. Called Lum’s, it became something of an institution, helping to popularise the Chinese-American food beloved today (think: orange chicken and BBQ ribs).

“The restaurant is how we came to this country,” she explains. “It closed in 1982, so I wasn’t born. But it was so important. The way they talk about it is like a family member that passed away.”

Lum’s new TV show about it is pleasingly warm and personal, with much of its gentle humour coming less from the supposedly awkward personality that inspired Lum’s stage name than her deep appreciation for food and hospitality. Have you ever seen someone scream “Oh my God, not the cilantro!” in ecstatic anticipation of a herb? I have, and it’s charming. But ultimately, Unlikely Cook is a love letter to Lum’s magnetic, occasionally foul-mouthed, paternal grandmother; the woman who raised her when she lost her mother at just four years old.

Several months after I meet Lum, I see the Instagram post announcing her grandmother’s death. But, for now, I ask about the woman who has loomed so large over her creative work, and regularly steals the show in Unlikely Cook. How easy is it working with your own grandma?

“It’s crazy. I’ve been asking my grandma to be in things since my first [TV] job, which was on MTV’s Girl Code,” Lum explains. Grandma obliged, starring in the brilliantly named episode Bad Sex, Grandparents, Eating Habits.

“I’m always a little worried, thinking: ‘Oh my God, what are you going to say?’ But she has such a lovely on-camera affect. It just kind of clicks.”

“With this [project], she’s calling me at all hours of the night, we’re staying up talking. Actually, she called me a week ago and was like, ‘I’m just thinking about the menu, and we should put a pu pu platter – but we shouldn’t call it pu pu, because, you know, it means shit so we should call it the volcano platter.’ It’s giving her excitement again.”

Between the family appearances and actor Jimmy O Yang’s star turn (Lum’s real-life best friend) Unlikely Cook may be Lum’s most biographical work yet. Which is saying something given her hit 2020 comedy television show was literally called Awkwafina Is Nora from Queens, and starred her as directionless, awkward Nora living in – you guessed it – Flushing, with her widowed father and boisterous grandmother.

For fans of Nora from Queens, there may be a particular, parasocial joy in watching Unlikely Cook. The sitcom could be absurd (Nora’s grandma accidentally growing cannabis, for instance), but you always sensed some emotional truth beneath it. Now we get the real Nora Lum.

“Oh my God, yeah,” she exclaims. She refers to an episode where she is stressed. “That episode was bizarre to watch. Because I have never seen myself be serious, be panicked. That’s never been recorded.”

“There was something about it where I actually felt bad. I felt bad for my exes, my friends. I was watching myself back like, ‘Chill out, girl!’”

I didn’t have her pegged as the self-conscious type, I say, what with working so frequently from her real life. “I’ve never been documentarised in quite this way,” she explains. “There’s a part of me that’s like, oh my God, you let people see this crazy, unbridled version of you?! I still don’t know how to deal with that. But I do feel that whatever is honest, it can’t be the worst.”

To be fair, food is emotional stuff, and so often bound up in questions of identity, history and, especially in the immigrant context, family sacrifice. I ask Lum about her observation in the documentary that a generation of elders grafted in restaurants so their kids didn’t have to. They could be lawyers instead.

“The truth is that a lot of the [older] people we met didn’t want their children to go back into the restaurant business. For my great-grandpa’s generation, when they came over they were relegated to either laundromats or restaurants, cooking food that has historically been demonised,” Lum says. “But then again, it’s also something that people love. There are more Chinese restaurants in America than there are McDonald’s, KFC, Burger King, all of that.”

But while the restaurant business gave Lum’s family life, it also took a lot of it. Her grandmother had her own restaurant for a time, but when it failed, Lum’s grandparents were forced to file for bankruptcy, losing both their business and home. For a while, the whole family lived in a one-bedroom apartment.

“I think her business failing was really hard on her. She would fold the napkins in the back. She would launder napkins in our home. And she would be the most amazing maître d’ that the whole town knew. I don’t think she ever really recovered from it.”

Would opening a permanent Lum’s be a way of rewriting that history?

after newsletter promotion

“I think giving back – if I’m in a position to do that – does feel like this full-circle moment where I could still make my family proud in that way. It would definitely be something for her.”

All this talk of making family proud and honouring their sacrifices is something I know well, having also been raised in an immigrant household. Did Lum agonise over her choice of a creative career as much as I did when I chose English lit over law – something I loved over something that might more reliably make good on what my family gave me?

“No, because I don’t think I was smart enough to get into law school,” she laughs.

“Oh, I doubt that’s true,” I reply.

“I’m actually not a good student. I went to summer school for gym. For gym. If you fail a class during the year, you can make it up over the summer. But it’s like a punishment, right? Every day I was taking two periods of gym, because I had failed so many times.”

She continues: “Do you know what Earth science is? The rock one? It’s the easy rock one. It’s not even chemistry. I had to take the Earth science [exam] five times, dude.

“So I think my family were just thinking, well, she has nothing to lose. Besides I wasn’t doing it off their dime, so I think maybe they were just happy I was doing something. But my dad really wanted me to be a meat inspector. I’m still on those government job registries that he signed me up for. He’s like, “Meat inspector, that’s a really good job.”

“It is a good job,” I concur.

“It is! Great entry level salary. And you always, always need a meat inspector,” she says.

“You could start now,” I offer.

“I know, I know,” she laughs, and I wonder if she has the same idea I have. Awkwafina is the Meat Inspector, coming soon to Apple TV.

OK, back to business. Watching Unlikely Cook, I couldn’t help thinking about the politics of America right now. After all, a show celebrating the work of immigrants feels significant in the age of Trump and ICE. Was that intentional?

“No, not at all. But if you want to tell the story of Chinese-American food, immigrant culture is something you can’t ignore. It’s also a deep part of our identity as second-generation Asian Americans, it’s part of how we see the world. And it’s a hard thing to see right now in America.”

Our time is nearly up. But wait, I’m still not sure, does this mean someday there will be a permanent Lum’s? “It’s still in the works of being figured out,” she says.

But clearly, in Nora Lum herself, something has stuck. “After this show, I did start dabbling a little,” she says. While shooting a film in Kentucky, she took to cooking her own breakfast, “a four-egg omelette with spinach and cheese”, she says with faint pride. It’s not quite as impressive as Chinese buns. But maybe they’ll come soon.

Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook is on Apple TV from Friday.

To baldly go: Patrick Stewart was an icon for bald men everywhere

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 12:27:55 GMT

The actor was an exemplary bald star, embracing his hair loss and the freedoms it brought. He didn’t go grey or recede – and he didn’t wear a wig like William Shatner as Captain Kirk

Patrick Stewart, Star Trek and X-Men actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86

Patrick Stewart managed to be lots of different things at once. He was a towering figure on stage. He was a literal superhero onscreen. And, at times, he wasn’t above sending himself up. It also needs to be said that he was a bald man.

And a pioneering one at that. Nowhere was this more clear than during his stint on Star Trek: The Next Generation. Previously, Star Trek had been a kind of space-set action show, where the relentlessly virile Captain Kirk would beam down to new planets to either punch or get off with all the aliens there. But then came its successor, and Kirk was replaced by a nonviolent intellectual called Jean-Luc. Worse still, he didn’t have any hair. What a sign of weakness.

But Patrick Stewart made it work. Not only was his cool temperament a nice change of pace from the 1960s take, but his sex appeal was undeniable. Indeed, in 1992 TV Guide readers voted him television’s “most bodacious” man. Stewart received 54% of the vote, putting him ahead of much hairier contenders including Luke Perry and Burt Reynolds.

Not that he didn’t have his critics. When Picard’s casting was announced to the world, it is said that a reporter complained to Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry that it didn’t make any sense. After all, the show was set in a future where space travel and teleportation were accepted as the norm, so wouldn’t it stand to reason that humanity would have created a cure for male pattern baldness? According to Stewart, Roddenberry’s response was that, by the 24th century, humanity will have evolved to the point where it no longer cares about baldness.

Stewart lost his hair in his teens, and was open about the effect this had on his psyche, telling Rolling Stone that he was so worried about how baldness might affect his love life that he spent more than he could afford on a wig. However, by ditching the hairpiece, Stewart became an icon for the bald.

When you lose your hair, you begin casting around for other bald men, because in a small way this helps normalise it. Stewart found himself a magnet for this, telling The New Yorker in 2023, “How many times have I been spoken to in the street by somebody who would pull off his cap, revealing a bald head, and say, ‘You saved my life!’”

Again, this is because Stewart was an exemplary bald. So often when men go bald they end up overcompensating by inflating themselves to preemptively ward off negative comments. Look at The Rock, and how much more aggressively he bulked out after he lost his hair. Look at Jeff Bezos, who reacted to baldness by pumping iron and building willy-shaped space rockets. Now compare this to Stewart, who pointed towards a different path of culture and elegance and refinement, embracing his baldness without ever apologising for it.

More than anything, though, you just have to look at the reactions to his death to see the real legacy of Patrick Stewart’s baldness. People were generally staggered to learn that he was 86 years old. This is because, as all bald people know, losing your hair ages you, but only temporarily. He was 47 years old when Star Trek: The Next Generation premiered in 1987, but he arguably looked a decade older than that. But then he carried on looking that age for decades afterwards. He didn’t go grey, or recede, or adopt an unflattering dye job, or any of the other things that makes men look old, because he didn’t have any hair. And unlike Captain Kirk, he never wore a high-end hairpiece. Patrick Stewart played the long game, and he won. O captain, my captain.

Police Scotland investigate Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s visit to Balmoral

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 12:11:16 GMT

Force says it has received ‘information’ on pair’s stay at royal estate as reported guests of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor

Detectives in Scotland are investigating Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s stay at Balmoral castle as reported guests of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor amid allegations that women were trafficked to the royal estate.

Police Scotland said it had received “information” and inquiries were at a “very early stage” into the time the disgraced royal spent with the child sex offender at Balmoral.

The late Epstein, who was convicted in 2008 of soliciting sex from girls, and Maxwell, who was convicted in 2021 of sex trafficking a minor, stayed at Balmoral in 1999.

Pictures previously released by the US Department of Justice appear to show Andrew and Epstein shooting on the estate.

The Daily Express has reported that the inquiries relate to claims that women were trafficked to the estate.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We have received information and active inquiries are ongoing, but these are at a very early stage. All inquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries. We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further.”

Other investigations linked to the release of the Epstein files were ongoing within several forces, including Thames Valley police, the Metropolitan police and Surrey police, the National Police Chiefs’ Council confirmed.

An NPCC spokesperson said: “Identifying any further potential offending, suspects, victims or witnesses is a complex process and will take time, but UK policing remains committed to carrying out a meticulous assessment of the material released by the US Department of Justice.”

There was no national investigation at present, the NPCC said.

The former Duke of York was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office on 19 February this year, his 66th birthday, after allegations he had shared sensitive information with Epstein during his time as a UK trade envoy. He was interviewed under caution before being released under investigation. He denies wrongdoing, with the police investigation continuing.

An email released in a tranche of the Epstein files last year and signed by “A” asked the disgraced British socialite Maxwell for “inappropriate friends”. In one of four emails sent to Maxwell in August 2001 by someone using the name the Invisible Man, the sender told her their “valet” had recently died and they had “left the RN”.

Mountbatten-Windsor left the Royal Navy the month before the email was sent. Another email from the same individual, dated 16 August 2001, said they were at “Balmoral summer camp for the royal family” before asking Maxwell: “Have you found me some inappropriate friends?”

In March 2002, an email from Maxwell to the Invisible Man said she had passed on a message to an unnamed individual, with that message beginning: “I just gave Andrew your telephone no.”

The message from Maxwell to the unidentified person also said “Andrew” would be “very happy” if he did some “two legged sight seeing”.

Andrew was the UK’s special representative for international trade and investment from 2001-11, when he stepped down amid controversy over his friendship with Epstein.

He received no salary for travelling around the world and the UK promoting Britain’s business interests, but criticisms were made about the thousands of pounds spent each year on his expenses and travel costs.

His decision to quit the role came in the same year he was pictured with his arm around his primary accuser, Virginia Giuffre, who said she had been trafficked to the former duke at the home of Maxwell.

Andrew paid Giuffre, a woman he has claimed never to have met, millions of pounds to settle a civil suit in the US in 2022.

Giuffre died by suicide, aged 41, in April 2025.

The academy system needs a refresh but now is the time for Carrick to trust in youth

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 12:00:52 GMT

Manchester United’s most famous eras were built around their academy products, so why not give the current crop a chance to shine?

Watching Manchester United succumb meekly against Como and Bournemouth brought to mind questions and comparisons with yesteryear. Two of United’s most famous eras were built around their youth players: the Busby Babes and the Class of ’92. Could this be a moment for Michael Carrick to give their most talented academy products a meaningful chance?

In February 2025 I saw United beat Arsenal 3-2 in the FA Youth Cup at the Emirates Stadium. Jack and Tyler Fletcher did well for United and so did Harry Amass, a signing from Watford. Max Dowman, a generational talent, starred for Arsenal.

Not one of that United team has established themselves in the first team. Amass, a left-back, has two substitute appearances this season. The winger Shea Lacey, part of the same under-18s squad, has come on four times and got a Carabao Cup start.

Supporters, not least at Old Trafford, like players from the academy. The two United youth products who are regulars, Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford, are well established. I look at some of the club’s big signings and wonder: do they see themselves as real Manchester United players? With youth-team products you get spirit and identity – a deep pride in the shirt. That isn’t enough but to really assess them they need a proper chance.

You have to give a player a minimum of three starts in a row to see whether they have the potential to be a regular. Some players at United and elsewhere get an occasional Carabao Cup start and that’s it.

It is interesting that JJ Gabriel, a highly rated 16-year-old at United, and his advisers appear to think he could be better off elsewhere. Other young English players have made similar moves. Noni Madueke, for instance, left Tottenham for PSV at 16, got games and came back to sign for Chelsea, then Arsenal.

This is a wider issue than what is going on at United. The purpose of a youth system should be to produce players for the senior team – not to be a trading post, a way of raising funds to buy often mediocre players from abroad.

Tottenham have brought through internationals including Sol Campbell, Ledley King, Harry Kane and Andros Townsend over the past 30 years or so. This season their only homegrown player with a Premier League appearance is Mikey Moore, and he was sent back on loan – this time to Cologne – in August.

The loan system can be beneficial – look at Kane. I saw him at Leyton Orient on his first loan from Spurs and wasn’t sure he had the pace for the highest level. When he came back injured from a loan at Norwich, his rehab work, including weights in the gym, left him feeling fitter and quicker.

It got to a point where Tim Sherwood, Tottenham’s technical coordinator, was banging on the door for Kane to get a first-team chance. He got it, took it and this week won the Ballon d’Or.

Often as an academy player you need a sympathetic manager and strong advocate. Three players Spurs acquired for their academy were sold this summer: Alfie Devine to Preston and Will Lankshear and Ashley Phillips to Middlesbrough. Were they not deserving of an opportunity?

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Liverpool have fielded a scouser every season since 1892 but named a 25-man Premier League squad in August without a player born in the city. They do have young English players and two – Rio Ngumoha and Trey Nyoni – have started non‑Carabao Cup ties this season, but looking across the Premier League I worry our national team talent pool is being eroded.

The academy system needs refreshing. Principally, under-21 football should be scrapped. There are 18-year-olds retained only so clubs have a big enough squad to support the one player who could become a diamond. A boy should be released at latest 18. Those who stay should be in the first team or on loan.

Young players need the competitiveness of senior football as soon as possible. Academy football is tidy and highly technical but has little resemblance to the frenetic, physical senior game. It also doesn’t test whether a boy has the mentality to cope in a tough dressing room where older players don’t want you taking their place. As a young player at Nottingham Forest I dribbled in training past an older teammate who warned: “Do that again, son, and I’ll break your leg.” It’s not like that any more but you need a certain character.

Too many over-18s are released from Premier League academies and want an EFL club without having the CV for that. Can they cope physically? Can they be trusted by a manager who has a short time to do well or faces the sack?

Top managers are also under pressure to win and so can be reluctant to give youth a chance. As a minimum they should be watching academy games when they can and asking: “Who have you got who could become a first-team regular?” Some managers separate themselves from the academy as if it’s another club.

Carrick watching United’s under‑21s this week showed he does take an interest. Now is his moment to be brave.

England rugby league reaches defining moment after men face early World Cup exit

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 11:32:49 GMT

Pool B + C: England 34-12 Papua New Guinea

Women’s side crash out after defeat by Samoa

Game over. Two ultimately straightforward victories from three group games would ordinarily be enough to secure qualification in the Rugby League World Cup, but the format means that, barring a rugby league miracle from Tonga on Sunday, England are heading home early.

That format – 10 teams in lopsided groups and England in a unique position of being effectively out after defeat on the opening weekend – has been a point of discussion since that defeat by the Tongans a fortnight ago. But at some stage, the attention has to turn internally and the tough, uncompromising questions have to be asked of English rugby league.

Those questions can wait for another 48 hours after England defeated Papua New Guinea to ensure qualification for the semi-finals remains mathematically possible. But on a day when they had to not only win, but erode away a 68-point margin on Samoa before hoping they slipped up against Tonga later this weekend, the game is now almost up. A 22-point winning margin here was simply not enough.

Tonga are capable of beating Samoa, without question. But given how their biggest-ever winning margin in that ferocious Pasifika rivalry is 32 points, it is safe to assume that head coach Brian McDermott and his side can start packing their suitcases now. England or Great Britain, for the first time in the history of the Rugby League World Cup, will not be in the last-four.

It had all begun so brightly in Wollongong, though. For the opening 20 minutes England were sensational, opening up a 22-0 lead at a rate which suggested they could rack up the points they needed; with 67 enough to ensure a Tongan win of any kind on Sunday in Sydney would be enough to sneak through to the semi-finals.

But England fell away from their gameplan in spectacular fashion. It would take them another 50 minutes to score a fifth try and by then Papua New Guinea had scored twice to take the points-difference permutations off the table. Late tries from Morgan Knowles and Mikey Lewis at least ensured it would be two wins from three, but England’s journey should end here.

This should serve as a defining moment for English administrators who, for too long, have had their heads buried in the sand. Within the space of four hours in Wollongong, their men’s and women’s teams were effectively sent home on what should be looked back upon as a dark day for the game.

An obsession with club rugby league, a congested domestic calendar which means England do not even have mid-season camps, let alone Test matches, and a decision to increase the overseas quota in Super League last year are all contributory factors to this mess.

They have a monumental task ahead to reverse that decline; it should start with agreeing a partnership with the NRL to allow them to get a grip on the English game, but that would rely on those in charge agreeing to take a step back and letting the grown-ups of rugby league run things efficiently.

McDermott wants to continue through to the next World Cup in 2030, and he should be given the chance – but he needs help from those above him. “It feels like we’ve lost the game,” he reflected post-match. “Something remarkable is going to have to happen now for us to go through. If all we’d needed to do was win, we’d have handled it better … but it looks like we’re going out.”

The required margin of victory looked entirely likely early on. Tries from Matty Ashton, AJ Brimson, Dom Young and Harry Smith all came from front-foot, attacking rugby that had the Kumuls scrambling. Leading 22-0 after the opening quarter, the points required felt within reach: but England spurned at least three more glorious chances as half-time approached.

They drifted from the rugby which had served them so well early on, allowing Papua New Guinea a foothold. Dudley Dotoi and Gairo Voro’s tries within five minutes after the break suddenly then made it 24-12 and as England continued to labour with the ball, it was now suddenly about holding on to win, not winning big. Thankfully, they were at least able to do that.

But when their fate is officially sealed on Sunday, the inquest should really begin into how English rugby league has found itself in the position among international rugby league’s new-age pecking order it is in. Talk about who should coach the team or who should play half-back are distractions. If those in charge do not wake up, England will continue to drift from the world’s elite.

England 6-24 Samoa

Meanwhile, England’s women have failed to reach the final stages of a Rugby League World Cup for the first time, as the increasing gulf between the northern and southern hemispheres was once again exposed in a 6-24 defeat to Samoa which ends their tournament prematurely.

Stuart Barrow’s side were in a winner-takes-all showdown in Wollongong against the Samoans, who were looking to reach the semi-finals of the World Cup for the first time. Their star-studded side, packed with NRLW talent, ultimately got the job done to inflict more misery on English rugby league and underline how they are being left behind on the international stage.

England’s 78-0 defeat to Australia last week felt damaging enough, but failing to qualify from a group for the very first time is another damning indictment of where the English game now appears to sit in the pecking order. There will be a lengthy inquest back home for not just the men’s side, but the women’s too.

Credit must go to Samoa too, though. Their rise in the international game has mirrored that of the men’s and while they too were beaten heavily by Australia in the opening weekend of the group stage, they are deservedly in the semi-finals for the very first time. They were much the stronger of the two sides in Wollongong and worthy winners.

It did not take long for Samoa’s superiority to shine. The outstanding Freedom Crichton Ropati crossed twice in the right corner in the early exchanges, before the Parramatta Eels winger completed her hat-trick on the stroke of half-time. In contrast, England had showed little promise when they were in possession and looked comfortably second best.

They had to score first after the break, but instead went further behind when Mercedez Taulelei-Siala crossed to make it 16-0, with only missed goal kicks from the Samoans keeping it somewhat respectable. Evie Cousins would take advantage of a marvellous Hollie-Mae Dodd break to get England on the board, but it was already looking like nothing more than consolation.

That proved the case when Fanua Rimoni’s late try put the seal on a wonderful win for Samoa, and ensured England would be heading home early. The sobering reality for the women’s game in England is that there does not appear to be a quick fix to close the gap, however.

The NRLW is making huge strides year on year, with players now fully professional and the talent pool growing at an exponential rate. There is progress in England, but much slower – with only a handful of competitive teams, and none yet professional.

Barrow opted to take a young squad to Australia, with 11 of the group that travelled 23 or under. That is perhaps with the 2030 tournament in mind, but with the disparity in investment between the two hemispheres only widening in women’s rugby league, England will head home early knowing there is a difficult few years ahead: and the prospect of the gulf only getting wider.

Digested week: The Traitors suddenly feels tired – time for a politicians version?

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 11:00:56 GMT

Liz Truss is like a broken record, Harry Kane is for ever Spurs, and the celebs in the castle are getting on my nerves

You would have thought someone would have made an intervention by now. To save Liz Truss from the worst excesses and delusions of herself. Most former prime ministers – and there are enough of them by now – make the transition into civilian life with little fuss. More or less. John Major found himself elevated from national joke to statesman after 20 years; Tony Blair took the grandiose step of establishing his very own institute; Boris Johnson took his grumblings to the Daily Mail where he is now more or less ignored; Theresa May opted for obscurity; we have yet to find out Keir Starmer’s next move. Yet Liz Truss seems permanently scarred by her 49 days in office and its abrupt ending. Constantly feeling the need to pick away at the wound that will never heal.

She has been abandoned by a Tory party for whom she is nothing but an embarrassment and now finds herself posting conversations on YouTube with people as deranged as herself for just a handful of viewers. And now she has written a 95-page book that is essentially a distillation of her previous book. Just even worse and a bit more desperate. Having read the book for a Digested Read, I would suggest you give it a miss. It reads as one extended cry for help. Still insisting that her budget was derailed by the Bank selling gilts the day before – something she had personally signed off – and that the establishment had been out to get her. She is like a broken record. Time for her family and friends to step in.

There are some footballers who will be for ever Tottenham. At least for me. There was Jimmy Greaves. He may have played for Chelsea, AC Milan and West Ham too but it is White Hart Lane for which he is most remembered. Likewise Gareth Bale. He won all sorts with Real Madrid but for Spurs fans he will always be one of us. Even if, in retirement, he seems at his happiest when he is playing golf. Then there is Harry Kane. Arguably the greatest of the three. The footballer who seemed to have less raw talent than Greaves and Bale but forged himself into the world’s best striker by sheer will and hard work.

I was lucky to see almost all of the home games – and many of the away ones – during Kane’s 11-year stay at the club. It would be nice to be able to say I spotted his ability from the off. But I didn’t. I assumed that, like many academy players who were being sent out on loan, he would eventually be shipped out to a lower league club. But when he did get his first-team chance, he scored goals. And kept on scoring them for a decade. A proper team player. As happy making goals for the team as he was knocking them in. Well, almost. A striker measures their seasons in goals. And he acknowledged the fans. When the team had played badly and lost, most of the rest of the players couldn’t wait to leave the pitch. Harry always made sure to thank the fans for their support.

Nor was I that sad when he joined Bayern Munich. I thought he had earned the move. He had given us more than enough and deserved the chance to play for a club that regularly won something. This week he won the Ballon d’Or and I couldn’t have been happier. Some may have thought it a reward for all the goals he scored for Bayern and England in the last year. I liked to think of it as the culmination of a journey. Come on you Spurs.

Budget day comes with its own set of rituals. First the photos of the chancellor holding up the red box outside No 11. In the Commons, the budget speech is always preceded by prime minister’s questions. Normally, PMQs are the high spot of the Commons week, but on budget day both the prime minister and the leader of the opposition know that no one is really listening and so they rather just go through the motions. No point in wasting your best lines if no one is going to write them up.

If the budget statement is a tough gig for reporters trying to make an instant assessment of its economic impact, it’s a nightmare for the leader of the opposition. She has to make an instant reply with only what’s already been leaked to back it up. So what you normally get is 20 minutes of “it’s all terrible” and “we wouldn’t have done any of it”. It’s only a day later, when economists and politicians have had a chance to go through the numbers line by line, that a proper assessment can be made.

John Healey isn’t everyone’s go-to guy as the standard bearer for Andy Burnham’s new brand of optimism. His is the voice of despair, a harbinger of the apocalypse. So it was hard going listening to him rattle off 98 not very big measures designed to help with the cost of living through what is forecast to be the toughest decade for the country on record. Healey said he was trying to give everyone some “breathing space”. Very Gen Z. Everyone wants some breathing space these days. But it sounded most that it was the government that needed the breathing space, with the tricky decisions on defence and the welfare bill parked until the next budget. Or the election. Whichever comes sooner.

One person who wasn’t in the Commons to hear the budget was Nigel Farage. He claimed someone had moved his prayer card. This sounded about as plausible as Burnham claiming he couldn’t make it to PMQs because Lucy Powell had taken his seat. If a party leader needs a seat, one can always be found. At the very least, a junior MP is told to make way. If Nige wasn’t in the Commons, it was because he couldn’t be bothered to turn up.

It’s amazing how quickly the unbearable becomes bearable. When we first started to go to the Marsden in Sutton for Jill’s chemo, it all seemed overwhelming and terrifying. Today, as we went back for the latest round, it feels if not comfortable then reassuringly familiar. Jill sometimes sleeps, sometimes reads a book on her Kindle, during the infusions. I sit beside her and watch the proceedings in parliament and write the sketch and diary. Like now. The wifi is better than at home. The Oak Centre, where the treatment takes place, is modern and state-of-the-art. More like what I imagine the BA business class lounge at Heathrow to be. A friend whose husband has Alzheimer’s couldn’t believe just how welcoming the centre was. There’s so much more money being invested in cancer than there is in dementia. The best time for a chemo slot is first thing in the morning. That way you can be sure to get a parking slot – free if you are having treatment – and you can also get a window bay in the centre.

For the staff, nothing is ever too much trouble: you never feel as if you are being rushed and they are happy to talk through your fears. Every patient facing their worst nightmare and being held and understood. Made safe. You can always tell where the other patients are in their cycle. There was the Indian woman with the most beautiful hair, hoping the cold cap would do its job. It probably wouldn’t. Then there was the middle-aged bloke who arrived, said hello to the nurses and was asleep in minutes. You could hear the snores from the other end of the room. Best of all is the trolley offering free drinks and sandwiches. It’s staffed by volunteers. My favourite is Sandra who joined the team having been a patient first. Another friend, whose wife died of cancer a few years ago, still volunteers at the hospice where she had palliative care. He makes cocktails for everyone once a week. I call that style.

My bad. Having previously raved about Celebrity Traitors, I feel somewhat embarrassed to say I have changed my mind. Halfway through last Friday’s episode, I realised not just that I was no longer enjoying myself but also that the celebs were actively irritating me. The whole format suddenly felt tired. As if the show had come to the end of its shelf life mid-run. I no longer cared what happened during the missions, murders and banishments. I just wanted someone – anyone – to go as soon as possible. I didn’t want to hear one more celeb saying “I really love you. We’re going to be best friends for life” when the only time they are likely to meet in the future is on a panel show.

James Acaster’s round table admission of guilt was an epic failure of self-awareness. The claim that he had been playing the game as “faithful” traitor was comically absurd. He had lasted that long precisely because he had played a traitor’s game so well. Mind you, I am planning to watch to the end, out of sheer “I’ve started so I will finish” bloody-mindedness. But the producers do need to think of ways of refreshing the look for next year’s version or it won’t be just me who is bored. I still think there is potential for a politicians version. If you’re near Worcester on 26 November, come to my show at Huntingdon Hall. We can try to make it happen.

The Guardian’s year in review 2026: On Tuesday 1 December, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. With Zoe Williams, John Crace, Pippa Crerar, Jonathan Liew and Lucy Mangan. Book tickets here or at guardian. live

The world needs the United Nations more than ever. It needs a new lease on life

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 10:00:52 GMT

We need neither ‘peace in our time’ nor ‘perpetual peace’ – but enough peace to keep civilization

To save the United Nations from the irrelevance in which it now wallows, the next secretary general will require the concerted backing of the few powers that govern the security council.

The paradox is that the great powers who created the institution in the 1940s and recently treat it with a cavalier cynicism are now the ones who need it most, as does the rest of the world.

This is not about nostalgia for what was created after the second world war. That world has changed. We are no longer in the cold war. But it is carelessness of high order to assume that some mystical process will create a world while, in the meantime, the most powerful give license to some dangerous pathologies that have brought us to ruin in the past.

The resort to war over dialogue and diplomacy has reared its head again. Restraint has given way to calculated recklessness. Changing facts on the ground before talking now creates leverage, and that is why we see an unprecedented multiplication of centers of violence. Militias and mercenaries abound.

Collective security to which all commit to be effective is now supplanted by a petulant isolationism. Revolutionary new technologies have spurred a rush to secure minerals and supply routes upending traditional notions of sovereignty. Drone warfare has made violence much more affordable. Frontiers are now up for grabs.

The permanent members of the security council, anachronistically still composed of the victors of the second world war, have a tall order. Quarrels that are as old as tribes, communities and nations now have new, more lethal weapons.

Civil wars, border wars and the return of imperial ambition are not relics. They drive the war in Ukraine, the drift toward conflict in the Horn of Africa, the instability around the Gulf and the Red Sea, and the standoff over Taiwan.

These conflicts are now multiplying at a scale and speed in a time when global regulatory arrangements over existential threats are denigrated. Proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, pandemics, climate change will either be fueled or managed by artificial intelligence.

As AI is woven into military planning, early warning and command systems, it compresses the time leaders have to think before they act, and it multiplies the tools of deception and destabilization. A world that learned, slowly and at great risk, to live with nuclear weapons must now learn to live with machines that may shape decisions about using them.

These dangers can only be contained if we dispense with some misplaced assumptions.

The first is that the UN is a club of the like-minded. It was never meant to be. The UN exists so that states that distrust or even detest one another have somewhere to meet – a place that offers hospitality to adversaries.

If the hard conversations about war and technology do not happen there, where else will they happen in a way that protects the rest of humanity? It is about co-existence, not convergence.

The second assumption is that power can be evenly distributed. It cannot. Pretending otherwise is idealism to the point of fault. A handful of states possess the disproportionate capacity to contain these dangers or to unleash them. In practice, today this means the United States, China and Russia.

But there is no reason to exclude India or a better-integrated European Union. Even if they do not trust one another, they need only recognize a shared interest in a world that remains manageable.

This harsh reality should temper the fashionable faith in “middle powers”. Their activism is understandable, even admirable: they see the great powers changing character and are trying to respond. But they are called middle powers for a reason. They cannot, on their own, end a major war or govern a technology developed mostly elsewhere.

This does not mean that might makes right. Neither does it mean that complicated times need simple answers which would be a repudiation of politics at the international level. Power checked by reasonable deliberation, negotiation and diplomacy is a core principle that inspired the charter of the United Nations. This moment calls for a rededication to principled pragmatism.

History has much to teach. When the plague swept Europe in the 14th century, the city states of Italy established the practice of quarantines and an early form of health certification. The science may have been wrong and the system imperfect. But it worked well enough, and it rested on self-interest, not virtue.

Since the mid-20th century, in a radically different technological era, nuclear proliferation and the risk of nuclear war have been contained, so far, through a lengthy process of negotiation and agreements.

Imagine a renewed UN that is a problem-solver rather than a bystander, a credible forum rather than a costly talking shop, and the prime instrument for collective action.

None of this happens unless the great powers want it to. Choosing a secretary general is one of the few moments when they must agree on a qualified person and a timely agenda. The superpowers, middle powers and emerging powers of the global south may each have reasons for skepticism. But they share a stronger reason to make this effort.

We need neither “peace in our time” nor “perpetual peace” – but enough peace to keep civilization.

Alex Rondos is a former envoy of the European Union. Mark Medish is a former senior US national security and treasury official

‘I left shellshocked’: writers on their scariest non-horror movies

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 09:00:50 GMT

For Halloween, Guardian writers have picked the most efficiently terrifying films outside of the horror genre from How to Have Sex to The Hunchback of Notre Dame

Minor spoilers ahead

Hiding in plain sight throughout Lee Chang-dong’s deliciously enigmatic Burning, in which a spirited young woman (Jeon Jong-seo) disappears, and a wealthy playboy (Steven Yeun) gives serial killer vibes, is a disaffected male rage. That’s perhaps the most commonplace horror of our times, whether on the internet or politics, and you feel the tremors of it steadily breaking the surface in Yoo Ah-in’s performance. He plays Jong-su, an aspiring writer, quietly frustrated with his lot in life. Jong-su works odd jobs and tends to his incarcerated father’s dilapidated farm, growing more desperate to grasp some sense of control over the world around him, which is where the scary part comes in. Lee is the master dramatist who with Burning tilts violently into thriller territory, navigating elements from Taxi Driver, The Vanishing and Michael Haneke’s Caché, using the language of horror movies to conjure up a creeping anxiety and dread that erupts into pure existential fear. Radheyan Simonpillai

Burning is available to watch on Mubi and Tubi in the US, to rent digitally in the UK, and on Netflix in Australia

The scariest non-horror movie for me is Disney’s The Hunchback of Notre Dame. The scene where Quasimodo is bound to a pillory where the townspeople throw food and jeer at him because of his appearance and disability will for ever be seared into my brain since I first watched it as a six-year-old child. To this day, I still believe that I was far too young to witness that particular depth of human cruelty even though it’s very real. Not to mention that the story deals with xenophobia and bigotry towards the Romany people and sexual predation from a religious leader that takes the basic idea of good versus evil to a whole new level. The Hunchback of Notre Dame reminds me that you don’t need jumpscares and gore to frighten someone. Sometimes, the real monsters are human beings with a bit of social standing over someone else due to money, beauty, authority or all of the above. Morgan Jerkins

The Hunchback of Notre Dame is available on Disney+

An insane loner motivated by his all-consuming misogyny perches beside his bedroom window, methodically shooting women on the street below. He writes of his compulsion to kill in a series of letters to police and begs the authorities to hurry up and catch him. This grimly prescient noir from 1952 feels all too familiar for modern viewers who are numb to stories of gun violence and incel culture. It’s a disturbingly acute portrait of urban alienation and the destructive nature of obsession, released more than two decades before Taxi Driver epitomized those themes. Equally haunting is The Sniper’s backstory. Director Edward Dmytryk was one of the blacklisted Hollywood Ten who refused to testify in front of the House Un-American Activities Committee. He later reversed course after a six-month prison sentence, ghoulishly ratting on his contemporaries and ending countless careers. Alaina Demopoulos

The Sniper is available on YouTube in the US and to rent digitally in the UK and Australia

In Stanley Kubrick’s magisterial 2001, human creativity is such a mysterious and foreboding thing that it isn’t even couched as of this world – rather, an eerie alien monolith gives it to the primates who later evolve to be human beings. The film will for ever be remembered for its visionary jump cut from a bone spinning in slow motion – tossed triumphantly into the air by a primate in a fit of conquering rage – to an orbiting space satellite carrying nuclear weapons: in one deft motion Kubrick encapsulates the history of creativity as a carrier of our liberation, but also our destructive potential. From there, what unfolds is a carefully choreographed dance of death between humanity’s ability to responsibly discharge its ever-growing technological powers and the devices that become more and more dangerous to our survival as a species. Although Kubrick ends the movie on a note of hope and transcendence, what sticks with me more is the existential terror that one of our greatest strengths as beings will ultimately lead to our collapse. In an age of extremes where we are regularly reminded of the many technologically fueled threats to global civilization, it’s hard not to feel that fear. In 2001, astronaut-protagonist Dave Bowman manages to save himself – and thus take the next leap in human evolution – by simply disconnecting the runaway AI known as HAL 9000, but in our world we’ve already passed the point where that would have been possible. Veronica Esposito

2001: A Space Odyssey is available on HBO Max

There’s so much I loved about growing up in the 80s: the funny pages, the power ballads, going for a drive, malls of genuine value – entertainment and otherwise. But one thing I did not love and still don’t was the era’s obsession with animatronic realism, of stuffed animals come disturbingly to life. And by far the worst offender was Howard the Duck. Here was a human adult-sized mallard foisted from his alien nest on to the unwitting citizens of Cleveland, Ohio, looking for all the world like a Donald Duck mascot who had fallen into a vat of primordial ooze (with those golf ball eyes screaming Help!). That Howard also happens to be a martial arts-wielding feminist with an appreciation for hair bands never endeared him to me more than the Dark Overlord who’s also summoned from deep space to … fuck with him? With us? (His true goals still remain somewhat unclear.) My nine-year-old mind was not prepared to see him in bed with Lea Thompson, and rarely does a Halloween go by when some part of me isn’t bracing for a surprise reunion with this quack at a backwoods haunted house. You simply cannot release a movie like this two years after Child’s Play and expect people not to mistake it for a horror. I wonder if the comics company that spawned this duck ever recovered … Andrew Lawrence

Howard the Duck is available to rent digitally in the US, on YouTube in the UK and to rent digitally in Australia

Remember the backseat scene in Bo Burnham’s excellent Eighth Grade, where a horny teen tries to seduce its young lead through a coercive game of truth or dare until her guilelessness catches up to his intentions? How to Have Sex is that unbearable, all-too-recognizable dread blown up to 91 minutes. In an extraordinary breakout performance, Mia McKenna-Bruce plays a 16-year-old on holiday in Greece with two more developed girlfriends. As they flirt with boys and party endlessly, she realizes that keeping up with a shot count might not equal sexual maturity. What’s brilliant about writer-director Molly Manning Walker’s debut is that the worst rarely ever happens: the girls can stumble home down a dark alley and make it back all right, but the threat of the worst-case scenario suffuses every single frame. It’s a queasy, unforgettable viewing experience, activating both parental and innocent impulses as we hope for the best for McKenna-Bruce’s fully realized heroine. Juan A Ramirez

How to Have Sex is available on Netflix and Mubi in the US, on Mubi in the UK and on SBS on Demand in Australia

The horror movie my friends and I were supposed to see that day was The Rage: Carrie 2, a little-seen sequel to the 1976 masterpiece. We did see it – I’d even call it mildly underrated! – and it was indeed a horror film, albeit not the scariest one. But the movie that sent us off into the night so rattled that my buddy briefly drove down the wrong direction of a one-way street was what we casually ducked into afterward: 8mm, a thriller starring Nicolas Cage. Cage was the draw there, so I didn’t think much either way about the subject matter, which was snuff films; Cage plays a private investigator hired to find out if such a film, starring a teenage runaway, is real. I understand why critics at the time mostly shrugged the Joel Schumacher movie off as exploitative, histrionic and even cheesy, but screenwriter Andrew Kevin Walker knows his way around bringing rococo horrors into a stylized version of the real world (he also wrote Seven), sneaking horror into more quasi-respectable genres. The movie’s detective-thriller trappings are probably what ultimately made its more over-the-top elements, including multiple gruesome deaths, an extended confrontation between Cage and a creep played by James Gandolfini, and Cage tracking down a mysterious snuff-film performer called Machine, so viscerally upsetting. My two buddies and I left shellshocked. I like to pretend that I haven’t revisited 8mm since its 1999 release because I’d be embarrassed by how affected I was by such shlock, but the truth is, I’m still a little afraid of the damn thing. Jesse Hassenger

8mm is available to rent digitally in the US, the UK and Australia

There are many reasons why Awake – the melodramatic thriller in which Hayden Christensen plays a wealthy finance bro who undergoes a heart transplant but remains conscious for the entire operation – continues to scare me the more I think about it. First, the idea of anesthesia failing is terrifying enough. But being paralyzed and unable to communicate that it’s not working? That feels unnecessary. Then there are the film’s many competing plot points. Christensen’s billionaire protagonist, Clay (a name I’ve yet to encounter in nearly a decade in the US), is apparently saint-like. While awake on the operating table, he gleans that his friend and cardiac surgeon (Terrence Howard) is in cahoots with his new wife (Jessica Alba) to kill him. The film is largely confined to a New York hospital, which sounds like a compelling chamber drama? Well, you’d be wrong. Because there apparently isn’t enough anxiety in Joby Harold’s directorial debut, we also get Clay’s hallucinations, including memories of his abusive father. It becomes a race against time for Clay’s mother (Lena Olin), another benevolent billionaire, to stop the plot. Somehow, it only gets more unbelievable. Still, Awake is weirdly exhilarating. Everyone commits fully to the madness, acting with a capital A. Shrai Popat

Awake is available on Tubi in the US, to rent digitally in the UK and on Netflix in Australia

Todd Haynes’s 2019 legal drama, Dark Waters, tells a familiar American story: a principled lawyer goes up against a massive, unscrupulous corporation and loses. But there is a lot in this film, which was based on Nathaniel Rich’s 2016 New York Times profile of former corporate defense lawyer Robert Bilott, to make this duel terrifying. Throughout his career, Haynes has looked at how external forces contaminate the domestic sphere, and here, it’s no different: the obsessive spiral that sweeps Mark Ruffalo’s Bilott is nearly as scary as the complete indifference with which DuPont, the chemical corporation responsible for knowingly poisoning West Virginians with “forever chemicals”, regards human life. One image in the film haunts me more than others: Bilott kneels among stacks of paper that tower over him as menacingly as Nosferatu’s shadow. It’s a terror of scale – all that work won’t kill Bilott, but it will whittle him down to a wisp. To DuPont, crushing Bilott is as simple as swatting a fly. Once you see the horror, you can’t unsee it. Rafaela Bassili

Dark Waters is available to rent digitally in the US and the UK and on SBS on Demand in Australia

There’s something uniquely, nightmarishly terrifying about trying to defend yourself against a false accusation. It’s what makes documentaries about particularly egregious examples of injustice not just enraging but seriously scary – how mechanically efficient the system can be when it’s focused on destroying you, often as the result of something as random as bad luck. In Thomas Vinterberg’s almost unbearably clammy drama The Hunt, a claim is made and believed and it’s cleverly one we’re never kept in the dark about. We know instantly that Mads Mikkelsen’s kindly kindergarten teacher didn’t sexually abuse the young daughter of a friend who, through a confused blur of emotions, makes a comment that is seen as proof of something devastating. With every small decision then made by those around her, some initially understandable and some maddeningly ill-advised, a tight-knit community turns on someone they had previously embraced. It’s horrifying to watch for so many reasons, exposing just how incredibly fragile the trust and acceptance of others can be and how so many are happy to rely on grim preconceptions about men who work with children. What’s chilling is how unstoppable the spiral can often seem and, in a disquieting final scene, how unfathomable it can be to move on from even if the crime has been disproved. In The Hunt, a pitchfork is far scarier than a knife. Benjamin Lee

The Hunt is available on Tubi in the US and to rent digitally in the UK and Australia

There are many reasons why Zodiac, David Fincher’s 2007 film on the infamous serial killer, is considered one of the best detective movies of all time: its precise detail, its masterclass escalation of suspense, its immersive and unsettling mood. But the legacy of Zodiac, to me, isn’t Jake Gyllenhaal’s obsessive spiral, or the vexatious unsolved cryptograms, or even Guillermo del Toro’s viral tweet thread on the movie’s perfection. It is the unnerving re-enactment, about 20 minutes in, of a black-clad man striding in broad daylight toward a picnicking couple. At first he appears to be just another park visitor; only after a few paces can you see that he is masked, marked by an ominous symbol and carrying a gun. Fincher mostly keeps the camera trained on the female victim’s face, as her initial curiosity morphs to concern, then fear, then terror. That shift – when she knows something is off, but can’t yet tell it’s dire – pops into my mind when, say, a stranger approaches on an empty sidewalk, or when I am alone in a park. My dread has yet to ever be substantiated, but that scene is a pathway to panic: sometimes, as in this actual 1969 murder, your fear was right. Adrian Horton

Zodiac is available on YouTube and Paramount+ in the US, on Netflix and Amazon Prime in the UK, and on Netflix in Australia

As a committed avoider of actual horror movies, my most scary experiences at the cinema tend to sneak up on me when I’m not really expecting them. Both the original Vanishing and Jonathan Glazer’s Under the Skin contained scenes that temporarily put the fear of God into me, but I think for cumulative dread and general misery, Darren Aronofsky’s mighty adaptation of Hubert Selby Jr’s junkie novel stands supreme. As its title indicates, Requiem is a nightmare inversion of the American dream: after attempting to go into business with a “pound of pure”, the three youthful protagonists, played by Jared Leto, Marlon Wayans and Jennifer Connelly in manifestly career-high performances, end up having an arm amputated, being battered by prison guards and being forced into gruesome sex work, respectively. In this film, heroin is the equivalent of the creepy killer doll, or hulking monster no one else can see; it’s the silent, remorseless slayer THAT CAN’T BE STOPPED. And that’s not even counting the fourth protag, Ellen Burstyn’s gameshow wannabe, so hopped up on speed-laced diet pills that she goes into amphetamine psychosis. This isn’t a tale of terror, as such, but their collective descent into abject misery is as profoundly disturbing an experience as cinema has ever recorded. Andrew Pulver

Requiem for a Dream is available on Peacock and Tubi in the US and to rent digitally in the UK and Australia

‘It’s been a whirlwind’: the Essex lawyer who quit her job and became voice of Netflix’s hit show Spike

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 09:00:50 GMT

Emily McGonagle was watching cartoons with her sons when she decided to embark on a career change. A decade on, she is a star of a globally popular children’s series

Emily McGonagle was on maternity leave from her job as a lawyer, juggling the care of her new baby and her toddler son, when the daily diet of TV cartoons made her think about an unlikely career change.

Watching Peppa Pig and Paw Patrol, her older son’s favourites, “it occurred to me: who does this job?”, says the 42-year-old from Essex. “How do you get into it? Even when I was watching TV commercials, I’d think: well, how do you do that?”

McGonagle had been commuting to her demanding legal job in London from the family home in Colchester, but was ready for a more flexible work-life balance. She had always loved performing in school plays and knew she had a talent for accents – so why not look into how to become a voice actor?

A decade on, she is voicing one of the most popular Netflix TV shows in the world. McGonagle plays eight characters in an animated series called Spike about a young dragon and his friends. When the programme launched on the streaming network on 12 October it quickly became the seventh-most-watched programme globally in any genre.

“These past few weeks have been a bit of a whirlwind and very surreal,” says McGonagle. “It’s just amazing to me that one day I was watching Peppa Pig with my kids wondering how you get into it, and today I’m turning on Netflix and seeing Spike next to Peppa Pig in the top 10. It is honestly amazing. I could never in my wildest dreams have imagined that I would get to this point.”

When first looking into the industry as a young mum, she says: “I realised that with the right training and setup with professional audio equipment, I could do it from home – which was a revelation to me because I had assumed everything was done in a studio.”

With the support of her husband, Ciarán, she converted a large wardrobe into a soundproofed vocal booth and began auditioning for voiceover jobs that were offered online. She started with a few corporate training videos, before getting some commercial TV and radio adverts, even voicing a Formula One-themed go-kart ride.

But the ambition to work in children’s animation never wavered, so she looked into drama classes at her local theatre, then took some specialist courses in acting for voice animation. The roles in Spike came about when McGonagle saw the project advertised “on LinkedIn, of all places” by the Lithuanian animation company behind it. Originally screened on YouTube, its snowballing popularity among hard-pressed preschooler parents eventually attracted the attention of Netflix.

Voicing multiple different characters in the same project can be a challenge, says McGonagle (She provides the voices for 20 in the video game Game of Thrones: Kingsroad, “and that was a lot”).

How does she keep them distinctive? “I write a bio for my characters and think about what they look like, how old they are, where they might be from and give them some backstory in order to bring that character to life. And then I will adapt my voice to make it younger, make it older, or I might add an accent. It’s all about the way in which you move your body and even your mouth itself.”

The characters she voices in Spike include the main character’s mother, a girl giraffe, a boy elephant, and the canine police officer. Some speak with various English accents, some American. “Those were just the accents and characters I put forward when I auditioned,” she says. “It’s not ultimately my decision.”

“It’s a very international team and we do all communicate online but there haven’t been any in-person meetups. We have spoken on Zoom calls but nobody has ever met in person because we all have our own home studios,” she says.

McGonagle’s sons, Finn and Jack, are now 11 and nine, and far too old for preschool dragons. They must be proud of her unusual career path, though? “They’re not really that bothered by it, which is probably a good thing,” she says. When she read them bedtime stories when they were younger, “honestly, they would just tell me: ‘Ah stop, don’t do the voices’.

“Quite often I’ll be going around the house talking in different voices just to practise and they do get annoyed with it.”

The hill I will die on: Dumplings are the ultimate proof of our common humanity

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 08:00:49 GMT

Across nations and classes, there is one thing we can all agree on – that putting delicious things inside dough is a good idea

On a recent Saturday morning in Paris, I made a life-changing discovery. It came in the frozen aisle of an Asian supermarket: you can buy premade dumpling wrappers. Take a moment to think about the implications of this. Chinese shrimp wontons? Ukrainian potato varenyky? Italian veal ravioli? You’re halfway there before you’ve even chopped an onion (as long as you’re not precious about using exactly the right dough for each recipe).

Since then, I’ve fallen into a full-blown dumpling rabbit hole, my nights spent on YouTube, watching grandmothers sitting in circles, pinching dough. So many shapes. So many techniques. Team inward pleats or outward?

Columbia University Press has just published The Epic History of Macaroni and Cheese: From Ancient Rome to Modern America. But clearly someone should also write The Long Arc of Putting Things in Dough: A Transcultural History. Because what does it say about humanity that all around the globe, at various points in history, people have invented some version of a delicious thing wrapped in dough?

Perhaps we all secretly long to be dumplings; there is certainly something reassuring about being enclosed. The French philosopher Claire Marin calls this a nostalgia for our “lost envelopment” – a longing to return to that primordial experience of being fully embraced in the womb.

Indeed, how fortunate is a filling’s existence: held, knowing it is exactly where it belongs. Desired, yet protected. And entirely individual, but never alone; dumplings are herd beings. Plus, they’re cute. So much so that squishy mystery dumplings have become the latest trend toy. The Labubu is so 2025.

Perhaps we need to go back to the stone age to understand the worldwide dumpling craze.

In her 1986 essay The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction, the American novelist Ursula K Le Guin suggested that our narrative of human history may be badly skewed. We picture early humans as men chasing bison. Yet the first human tool may have been a basket, not a spear. Gathering probably provided most of the calories; hunting was more often a hobby to kill time. And the fact that we say “hunter-gatherers” rather than “gatherer-hunters” is probably another vestige of the patriarchy.

“It is a human thing to do,” Le Guin writes, “to put something you want, because it’s useful, edible or beautiful, into a bag … and then take it home with you.”

Dumplings, those lovely edible containers, take this human instinct and make it culinary.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Whatever the reasons for the dumpling’s global triumph, it fills me with hope. Every time I eat Afghan mantu, Argentinian empanadas or Austrian kasnudeln, I feel that these little envelopes are trying to teach me a small lesson in universalism.

Forget the clash of civilisations. Dumplings, whether you like them or not, are the ultimate proof of our common humanity.

Joseph de Weck is an associate fellow with the German Council on Foreign Relations and writes for Guardian Europe from Zürich and Paris

Opening the EU debate again is clearly a political minefield. But we have to do it

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 06:00:47 GMT

Andy Burnham must tread cautiously, but Brexit was a very grave act of self-harm – and he is right to address it

Andy Burnham’s opening debate on whether Britain should rejoin the EU is divisive, painful and politically risky. That is why it should be welcomed. To jeopardise his popularity so soon after coming to office might seem reckless, but the issue is urgent and not going away. Brexit is continuing to damage the nation’s economy. The prime minister’s job is to challenge, if not reform it.

The Brexit decade has evoked a bizarre sense of guilt among Britons. Opinion polls show nearly 60% regard it as a mistake, with just a third still in favour. Almost a quarter of those who voted for Brexit now regret it. While early forecasts of economic disaster were proved wrong, the accumulated cost of cutting links with Britain’s biggest trading partner is estimated at 6-8% of GDP.

This is huge. It must rank as the greatest act of self-harm by a British government in modern times.

A year ago Keir Starmer began to ease some of the barriers, with modest deals on youth exchange and meat exports. Burnham wants to take this further, with negotiations resuming in Brussels next month. Yesterday in the Commons he cited damage to the car industry, while agriculture remains mired in dozens of pages of regulation. Fish rots in inspection sheds, and cars and passengers queue for hours at borders.

Yet if something must be done, the question remains: what? Burnham emphasises that he would not renege on Labour’s 2024 election pledge to honour the referendum in this parliament. But he certainly wants a revival of the debate and has a personal hope to see Brexit reversed one day. For now he seeks “an honest discussion … an open conversation” on where future negotiations might lead. He murmured the possibility of free movement of people for EU passport holders. The subject’s delicacy was demonstrated as Westminster Brexiters reacted like scalded cats. “Betrayal … catastrophe”, cried Reform UK’s Nigel Farage.

A reason for Burnham to proceed cautiously is that the public’s regret over Brexit is not matched by agreement on what should take its place. While 55% of all Britons would support rejoining the EU, that falls to 35% if the condition is surrendering the UK’s previous opt-outs – which would mean joining the euro and participating in the Schengen passport-free travel zone.

There could be a middle-ground Brexit model, including a bespoke place for Britain within a wider European economic area. But this in turn might be unacceptable to some existing EU countries. An alternative could include membership of the European Free Trade Association or a customs union.

The truth is Britain has always been ambivalent in its attitude to European unions. Ireland and Denmark had in the past reversed anti-EU referendums by negotiating opt-outs with Brussels. David Cameron attempted no such remedy in 2016. He simply resigned.

During the post-referendum Commons debates it was clear that many MPs would have favoured a “soft Brexit” option, its form as yet unclear. A responsible parliament at the time might have formed a coalition to pursue such an option. As it was, Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour party preferred to exploit Theresa May’s internal divisions and leave the way open for Boris Johnson and his “hard Brexiters”. Manning Westminster’s party barricades took precedence over seeking a sensible compromise with Brussels.

Burnham must therefore tread with care. Westminster’s political culture slithers instinctively into conflict mode without thought for the message that this sends to the outside world. Plenty of Europeans remain sceptical of whether Britain truly wants to rejoin the EU, and will resist any demand for extensive opt-outs or concessions. But that is for another day. For now, Labour is committed to honour its referendum manifesto promise.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Burnham is right to open the conversation. But he must first detoxify Brexit and diminish its prominence – and that of the party whose existence depends on it, Reform. For the time being, as there is no question of rejoining the EU, there is no issue of British sovereignty. The negotiations should be boring, over regulations, conventions and protocols. These would inevitably involve compromise – but compromise that ensures both parties come away with something gained.

One solution would be to do what was not done after 2016: establish a strong cross-party Commons committee to monitor the November talks and take Burnham’s conversation forward. This should concentrate on reducing barriers to trade and growth, and promoting cultural and security relations with Europe. To put it mildly, Europe needs such concentration, and badly. On that, surely Westminster can agree.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist
