On Star Trek, Patrick Stewart could make anyone feel hopeful for humanity

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 05:00:48 GMT

As Jean-Luc Picard in seven seasons, four films and a sequel, Stewart made us believe the most interesting person in the room might also be the most humane

Patrick Stewart dies age 86

His life in pictures

Patrick Stewart brought gravitas and complexity to the screen, from Star Trek to X-Men

‘He stood for the best of us’: William Shatner and more pay tribute

What might humanity look like in 400 years’ time if we really do become wiser and more compassionate with each passing decade? The creators of Star Trek: The Next Generation clearly felt the answer closely resembled Patrick Stewart, who has died aged 86 after a short illness. Their decision may well have opened up an entirely new future for Gene Roddenberry’s enduring, resolutely utopian space saga.

Prior to the casting of the classically trained Yorkshireman in 1987, Star Trek was best known for the interplay between William Shatner’s charismatic, impulsive Captain Kirk and Leonard Nimoy’s drily logical Spock. Stewart brought something of both men to the captain’s chair as Jean-Luc Picard, combining analytical rigour with a depth of feeling his imposing formality could never quite conceal.

The bald, cerebral Englishman was a bold choice to succeed Shatner’s swaggering Canadian alpha male – but his ability to bring quiet authority and conviction to even the most outlandish of scenes gave the Enterprise an entirely different centre of gravity. Through seven seasons and four feature films, Stewart made audiences believe that the most interesting person in the room might also be the most thoughtful and humane.

The difference between the two captains is perhaps best exemplified in the famous 1989 episode The Measure of a Man, in which Picard must defend the android Data against an overzealous Starfleet scientist’s attempts to dismantle him in the name of progress. Where Shatner might have chewed up all the available scenery before challenging the prosecution to a shirtless fistfight in a nearby space quarry, Stewart lets the legal arguments themselves become the drama. His measured questions on the nature of sentience expose the enormity of what is being proposed, the gathering anger in his voice conveying a civilised man discovering how much barbarism still lurks within his supposedly enlightened society.

Stewart also gave Star Trek an emotional scale to match the extravagance of its ideas. In the 1992 episode The Inner Light, an alien probe from a long-dead civilisation entrusts Picard with decades of another man’s existence so that it might live on in his memory. He acquires a wife, children and a whole domestic life, even entering old age, before suddenly awakening aboard his ship to discover that only minutes have passed. The premise has something of Borges about it, an entire existence unfolding in a few minutes. Stewart makes us feel the weight of years that nobody else aboard the Enterprise has lived; he later called it his favourite episode.

It was perhaps inevitable that this blend of intellectual ambition and emotional intimacy didn’t always translate so effectively to the more bombastic world of the big screen, where Picard and his crew arrived in 1994 with the uneven Star Trek Generations. At times it was tempting to wonder if Stewart might have been better suited to the pre-blockbuster science fiction of the early 1970s, when Solaris and Silent Running could build entire worlds around questions of memory or conscience. The Star Trek films sometimes seemed uncertain about what to do with an actor who could make deliberation so compelling, handing him a phaser when unpicking a moral conundrum may have better suited his skills. It didn’t help that the Picard-era movies were made on substantially lower budgets than many of their contemporary sci-fi rivals, and often really looked like it.

And yet, even here, there were victories that only Stewart could have pulled off. First Contact (1996) cast Picard as a Captain Ahab-style avenger pursuing the technological white whale known as the Borg, which had briefly assimilated him into its remorseless hive mind during the TV show. Few other actors could have taken their best-known character into such unfamiliar territory unscathed, but Stewart’s years performing Shakespeare had prepared him for men whose public authority conceals private torment. He understood how eloquence could give destructive passions the appearance of reason, and how frightening rage becomes when it erupts from someone we have spent years watching display formidable self-control. By disrupting the qualities that had made his Picard so reassuring, Stewart was able to show how profoundly the Borg had wounded him.

The final Next Generation-era movie was 2002’s poorly received Star Trek: Nemesis, by which time Stewart had found a new multiplex audience as Charles Xavier in 2000’s X-Men. Despite his continuing prominence in genre fare, he never returned for the rebooted film series that began with 2009’s JJ Abrams-directed Star Trek, which instead turned to Nimoy for its elder-statesman gravitas.

Television eventually welcomed him back in Star Trek: Picard, which ran for three seasons from 2020, reuniting him with his old Enterprise colleagues for its highly acclaimed final run. Once a gamble on Star Trek’s future, Stewart had become one of the great reasons to revisit its past. His success helped establish that the saga could flourish beyond its original cast, opening the way for the political intrigue of Deep Space Nine and the stranded explorers of Voyager. And his legacy is perhaps even more apparent today in the tonal confidence of Strange New Worlds, which shares The Next Generation’s willingness to move between moral inquiry, cosmic peril and outright whimsy.

As much as anyone, Stewart gave Roddenberry’s faith in progress a persuasive human form. If Star Trek was always about showing us how far humankind might travel in the next four centuries, he helped us believe we might actually have grown up by the time we got there.

Could 2026 be the year that democracy fought back?

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 05:00:47 GMT

Elections are never enough by themselves, but the stunning results from Serbia, Brazil and Hungary have given us hope in dark times

It is undoubtedly too early to declare victory, but the recent electoral defeats of Viktor Orbán, Aleksandar Vučić and Flávio Bolsonaro make me wonder: is 2026 turning out to be the year democracy slowly, but surely, fought back?

Even in Israel, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s reigning bloc lost its parliamentary majority and saw the spectacular rise of Arab parties. Though the opposition may not be able to form a government yet, it does have the larger parliamentary bloc.

The shift began with an astonishing election result in Hungary in April. Against all odds, Orbán, the EU’s most deeply entrenched autocrat, was unseated by challenger Péter Magyar. Over his long years in office, Orbán had done everything possible to consolidate and perpetuate his authoritarian grip on power. The media were in his pocket, the judiciary ate from his hand and academic freedom was systematically curtailed. Yet a broad civic movement coalesced around Magyar’s party and succeeded in ousting him. The banks of the Danube witnessed their most exuberant night of celebration this century.

Joy was equally palpable last Sunday night, 300km down the river in Belgrade. There in Serbia, the Student List, a bottom-up alliance of students, academics and angry citizens, unexpectedly sent Vučić packing. Vučić had held a tight grip on power since 2014, first as prime minister, then president, relying on a familiar cocktail of far-right bravado, financial scandals and contempt for the rule of law: the winning formula of recent years. But there seems to be a limit to what citizens are ready to accept. Vučić’s fate was sealed after the newly constructed roof canopy of the Novi Sad train station collapsed in 2024, killing 16 people and triggering widespread public fury against systemic corruption.

Then came the biggest news of all on Monday morning, when Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defied expectations to emerge victorious in Brazil’s presidential election. In the first round, Flávio Bolsonaro had been in the lead, and almost every poll predicted he would win the run-off. Many Brazilians braced themselves for an administration at least as radical-right as his father’s. Instead, Lula, the son of poor, illiterate farmers and a former factory worker himself, surprised friend and foe alike by winning the presidency of Latin America’s largest economy for the fourth time.

Commentators were quick to point out that Lula’s victory halted a winning streak for rightwing populists across Latin America. That is certainly true, but zooming out reveals a broader pattern. This is not primarily a story of left v right, but rather of democrats v post-democrats. Hungary’s Magyar is by no means a leftist; he is a centre-right leader who was once a member of Orbán’s own party. In Serbia, the Student List was headed by Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist and university professor with no pronounced ideological profile. While he champions liberal values such as press freedom and the rule of law, his stance on Kosovo aligns with traditional Serbian nationalism: it should not be independent.

What Magyar, Srdanović and Lula share – despite significant political differences – is a fundamental belief that the rules of the democratic game must be respected. Elections must be fair, judges and journalists must work independently, and checks and balances exist for a reason.

Post-democrats, by contrast, treat laws and international agreements as mere suggestions, a convenient menu of policy options from which they can cherrypick. They use elections to gain power, only to hollow out democratic institutions once they are in office and maximise their private business profits. As corruption is key, they have to remain in power to stay out of jail. Opposing voices must be muzzled and critical media prosecuted. Post-democrats only keep the outer shell of democracy. Bolsonaro Jr took a page from Donald Trump’s playbook: election results are declared unimpeachable when he wins, and rigged when he loses. Similarly, Netanyahu is now attempting to discredit the Israeli election outcome, by suggesting Qatar interfered on behalf of the Palestinian parties.

Post-democrats have been on the rise for years, and it is terrifying. Since 2000, we have witnessed a steady, deliberate dismantling of democratic achievements across every continent. Anyone reading the latest international Democracy Report, produced by the V-Dem Institute, could easily despair. In terms of overall democratic health, it finds that we have effectively regressed to the levels of 1978. Only 7% of the world’s population live in liberal democracies.

Yet after years of alarming headlines about global democratic backsliding, the news from Budapest, Belgrade and Brasília offers rays of hope in dark times. So does the massive wave of Gen Z protests this year, from India and the Philippines to Albania, Argentina and Chile. Huge crowds of young people have taken to the streets to challenge autocratic power and corruption in their countries.

Could liberal democracy be finding its second wind? Is it actually possible to defeat autocrats and authoritarian regimes after all? Could this mark the beginning of a democratic revival that might extend to the US next week? Most polls suggest that the Democrats stand a strong chance of reclaiming at least the House of Representatives in the upcoming US midterms.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Meanwhile, the delegitimisation of Arab voters in Israel this week reminds us of the limitations of change via the ballot box. Elections can help us get rid of post-democrats, but in deeply divided societies they are not enough to heal. The individual, silent act of voting must be complemented with collective processes of deliberation.

Nonetheless, globally, 2026 may come to rank as the best year for democracy in more than a quarter of a century. Could this be the turning point?

What this tells us ahead of critical elections in some of the EU’s largest member states in the year ahead – France, Spain, Germany and Poland – remains anyone’s guess. Looking at the momentum of the AfD in Germany, rightwing populist parties with post-democratic tendencies remain very much alive in Europe. And Vox could be part of a People’s party-led government in Spain in a matter of weeks. But Hungary, Serbia and Brazil have delivered a vital reminder: the rise of autocrats and their permanence in power are not immutable laws of nature. Soon enough, post-democracies may start to feel passé.

David Van Reybrouck is a Belgian author and philosopher laureate for the Low Countries. He is the author of Against Elections: The Case for Democracy, and the initiator of Democracy27

The White House Farm massacre phone calls: could a single disputed digit set Jeremy Bamber free?

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 05:00:47 GMT

He has been in prison for 41 years for killing five members of his family. But if a phone call was made to the police by Bamber’s father on the night of the murders – as his team believes – one of the UK’s most notorious criminals could be exonerated

On 7 August 1985, five people were found dead at White House Farm in Essex, England: 28-year-old Sheila Caffell (known to her family as Bambi); her six-year-old twin sons, Daniel and Nicholas; and her 61-year-old adoptive parents, June and Nevill Bamber. All five had been shot with a rifle. Caffell’s 24-year-old brother, Jeremy Bamber, who was also adopted, had called to alert Essex police to a disturbance inside the farmhouse – he said his father had called to tell him – and had been outside with the police for four hours before the bodies were discovered. Caffell, who had recently been hospitalised with schizoaffective disorder and is said to have feared her children were going to be taken into foster care, was found with the rifle lying on her chest, pointing towards her neck. There were two gunshot wounds to her neck and chin and a bloodied Bible by her side.

The case was initially thought to be open and shut, a tragic murder-suicide committed by Caffell. But a month later, Bamber was arrested after relatives went to the police to voice their suspicions about him; his former girlfriend Julie Mugford then told police he had made a confession to her. The relatives went on to inherit from Nevill and June Bamber’s considerable estate after Bamber’s convictions. It was later discovered that Mugford had agreed to sell the story of their relationship to the News of the World for £25,000 if Bamber was convicted. Essex police and crown prosecutors had also agreed to drop charges against her for burglary, chequebook fraud and selling cannabis, because “prosecuting her could jeopardise her availability or credibility as a key witness” against Bamber.

Bamber was found guilty of the murders and has now been in prison for 41 years, but questions have always been asked about the safety of his conviction. These have grown recently. The proper body to examine these is the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), but it has already taken the CCRC four years to consider less than half the evidence that Bamber has submitted to them. In July 2025, it concluded that the first four of 10 points did not meet the high evidentiary threshold needed to refer the case back to the court of appeal.

In the third piece in our series considering discrete pieces of evidence, we analyse discrepancies in timelines recorded by Essex police that could prove Bamber’s innocence.

“Imagine how stupid I’d have to be to put myself in the frame for murdering my family by telling the police I’d received a phone call when I hadn’t,” Jeremy Bamber says. “Like most people, I assumed the police would have been able to trace the call. If it turned out Dad hadn’t called me, I’d have basically been handing myself in.”

Bamber is writing to me from Wakefield prison. For the past 41 years, he has been locked up for the murder of five members of his family, while always protesting his innocence.

In his letter, he is referring to a phone call he made to Essex police from his cottage in the middle of the night on 7 August 1985. Bamber, now 65, told the police his father, Nevill, had just called him to say Bamber’s sister, Sheila Caffell, had “gone crazy” at the family home, White House Farm, and got hold of one of Nevill’s guns. Bamber said the line had then gone dead. His call to Essex police has never been disputed. What has been disputed is his claim that Nevill called him.

At Bamber’s trial, the prosecution claimed he had made up the call to provide himself with a false alibi. They argued that he had killed the five members of his family at White House Farm between 12am and 3am, before cycling back to his cottage and calling the police himself.

This is a story about telephone calls, technology and timings. It is also a story about a single disputed digit in police logs, which could prove Bamber’s innocence. A digit that, at the time of the trial in 1986, neither the jury nor Bamber’s defence team could possibly have understood was so significant. It was only 25 years later, when 347,000 documents relating to the case were released, that its importance became clear.

The digit relates to the time Bamber called the police. At trial, there was confusion about whether it was 3.26am or 3.36am. The presiding judge, Sir Maurice Drake, told the jury to accept a timing of 3.26am. But a series of police logs and statements that were not disclosed at trial suggest Bamber made the call at 3.36am.

It appeared to be an obscure time-keeping argument in court, of little real significance. But it seems there is evidence that the jury was misled and that the differing times in fact refer to two different calls – the first made by Nevill and the second by Jeremy Bamber. And if Nevill did call the police to report his daughter had gone “berserk” with a gun, his son should not be in prison.

Chelmsford crown court, October 1986. PC Michael James West, who took Bamber’s call at Chelmsford police station in the early hours of 7 August 1985, takes the stand to give evidence for the prosecution. He explains that he works in the control room, a radio and telephone hub for the Chelmsford division, where the unit’s calls are received and officers are allocated their tasks. PC West says he filled out an event log, called a C1, as the conversation took place with Bamber, and that the practice is to log the time at the beginning of the conversation. Surprisingly, that C1 call log is not available to the jury. West tells Anthony Arlidge, the QC for the prosecution, that he recorded the time of 3.36am using the digital clock on the wall in the control room.

Arlidge doesn’t mention the time again. It is only when Geoffrey Rivlin, counsel for the defence, cross-examines West that he is challenged about the purported inconsistencies in his record-keeping.

In his first statement, made two days after the murder, West said he received the call from Jeremy Bamber at 3.26am. In a more detailed statement a month later, the time had changed to 3.36am. Rivlin suggested in court that West had got the time wrong when he changed it and that the call was made, as he had said in his first statement, at 3.26am.

Rivlin: I would like to ask you about times first, if I may. The time you have recorded was 03.36.

West: That is correct.

Rivlin: Is it right that you may have misread the clock and the time may have been 03.26?

West: I was informed I actually spoke to the information room at a time prior to the one that I have recorded so I can only assume that I have wrote – I actually recorded the wrong time, as it were.

But then West, it seems, becomes defensive. He is reluctant to say he made a mistake or that the clock was inaccurate.

Rivlin: The situation is, you looked at the clock and recorded 03.36. You were told subsequently that was almost certainly wrong and you said you may have misread the clock.

West: Well, there is a dispute over the times. I don’t know whose time is right and whose time is wrong.

Rivlin: Let me ask you this question. As regards the clock in the control room at the police station, is that accurate?

West:. Yes, it is.

Rivlin: Are you sure about that?

West: It has on occasion been inaccurate, but on very few occasions.

Rivlin: Would you agree with this, that the control room wall clock rarely shows an accurate time?

West: I would have to disagree with that.

Rivlin: You disagree?

West: Yes.

Rivlin: At all events, perhaps we need take it no further than this, that you did subsequently agree you may have misread the clock?

West: It is possible, although certainly there is a variance in times, yes.

This exchange must have been baffling for the jury. West appeared unwilling to concede that he got the time wrong. Rivlin seemed to suggest the difference between 3.26am and 3.36am was highly significant, but never explained why. He was determined that 3.26am should be recognised as the correct time, but the jury was given no explanation for his insistence.

The reason Rivlin was adamant that the call was made at 3.26am is simply because he thought it looked better for the man he was defending. Bamber had said he received the call from his father at about 3.15am, then rang his girlfriend, Julie Mugford, before calling the police. What kind of man waits 20 minutes and speaks to his girlfriend before contacting the police in such an emergency? Ten minutes, Rivlin thought, would seem more acceptable to a jury.

But Bamber says that is looking at it with the benefit of hindsight: “The last thing I thought when Dad called me was that this was going to end up with my whole family killed.” There had been previous incidents with Caffell, who had a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder and had been hospitalised after a psychotic episode five months before the murders. But none had ended in disaster.

The evening before the killings, Bamber had been at White House Farm and had taken out his father’s .22 rifle, to try to shoot rabbits. When he returned to the farmhouse, he had removed the magazine and the bullet in the breech of the rifle and left those items, and the gun itself, on a bench in the annexe of his parents’ kitchen.

He didn’t fear for the worst when he got the phone call from Nevill, he tells me, because he knew the gun was unloaded. “I assumed my dad, who was 6ft 4in and a strong man, would take the gun off Sheila and that she would calm down.”

As for waiting 20 minutes before calling the police, Bamber has always claimed his father was cut off in the middle of their conversation and that he tried a number of times to call him back, but kept getting the engaged tone. He says he then called Mugford at 3.30am and asked her what she thought he should do. Mugford – who told police a month after the murders, just after Bamber ended their relationship, that he had confessed the killings to her – advised him to “go back to bed”.

He ignored her and at 3.36am, he says, he called the police. “If I’d made up the call from Dad, why on earth would I have said I took 20 minutes to call the police? I would have said I called the police immediately.” Bamber is telling me this in letters sent a few months ago, before the prison banned him from discussing his case with journalists.

But the 3.26am timing of the call appeared to be supported by a rolling log made by a civilian phone operator, Malcolm Bonnett. He was situated at Essex police HQ, a building roughly a mile away from Chelmsford police station, where West was stationed.

Bonnett’s job was to log radio messages and send help from the police and other emergency services. Emergency 999 calls came in to Bonnett, but he also took phone calls from local police stations and officers such as West.

The Bonnett log was shown to the jury at the trial – exhibit 29. It was presented to the court as his record of a call West made to him about the phone call he had received from a Mr Bamber. The jury was told that the Mr Bamber in question was Jeremy. Bonnett’s rolling log starts with an entry at 3.26am. The subject line for this call is “Daughter gone berserk”. This is the only document the jury were shown in regard to the time of the call. It was never explained why West’s C1 log of the phone call was not included in the bundle given to the jury. They had no idea why West had logged the time as 3.36am or why the confusion in court when it was suggested he had got it wrong.

Something didn’t add up. At the trial, it was unclear whether West or Bonnett actually sent out the police cars. Both appear to claim to have done so. West said he radioed the officers asking them to attend the scene, but Bonnett also said that after receiving the call from West about the incident he sent the first police car, CA7, to White House Farm at 03.35am, followed by another car, CA5, at 03.36am. These timings only made sense if West had taken the call from Bamber at 3.26am.

After West and Bonnett’s evidence, the time of Bamber’s call played no part in the trial until the summing up, in which Drake stated that the clocks in the information room were later checked and found to be correct. He advised the jury to accept the true time of Bamber’s call as 3.26am. “You would, in effect, be giving the defence case the benefit of a doubt, and I will suggest that you may – although it is always a matter for you – work on the timing of 03.26 as the time when the phone call was made to Chelmsford police station, and accept that Police Constable West quite simply made a mistake when reading the clock, or writing down 03.36.”

In fact, though, insisting that the call was made at 3.26am gave Bamber anything but the benefit of the doubt. Instead, it put him in the time frame for the murder, because the chronology now made sense: Bamber called West at 3.26am, and West called local officers, who set off for White House Farm at 3.35am.

After a month-long trial, the jury came back with a 10-2 majority on 28 October 1986. Bamber was convicted of one of the most notorious crimes in British history and sentenced to life with a recommended minimum of 25 years. This was later extended to a whole-life tariff by the then home secretary Douglas Hurd in 1988, although Bamber was not made aware of this until 1994.

Fast-forward 25 years. It’s 2011 and Bamber now spends most of his life in prison searching for exculpatory evidence. There is also a campaign team working on his behalf to try to get his conviction overturned. He belatedly receives 347,000 pages of documents, initially withheld by Essex police, after public interest immunity laws are amended in favour of greater disclosure.

This is when Bamber’s team becomes convinced it has found the smoking gun. Amid the myriad documents is the C1 form that West filled in as he was speaking to Bamber on 7 August 1985. Astonishingly, this log wasn’t even included in the exhibit list, which includes every document that can potentially be shown to the jury. The time recorded on it is 3.36am, as he stated at trial. At the top, it clearly states who has made the call and from what address – Mr Bamber, 9 Head Street, Goldhanger. The subject is “Distress call”.

When West’s C1 log is compared with Bonnett’s log, important differences, apart from the times of the call, become obvious. In West’s C1 log of Bamber’s call, it says: “Father phoned (aged 62). Please come over your sister has gone crazy and has the gun. Phone went dead. Sister Sheila Bamber age 27 has history of mental illness.” This is clearly Bamber relating the call from his father – hence the reference to father and sister.

By contrast, the opening of Bonnett’s rolling log, which begins at 3.26am, is told from a wholly different perspective. For a start, it refers to Caffell as “daughter” rather than “sister”. The subject of the log is “Daughter gone berserk” and it says “Daughter Sheila Bamber aged 26 yrs has got hold of one of my guns”. The guns at White House Farm belonged to Nevill. In West’s C1 log it refers to the gun. Both logs get Caffell’s age wrong. Bonnett’s says she is 26, West’s 27. In fact, she had celebrated her 28th birthday a couple of weeks earlier. In West’s log, Bamber has mistakenly added an extra year to his father’s age. In Bonnett’s log, no age is given.

Then there is the different way in which the caller’s name and address is logged. The convention in police logs is to start with the informant’s name and address, because it immediately establishes who is providing the information, and it means they are traceable if contact is lost. Bonnett’s log of West’s call refers to “Mr Bamber, White House Farm, Tollshunt D’Arcy”. West’s log refers to “Mr Bamber, 9 Head Street, Goldhanger”. Next to the address for White House Farm is the phone number. Bonnett’s rolling log doesn’t have a number for the farm till 03.56am, when the police confirm that the phone is off the hook.

In addition, Bonnett’s 3.26am log makes no mention of Caffell’s history of mental health problems, a crucial fact that any officers dispatched to the scene should have been informed of. The differences in perspective and facts between Bonnett’s log and West’s log would surely have been spelled out by Rivlin for the defence if both had been available.

There is a line space in Bonnett’s log after the initial paragraph, and then it states: “Message passed on to CD [Control Chelmsford, the code used to refer to the central radio control room where West was stationed] by the son of Mr Bamber after the phone went dead”. The line space suggests it could be a new entry.

When Bamber’s team came across West’s C1 form, they were convinced that this explained the confusion between 3.26am and 3.36am and why the first police car had been dispatched before Bamber’s call: there had been two distinct calls. They believed that the first section of Bonnett’s log referred to a call from Bamber’s father, Nevill, and that this was the information the police appeared to have responded to. This would finally explain how a car had been sent to White House Farm before West said he took Bamber’s call. And, crucially, it would prove Bamber’s innocence.

“At the trial, I had no idea why they were making such a fuss about whether I’d made my call at 03.26am or 03.36am,” Bamber writes. “It was only when we finally saw the log from West 25 years after I was first jailed that it became obvious there must have been two calls. The language is different, the perspective’s different, the information provided is different. It can only be two different people reporting the same incident as they see it.”

In 2016, a documents expert, Dr Chris Davies, studied the new evidence and concluded that the most likely reason for the inconsistencies was that there were two phone calls. “I consider that this would be my preferred explanation for them,” he said. If Nevill called the police at 3.26am to say his daughter had “gone berserk” and had the gun, it puts Bamber in the clear.

If there was an earlier call from Nevill Bamber, there are various theories about who may have taken it, including Malcolm Bonnett (who died in 2023) and officers who were in the control room with PC West (there were at least two others).

Bamber’s team felt that the 3.26am and 3.36am logs finally enabled them to make sense of a mystery from the original investigation: why had the police devoted so much energy to trying to prove that Bamber could have cycled from White House Farm back home to Goldhanger in 10 minutes, before finally concluding that it was impossible? This early police theory appears to have allowed for two calls – one from White House Farm at 3.26am and the other from Goldhanger at 3.36am, both made by Bamber.

Fifteen years on from the disclosure of West’s C1 log, Bamber’s team are still scouring the 347,000 documents that were released to them. In 2020, they came across “pocket book no.49”, belonging to DC Stephen Myall, one of the three officers originally radioed, alongside PS Bews and PC Saxby, asking them to attend the incident at 3.30am, six minutes before West stated on his C1 log that he received the call from Bamber. At the time, they were on an undercover foot patrol of an industrial estate after a spate of burglaries.

In his pocketbook, Myall wrote that he, Bews and Saxby immediately returned to Witham police station when, at “03.37am approx”, they received a phone call from West about the incident at White House Farm. “The Officer (PC West) at CD Control was on the phone and told us that he was relating information to us and still had the informant (Jeremy Bamber) on the other telephone.” Myall wrote that Bamber had told West that his father had said “words to the effect of ‘Come quick, your sister’s gone berserk. She’s got a gun’. The telephone had then gone dead.”

Bamber’s team believes it is now clear that Bews, Saxby and Myall were contacted by radio at 03.30am, as a result of a call from Nevill at 03.26am. The police officers were not at Witham police station at that point, but immediately returned from the nearby industrial estate to collect the police car, which they hadn’t taken with them on the undercover job. West then contacted Witham police station, by telephone, at 3.37am, having spoken to Bamber for a minute, from 03.36am.

The CCRC, the body that investigates alleged miscarriages of justice, has examined Bamber’s convictions three times. In 2002, it sent the case back to the court of appeal, but the judges concluded: “The more we examined the detail of the case, the more likely we thought it to be that the jury were right.”

In 2011, the CCRC refused to refer the case, stating that the evidence did not raise a real possibility that the court would find Bamber’s convictions unsafe. In 2021, his legal team made a new submission, consisting of 10 points. The CCRC has been widely criticised in recent years for its tardiness and its poor referral rate. In 2024/25, only 2% of cases – 31 out of 1,541 applications – were referred back to the court of appeal. (This rate has improved considerably since Dame Vera Baird became interim chair in June 2025.) By July 2025, the CCRC had examined four of the 10 points in Bamber’s submission and declared that, on the basis of these four points, it would not be referring the case back, although it would continue to explore the remaining six points.

One of the four points that was dismissed was the discrepancy between 3.26am and 3.36am being recorded as the time of Bamber’s call to the police. The CCRC remains adamant that the different timings are a result of police error and that there was only one call, from Bamber, at 3.26am. This is despite the C1 log from West stating it was at 3.36am and despite Myall’s record stating that West had Bamber on the phone at 3.37am.

The CCRC also claims that the issue of the call timings “had been dealt with at trial”. This is plain wrong. At trial, and at his 2002 appeal, Bamber’s team had no idea that there were two logs suggesting two calls to police about the same incident.

Since the 2021 submission to the CCRC, more valuable evidence has been uncovered. After the trial, Drake ordered the Dickinson review, an internal inquiry by Essex police into what the Times called the “blunders, omissions and ineptitude” of the force’s early investigation into the murders. The review would examine, for example, why the crime scene was grossly contaminated; the destruction and mismanagement of vital evidence; and the timeline and call-log inconsistencies.

The findings of the inquiry have never been made fully public. However, some documents from the review were released to Bamber’s lawyers in 2011 after a legal challenge. His defence team only recently discovered that the Dickinson review supports the 3.36am timing of Bamber’s call in its timeline of events on the day. It states that Bamber called West at 3.36am and, at 3.37am, “PS Bews, PC Myall & Saxby [were] at Witham. Receive telephone message from PC West. Despatched to White House Farm.” All these references are consistent with the first call to the police having been made by Nevill at 3.26am, officers being asked to attend White House Farm, then West taking a second call from Bamber at 3.36am.

Today, West works for the Masons. I contact him to suggest that his original log, which stated that Bamber called the police at 3.36am, was in fact accurate and consistent with the statements provided by other officers. He tells me he cannot recall the details, 41 years on, without seeing the specific documents and suggests that we meet face to face.

After this conversation, West does not respond to my calls. I text him with an explanation of why I believe his initial record of 3.36am was correct and suggest that a separate call may have been made at 3.26am. But he is having none of it: “Simon, I have nothing to add to anything that has been said and absolutely no comment on any of your rather ridiculous postulations. Jeremy Bamber was found guilty and remains a convicted felon. No one seems to ask: ‘What if that was the correct decision?’”

Meanwhile, Bamber’s team continue to try to piece together the missing pieces of the jigsaw. A few months ago, they re-examined PC West’s trial transcript and came across an astonishing exchange between him and defence council Geoffrey Rivlin.

Rivlin: You made it clear to him [Bamber] that police officers would be sent to the house.

West: Police officers had already been sent when I spoke to him, yes.

Here, PC West states that police officers had already been sent when he was speaking to Bamber. But if the police only received one call alerting them to the incident and the time of it was 3.26am, as the CCRC and Essex Police now insist, that would mean the first car had left before then. Yet the earliest mention of a radio call to officers is 03.30am and officers leaving is 03.35am. On the other hand if we stick with the 03.36am timing on West’s log, it only makes sense if there had been an earlier call because of the radio call to local officers at 03.30am and the leaving time of 03.35am.

This was the closest the jury ever came to hearing that the police appeared to have received two different calls about the incident. Unfortunately, neither the defence nor the jury picked up on West’s answer that officers had already been sent to White House Farm when he spoke to Jeremy Bamber.

When asked to comment about the failure to disclose evidence and inconsistencies in officers’ logs, a spokesperson for Essex Police said: “In August 1985, the lives of five people, including two children, were needlessly, tragically and callously cut short when they were murdered in their own home by Jeremy Bamber. In the years that followed, this case has been the subject of several appeals and reviews by the court of appeal and the Criminal Cases Review Commission – all of these processes have never found anything other than Bamber is the person responsible for killing his adoptive parents Nevill and June, sister Sheila Caffell and her two sons Nicholas and Daniel.”

A CCRC spokesperson said: “Mr Bamber has made three applications to the CCRC. The first application led to a referral to the Court of Appeal in 2001. His conviction was subsequently upheld. The second application to the CCRC in 2004 did not result in a referral. A third application received in 2021 is currently under review. A provisional decision on part of this latest application was issued to his legal representatives, and they responded to us in January this year. Work now continues to consider additional matters which were raised in Mr Bamber’s application. It would be inappropriate for us to discuss the case or make any further comment while the application is being reviewed.”

Those convinced of Bamber’s guilt maintain that Nevill Bamber’s calls to his son and the police never happened. Which takes us back to the first statements Bamber made when he was arrested. At the end of an aggressive 11-hour interrogation by Essex Police on 10 September 1985, Bamber is getting frustrated with all the questioning about the phone call he claims to have received from his father. He suggests there is one easy way of settling the issue. Get hold of British Telecom’s records. Bamber is apparently convinced this will provide him with an alibi and prove that he is telling the truth. If his father never called him, this is a kamikaze defence. All Essex Police need do is check BT’s records, and if there isn’t a call from White House Farm, he has implicated himself.

Bamber: Telecom must be able to tell you the times of phone calls on my parents’ phone.

Officer: What d’you mean by that?

Bamber: It would be proof that I received a phone call from my father.

Officer: If I tell you that Telecom can’t give such details then your theory can’t be checked.

Bamber: I thought Telecom could.

But it couldn’t. Or at least that’s what he was told. Despite an extensive advertising campaign in Essex stating that phone records were being digitised at the time, Essex Police said that calls in the area could not yet be itemised and bills still relied on an anonymised meter system. Years later, documents emerged showing that Telecom did indeed have itemised bills of earlier calls made from Bamber’s home phone number, though these were long-distance calls.

One aspect of the Bamber case that must have shocked the judge was how much evidence was destroyed on the day of the murders. At the time, the police believed it to be an open-and-shut murder-suicide. But that can never excuse the destruction of bloodied mattresses and bed linen.

However, in 1996, 11 years after the murders, an even more shocking obliteration of evidence took place. Although it was known that Bamber was preparing an appeal for the Home Office (which was subsequently inherited by the newly formed CCRC, in 1997), Essex police unilaterally destroyed vital evidence. Among the list of exhibits that were destroyed are bullets, blood samples and swabs, all of which may have provided exculpatory evidence for Bamber as DNA testing became ever more sophisticated. It was particularly alarming that Essex Police destroyed Sheila Caffell’s heavily bloodstained night dress, which may have shown her to have been in contact with the other victims, who were also very bloodied.

As so often in Bamber’s case, the document listing the evidentiary material and whether it was to be filed or destroyed is incomplete. Here it starts at number 167 and finishes at 661. At numbers 598 and 599, it says “British Telecom extract of calls”, citing the telephone numbers for Bamber’s home and White House Farm. By the side of both entries, it says “Destroy”.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Researchers are exploring novel ways to treat, even prevent, the brain disease C. T. E. One of the most surprising: near-infrared light.

Marcus Mailei, who began playing football at age 7, with a headset that delivers near-infrared light to his scalp and inside his nose, a treatment known as photobiomodulation. Credit... Kim Raff for The New York Times

Supported by

By Lynne Peeples

A college football team in Utah is donning some curious caps this season. As part of their regular recovery routine, many Brigham Young University players are wearing headsets that shine near-infrared light onto their scalps — and up their noses.

Emerging science suggests that the devices may help the brain be more resilient to damage, potentially reducing the risk of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a degenerative disease associated with repeated head trauma.

Researchers first introduced the headsets to B. Y. U. football as part of a small, randomized trial in 2021. Based on that study’s results — signs of reduced brain inflammation among users over the season — the team ordered more.

Near-infrared light is just one of a number of surprising therapeutic approaches for C. T. E. that scientists are investigating. Some see promise in manipulating the gut microbiome; others are exploring the potential of stimulating the vagus nerve, eliciting a psychedelic experience or repurposing drugs that might quiet inflammation in the brain.

All the research is driven by mounting concerns over the long-term brain health of contact-sport athletes. A study published on Wednesday used a statistical model to estimate that three in four former National Football League players who died between 2008 and 2023 most likely had signs of C. T. E. in their brains at death.

Chris Nowinski, a neuroscientist and chief executive of the Concussion & CTE Foundation, and a coauthor of the study, described C. T. E. as a “massive public health issue.”

Dr. Allen Sills, the N. F. L.’s chief medical officer, said he is closely watching research developments.

“All clinicians hope that we will soon have better diagnostic and therapeutic options for patients,” he said. “We just have so much more to learn about the pathophysiology of many neurodegenerative diseases and which parts of the cascade are most robust for intervention.”

It’s not only a problem in sports. The Coast Guard acknowledged for the first time in July that rough seas can cause repeated brain trauma to small-boat crews.

And by some estimates, the number of intimate partner violence survivors living with long-term effects from brain injury dwarfs that of football players.

At the moment, there is no widely recognized treatment for C. T. E., and it can only be definitively diagnosed after death. But worried athletes and former athletes are not waiting for the research to arrive.

Marcus Mailei began playing football at age 7. After a brief injury-riddled stint in the N. F. L., the fullback hung up his cleats at age 24.

Disturbing changes slowly surfaced over the next several years. Mr. Mailei became increasingly irritable. He grew more socially anxious, even paranoid, about the intentions of family and friends, or about planes flying overhead.

His wife, Kristen Mailei, began to fear for his safety, as well as their family’s. One day, she stumbled across an article about another former player whose similar symptoms subsided after using a near-infrared light headset.

“It was a Hail Mary,” she said.

In 2020, Marcus began wearing a headset a few days a week, 20 minutes at a time. “After about a year, I felt like my feet were back on the ground,” said Mr. Mailei, now 39 and a community college teacher and coach in Utah.

The treatment, called photobiomodulation, or PBM, emerged in the 1960s after Hungarian scientists accidentally discovered that low-level red light stimulated hair growth in rodents.

Decades later, researchers began to investigate whether longer wavelengths of near-infrared light — which are invisible to the human eye and penetrate more deeply than visible red wavelengths — could affect brain tissue.

Studies in animals and humans showed that, depending on the device, a small fraction of near-infrared photons targeted at the scalp can reach the brain. That appears to be enough to trigger shifts in blood flow, communication between brain regions, and how cells produce and use energy.

PBM is widely available in clinics as a treatment for wounds, inflammation and more. But much of the science regarding its effects on both the brain and body remains unsettled, including optimal wavelengths, intensities and durations.

The headsets used in the B. Y. U. studies include a component that sends photons up the nose, which preliminary research suggests may be a more efficient route for getting photons to certain parts of the brain.

After PBM studies continued to show improvements in people with lingering head injury symptoms, researchers at the University of Utah decided to see if it could also be used to intervene earlier.

“If we can prevent damage from happening, that’s even better,” said Hannah Lindsay, a neurologist at the University of Utah School of Medicine and coauthor of the study of the B. Y. U. football team.

During the 2021 football season, dozens of B. Y. U. players used a near-infrared light headset three times a week. Half of the players were randomized to receive active light therapy and the other half to use identical headsets that did not produce light.

Based on a final analysis of 26 players, researchers saw that the brains of athletes who received PBM did not accumulate the same widespread inflammation and wiring damage as those in the placebo group.

What’s more, the neuroinflammatory changes in this group were concentrated in brain regions known to be the most vulnerable to the rotational twisting and sheering forces common in football.

Other research adds support. John Mitrofanis, a neuroscientist at the University of Grenoble Alpes in France, has helped demonstrate that pretreating an animal with near-infrared light makes its brain, he said, “more likely to stave off whatever insult it’s going to be hit with.”

A small, randomized study at Massachusetts General Hospital also showed improved markers of early recovery for patients treated with PBM within three days of a traumatic brain injury.

“More and more data comes out showing that this is real,” said the study coauthor Eva Ratai, a neuroradiologist at Mass General Research Institute.

Not all trials have shown significant benefits, however. Some experts caution that PBM needs much more research before it can be recommended to athletes at risk.

“The idea that red-light therapy could stop brain damage acutely is a massive claim that lacks significant evidence,” said Dr. Nowinski. “It’s also a risky claim if we’re actually trying to convince people to change their behaviors.”

Larger and more rigorous trials are in the works. The Utah research team recently received a $4.6 million grant from the Department of Defense to study PBM for persistent symptoms of mild traumatic brain injury in 300 service members, veterans and first responders.

Dr. Jean-François Chermann, a neurologist in Paris who specializes in sports-related concussions, is planning one of at least two separate clinical trials in France of PBM for rugby players.

Dr. Chermann recently treated 60 elite players whose concussion symptoms had lingered for at least three months. After eight or more sessions, according to his not-yet-published results, about 80 percent had significant improvement.

“But some people didn’t respond at all,” he said.

Near-infrared light is far from the only C. T. E. treatment that scientists are evaluating.

Daniel Carcillo played 10 years in the National Hockey League, winning two Stanley Cups and engaging in 164 fights. He subsequently developed symptoms associated with C. T. E.

Mr. Carcillo, now 41, said he made himself a “guinea pig” to all kinds of treatments — hyperbaric chamber therapy, craniosacral massage. Nothing seemed to work.

Finally, after reading promising research on psychedelics, he participated in a guided psilocybin session. (Psilocybin is the psychedelic compound in “magic mushrooms.”)

“I’ve now been symptom free for seven years,” he said. “I’ve never been happier or healthier.”

Frederick Barrett, director of the Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research at Johns Hopkins University, said he hears similar stories from former athletes.

The “plural of anecdote is not data,” he said. Yet Dr. Barrett suggests the emerging evidence is sufficient to justify investigating psychedelics as a treatment for T. B. I. and C. T. E.

One study published in September, for example, showed that doses of psilocybin after repeated mild head impacts helped protect rats’ brains by rebuilding networks and boosting cell repair, as well as by reducing swelling and the toxic buildup of tau protein. The N. H. L. declined to comment on this and other experimental treatments.

Drugs already on the market might also be repurposed to protect against brain injury. Baricitinib, a high potency anti-inflammatory medication used to treat rheumatoid arthritis and other conditions, is under investigation in a new open-label trial of depressed football players.

Depression can be a “precursor to full blown C. T. E.”, as well as to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases, said Andrew Miller, a psychiatrist at Emory University and trial investigator. “Inflammation is playing a major role in all these diseases.”

The trial will explore if, by blocking inflammation, the drug can arrest disease “before cognitive calamity,” he said.

The influence of the gut microbiome on inflammation is among reasons that it, too, is on the radar. A recent small study linked mild, non-concussive blows to the head during football with changes in the microbiome.

Mounting research suggests it’s a two-way street: Manipulating the microbiome also appears to affect inflammation and tissue damage in the brain.

The N. F. L. Players Association is supporting microbiome trials. One is collecting blood and stool samples while tracking head injuries among 120 male and female college athletes in Houston.

A separate trial has been looking at veterans and people coming into the emergency room after a T. B. I. Those findings, currently under review, suggest that the microbiome might dictate recovery or be a target for interventions, said Lisa Brenner, director of the VA Brain Health Coordinating Center at the University of Colorado Anschutz and trial investigator.

Much more work is needed, scientists say, but specific probiotic strains or fecal transplants could one day be a plausible treatment for the brain.

“We think about recovery from a brain injury happening in the brain, but it could be happening in the body, too,” said Dr. Brenner.

New animal research even hints that tapping into the bone-brain connection — by compressing the shin bone — could promote recovery after brain injury.

Some of these novel strategies may overlap. Researchers have applied PBM to the abdomen, targeting the gut microbiome. Others have found possible synergy between PBM and vagus nerve stimulation; at least one headset now incorporates both treatments.

More standard psychiatric treatments — from neurofeedback to noninvasive brain stimulation — could make the treatments more effective. One of the three arms in the Utah team’s new clinical trial will combine PBM with computerized cognitive rehabilitation.

Scientists agree that the very best solution is to prevent head injuries in the first place. In the case of football, more advanced helmets and protective rules, such as limits on full-contact practices and changes to kickoffs, help.

Dr. Sills said the N. F. L. is continuing to look for further opportunities to “get rid of avoidable head impacts.”

But such efforts still don’t eliminate the risks. And as Dr. Nowinski points out, abstinence is “a difficult sell to young people and to their parents.”

The Maileis’ oldest son plays football and recently suffered a concussion. “I strapped the light on his head the next day,” said Ms. Mailei. “I’m terrified of him playing, but he loves it so much.”

Obamacare Dealt Yet Another Blow as Premiums Rise Again

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

Premiums will jump by 13 percent for next year, though much of the price increase will be offset by subsidies. But customers who earn over $64,000 will pay more, on top of this year’s huge increases.

By Reed Abelson and Margot Sanger-Katz

The reporters have been covering the Obamacare marketplaces since they opened in 2014.

Millions of Americans who depend on Obamacare for their health insurance face another double-digit price increase next year, adding to the financial toll that has already driven millions of others to drop coverage since last year.

The price increases largely reflect higher medical costs across the country. But they also are a signal of the latest blow to Obamacare under the Trump administration, which has overseen the expiration of tax credits that helped Americans pay for coverage and has erected new barriers to enrollment in an effort to root out what it describes as widespread fraud.

The average price of health insurance in the Obamacare marketplaces will rise by 13 percent next year, according to an analysis on Friday by KFF, the health research group.

The Trump administration on Friday published new prices for 2027 in 30 states with markets managed by the federal government. Using that data and state figures, KFF calculated the increase nationwide.

The large premium increases for Obamacare plans are similar to changes expected in other health insurance markets, though slightly higher. Reports by several consulting firms projected that premiums for employer plans, which cover around 150 million people, could go up by about 10 percent in 2027. Premiums for federal workers are increasing by more than 10 percent.

Public opinion polls have shown that the cost of health care has been among voters’ top economic concerns going into the midterm elections on Tuesday. In a recent poll from KFF, about 60 percent of registered voters said they were worried about being able to afford health care for themselves and their families.

Kate and Mark Dwyer, a couple in rural Oregon, have been wrestling with whether their budget can handle another annual increase. They had already shifted to the cheapest available Obamacare plan, leaving them on the hook for thousands of dollars in out-of-pocket costs.

Next year, the least expensive plan will increase their costs by more than $500 a month, to nearly $3,000, Ms. Dwyer said. That amounts to more than a third of her earnings at a nonprofit.

“We are looking at going without next year,” Ms. Dwyer said. “There is no middle ground. It’s either $3,000 or nothing.”

In an apparent nod to such concerns, the Trump administration sent many Obamacare customers $500 checks this month to offset their insurance premiums — a one-time payment just before the election.

Across the private and public health sectors, the increases have been driven by rising hospital prices, high payments under a consumer protection law that changed how some doctors are compensated, and the growing use of artificial intelligence in doctors’ offices, according to benefits consultants and industry analysts. Several large employers also pointed to a rising bill for expensive specialty prescriptions, like cancer drugs and GLP-1 medicines.

The Trump administration released the numbers quietly on Friday afternoon as a data file. A government fact sheet about open enrollment published shortly afterward did not mention the premium increase, but noted that three-quarters of Obamacare customers with subsidies can still find plans for less than $50 a month.

Open enrollment and shopping for plans begins Sunday, just two days before the midterm elections, in which affordability and the higher prices for groceries, gasoline and health care have been a central issue.

Although the federal government reported that 19.2 million people were enrolled in Obamacare coverage early this year, more recent estimates indicate a lower total.

Roughly 10 percent are older consumers who earned more than $63,840, a group largely composed of self-employed workers, such as chiropractors, dentists, ranchers and farmers, as well as many early retirees. Many already faced premium increases exceeding $1,000 a month in 2026.

“This is a really small number of people,” said Cynthia Cox, the director of KFF’s program on the Affordable Care Act. “But these people are getting hit the hardest by rising health care costs, and they don’t get any help.”

The average cost for the cheapest bronze plan with a high deductible will be about $700 a month for a 50-year-old single person, according to Ms. Cox.

Obamacare customers who earn less than $64,000 a year make up most of the people enrolled in the program and will still benefit from income-based subsidies and will not have to pay higher out-of-pocket premium costs next year. For those people, taxpayer dollars will cover the extra cost.

But many with strained household budgets are struggling to pay their portion since their Obamacare premiums went up in 2026, and many have been forced to switch to plans with higher deductibles.

In 2026, premiums rose by an average of 26 percent, with the cost for all consumers more than doubling on average for the same plan, after the Republican-led Congress decided to let temporary federal subsidies expire.

Recent estimates from KFF, based on insurance filings with regulators, suggest that enrollment fell by nearly five million people, as of June.

A recent large survey released by the Commonwealth Fund, a foundation and research group that supports the Affordable Care Act, found the uninsured rate among working-age adults had risen since two years ago.

Democrats forced a record 43-day government shutdown last year, as they tried to leverage government funding on an extension of the subsidies or health care tax credits. Aides to the House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, a Democrat from New York, have said he will schedule a vote to restore the extra subsidies in the first days of the next Congress if Democrats win a majority in the midterm elections.

The data on premium costs were published on Friday just before the start of next year’s enrollment period, which runs from Nov. 1 to Jan. 15. People in most states who want to buy Obamacare insurance for next year need to sign up during that period. (A handful of states keep the enrollment period open longer.)

Increases for consumers who renew their current plans could be higher than the average increase.

“We really do encourage people to shop and compare” among the plans they are offered, said Anthony Wright, the executive director for Families USA, a left-leaning consumer advocacy group. The average price increase can mask tremendous variation in the cost of a policy, he said.

To lower the cost of coverage, many people switched from more comprehensive plans to so-called bronze coverage this year, which often offers lower premiums and much higher deductibles. The average A. C. A. deductible rose to a record high of nearly $4,000 in 2026. As they consider plans for next year, those people may no longer be able to avoid a price increase by switching to a skimpier plan.

Caroline Pearson, the executive director at the Peterson Center on Healthcare, a group focused on lowering health care spending, said she had been watching the market closely for signs of instability, given last year’s big price shock. But she described the newly published increase as “consistent with the rate increases we are expecting” for employers and their workers.

But few people covered by an employer health plan are exposed to the full cost of insurance like unsubsidized Obamacare consumers. Employers pick up more than half of the tab for the typical person in work-based coverage, and such insurance premiums are deductible from people’s taxes.

Administration officials attribute some of that drop-off to its efforts to reduce fraudulent enrollment, arguing that brokers had enrolled fake consumers in subsidized coverage.

In September, Vice President JD Vance announced the government had canceled coverage that he said brokers arranged for about 750,000 people whose records lacked Social Security numbers and who had not used or contacted their health insurer through August. He and other administration officials argued there was evidence of additional fraud.

But the Commonwealth survey suggests that some people who have dropped Obamacare coverage may now be going without any health insurance.

Reed Abelson covers the business of health care, focusing on how financial incentives are affecting the delivery of care, from the costs to consumers to the profits to providers.

Margot Sanger-Katz is a reporter covering health care policy and public health for the Upshot section of The Times.
