Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Strategies

Factors like inflation, interest rates, A. I. and the war with Iran are far more important, our columnist says.

Credit... Video by Ben Voldman

Supported by

By Jeff Sommer

Jeff Sommer writes Strategies, a weekly column on markets, finance and the economy.

Midterm elections are the elephant in the room. But not in financial markets.

Instead, what’s driving the markets are interest rates, inflation, artificial intelligence, tariffs, the Iran conflict and the price of oil.

The midterms? On a personal level, I’m transfixed by the political news. But as a close observer of the markets, I’ve concluded that, for the short term, at least, the elections scarcely matter.

For one thing, financial markets are forward-looking. Prices already have certain political expectations baked into them, foremost among them the historical fact that the political party that controls the White House has typically lost ground in the midterms. That’s exactly what the polls and prediction markets anticipate for Tuesday’s elections, and it’s what the markets have been assuming for months.

Even if this broad assumption turns out to be correct, of course, plenty of urgent political questions still need to be answered. Will the Democrats control both houses of Congress, just one or none? Will this election represent a turning point for U. S. democracy? These are serious issues, no doubt.

For the markets, however, the consensus projections are simple: Democrats will control at least one chamber of Congress, the House. With a Republican in the White House, that’s a recipe for political gridlock — in which neither party can enact major legislation. It’s not a good situation if you want to get things done. But Wall Street loves gridlock because it abhors political interference — or so some analysts say every election cycle.

As I pointed out back in 2010, however, the evidence for markets’ supposed preference for gridlock, or for any other political alignment, is flimsy when you look at actual financial returns.

That’s still the case.

Since 1930, in the year after a president’s political party lost control of the House in the midterms, the S&P 500 or its predecessors rose an average 8.8 percent. But the S&P 500 rose an average 14 percent in the year after all midterm elections. This data comes from a recent study by Ed Clissold, chief U. S. strategist, and Thanh Nguyen, senior analyst, for Ned Davis Research, an independent financial research company.

The broader truth seems to be that, with occasional exceptions, overall stock market returns generally don’t depend on politics, one way or another.

Explicitly political investment strategies haven’t kept up with the overall market this year, as I noted in July. Consider these updated returns, including reinvested dividends, for this year through Friday, according to FactSet.

Truth Social America First E. T. F. (with the ticker MAGA), which calls itself a vehicle for investing “in companies that align with your Republican political beliefs.” It was up 11.2 percent.

Democratic Large Core E. T. F. (ticker DEMZ), which contains S&P 500 companies “that have made over 75 percent of their political contributions to Democratic causes and candidates.” It gained 11 percent.

The benchmark S&P 500, by contrast, was up 13.8 percent, with dividends.

Just holding the broad market was a better strategy. The so-called Democratic fund’s performance was closest to the S&P 500’s, though it lagged the benchmark, perhaps because it excluded the stock with the best returns in the S&P 500 this year: Moderna, the biotechnology company, which was up more than 600 percent, according to FactSet.

The MAGA fund excluded so many tech companies, like Moderna, Advanced Micro Devices, Nvidia, Alphabet and Apple, that it amounted to a tilt against tech. That was a bad move in the current stock market.

While politics haven’t mattered much for stocks, tech — and specifically A. I. — definitely has.

That was clear this past week. Documents filed on Monday by Anthropic, the giant A. I. start-up that plans to go public before the end of the year, bolstered the stock market. And the company’s prospectus suggests that its significance goes way beyond that.

“We believe that A. I. is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” the document said. It warned that “consequential” could mean horrific.

“Sufficiently advanced A. I. systems,” the prospectus continued, “could, if not developed, deployed and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

Yet the company also said it was generating revenue on an astounding scale. For the first half of the year, its sales were $16.3 billion, up nearly fourteenfold from the same period a year ago. Its losses for the same period were $80.7 billion, however — a reminder that it is an open question whether eventual profits from A. I. will ever justify the mammoth sums required to build A. I. infrastructure.

Stock market volatility began rising in recent weeks on concerns about A. I. spending by giants like Alphabet, Meta and Amazon, and by financially pressured companies like CoreWeave and Oracle, whose data center bonds have sunk in value.

The stock market, though, is still being supported by soaring corporate earnings, thanks in no small part to profits from chipmakers like Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices. This A. I. boom has created an extraordinarily concentrated stock market, adding risk to investor portfolios. Should A. I. stocks or bonds weaken further, important parts of the stock and bond markets could be in jeopardy.

The bond market has already been through plenty of turmoil, with benchmark 10-year Treasury rates soaring above 5.3 percent in September, up from 4.2 percent at the beginning of this year.

French sovereign bonds weakened during the national demonstrations over the high cost of living and deteriorating school conditions, and bonds of other European nations, with swelling amounts of debt, have been hit hard.

Those seeking safety — whether from troubled European bonds, A. I. bonds or the shaky stock market — moved back into Treasury bonds this month. That increased demand appears to have raised bond prices and lowered yields, which move in opposite directions.

At the same time, short-term interest rates have been rising, along with the rate of inflation.

The Federal Reserve on Wednesday held steady on its policy rate, the short-term Federal funds rate, at a range of 3.75 to 4 percent. But the Fed raised rates in September for the first time in three years, and with the inflation rate still well above the Fed’s 2 percent annual target, the markets expect the central bank to raise rates three more times from December through June. The central bank may have delayed raising rates before the midterm elections at least partly to avoid a heightened conflict with President Trump, who has demanded lower rates for months.

Higher interest rates in the bond and money markets mean that loans of virtually all kinds, from credit cards and automobiles to business loans and mortgages, cost more. That’s causing hardship for millions of people and slowing economic growth.

Furthermore, if rates keep rising, bond prices will fall further, and stocks are likely to be damaged, for two reasons: Corporate profits will be harder to maintain if financing costs are higher, and stocks will be unattractive compared with bonds offering higher interest rates. Investors will need to keep track of interest rates to protect themselves in the stock and bond markets.

On the other hand, as I pointed out last week, money market funds, Treasury bills, high-yield savings accounts and certificates of deposit are paying ever-higher interest rates just for parking your money. The average rate in the 100 largest money market funds tracked by Crane Data rose to 3.75 percent on Friday, from 3.71 percent the previous week, and is likely to surpass 4 percent in December if the Fed raises rates as expected.

Why have interest rates risen this year? There are many reasons, but one is glaring, and it is a matter of geopolitics: the war with Iran. Rates began to soar, along with oil prices and inflation, after the United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. As one consequence, energy stocks have spiked more than 50 percent this year, the most of any sector in the S&P 500.

Whether the conflict in the Middle East escalates after the midterms is another critical question for the markets. That will depend on decisions by President Trump and leaders in the Middle East, though a reconfigured Congress could conceivably begin to play a larger role in foreign policy.

But betting on politics, or geopolitics, strikes me as an unwise financial strategy. Such investing hasn’t worked reliably over the last century.

Instead, for people with long horizons, sticking with broad investments in the markets has been a winning approach. I expect that will continue to be the case, whatever the outcome of the midterm elections.

Jeff Sommer writes Strategies, a weekly column on markets, finance and the economy.

‘My Body Hurts’: Christa Pike Describes Pain and Isolation After Botched Execution

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Christa Pike’s Botched Execution

Advertisement

Supported by

Ms. Pike, who was convicted of a 1995 murder, released her first statement since the failed attempt to execute her last month.

By Emily Cochrane

Reporting from Nashville

In her first comments since Tennessee botched her execution last month, Christa Pike said that she was in constant pain and that she had been kept largely in isolation.

“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” she said, according to a statement released Friday. “My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak.”

Ms. Pike, 50, received the death penalty for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate in Knoxville, Tenn. Ms. Pike, then 18, was one of three students who lured Ms. Slemmer into the woods, slashed at her with a box cutter and beat her.

In the statement, which she dictated to her legal team, Ms. Pike said she had been prepared to die the morning of Sept. 30. She had said her goodbyes to her loved ones and supporters. She told the people in the death chamber she was leaving them “in loving kindness.”

But then she woke up alone, confused and in pain, according to the statement. She was the first person to survive after receiving a lethal dose of the drug pentobarbital.

“I had not contemplated life beyond that night,” Ms. Pike said, “and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position.”

She added, “I am searching for meaning in what happened to me.”

The mother of Ms. Slemmer, May Martinez, was in favor of the execution and has rejected Ms. Pike’s expressions of remorse in the years since the crime. Ms. Pike said she was thinking about Ms. Slemmer’s family and “the terrible pain and loss they have endured.”

The execution, initially delayed in a flurry of last-minute legal maneuvering, went ahead the evening of Sept. 30. In court documents this month, Randy Spivey, one of Ms. Pike’s lawyers who witnessed the execution, described nearly an hour in which members of the team responsible for placing the IV struggled to do so.

At one point, Mr. Spivey said, one team member said that a vein “might be blowing,” acknowledging that a vein might have been damaged in the process. In excerpts from a 2025 deposition released in court this week, Kenneth Nelson, the warden at the prison where executions take place, said the team contracted for the execution did not practice what to do if they had a hard time inserting an IV.

It took about 30 minutes to verify the authenticity of the first 911 call for an ambulance from the prison. Ms. Pike was in a private Nashville hospital for more than a week, where staff “treated me with compassion, dignity and respect,” she said.

The botched handling of the execution has drawn scrutiny as the state’s second failed attempt at capital punishment this year. After Ms. Pike’s execution attempt, Frank Strada, the embattled head of the Tennessee Department of Correction, said he would step down.

Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican who is term-limited, paused all executions for the remainder of his term and ordered an independent investigation into the practice. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for governor, has said she believes Ms. Pike should face execution a second time, calling for the use of the electric chair instead of lethal injection.

Ms. Pike’s legal team has asked Mr. Lee to consider granting her clemency, allowing her to spend the remainder of her life in prison. On Wednesday, Mr. Lee told reporters, “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”

Ms. Pike spent most of her three decades in prison in isolation, until a 2024 settlement allowed her some physical interaction with other women in the prison. In her statement Friday, she said being alone in the infirmary was a painful repeat of that treatment, even as her recovery continued.

“I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger,” she said.

On Friday, her lawyers accused the Tennessee Department of Correction of violating the terms of the settlement agreement, saying the agency had denied a request that she be housed with other women receiving temporary medical care and unlawfully kept her in isolation without an end date.

“A medical need caused by the state’s own horrific misconduct does not authorize” a violation of the agreement, the lawyers wrote in an emergency filing to enforce the agreement.

The emergency request also sheds some light on the aftermath of the execution attempt. Her lawyers raised questions about whether she was getting her prescribed medication. They also asked for a one-time exemption to the limit on commissary purchases because Ms. Pike wanted to repurchase things, including clothes, that she had given away before her execution.

The Department of Correction declined to comment.

Ms. Pike’s long-term prognosis, her legal team said, remains unclear.

“I don’t know why I survived that night — I don’t know what comes next,” Ms. Pike said. She added, “For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time.”

Emily Cochrane is a national reporter for The Times covering the American South, based in Nashville.

Marvin R. Shanken Has Died. His Magazine Changed How We Drink Wine.

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

He bought a struggling industry newsletter called Wine Spectator in 1979 and turned it into one of America’s leading tastemakers. He was 83.

By Clay Risen

Marvin R. Shanken, who transformed a struggling newsletter called Wine Spectator into one of the country’s leading arbiters of what Americans think about what they drink — and, in the process, helped turn Napa into a byword for luxury around the world — died on Thursday at his home in Manhattan. He was 83.

His wife, Hazel Shanken, said the cause was glioblastoma.

Mr. Shanken’s career covering the wine industry began in the early 1970s, just as American wine was emerging from the shadow of France and Italy. In 1979, after running Impact, a trade publication, he bought Wine Spectator, then based in San Diego, for just $40,000, or about $163,000 today.

Over the next decade, he moved the newsletter to San Francisco, reinvented it as a large-format glossy magazine and boosted subscriptions from about 5,000 to more than 100,000.

By mixing news, profiles, lifestyle features and extensive wine reviews, Mr. Shanken made a powerful case that wines from Napa, Sonoma and other pockets of the West Coast could be every bit as impressive as those from Bordeaux or Tuscany.

The stock market boom of the 1980s, combined with the evolving tastes of the baby boomers, catalyzed a golden age for American wine. Mr. Shanken positioned Wine Spectator as its advocate, interpreter and magistrate; a good review in the magazine could mean a fortune in sales for a winery.

“He made a big difference for all of us in the wine business as we were all growing together, especially here in California,” Bill Harlan, who founded the widely acclaimed Harlan Estate vineyard and winery in Napa in 1984, said in an interview.

As the independent critic Robert M. Parker Jr. did in his influential newsletter, Wine Advocate, Mr. Shanken’s writers and reviewers embraced a 100-point scale for evaluating wine, along with a specific suite of wine styles: big cabernet sauvignons, buttery Chardonnays and oaky sauvignon blancs.

Although the 100-point scale has its critics, many of whom consider it reductive, it gave new consumers an easy way to decide what to drink, and to understand what they were drinking.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

“Marvin Shanken’s vision for making wine knowledge accessible was unparalleled — not only by embracing a system for a simple, relative-quality rating, but by always including notes on the wines and in-depth profiles of the people behind the wines,” David Duncan, the proprietor and executive chairman of Silver Oak Cellars, a Napa winery renowned for its cabernets, wrote in an email.

Mr. Shanken was an empire builder. Alongside Wine Spectator, he added Cigar Aficionado in 1992 and Whisky Advocate in 2010; he took over the New York Wine Experience, an elite annual gathering of top wineries, in 1981; and he ran an extensive festival and conference business. He also owned a collection of influential trade magazines that quietly provided a significant chunk of his revenue.

Thanks in no small part to Mr. Shanken, the modern California wine industry, which began in the 1970s as an insurgency against the dominance of Old World winemaking, had by the 2000s become a cornerstone of the establishment and a magnet for money.

“More than any other publication, Wine Spectator established the ‘wine country lifestyle,’” W. Blake Gray, the U. S. editor of the website Wine-Searcher, said in an interview. “Wine Spectator spoke to one type of reader: wealthy.”

Mr. Shanken reveled in his power. He liked to show journalists around his Manhattan office, which had its own sprawling wine cellar and a walk-in humidor. Sometimes he showed them a smaller humidor that Milton Berle gave to John F. Kennedy as a gift in 1961; Mr. Shanken bought it at auction in 1996 for $574,000.

His office walls were decorated with photos of him socializing with presidents, tycoons and movie stars. One showed him with Michael Milken, the disgraced financier, and Rudolph W. Giuliani, who as U. S. attorney had brought Mr. Milken to justice.

“He put him in jail, and I brought the two of them together,” Mr. Shanken told The Wall Street Journal in 2015.

A former investment banker, Mr. Shanken was proud of his lack of publishing experience. Despite his immense business success, he liked to say that he rarely made decisions based on financial analysis — fittingly, he said, he went with his gut.

“I have never done feasibility studies,” he told the website Mr. Magazine in 2012. “I’ve never done focus groups. I’ve never done any of this stuff. Usually, my stomach leads my mind. I basically operate on instincts, for better or worse.”

Marvin Ray Shanken was born on Oct. 4, 1943, in New Haven, Conn. His parents, Oscar and Evelyn (Fishman) Shanken, ran a jewelry store.

He graduated in 1965 from the University of Miami with a degree in business. He liked to brag that, despite coming in last in his class, he took enough extra classes to get into the business school at American University. He received a master’s degree in business administration in 1968.

He then joined a small investment firm in New York, where he focused on real estate. He knew little about wine until 1971, when he helped close a deal for a client who was buying a winery.

At a celebratory dinner, the client told him to order any wine he wanted. Mr. Shanken selected a 1961 Petrus, still considered one of the greatest merlots ever made.

“We drank it, and bells went off,” he wrote in Wine Spectator earlier this year. “I experienced a taste that I’d never ever had before. And for the first time, I awoke to the delicious nature of a beverage called wine.”

As he became more interested in the industry, he was surprised at how hard it was to gather information. In 1972, he took over Impact, then a tiny industry newsletter, and expanded it to include extensive data reporting, as well as a conference arm.

Seven years later, Robert Morrisey, who had founded Wine Spectator in 1976, asked him to buy the publication, which was losing money and in danger of being shut down.

Mr. Shanken’s first marriage, to Patricia Rubin, ended in divorce. He married Hazel Rudy in 1981.

Along with her, he is survived by three daughters, Samantha Shanken Baker, Allison Cohen and Jessica Shanken Reid; four grandchildren; and two sisters, Elaine Shanken Fischer and Susan Shanken Rosenzweig.

The long-running dominance of Wine Spectator — it celebrated its 50th birthday this year — inevitably invited criticism, especially from younger winemakers and experts who assailed its preference for certain styles of wine, and for promoting wine as part of a luxury lifestyle.

“In 2026, unfortunately the wine business has fallen, and Spectator’s positioning of wine as an accessory for the wealthy is part of the reason,” Mr. Gray, the U. S. editor of Wine-Searcher, said. “Shanken didn’t invent wine snobbery, but he did Americanize it.”

Still, Mr. Gray allowed that Mr. Shanken deserved credit for almost single-handedly transforming American wine.

“It was an extremely influential publication that, along with Robert Parker, actually affected the way wine was made,” he said. “Wine Spectator could make wineries halfway around the world change the way they made wine.”

Clay Risen is a Times reporter on the Obituaries desk.

How Curry Barker Makes a Sad Face Terrifying in ‘Obsession’

The New York Times October 30, 2026

What to Watch

Advertisement

Supported by

Anatomy of a Scene

Barker, the film’s writer and director, explains how lingering shots heighten the tension and awkwardness in a party scene.

By Mekado Murphy

In “Anatomy of a Scene,” we ask directors to reveal the secrets that go into making key scenes in their movies. See new episodes in the series on Fridays. You can also watch our collection of more than 350 videos on YouTube and subscribe to our YouTube channel.

If you ever find yourself in possession of a One Wish Willow novelty item, you might want to trash it immediately. In the hit film “Obsession” (streaming on Peacock), Bear (Michael Johnston) has not heeded that warning. He uses the devise to wish that his longtime crush, Nikki (Inde Navarrette), would love him more than anyone. And boy, does that wish come true, to sinister effect.

By this point in the film, Nikki’s behavior has already grown unnerving. Things take an even worse turn in this scene when she crashes a get-together Bear is attending and causes a stir during a party game, creating tension throughout the entire room.

Discussing the scene in an interview, the film’s writer-director, Curry Barker, said, “I really wanted to capture the awkwardness of the situation.” To heighten the discomfort, Barker opted to “stay on frames a little longer than you typically would to kind of linger and make you feel uncomfortable.” He wanted the audience to feel like party guests themselves, wallowing in the awkwardness.

The scene ends with a shocking moment of violence that propels the narrative.

“I wanted the party scene to be a big turning point in this movie, and I thought, if there’s going to be something horrific that happens, I want it to take place in a public forum like a party,” Barker said. “I thought it’d be really interesting to see her in her full craziness.”

Judge Appoints Special Master to Determine if Trump Officials Lied in Golf Course Suit

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Judge Ana C. Reyes said an outside investigator would help determine whether parks officials or Justice Department lawyers withheld plans for Washington’s East Potomac Park.

By Zach Montague

Reporting from Washington

A federal judge appointed a special master on Friday to investigate the possibility that the Trump administration concealed plans to overhaul East Potomac Park in Washington as the president called for construction of a professional golf course at the site.

The appointment of an outside investigator represented an escalation in a confrontation between Judge Ana C. Reyes and the Trump administration over a municipal golf course and park in the nation’s capital.

Judge Reyes, who was appointed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr., had repeatedly clashed with the Justice Department in the case. She has displayed frustration with what she described as misleading attempts by officials to downplay how firm the federal government’s plans were for the park.

Her order followed a remarkable standoff with Stanley Woodward Jr., the third most senior official at the Justice Department, at a hearing Friday. At issue was whether he had personally lied in court when he told Judge Reyes that there was no immediate plan to close the course or start construction. Those comments came days after President Trump had announced on social media that work was scheduled to begin “IMMEDIATELY!”

The government acknowledged in a filing this week that it planned to close most of the park Nov. 15.

Judge Reyes emphasized on Friday that her decision did not amount to a finding that either Interior Department officials or the Justice Department lawyers had violated any rules of personal conduct. But she had already concluded at an earlier stage of the lawsuit that one senior official, Gregory Wischer, had probably withheld some of what he knew about the agency’s plans for the site.

Mr. Trump has spoken publicly for months about his desire to replace the municipal golf course in the park with a larger, more difficult one that could host professional tournaments, closely resembling the courses he owns and operates elsewhere.

A preservationist organization and two local residents sued in February to stop the current course from being replaced.

President Trump’s proposed overhaul of a Washington golf course and park could sacrifice features long popular with locals.

Government lawyers repeatedly told Judge Reyes that planning to fulfill Mr. Trump’s vision was in its preliminary stages, arguing it would be premature for her to order construction blocked. With those assurances in hand, Judge Reyes declined to take pre-emptive actions to dictate what decisions the federal government could make about the property’s management.

Instead, for months she ordered the Justice Department to simply notify the court if and when the federal government began taking steps to carry out the redesign, to allow time for her to explore the project’s legality.

Then, earlier this month, the Justice Department alerted the court just before 5 p. m. on the Friday of a holiday weekend that it intended to begin cutting trees at the park, describing the work as part of a routine “tree maintenance plan” to remove dead and diseased trees. Within hours, the Interior Department cleared more than 400 trees, a move the group suing interpreted as the beginning of Mr. Trump’s redevelopment. Judge Reyes quickly intervened and ordered the cutting halted.

During the hearing on Friday, she repeatedly pressed Mr. Woodward, who joined the case after the tree dispute, to clarify whether everything he had told the court to this point had been accurate. During his last appearance, she had forced Mr. Woodward to explain recent social media posts in which Mr. Trump announced that the park would close on Nov. 15 for an approximately 14-month renovation. Mr. Trump said he had secured a design by a prominent golf course architect, with whom he was photographed touring the course in June.

Mr. Woodward maintained that even after Mr. Trump’s posts, there was no “final” plan to shut the course. He also insisted that officials had been kept largely in the dark about the specifics of when and how Mr. Trump’s plan would unfold.

Judge Reyes said the special master would be tasked with determining whether the hurried tree removal was “designed to evade judicial review” and whether the Justice Department had provided false assurances that no concrete decisions had been reached.

She said the investigation would also focus on whether the Interior Department and National Park Service were truly out of the loop or if in fact top officials had been briefed on Mr. Trump’s plans and were taking steps to realize them.

Zach Montague is a Times reporter covering the federal courts, including the legal disputes over the Trump administration’s agenda.

U. S. to Send Dozens Back to Afghanistan, Despite Risk of Persecution

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The Trump administration plans to fly the Afghan immigrants from Louisiana to Pakistan, where they are expected to be expelled over the border to Afghanistan.

By Pranav BaskarHamed Aleaziz and Elian Peltier

The Trump administration has detained dozens of Afghan immigrants in Louisiana and plans to deport them to Afghanistan, according to three U. S. officials. The group includes people who could face discrimination or persecution under the Taliban, including relatives of people who helped the U. S. military and at least one gay man.

More than 150 Afghan immigrants are expected to be deported, one official said, making this one of the largest single expulsions of Afghans.

By sending them to Pakistan — which would then send them to Afghanistan — the Trump administration has found a way around the hurdles that have so far prevented vulnerable Afghans from being sent back to face repression or retaliation by the Taliban.

Lacking diplomatic relations with the Taliban, the United States cannot arrange deportations to Afghanistan. And some Afghans living in America have been granted legal protections from U. S. judges, which prevent them from being sent back to Afghanistan because of the persecution they would likely face under the Taliban government.

The officials say the deportation is, in effect, to Afghanistan, and that is what the detainees have been told by ICE. But Pakistan will oversee their expulsion over the border to Afghanistan.

The first flight is expected to leave as soon as Nov. 2.

One of the Afghans marked for deportation is Mohammad, 47, who said he was detained last year by federal agents while charging his electric car and had been held in Oklahoma. Last week, he was moved to a prison in Louisiana to be deported, he said in a phone interview from the prison. He said his family left Afghanistan as refugees in 1981, when he was 2 years old, after the Soviet Union invaded.

Over four decades, Mohammad navigated life in America. After serving time in his early 20s for two felonies, he lost his permanent residency. Mohammad said he came to accept being gay and married an American man in 2020.

“That right there is automatic grounds for imprisonment and execution there,” Mohammad said. In Afghanistan, homosexuality is punishable by death. He spoke on the condition that he be identified only by his middle name, explaining, “I am afraid for my life.”

In court filings for another case, an Afghan man said that he was arrested and tortured by the Taliban in 2023 because of his wife’s affiliation with the previous government. She had helped the U. S. military as a soldier with the Afghan Army and as a member of the women’s police force, a group that the Taliban singled out for retribution when they returned to power.

He entered the U. S. illegally in 2024, was arrested by border patrol and has been in ICE detention since then. His asylum application had been denied by a U. S. judge. His lawyer shared the documents describing his case on condition that the man not be named.

U. S. law prohibits the government from deporting people to countries where courts have ruled they would most likely face persecution. It is not known if any of the Afghans being sent back in November have such court protections.

The United States has not announced the deportation plan, elements of which were first reported by Bloomberg. The New York Times pieced it together through interviews with lawyers for some of the people detained and with the three U. S. officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a confidential policy. The Times also obtained documents to verify Mohammad’s criminal history, marriage and the plan to deport him.

Court filings for one of the Afghans indicate that he has been put on a manifest for a special chartered flight that leaves Alexandria, La., during the first week of November. Lawyers representing the two other Afghan immigrants shared emails from federal officials informing them that their clients would be deported to Afghanistan in early November.

A spokesman for the Department of Homeland Security said that ICE “does not comment on prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details.”

In recent days, the Afghan immigrants have been moved from detention centers all over the country by U. S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to immigration detention facilities in Louisiana. Detainees and lawyers said they were given little information, other than that they are being sent to Afghanistan.

Melissa Medrano Henry, Mohammad’s lawyer, said the federal government had informed her that it had obtained travel documents for her client from Afghan authorities — meaning, the Taliban — but had yet to produce them or explain how the documents were obtained. She has filed emergency motions to block his deportation, but a judge has not yet made a decision.

While past U. S. administrations have deported small numbers of Afghans to Afghanistan, also relying on intermediary countries, those flights were reserved for people with serious criminal charges, often related to terrorism. Data from the Deportation Data Project, an effort by the University of California, Berkeley and U. C. L. A. to use public records requests to analyze ICE data, shows that in the past four years, the United States has sent about 97 Afghans back.

Next week’s planned deportation flight is the most expansive effort so far to include Afghans in the wider dragnet to carry out mass deportations. The group includes a mix of people who came to the United States legally and illegally, and some with criminal records. Lawyers for some of the detainees are challenging their deportations.

Over the past two years, the Trump administration has restricted immigration for Afghans who helped the American war effort, deported others to countries in Africa, and pushed some, who are stranded in a former U. S. military camp in Qatar, to return voluntarily.

Spokesmen for Pakistan’s ministries of interior and foreign affairs did not respond to requests for comment.

Pakistan is in the midst of its own campaign of mass deportation of Afghan refugees, as well as campaigns of public harassment and intimidation to push them out. Since 2023, Pakistan’s government has expelled or forced to return more than 2.7 million Afghan citizens to Afghanistan, calling their presence a national security threat.

Taliban government officials did not respond to requests for comment.

Pakistan’s mass expulsions of Afghans is one of several tools it has used to try to pressure the Taliban government, which it accuses of harboring terrorist groups that stage relentless attacks on Pakistani soil. It has vowed to expel all Afghans — about 1.5 million still live in Pakistan — no matter their immigration status.

In recent months, it has revoked or not renewed the visas of Afghan health care professionals who had moved to Pakistan to complete specialized training. Hundreds of Afghan doctors have been laid off and are at risk of expulsion.

Zainullah Niazmand, an Afghan cardiac surgeon practicing in the Pakistani city of Lahore, said he believed the Pakistani government, having first expelled Afghan refugees, traders and day laborers, was now intensifying pressure on the Taliban government by sending back doctors. His visa was revoked last year and he, his wife and their 3-year-old daughter are at risk of expulsion.

Mohammad, the Afghan immigrant detained in Louisiana, said he feels like he is paying for a mistake he made when he was young. After two felony convictions in 2003, for robbery and for making threats to a school, according to the government documents for his case, he said he spent about three years in prison, lost his green card and spent two decades rebuilding his life while checking in regularly with ICE.

“I was so scared to get married. I was so scared to get into a serious relationship, to try to have and maintain a regular life out of fear that one day, something like this could happen,” he said. “The one thing that I did hold dear and close to me in my life in this country was having the freedom to choose how I want to live my life. That’s being stripped away from me.”

In detention, as he awaits a flight to a country he has never known, Mohammad says he is growing his beard and trying to relearn Islamic prayers, fearful of what life will be like under the Taliban.

Yaqoob Akbary contributed reporting from Kabul, Afghanistan.

I got to know Mohammad, the Afghan man quoted in this story, over several calls he made from a prison phone. Often, he reflected about his fear of being deported in the coming days, his confusion about what would come next. But he also said something about identity that stuck with me: “For most of my life, I felt too Afghan to be American, and too American to be Afghan.” His lawyer is trying to stop him from being sent back, but he’s waiting for a judge to decide whether to put an emergency hold on his deportation.

Pranav Baskar is an international reporter at The Times, based in New York.

Hamed Aleaziz covers the Department of Homeland Security and immigration policy for The Times.

Elian Peltier is The Times’s bureau chief for Pakistan and Afghanistan, based in Islamabad.

Binance’s $6.3 Billion Hack Is Just the Start of a Risky New Era

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The largest cyber heist in history came as attackers increasingly use artificial intelligence and other advanced techniques to steal crypto and quickly launder the funds.

By David Yaffe-Bellany and Dustin Volz

David Yaffe-Bellany reports on the cryptocurrency industry, and Dustin Volz reports on cybersecurity.

In February 2025, a team of North Korean hackers stole $1.5 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange Bybit — a dark day for the industry and the largest crypto heist ever recorded.

Now that number looks paltry.

Binance, the world’s biggest crypto exchange, set an unwanted record on Thursday, losing $6.3 billion to hackers in an eye-popping attack that highlighted the deep vulnerabilities in crypto’s financial infrastructure.

For years, the industry has struggled to prevent thefts. Now, the risks are growing even more extreme as attackers use artificial intelligence and other advanced techniques to steal funds and quickly launder them, crypto analysts and security experts said.

The Binance attacker used “laundering patterns we have not seen before,” the crypto analytics firm Chainalysis wrote in a blog post on Friday. “Thousands of transactions in a short period suggest that the attackers are using automation to obscure the trail of funds.”

The details of how Binance was breached are still coming into focus. Both Chainalysis and TRM Labs, another analytics firm, attributed the hack to North Korea, which has targeted crypto companies for years. Binance initially said the attacker appeared to have compromised a laptop belonging to one of its engineers, before clarifying that further investigation had uncovered “additional points of breach.”

Binance has promised to make customers whole and said it had set aside more than $6.3 billion in company funds to cover the losses. (Binance processes billions of dollars in transactions every day.) Of the total that was stolen, $3 billion has been frozen by other companies, including Circle and Tether, two large issuers of digital coins that have the ability to stop the movement of stolen funds.

That means North Korea won’t have access to those coins, and Binance said it was working on recovering them. But the hackers have already moved $2.4 billion in crypto “beyond any issuer’s reach,” according to TRM.

Those losses may be only the beginning, as the crypto world reckons with an era of fast-evolving hacking techniques and growing risks. Even as President Trump has endorsed the industry and sought to bring it into the mainstream, some crypto firms still struggle with the basic work of any financial company — keeping customer money safe.

“A. I. is undoubtedly turbocharging the ability of hackers to find and exploit subtle flaws in various parts of the crypto ecosystem,” said Eswar Prasad, a Cornell University economics professor who tracks the crypto industry. “The scale and scope of such attacks is likely to intensify.”

Still, North Korea’s inventive army of hackers could probably have pulled off the Binance heist without A. I., even if the technology proved useful during the operation, some cybersecurity experts said.

“North Korea had sophisticated threat actors that could have done this pre-A. I.,” said Joshua Saxe, the chief technology officer of the A. I. security firm Abundant Security. “That said, it’s hard not to think about the relationship between megaheists like this and what A. I. is doing to democratize advanced hacking. Many more actors can attempt this kind of thing now, thanks to A. I. tools.”

Crypto has struggled with major thefts since the technology’s inception in 2008. Industry pioneers viewed digital coins as a renegade alternative to banks — a type of money outside the supervision of governments or big businesses. From the beginning, that philosophy made crypto vulnerable.

Many crypto investors keep funds in their own online wallets. But if they lose a password, the money is gone forever. Others rely on exchanges like Binance, which behave something like banks, storing funds for customers. But exchanges are not subject to the same regulatory systems that govern banks and other traditional financial companies, and have often lacked effective guardrails against crime.

In February 2025, North Korean hackers tricked the chief executive of Bybit, Ben Zhou, into authorizing a seemingly routine transaction that handed them control of the exchange’s system. They had exploited a gaping hole in ByBit’s defenses — a free software product that the company used to protect customer deposits. The thieves extracted $1.5 billion in digital coins.

At the time, a security firm called the losses “completely preventable.” Ultimately, Bybit weathered the crisis by drawing on corporate reserves and borrowing funds from other crypto companies.

The attack on Binance appears more serious.

After it was founded in 2017, the exchange quickly became the largest and most important company in the crypto industry, processing as much as two-thirds of all digital currency transactions. It provides a marketplace for people to buy popular coins like Bitcoin and Ether, converting traditional currencies into crypto.

On Thursday, as soon as Binance’s system was breached, its founder, Changpeng Zhao, assured customers that they would not lose any money.

“It hurts, but we will survive,” he wrote on X, adding a muscle emoji.

Mr. Zhao has a long history of legal and regulatory problems. Binance pleaded guilty to money-laundering violations in 2023 and paid a $4.3 billion fine to the U. S. government. After serving a four-month prison sentence, Mr. Zhao was pardoned by Mr. Trump last year. Binance also forged a business relationship with World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto company.

News of the Binance hack started to spread on social media on Thursday afternoon. Because most crypto transactions are publicly visible, industry analysts tracked sudden withdrawals from the exchange on the blockchain, the ledger of digital currency movements. But while transactions happen openly, the money often moves too quickly for companies to respond, and it can be difficult to determine who controls particular accounts.

The stolen funds began leaving Binance around 4:20 p. m. on Thursday, according to Chainalysis. Soon the thieves started moving the money in a sequence suggesting “a programmatic process” for laundering funds.

Chainalysis attributed the attack to North Korea partly because it observed stolen Binance funds “commingling” with funds stolen last month in a hack that targeted Bitget, another crypto exchange. In its analysis, TRM said the Binance hack was the work of TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit.

In a statement, the F. B. I. said it was “aware of the incident” and “engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts and coordinate appropriate investigative steps.”

Western intelligence officials for years have warned that crypto theft is one of the main ways that North Korea’s regime evades punishing international sanctions and funds its nuclear weapons program, which it considers crucial to its survival.

The Binance hack appears to be an especially lucrative payday. Tom Robinson, the chief scientist and a co-founder of Elliptic, a crypto analytics firm, said it would nearly double the sum of all of North Korea’s known crypto thefts. Mr. Robinson said Elliptic agreed with other firms that North Korea was probably the culprit, but noted that North Korean groups usually were much faster and more efficient at moving funds and avoiding freezes.

North Korean hackers “know that unlike big banks, crypto exchange security is often terrible,” said Ciaran Martin, the former head of national cyberdefense in the United Kingdom. “They’re good at exploiting that.”

He added, “This is their best day at the office yet.”

David Yaffe-Bellany writes about the crypto industry for The Times from New York. He can be reached at davidyb@nytimes. com.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

The day that changed modern China also taught me how to recognize true courage.

Credit... Peter Turnley/Getty Images. Illustration by Matt Dorfman

Supported by

By Nicholas Kristof

Nicholas Kristof, who was Beijing bureau chief for The Times from 1988 to 1993, is now a columnist for Opinion.

This story is part of a series marking 175 years of eyewitness journalism from The New York Times. Read more here.

As I pedaled my bicycle toward the gunfire and Tiananmen Square, dodging people in crowds fleeing in the opposite direction, I kept thinking: What a crazy occupation this is.

For weeks during the spring of 1989, the question preoccupying the world had been whether the student-led Tiananmen demonstrations paralyzing China would end with a democratic revolution or with massacres. That night, June 3, the phone began ringing in the apartment in Beijing I shared with my wife and fellow New York Times correspondent, Sheryl WuDunn. We had our answer: Tens of thousands of army troops were forcing their way into central Beijing, mowing down crowds of unarmed protesters and bystanders who tried to resist.

So I jumped on my bicycle, legs pumping madly, careening around tank traps students had set up, so I could report on a modern army waging war on its people.

It was probably the most important story I’ve covered and I got at least one big thing wrong — I’ll get to that — but I did manage to reach Tiananmen Square before the troops. I parked my bicycle near the famous portrait of Chairman Mao and began interviewing people in the throng of students and workers.

Although it was already dark, the square was lit by overhead lights and by the glow of two armored personnel carriers that protesters had set ablaze. At first, the troops, arriving by the truckload, fired over our heads. Then they lowered their aim and fired right at us.

The gunfire was episodic, coming in cacophonous bursts every few minutes. People would fall, we would retreat, the guns would fall silent for a time and our retreat would halt.

I was rushing around, interviewing people in Chinese, always trying to keep a layer of protesters between me and the bullets. Until I realized that I was taller than almost everyone around me, so that a valuable few upper inches of me were still exposed. I began stooping as I spoke to people.

“General strike!” the crowd shouted. “General strike!” Some people hurled rocks or Molotov cocktails toward the troops, but they couldn’t hit the soldiers — and then there would be another round of gunfire, and more would drop.

Groups of protesters commandeered two buses in hopes of reaching the troops. About a dozen young people boarded each bus, holding iron bars or other weapons with which they intended to attack the soldiers. The crowd screamed encouragement, but their courage was misplaced. As the protesters drove the buses toward the troops, the soldiers opened fire. The buses came to a halt, one of them on fire, and in a moment, these young people transformed from heroes into corpses.

I found myself in the midst of a massacre. With each round of gunfire, we were pushed backward on the blood-soaked Avenue of Eternal Peace. My bicycle was now close to the troops and not recoverable, so I ran to a nearby hospital to count corpses, and then back home. I had forgotten that it was a Saturday evening, which for the paper meant early deadlines.

When I didn’t return on time, Sheryl, who had filed her own story about the slaughter, was increasingly fearful that I had been shot. “There’s no point in worrying,” the foreign editor, Joseph Lelyveld, kept telling her on the phone; the anxiety in his voice made her worry even more. He tried to distract her by asking her to reach out to all the hospitals to document the death toll — a request that didn’t help Sheryl’s mood.

Finally, I burst in, hugged Sheryl, called New York to reassure editors there that I was fine and then filed my story by telex — a few paragraphs at a time, as I wrote them. I had never been so sad to have my byline and Sheryl’s under a banner headline across the front page.

Guilt nagged at me that night, and this brings me to my first great mistake in covering the crisis. During the demonstrations in the weeks before the bloodshed, I had periodically written condescendingly that the workers and peasants in the protest movement talked about democracy but couldn’t define it. I had suggested that they were driven by anger at inflation and corruption but didn’t necessarily believe in democracy for Tibetans or fully embrace the kind of free and pluralistic society they spoke of so glowingly.

There was something to this idea, but that night in June I had seen extraordinary courage from the workers and peasants. I was terrified that evening — my notebook was so damp with sweat from fear that I had trouble writing in it — and the bravest people of all were the poorly educated laborers from the countryside who drove bicycle rickshaws. Whenever there was a pause in the shooting, they would pedal their carts into the fray to pick up the bodies of students who had been killed or injured, then turn around and race to the hospitals. They might not have been able to define democracy but they were ready to die for it.

Another hard lesson I learned covering Tiananmen: Victims lie or, more charitably, misremember. It’s human nature to doubt oppressors and believe victims, but in the aftermath of the massacre there were many “eyewitness” accounts claiming that thousands or tens of thousands of students had been slaughtered in Tiananmen Square; that huge numbers of them had been shot from machine gun emplacements there; or that many were killed when tanks rolled over tents with students inside. None of this was true.

Since then, I’ve seen many times in my career that perpetrators of atrocities lie to cover up their abuses, and that victims respond with exaggerations of their own. This has taught me that we must be as vigilant in verifying accounts of victims as we are in grilling oppressors. While many estimates of the Tiananmen death toll are in the thousands, I’m reasonably sure these are wrong. Sheryl and I made great efforts to cultivate sources at hospitals and morgues to determine the toll, and our best guess is that between 400 and 800 people were killed and several thousand injured.

Accessing hospitals was difficult. Soldiers turned us away at entrances and doctors were threatened if they spoke to journalists. Chinese citizens and even some officials cooperated nonetheless, because they wanted the truth to come out. Disenchanted employees at one hospital sneaked us inside through a tunnel system from a neighboring building. We found that even the hallways were filled with shooting victims.

One young wife was weeping beside the unconscious figure of her husband, an inventor with seven patents in his name. Despite her warnings, he had gone out when the shooting started, in order to support the students, and she loved and admired him for his courage. But, she added between sobs, she hated that he might leave her alone with their 4-year-old daughter.

Journalists like to project toughness, but I was shattered, physically and morally exhausted. We went days with barely a wink of sleep, and once, when we did nap, the army fired on our apartment compound with automatic weapons. Moving around Beijing to interview people, Sheryl and I were afraid of being shot, but worse was to see the hopeful, vibrant China we had been covering morph into a crushing dictatorship. I remember collapsing on my bed one day and finding tears trickling down my cheeks.

The Chinese government rewrote history, calling the protesters “hoodlums” who had engaged in “rioting.” The state media singled me out, denouncing me for spreading lies and “writing not news reports but fiction.” The next day I ordered lunch at an empty Sichuan restaurant, where the staff gathered in a corner, pointing to me and whispering. I feared they had recognized me and I wondered if they might poison my food. Then several waitresses approached my table. “Are you the one they mentioned on television last night?” one asked. “The reporter who lies?”

“Yes,” I said, and I started to explain, but she cut me off. “Never mind,” she said, beaming. “There’s no need to pay your bill. We’ll take care of it. We’re all ‘hoodlums’ here.”

As the government began mass arrests, one of our sources was a Chinese student whom we had inadvertently gotten into trouble. “Shawn,” as he called himself in English, was a student at Tsinghua University who had helped us cover the protests. Now he was being interrogated about his connection to us, yet he still dared to meet secretly with Sheryl — who is Chinese American and could melt into crowds in a way I could not — to update her on the crackdown at the universities. His courage was breathtaking, and we were frightened for him when he suddenly disappeared.

This incident brings me to another moment that I still turn over in my mind. More than a year after his disappearance, Shawn reappeared in Beijing, met with me in secret and explained what had happened: He had been imprisoned but had escaped and was on the run. Now he asked for my help in fleeing China.

One basic rule of being a foreign correspondent is that you obey local laws. You certainly don’t help an escaped felon leave the country. Yet here was a young man who had endured prison because he had helped us cover this story. If we didn’t assist him, he would almost certainly be caught.

What to do? I wanted to consult editors in New York, but that was impossible because my phones were tapped. In any case, no editor could recommend helping an escaped prisoner.

Another concern: I harbored a nagging doubt about Shawn’s story. He said he had escaped while working in the fields of a prison farm, but we had never heard of anyone escaping from a Chinese prison. I wondered, Could this be a setup? The Chinese prime minister at the time, Li Peng, disliked my coverage, and his office was looking for an excuse to expel me. Was Chinese state security hoping to entrap me so that the authorities could arrest and imprison me and close The Times’s bureau?

I wavered, but Sheryl had a firmer compass. She doubted that Shawn would agree to entrap me, and she insisted that, given the risks he had taken, we owed him our assistance. So we did help him, including providing money to finance his escape.

Shawn was able to slip into Hong Kong on Christmas Day, 1990, when he figured there would be fewer British police officers along the border. He called me that night, and the next day I flew to Hong Kong, where, with the help of Human Rights Watch, I negotiated to get him a visa to the United States. Shawn is now a U. S. citizen.

Once I was out of China and could speak freely on the phone, I confessed to the paper’s top editors what I had done. To my surprise, they were congratulatory rather than scolding. A retired executive editor, A. M. Rosenthal, confided that three decades earlier he had helped sneak someone from Communist Poland to the West. And a Times correspondent, Sydney Schanberg, had tried desperately (though unsuccessfully) to doctor a fake passport for a Cambodian colleague, Dith Pran, to save him from the Khmer Rouge slaughter. Dith Pran eventually made it out on his own and worked as a much-loved colleague in The Times’s newsroom, a constant reminder that we have complex human obligations as well as professional ones.

There’s nothing I’ve done in my career that was as unprofessional as helping Shawn. But there are also few things I’m prouder of.

Nicholas Kristof became a columnist for The Times Opinion desk in 2001 and has won two Pulitzer Prizes. His most recent book is the memoir “Chasing Hope: A Reporter’s Life.”

Prediction Markets Face Their Biggest Accuracy Test Yet: The Midterms

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

By Stuart A. Thompson

As polls closed in Brazil last week, online bettors appeared convinced that Flávio Bolsonaro would become president, placing his odds of winning around 80 percent.

They were wrong.

As ballots were counted, it became clear that Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva would prevail. The odds rapidly shifted as traders scrambled to place new bets on the winner.

Polymarket favored Flávio Bolsonaro going into Election Day. He lost.

Note: Brazil’s polls were scheduled to close at 5 p. m. local time. Some election results were reported around that time, but a Federal Supreme Court decision released around 5 p. m. extended voting by another two hours. Source: Polymarket

This year, the power of prediction markets is being tested like never before. Though the platforms, including Polymarket and Kalshi, have been around for several years, they exploded in popularity more recently by allowing bets on everything from who will win the World Series to how much consumers will spend on Cyber Monday.

The platforms are hoping the U. S. midterm elections will be their moment to shine — and help business boom — with a spate of accurate predictions that surpass polls and election forecasts in their ability to anticipate what will happen.

To attract new users and rake in fees associated with their betting activity, the companies have conducted a marketing blitz. Kalshi rented a giant billboard in Times Square, blaring odds about which party will control the Senate. Polymarket produced a TV spot depicting a failing political campaign with the tagline: “Watch the midterms move.”

Producing accurate predictions this year would be a boon for an industry that is facing increasing scrutiny from lawmakers, including over concerns regarding market manipulations and insider trading.

“I think in a week from now, this is going to be a pretty big story,” said Brett Goldstein, a research professor at Vanderbilt University and co-leader of a team that studies prediction markets. “And we’ll see which way the story goes.”

Studies have shown that prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi can be highly accurate. That does not mean that the odds-on favorite always wins, however.

Prediction markets allow users to place wagers on the outcome of an event. Much of the betting activity is focused on the outcome of sports, but elections have emerged as a popular category because campaigns take months to resolve and can accumulate millions of dollars in bets from amateurs and pros alike. As users place bets, the price for each option fluctuates, creating an always-moving set of odds that reflect the likelihood that something will happen.

A review of more than one million markets, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences this year, found that those odds were “well calibrated.” Strong favorites usually won, but not always.

But researchers believe they are on the brink of developing an even richer understanding of the markets’ predictive power once all the votes are tallied this year. Past findings do not necessarily reflect the platforms as they are today, with far more users and money coursing through the sites.

Dani Lever, a spokeswoman for Kalshi, compared betting markets to the stock market, saying that investors have always traded around elections. “By shifting the focus from what people want to happen to what they think will happen,” she said in an emailed statement, prediction markets can “filter out social media noise and pundit bias.” Polymarket did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

More than $221 million has flooded into markets related to the midterms, up from $92 million in the 2024 presidential race, according to a report called “Gambling on Democracy” from the Anti-Corruption Data Collective, a research group based in Washington focused on identifying and reducing corruption in private investment.

The rising popularity of prediction markets has been met with plenty of pushback over whether they possess any special predictive power at all.

In the 2024 presidential election, prediction markets showed far sooner than polls that Donald J. Trump would triumph over Kamala Harris, according to a study by the researchers at Vanderbilt University. Polls had narrowly but consistently favored Ms. Harris, the researchers had found.

“We need to watch these very closely,” said Mr. Goldstein, who worked on the study. “They may be telling us something closer to the truth.”

The platforms have also had notable misses this year. During this year’s primary elections, prediction markets gave Spencer Pratt, a conservative candidate for mayor of Los Angeles, a 75 percent chance of being on the Nov. 3 ballot. He came in third place during the primary, trailing by nearly 30,000 votes, and did not advance to the general election.

High quality polls released before the vote were divided, with half showing that Mr. Pratt would come in second, and half showing that Nithya Raman, the eventual second-place finisher, would be second.

Polymarket bettors favored Karen Bass, the incumbent mayor, and Spencer Pratt, a conservative challenger. They were wrong. Nithya Raman, a progressive candidate, came in second place and advanced to the general election.

Source: Polymarket

Pollsters and election modelers have taken special umbrage with the prediction markets, arguing that they mostly capture the beliefs of online gamblers and are otherwise largely reliant on existing polls.

“I don’t think we should be looking at prediction markets at all,” said G. Elliott Morris, an election forecaster who runs FiftyPlusOne, a polling and election forecasting website. “I think we have great direct measurements of public opinion from the polls.”

Mr. Morris said that some races on prediction markets showed signs that bettors believe polls would underestimate Republican support. Polls have made such mistakes in the past — undercounting support for President Trump in particular. But they were more precise during midterm elections over the past decade.

That may help explain a difference between modelers, polls and prediction markets in the Iowa Senate race. Polls have shown a race that is evenly split. Modelers, like Mr. Morris, have favored Josh Turek, the Democratic candidate. Prediction markets, including Polymarket, Kalshi and PredictIt, have favored Ashley Hinson, the Republican.

In most other tight Senate races, prediction markets have favored Democrats, including in Maine, where Susan Collins, the Republican incumbent who has held the office since 1997, trails behind Troy Jackson, a Democrat. Ms. Collins has trailed in every high quality poll taken in October, except one, where she was tied with Mr. Jackson.

In 2020, Ms. Collins had trailed in every poll released during the final four months of her re-election campaign. But on Election Day, she triumphed by more than 8 percentage points over the Democratic challenger — reflecting an overall miss in polling that underestimated support for Republicans that year.

Campaign managers are also beginning to watch prediction markets for signs of how to pivot their messaging.

For years, campaign strategists have studied how to read polls for such guidance. Eric Wilson, a Republican strategist, said that seeing a lot of undecideds in a poll was an instant sign that campaigns should spend more on name recognition, and avoid mentioning their opponent, for example.

Prediction markets might hold similar insights, he said, but strategists are still learning what to do with them.

“In many ways, it’s as valuable a signal as polling,” Mr. Wilson said. “We just don’t know what it’s saying.”

I've been reporting on prediction markets this midterm season and will be watching closely on Election Night to track how their predictions fare. (Check out my story on one bettor who has $1.5 million on the line: https://www. nytimes. com/2026/10/29/technology/polymarket-kalshi-midterm-election-betting-wagers. html). There's little question left that prediction markets have predictive power, but the more interesting question is whether they do much more than riff off the polls and work by election modelers. The answer might be found in the Iowa Senate race. Recent polls are divided, narrowly favoring the Democrat. Prediction markets are bullish on the Republican, Ashley Hinson. It's a rare case where there is a difference between how prediction markets see the race and what polls show. Another interesting race could be Nevada's Governor. Polls show a tight contest, but prediction markets have given remarkably high odds to the Democrat.

Stuart A. Thompson writes for The Times about online influence, including the people, places and institutions that shape the information we all consume.

As Picard, Patrick Stewart Had ‘Life-Changing’ Effects on Generations of Scientists

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Patrick Stewart (1940-2026)

Advertisement

Supported by

Stewart’s iconic “Star Trek” character inspired astronomers and astronauts in countless ways: “You were the captain of my childhood,” one astrophysicist said.

By Robin George Andrews

Patrick Stewart, who died on Wednesday, was many things to many people: a world-renowned actor, a knight of the realm, a patron of the arts, a tireless fighter for raising awareness of domestic abuse. And for millions, Mr. Stewart will chiefly be remembered as Jean-Luc Picard, the stoic, pacifist captain of the U. S. S. Enterprise who first appeared in “Star Trek: The Next Generation.”

Mr. Stewart’s iconic character was also a source of inspiration for thousands of space scientists.

On social media, the real-life explorers and chroniclers of the cosmos — including astronauts, astronomers and science communicators — mourned the loss of Mr. Stewart, often referring to him by his Starfleet rank. Grant Tremblay, an astrophysicist, wrote: “Ad astra legend. You were the captain of my childhood.” Chanda Prescod-Weinstein, a theoretical cosmologist and author, said: “Rest in peace, our Captain,” adding that his on-screen role was “life changing for me and so many.”

In a social media post, Mark McCaughrean, an astronomer based in Europe, said that he hoped Mr. Stewart “knew how influential that programme was across astronomy.” After all, he added, it’s no coincidence that the James Webb Space Telescope “was originally and for many years called the Next Generation Space Telescope.”

“Star Trek” has also encouraged some to pursue an unusual career path: protecting the planet from cosmic catastrophes. NASA’s Planetary Defense Coordination Office, in Washington, coordinates U. S. efforts to monitor space for asteroids headed toward Earth and conjure up spaceflight missions designed to swat them away. Both its founder, Lindley Johnson, and its acting planetary defense officer, Kelly Fast, have cited the show as a key inspiration for their work.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, in Greenbelt, Md., also chimed in with a post on X. “History will never forget the name Captain Picard,” it read. “Thank you for inspiring the Next Generation of explorers.”

NASA in particular has a long history with “Star Trek.” In 1976, the space agency unveiled the very first space shuttle. It was named Enterprise — a decision made after the White House received letters from almost 100,000 “Star Trek” fans.

Picard would doubtless have found common ground with many NASA scientists. The character once said, “Things are only impossible until they’re not,” something echoed in the motto of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory: Dare mighty things.

Unlike previous members of Starfleet, Picard was not a buccaneer. He was a diplomat (and an amateur archaeologist) as much as he was a galactic pathfinder. Picard was suffused with empathy and a yearning to see and understand as much about the universe as he could, as peacefully as possible.

In other words, Picard was an exemplary astronaut-scientist, providing inspiration for real-world space travelers.

During a panel for a film festival in 2017, Mr. Stewart told the story of a televised call he had with several astronauts aboard the International Space Station. “Before we get into this any further, Captain, I have to know: Why would you — a real astronaut — want to have a conversation with a fake one?” he recalled asking a crew member at the time. “He said, ‘Because I wouldn’t be here doing this if it weren’t for you.’”

The astronaut then told Mr. Stewart that he had something to show him on camera. “It was a photograph of him,” Mr. Stewart said, “and all his fellow crew members — not Photoshopped, but actually wearing ‘Star Trek’ uniforms.”

When asked about his desire to travel into space, Mr. Stewart said he was keen to follow in Picard’s footsteps. “I would go like a shot,” he said in a 2020 interview with AARP magazine.

“Star Trek” frequently showcased an optimistic version of humanity. By the 23rd century, humans had persisted through a series of global conflicts to become an interstellar species while also transforming Earth into a near utopia. Both Mr. Stewart and his fictional counterpart were wary of efforts to aggressively militarize the final frontier.

Today, the prospect of space warfare looms large, with the United States, Russia and China all showing strong interest in developing and deploying weapons into Earth orbit. In a 2014 interview, Mr. Stewart said that “Picard saw force as a last resort. Absolute last resort.”

Mr. Stewart never got his chance to venture into space. But it may not be long before he ends up there, in a manner of speaking. Several asteroids have been named after various “Star Trek” alumni, including Leonard Nimoy, the actor who played Mr. Spock, and Nichelle Nichols, who played Lieutenant Uhura.

Perhaps Mr. Stewart’s name will eventually be attached to a space rock, too. Astronomers: Make it so.
