What It’s Like to Be Caught Between Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Amy Chozick

Ms. Chozick, a former New York Times reporter, is the author of the novel “With Friends Like You.” She wrote from Los Angeles.

On opening weekend, someone posted on X: “Imagine how weird it would be to watch ‘You Can See Everything’ with Amy Chozick.”

Let me tell you how weird.

It was wild to watch disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her life partner, Billy Evans, reading the lengthy profile of Ms. Holmes that I wrote for The New York Times on a laptop, seemingly just as it was published. At one point, Mr. Evans reads a quote from Ms. Holmes about her depiction by actors in film and TV — “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created” — and says it doesn’t sound like something she would say. He suggests Ms. Holmes must instead have said, “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character they created.” She agreed.

I had no idea that a central theme of the film would revolve around this disputed quote, which essentially opens and closes the movie.

The Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim documentary is, as one review put it, “an existential vortex, challenging the concept of truth.” It might not even be, by some overly strict definitions, a documentary.

It is quite funny. I howled laughing at the uncomfortable weirdness of the depictions of the couple that Mr. Fielder and Mr. Oppenheim constructed. Ms. Holmes and Mr. Evans appeared to have let the filmmakers see everything, even showing Mr. Evans taking a shower. But when I saw the film, I kept thinking: Where is the nanny?

She was nowhere to be seen. Without her, the couple comes off as harried multitasking parents, literally rocking the baby with one foot.

I met Vanessa, the Salvadoran woman who was sometimes on hand to help care for their toddler and newborn, because I also spent several days inside the couple’s canary-yellow rental home in Del Mar, Calif. My article was published on May 7, 2023, 23 days before Ms. Holmes went to prison after being found guilty of fraud at her once-hot blood-testing-device company.

We went to the zoo and for tacos and smoothies. They even offered to let me stay with them. I declined. And by the looks of the bed they dusted off for Mr. Fielder, I think I made the right call.

I left in March. Mr. Fielder and his crew arrived in April. I was struck by the film’s opening text that said Ms. Holmes hadn’t spoken publicly in seven years, since my profile was published shortly after Mr. Fielder and his crew arrived.

Ms. Holmes and Mr. Evans seemed convinced that the longer you spend with them, in the cozy kitchen, playing with the kids, walking the dog on the beach, the more you’d be hypnotized, too. How could you not be? For them, access was a conduit to a type of exoneration. They are salespeople. Their humanity is what they now had to sell.

It’s why the couple extended so much access for my Times profile, hoping it would help reshape Ms. Holmes’s image and garner sympathy. Then my story came out.

Half the internet, and many of my former Times colleagues, derided the story as a “puff piece.” I was relentlessly trolled online by people who thought I was too easy on her. Ms. Holmes and Mr. Evans, meanwhile, apparently thought I’d been too hard on them.

So they might as well embrace Mr. Fielder and — as is explored in the documentary — ask for a cut of the film’s profits.

My time in Mr. Fielder’s vortex began in June 2025, when he reached out saying he’d love to “pick your brain” off the record. He’d also spent time with Holmes before she went to prison — we’d just missed each other — and was working on a documentary. I promised not to tell anyone about the project.

We spoke a couple of times, comparing notes about our surreal experiences with Ms. Holmes. We’d so nearly overlapped that she’d worn the same camel sweater. It almost felt like a support group. It’s a pretty small circle of people who understand the dizzying experience of sitting in that canary-yellow house by the Pacific, watching Ms. Holmes nurse her baby days before reporting to prison. We’d both stared into those unblinking eyes. Both offered her Kleenex when she cried. Mr. Evans offered us both breakfast. We both felt ourselves getting swept up by Ms. Holmes’s quiet magnetism.

I’d left the house thinking I had better check my wallet. Mr. Fielder seemed to be similarly conflicted.

I wasn’t particularly familiar with Mr. Fielder’s work, but I wanted to be helpful. I tentatively agreed to appear on camera. Why not? He seems like a mensch! I mentioned this to a friend, a rabid Fielder fan who also happens to work in communications. His advice: “ABORT! ABORT!”

I told Mr. Fielder I actually didn’t feel comfortable being on camera. I apologized and wished him luck. He was disappointed. He laid on the guilt (fair). He’d already rented the camera package and had a crew traveling my way as we speak. He promised he’d make it “very fun and easy.” I felt bad. I wanted to help a nice Canadian man make his documentary. I asked my friend what to do. His response: “LEAVE TOWN!”

I have to admit, I ghosted Mr. Fielder. As it turns out, ghosting Nathan Fielder is hard to do. He is unusually likable, persistent and persuasive — winningly awkward, as he seems to be on camera — and there’s something that makes you want to help him.

Then, in February 2026, Mr. Fielder contacted me again. He wanted help to “clarify a little thing.” Ah, yes, a little thing. Ms. Holmes, he explained, said I’d misquoted her.

In the film, after reading the quote, the couple call their P. R. team. And sure enough, back in 2023, I had heard from one of her publicists who explained that Ms. Holmes’s recollection of our conversation differed from what was published. Would I double-check the quote? At the time, I reviewed my notes with my editors, who stood by the reporting. Mr. Evans sent The Times an 80-second audio clip, but it didn’t contain the disputed exchange. We heard nothing further and considered the matter resolved. (I’ve explained the full backstory here.)

It surprised me, because Ms. Holmes and I had spoken so much about the persona she created at Theranos. When I showed up at their rental house, she looked and sounded like a completely different person from the girl boss people remembered. What was with the James Earl Jones inflection? The Steve Jobs turtlenecks? The red lipstick?

In my profile, Holmes explained that, having founded Theranos at 19, she’d created a public persona to be taken seriously in business.

Now, three years later, Mr. Fielder was asking about that quote. I informed my old editor, who advised that I not reply. Instead, we referred Mr. Fielder’s inquiry to the newspaper’s public-relations department, standard practice when a published article is being challenged.

When the documentary premiered at the Telluride Film Festival, I heard from friends who told me that my Times article was in the movie.

I sent several requests to A24, the film’s studio, asking to see it. It felt like every culture writer and midlevel executive in Hollywood had seen the movie and was asking me about it. I heard about a big screening in L. A. They said it was at capacity. A spokeswoman at a firm helping A24 offered “to assist with a ticket to a local theater” when it opens. (“No spoilers.”)

I texted Mr. Fielder to see if he could help. (Canadian mensch, and all.) He said he’d try, and then reminded me that I never did answer his question about the disputed “character I created” quote (single tear emoji). And somehow I felt guilty all over again. I apologized. I told him I knew it was too late, but to call me if he wanted me to explain.

I finally saw “You Can See Everything” as God and A24 intended at a 4:30 p. m. showing on opening day at the Landmark Theatres Sunset in Los Angeles.

I spit-laughed at the scene of Mr. Fielder sitting on the second floor of Beer Authority across the street from The New York Times building, eating nachos and trying to track me down. I haven’t worked on staff at the paper since 2022. I live in Los Angeles and write screenplays now. But hey, I appreciate a good establishing shot.

The documentary’s closing postscript says Mr. Fielder eventually got in touch with me, that I stood by my story, but didn’t provide evidence supporting the quote. That’s not exactly what happened. I never discussed the disputed quote with Mr. Fielder. I referred his inquiry to The Times, which has stood by the reporting.

I don’t know what Ms. Holmes told Mr. Fielder that didn’t make the cut, but the tone of their conversations on camera is different from my memory of how she and I interacted. With me, our talks felt very much mother-to-mother. After Theranos imploded, Ms. Holmes told me that she finally felt free: “I began my life again.” I remember thinking that she sounded a lot like someone who had finally broken out of a cult and been deprogrammed.

But then I remembered that Ms. Holmes had been running the cult. It was her vortex all along, and thanks to Mr. Fielder and Mr. Oppenheim, we all get to experience it.

Amy Chozick, a former New York Times reporter, is a screenwriter and author based in Los Angeles. Her debut novel, “With Friends Like You,” was published in July.

Patrick Stewart Was Regal, Stately and Quite Hilarious

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Patrick Stewart (1940-2026)

Advertisement

Supported by

An Appraisal

The actor used his booming voice and Shakespearean pedigree in the service of absurd (and often lewd) comedy.

By Maya Phillips

Sir Patrick Stewart: The name of the English actor, who died Wednesday at 86, was pretty much always synonymous with elegance and dignity. His stately baritone immediately lent gravitas to every character he played. There was a courtly polish, an Old English classicism, to not only his performances but his persona as an actor of the small screen, the big screen and the stage alike. But for all his refinement — or perhaps because of all his refinement — Stewart also developed a reputation for a loony, deadpan, often self-mocking sense of humor.

What’s the opposite of an august elder who’s been knighted by Queen Elizabeth II? A weird, dirty old man with some inappropriate kinks. That’s a type Stewart played a few times throughout his career. There was a memorable “Saturday Night Live” sketch in which he played the owner of an erotic bakery obsessed with decorating cakes depicting women peeing.

On “Extras,” he played an exaggerated version of himself who writes a screenplay about a man who uses mind powers to strip off women’s clothes. (“I still can’t believe he agreed to do this scene,” Ricky Gervais wrote in a tribute Thursday.)

For more than 100 episodes, Stewart also voiced the “American Dad!” character Avery Bullock, the viciously unhinged deputy director of the C. I. A. In one episode, he offered this caustic response to someone’s attempt at a “Star Trek” reference: “Some of us spent the late ’80s and early ’90s getting laid.”

Many of his voice-over roles similarly took comic advantage of his signature regal manner of speaking. As the narrator of the Seth MacFarlane movies “Ted” and “Ted 2,” and as the voice of a decapitated pig head in the Amazon series “Bait” earlier this year, Stewart rolled out strings of exquisite expletives and strange non sequiturs purposely, humorously, at odds with his formal intonation. There was nobody better at using over-the-top English pomposity in the service of unrelenting wryness.

After all, to Stewart even his noble name and title was something to be occasionally poked fun at and undermined for the sake of a joke. On X, his handle was the playful @SirPatStew, and once on “The Graham Norton Show” he joked how his favorite fan-dubbed nickname was “Beef Stew.” Stewart wasn’t just interested in voicing or playing the absurd character but playing caricatures of himself that were nods to his venerated title or career. In 1996, the Shakespearean great appeared on “Sesame Street” in full Elizabethan garb to recite a parody of the famous “Hamlet” soliloquy. “‘B’ or not a ‘B’: That is the question,” he intones, holding out the letter “B” as though it’s poor Yorick’s skull.

The Officiant Mooned the Guests at My Daughter’s Wedding. Help!

Nobody Wanted Montague Street. Now Everybody Does.

Big Izakaya Energy Comes to SoHo

Advertisement

In 2015, as the host of the Just for Laughs festival, Stewart walked onstage to grand courtly fanfare while wearing “Monty Python”-style knight armor and later recited an advance eulogy that included jokes about his “unwashed genitals” and his sexual penchant for janitorial equipment and stage props. A couple of years later, the man who once played Hamlet, King Lear and Othello found a very different role: the voice of Poop in “The Emoji Movie.”

In a 2017 appearance on “Conan,” Stewart shared that his sense of humor was something he learned to adopt early into his run on “Star Trek: The Next Generation.” The disciplined actor, who by his own admission was “boring and tiresome” when he began the role of Jean-Luc Picard, thanked his castmates for quickly teaching him how to embrace his silliness. “I think they made me live longer,” Stewart said. “I think maybe I wouldn’t be here if they had not taught me how to laugh more.”

Maya Phillips is an arts and culture critic for The Times.

In Dueling Health Messages, Democrats Focus on Cost and Republicans on Fraud

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

After concentrating on the high price of gas and groceries, Democrats are using health costs to make their case about an “affordability crisis.”

By Sheryl Gay Stolberg

Reporting from La Crosse, Wis.

When Representative Derrick Van Orden, an endangered Republican congressman in western Wisconsin, appeared recently with hospital executives, he said his goal was to root out fraud in Medicaid so that “every dollar that’s allocated” would “go to someone that needs medical care, or a hungry child.”

Rebecca Cooke, his Democratic challenger, has an entirely different health care message. Last week, she stood in front of a giant blue bus emblazoned with “Sick of It! Fix Health Care Now.” in a park overlooking a river marsh.

“I’ve talked to people here in the city of La Crosse, small-business owners who have seen their premiums go up from $400 to $1,800 a month,” Ms. Cooke said then, at an event hosted by “Protect Our Care,” a left-leaning nonprofit. “People are really, really hanging on by a thread here.”

The dueling messages in a crucial state encapsulate the different approaches to an issue high on voters’ minds in the final days of the campaign. As the 2026 midterm season barrels toward a close, the two parties are talking past each other on health care. Republicans see the big problem as fraud. Democrats say it is cost.

Polls show clear partisan differences in what voters think. A recent survey by KFF, a health policy research organization, found that Democrats were twice as likely as Republicans to say addressing health care costs was “extremely important.”

After spending much of 2026 citing the high price of gas and groceries as proof of an “affordability crisis,” it makes sense for Democrats to build their closing argument around health costs, said Celinda Lake, a Democratic strategist.

“A lot of races are finishing on it,” she said. “It’s the No. 1 cost-of-living issue where Democrats have the biggest advantage.”

Fraud in government programs is Republicans’ top issue, the KFF survey found, with more than half calling it “extremely important.” Mollyann Brodie, who oversees polling and research at KFF, said Republicans may be building messages around fraud to close the “enthusiasm gap” in what looks, for them, to be a tough year.

But Joel White, who advises Republicans on health policy, said talking about fraud will not address voters’ concerns about the cost of care.

“Very few people make the leap to say if you reduce fraud, I will pay less, this will make things more affordable,” said Joel White, who advises Republicans on health policy. “Republicans kind of hung their hat on the fraud and abuse angle and tried to make the affordability argument, and it’s kind of falling flat.”

Democrats have long had an advantage on health care. But in the past they focused primarily on access, especially as they fought to defend the Affordable Care Act, the 2010 law that created Obamacare. This year, two votes in Congress changed the health care landscape, pushing cost to the top of Democrats’ affordability agenda.

A set of enhanced Obamacare tax credits, enacted as a temporary measure during the pandemic to make premiums more affordable, expired in January after the Republican-controlled Congress refused to extend them. Premiums have shot up by 58 percent, according to an analysis by KFF, and deductibles have soared.

Ms. Cooke has her own story about that: She is one of an estimated five million Americans who gave up their insurance coverage, saying it was no longer affordable, when the Obamacare tax credits expired.

President Trump’s giant domestic spending bill, which passed last year, included $1 trillion in cuts to federal Medicaid spending over the next 10 years. Many of those cuts have not yet gone into effect, but they pose a threat to cash-starved rural hospitals and are estimated to swell the ranks of the uninsured from 30 million today to 37 million in 2036, according to the Congressional Budget Office.

The bill created a $50 million fund to shore up rural hospitals. Democrats like Ms. Cooke, a daughter of dairy farmers, say it is not nearly enough. Two hospitals closed in the district in 2024.

When Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. turned up at a local dairy farm with Mr. Van Orden, he highlighted both the fund and the health benefits of milk. Ms. Cooke called the visit “a slap in the face to rural Americans.”

Similar debates are unfolding around the country. In Pennsylvania, Representative Scott Perry, a seven-term Republican incumbent, is in a tough race against Janelle Stelson, a former TV news anchor. During a recent debate, Ms. Stelson, a Democrat, complained that Mr. Perry “voted for a bill that is threatening struggling hospitals” and would “take health care away from people who live here and need it.”

Mr. Perry shot back that insurers need to be more transparent about prices, so that patients “can shop around” and focus on “wellness, as opposed to sick care, which is what we have now” — a remark that echoes Mr. Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement. He said his vote on the domestic spending bill “actually saved Medicaid” because the real problem with health care is fraud.

“Pennsylvania is the state with the most Medicaid fraud cases of any state in the country,” Mr. Perry said.

Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said Republicans were “laser-focused on lowering health care costs for working families.”

Some Republicans in tight races have sought to claim the health cost issue for themselves.

Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, a physician and former public health official, sponsored the Lower Health Care Premiums for All Americans Act. It passed the House and died in the Senate. In Michigan, Representative Tom Barrett is backing the Great American Health Care Plan, but it is stuck in committee.

“It’s just sitting there,” complained Sarah Chamberlain, the president of the Republican Main Street Partnership, who would like to see House leaders take more interest in the issue.

More than 80 percent of voters say the economy and cost of living are their top concerns; 69 percent say health care is a top issue, according to a recent poll by The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. Voters say they are feeling the pinch from rising premiums and the high cost of drugs.

John Havlicek, a retired high school Spanish teacher and union activist who appeared with Ms. Cooke in La Crosse, gained local internet fame when he went to Washington, courtesy of the liberal Center for American Progress, and confronted Mr. Van Orden about the price of food and medicine.

Mr. Havlicek received a diagnosis of Type-2 diabetes 18 months ago, he said in an interview. When diet, exercise and a medicine to lower his blood sugar failed to improve his health, his doctor put him on a GLP-1 drug to treat the diabetes. The drug also causes weight loss. Mr. Havlicek’s health improved and he lost 30 pounds.

But then his insurance quit covering the drug, which cost $1,000 a month.

“I’m angry, I’m scared and I’m fighting,” he said.

Ms. Cooke is making her second attempt to unseat Mr. Van Orden, a retired Navy SEAL and two-term incumbent who describes himself as a “100 percent disabled veteran.” A string of federal officials — Mr. Trump, Mr. Kennedy, Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Kash Patel, the F. B. I. director — have campaigned with him.

The congressman is a die-hard Trump supporter: After the president approved a firing squad execution of the gunman who killed 13 people in Fort Hood, Texas, Mr. Van Orden made headlines with a social media post suggesting he wanted to participate.

But in a rare break with his party — and a sign of how much his constituents are concerned about the cost of care — he voted to extend the Obamacare tax credits. Mr. Van Orden said he could not “sit back and watch my constituents lose access to health care or face massive premium hikes,” though he called it a “temporary patch” for a broken health system.

Before becoming a candidate herself, Ms. Cooke ran a political consulting firm and a small shop specializing in “Made in America” goods. She also founded a nonprofit to help businesses owned by women. Republicans have painted her as a Democratic operative and tried to label her a socialist.

She calls herself a centrist. She supports expanding Medicare, but not Medicare for All, the proposed universal government-funded health program championed by Senator Bernie Sanders, independent of Vermont. Even so, Mr. Sanders has endorsed her and campaigned with her on Sunday. The Blue Dog PAC, which backs moderates, has endorsed her as well.

In 2022, after her first race, Ms. Cooke said, she sold her shop; she now works part time as a waitress. She was insured through Obamacare and the tax credits she received meant she did not have to pay anything “because I didn’t make enough income,” she said. But when the tax credits expired, her costs went up to $250 a month. She also pays $80 a month, out of pocket, for two prescriptions.

“I’m pretty healthy,” she said. “But fingers crossed.”

If she wins her election, she will have coverage again, paid for by the taxpayers, as do all members of Congress.

Sheryl Gay Stolberg is a correspondent based in Washington for The Times, covering Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Trump’s health agenda.

Mosquito Lasers

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

China has come up with an innovative way to kill the insects.

By Sam Sifton

I am the host of The Morning.

Check this out: A company in China has invented a $1,000 A. I.-enabled brick that tracks mosquitoes in flight and burns their wings off with a laser. The United States may be ahead of China in developing A. I. models, but the device is an example of how quickly China is putting powerful computing into consumer products.

The technology also has military potential. As Keith Bradsher, who saw a demonstration, writes, “It’s not hard to imagine how a system that tracks and shoots down mosquitoes today could be adapted to target drones tomorrow.”

What could go wrong? A lot. A laser powerful enough to dispatch a mosquito is powerful enough to damage your eyes. To protect people (and animals that are not mosquitoes), A. I. software recognizes them and prevents the laser from shooting, even in darkness. A camera also identifies shiny surfaces so beams don’t ricochet elsewhere.

Keith’s description of the device’s effectiveness is bracing:

For anyone who has ever wished mosquitoes a horrible death, this is a strikingly high-tech way to make that wish a reality. The laser delivers a gruesome end, though not a quick one. Mosquitoes whose wings have burned off can take hours or even days to die, lying on the ground and twitching slightly.

After the demonstration, Keith examined the fallen bugs. Their wings were gone, but their legs and bodies appeared intact. They couldn’t fly, even when he waved his hand directly over them.

See the device at work.

The best view in D. C. is from the top of the Washington Monument, 555 feet above the National Mall. Spin in a circle and you can take the nickel tour: the White House, the Capitol, the Reflecting Pool, the Lincoln Memorial, the Jefferson Memorial, all the hits.

It’s a great place, in other words, to see President Trump’s imprint on the city, even as his projects face legal challenges. To grasp the extent of his Washingtonian makeover (and to allow you to experience the grandeur of the urban landscape), Times journalists built a high-resolution panorama, using 32 overlapping, close-up images our photographers captured at the top of the monument. Then software stitched them together into a 360-degree projection that acts like a custom-made Google Street View built from the perspective of a soaring bird.

It’s super cool. You can zoom in on the new helipad Trump installed outside the White House, and the new ballroom rising where the East Wing once stood. There’s the Eisenhower Executive Office Building he thinks is the wrong color. See where he wants to raise a 250-foot arch, and where he wants to replace athletic fields with a statue garden dedicated to American heroes. And there in the distance, you can see East Potomac Park, where Trump has already removed hundreds of trees as he replaces a municipal golf course with a championship-level one.

A number of federal judges have said that Trump can’t build this element or that one without the approval of Congress. But the Republicans who control Congress have not pushed back on him, which is allowing him to remake Washington just the way he wants it. It’s starting. Come on up and see for yourself.

Patrick Stewart survived a grim childhood in England’s coal-mining north country to become an acclaimed Shakespearean actor. Then, in middle age, he took on the role that would bring him worldwide fame, playing the baritone-voiced starship captain Jean-Luc Picard in the “Star Trek” spinoff “The Next Generation.” Stewart died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles. He was 86.

Read his obituary.

Revisit seven of his most notable performances.

Other Big Stories

I don’t understand how one party or the other can simply redraw the congressional district maps. Aren’t there rules for how and when this can be done? Who sets them? | Carol Roach | Overland Park, Kansas

Yes, there are rules, but they vary by state. Typically, congressional districts are redrawn once a decade after the census to ensure they contain about the same number of people. But federal law allows more frequent redistricting. In states where the legislature controls the process (instead of an independent commission), a majority party can pass a new map. States can even change their rules when they want, something California voters did last fall. The Supreme Court also recently changed its interpretation of the Voting Rights Act, clearing the way for states to eliminate majority-minority districts by redrawing maps. — Eve Washington, a data journalist with The Upshot

Another Toll of the Violent Unrest in France: The Political Center

The New York Times October 30, 2026

Unrest in France

Advertisement

Supported by

Support for Édouard Philippe, the leading candidate from the centrist bloc, has eroded, while his far-right and far-left rivals benefit.

By Mark Landler

Reporting from Paris

Soon after President Emmanuel Macron of France spoke to a traumatized country, in the aftermath of riots that set cities aflame on Oct. 17, Mr. Macron’s former prime minister and aspiring successor, Édouard Philippe, responded to his old boss.

“Our country needs to be commanded,” Mr. Philippe wrote, scolding Mr. Macron for what he called a failure to restore order, protect shopkeepers from looters and engage protesting high-school students in dialogue.

For Mr. Philippe, the leading presidential candidate from France’s shrinking political center, it was not the first break with Mr. Macron. But his tempered tone suggested he was speaking more in sorrow than in anger. It was all but lost in an angry cacophony, underscoring how the upheaval is reshaping France’s politics: More extreme figures are sidelining centrists.

No major candidate has lost more support in the polls than Mr. Philippe since the protests erupted last month: roughly two percentage points, leaving him between 13 percent and 15 percent. He now trails the far-left candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, and remains well behind the far-right leader, Marine Le Pen, who claims the backing of about a third of those surveyed in most polls.

As things stand, Mr. Philippe, 55, would not make it into the second round of France’s two-round election system that starts in April. That would leave voters choosing between Ms. Le Pen and Mr. Mélenchon — a race she would likely win.

“Politics are getting more polarized, with the student movement and allegations of police brutality,” said Philippe Marlière, an expert on French politics at University College London. “The two extremes have their own repertoire for that. The moderate right is being squeezed between these two forces,” he continued. “They are being suffocated. There is no space for them to be heard.”

Mr. Philippe joins a beleaguered band of centrist politicians across Europe. Anger over rising prices, stagnant economies and declining prospects for young people has propelled populist parties on the far right and far left. That has flummoxed centrists like Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany; Keir Starmer, the ousted prime minister of Britain; and Mr. Macron himself.

A day after the riots, Ms. Le Pen warned about a “profound crisis of confidence and authority.” She spoke at a desk in front of a French flag, in a video that seemed designed to present her as a president in waiting. Mr. Mélenchon lashed out at the government for its handling of the protests, accusing it of “blind violence.”

Mr. Philippe, the mayor of the port city of Le Havre, sought to strike a law-and-order message, but less stridently. He met with shopkeepers in Paris whose properties were looted and vandalized. He patrolled with the police in the eastern French city of Charleville-Mézières.

Speaking to Le Point, a conservative French magazine, this week, Mr. Philippe also tried to highlight his right-wing credentials. Young people from immigrant backgrounds were overrepresented among those who rioted, he said, a claim the government has not backed up. He called it a “failure of integration in our country” and promised to cut in half the number of immigrants to France over the next five years.

Mr. Philippe’s representatives acknowledge that France’s fraught mood does not favor a sensible, center-right politician, one best known for serving Mr. Macron during the first three years of his presidency, most visibly during the Covid pandemic.

“There is a before and after Oct. 17,” said Arnaud Péricard, a spokesman for Mr. Philippe’s party, Horizons. “It’s a very complicated moment, where a lot of electors are losing their boundaries.”

Mr. Philippe had also come under scrutiny in an investigation of embezzlement of public funds involving the city hall in Le Havre. On Thursday, his lawyer confirmed a report in Agence France-Presse that Mr. Philippe had been designated as an “assisted witness” in the case. That legal status does not clear him but indicates that, for now, there is not enough evidence to charge him.

Mr. Péricard said Mr. Philippe’s campaign viewed the development as “very positive,” adding, “This matter is now behind him.”

Mr. Philippe’s strategy, he said, was to increase his public visibility in the coming days, but otherwise to ride out the current upheaval without losing his status as the leading centrist candidate. Front-runners in French presidential elections often stumble, Mr. Péricard noted, referring to Ms. Le Pen, and the campaign won’t shift into high gear until January.

“Édouard always describes himself as a diesel,” he said. “He’s slow to accelerate, but once he gets up to pace, he keeps it.”

For the moment, Mr. Philippe’s position seems secure, if only because the center is so fractured. His most direct rival on the center right, Gabriel Attal, another former prime minister, has also seen his poll numbers sag since the unrest broke out. Bruno Retailleau, a more hard-line figure, has faced competition from the mayor of Cannes, David Lisnard, an upstart hard-liner with a savvy social-media profile.

On Wednesday, Mr. Attal called for a primary vote to determine which centrist candidate should go on to face the far right and far left.

On the center left, Raphaël Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament, has also recently enjoyed a modest bounce in polls, though analysts question his staying power. They are waiting to see if François Hollande, the former Socialist president, will enter the race early next year.

Some in France yearn for a fresh face to shake up the race, much as Mr. Macron did in 2017, when he ran as a 39-year-old agent of reform. France’s economics minister, Roland Lescure, said this week that he believed a majority of people would vote for a moderate candidate if the right one emerged.

“We’ll see by the time January or February comes if someone can emerge or maybe some two can emerge” as a unifying figure, Mr. Lescure said to reporters. “There’s a bit of a silent majority that is still out there, that I think requires or demands an incarnation, which we haven’t been able to provide yet.”

Political analysts, however, said they were skeptical that any “white knight” would emerge, in part because of the challenges of building a viable campaign on short notice. Even before the recent unrest, the polarization of French politics would make a centrist coalition of the kind Mr. Macron assembled far-fetched today.

“His strength lies in having succeeded in consolidating an electoral base and in having created an electoral base that didn’t exist before him,” said Raphaël LLorca, an analyst at the Jean-Jaurès Foundation, a left-leaning research group in Paris. “Isn’t this, deep down, the end of Macronism, in the sense that each of his voters is returning to their own homes?”

Mr. Macron has never been more unpopular than he is now, which poses another hurdle for Mr. Philippe. Although he left the government in 2020, and even called on Mr. Macron to resign last October amid chaos over passing a budget, Mr. Philippe is identified as a veteran of his movement.

“Whatever credibility the government had evaporated on Oct. 17,” said Mujtaba Rahman, an expert on France at the Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy. “That context is damaging to Philippe by association.”

Ségolène Le Stradic and Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

Mark Landler is the Paris bureau chief of The Times, covering France, as well as American foreign policy in Europe and the Middle East. He has been a journalist for more than three decades.

The New York Times October 30, 2026

The Context

From France to Brazil, voters are railing against the status quo, even as the politics of disenchantment make lasting change nearly impossible.

By David Wallace-Wells

When Notre-Dame burned, in 2019, it looked to the world like a tragic bonfire of European cultural patrimony, sparked perhaps by a dropped cigarette. When the Limoges city hall went up in flames on Oct. 17 — ignited by arsonists amid France’s largest and most contentious protests in at least a generation — it seemed to reveal something more alarming: not just the ungovernability of the country but also the brokenness of the whole social compact. To many watching from abroad, it looked as if liberalism itself were burning.

There were 800,000 people marching in the streets that day, demonstrations several times the size of the largest protests against climate-motivated gas taxes in 2018, which were mounted by rural voters who came to be known as the gilets jaunes, or Yellow Vests. What began as a movement of students angered by the poor condition of their schools — and the sense that their futures were now determined by an unfamiliar black-box algorithm that would deliver their university placement with all the consideration of a free chatbot — had, by then, fused with growing outrage over sharp increases in the cost of living and frustration with the broken promises of the French state.

Thousands of veterans of the gilets jaunes, as well as trade unions, firefighters and schoolteachers, had joined the students. Labor leaders called for a general strike, and students at the right-leaning Alsace law school joined in, in solidarity. Protesters were often beaten back, arrested or tear-gassed by police, and into the apparent chaos swarmed masked youths rioting and looting without such obvious political intent. Still, 72 percent of the country has said it supports the demands of the protesters, and on the following Saturday, 800,000 people again took to the streets. Right-wing observers in France and abroad, meanwhile, fretted about the menace of anarchism and “Islamo-lefitism.”

To many Americans, this may just seem like France being France, where revolutionary cosplay has been a rite of passage for generations and where the streets of Paris, it’s often joked, represent the fourth branch of government. But the school protests that engulfed the capital earlier this month originated not in France but on Mayotte, a French territory made up of tiny islands in the Indian Ocean, 5,000 miles away. They then jumped across Africa and the Atlantic to French Guiana, a faraway French outpost of the European Union, tucked between Brazil and Suriname. When the rage that burned in the periphery finally arrived in what the French sometimes call “the hexagon,” it ignited first in provincial cities, then in the banlieues, or suburbs, and only last in central Paris.

The phenomenon is, in fact, a global one: generational frustration with the basic bargain of the status quo, and such deep-seated exasperation with existing institutions and establishment politics that building an enduring governing majority starts to look like an impossible task.

In India, a remarkable cross-class Gen Z coalition has come out to protest corruption, disenfranchisement and above all the rule of Narendra Modi. There has been similar generational unrest in Italy and Spain and Belgium — and even Albania, where Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump’s play to develop Sazan Island as a luxury resort inspired a national uprising. There have been genuine Gen Z revolutions in Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka in recent years, and a student movement just ousted Serbia’s populist authoritarian president.

In Brazil, in the several weeks between the first round of national elections and the second, millions took to the streets and then swarmed to the polls to deliver a contradictory result. The far-right scion Flávio Bolsonaro, who triumphed in the first vote, failed in the second — the first time in the country’s modern history that the outcome flipped between the initial round and the runoff. The leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was returned to office, in a heroic comeback immediately celebrated by liberals the world over.

But in his fourth term, the progressive icon will be dealing with the most reactionary Congress in modern Brazilian history, an opposition led by four other members of the Bolsonaro family, widespread skepticism about the validity of the results and almost universal distrust of the country’s Supreme Court. The shock result may make Lula look like the world’s most successful 21st-century politician, as many of his admirers have argued. But it also lands the country in what looks like irresolvable political deadlock. And it’s not exactly a healthy sign that the man he defeated fled the country.

In the United States, the road to the midterms hasn’t been blockaded by mass protest or pockmarked by social unrest. But even a blue wave on Election Day seems likely to yield only a quarrelsome divided government and a lame-duck version of Donald Trump’s imperial presidency. An ascendant Democratic Party still isn’t clear what it stands for, or what to fight for, or how long its claim on political power is likely to last.

That the country lurches from one so-called vibe shift to another is a sign that the enduring vibe is dissatisfaction. Almost certainly, 2026 will be the seventh straight election to deliver a repudiation of the party holding the presidency. Quite likely, that will happen again in 2028. Perhaps it will open a new horizon for American politics. Or perhaps it will just mean the other party becomes once again the source of disappointment and rage.

The mood of political futility didn’t arrive with price spikes from the Iran war and crippling heat waves sweeping Europe this summer. In 2024, when more people went to vote in elections around the world than in any previous year in human history, the party in power lost ground almost everywhere, in what some have called “a bonfire of the incumbents.”

This was a remarkably uniform judgment against the political order that had governed much of the world since roughly the end of the Cold War. But the conventional explanation for why was straightforward. Populist resentment had been growing almost everywhere since the financial crisis of 2008, yielding a dark global weather system into which rapid inflation, mass migration and pandemic backlash arrived to create a perfect storm of anti-incumbency.

Each of those crises has cooled since 2024, with the pandemic increasingly in the rearview mirror, the postpandemic surge in global migration down considerably from its 2023 peak and inflation more manageable almost everywhere (despite the war in Iran). But the mood simply hasn’t changed much. Global politics is still defined not by what political scientists long ago identified as the incumbency advantage but by its opposite: a structural preference for those out of power and a reflexive hostility toward those already wielding it.

For a decade now, the anti-establishment turn has looked like a crisis to the champions of the old order, confused by what might have produced it — with the threatened disruption of A. I. now added to the list. But just as important may be where it all leaves us: with what feels like a new political metabolism that chews through majorities and renders even inspiring victories short-lived. The resulting whiplash isn’t just discombobulating; it also risks becoming self-perpetuating. Voters dissatisfied with the way things stand are quick to turn on new leaders, depriving their governments of the popular legitimacy necessary to achieve anything lasting, only to then blame them for that failure too.

The global pattern isn’t entirely uniform: Left-of-center leaders in Mexico and Canada are remarkably popular, and charismatic politicians like Lula or Trump can win additional time in office even in the face of widespread disappointment and frustration.

Yet the broader pattern still looks fairly clear. The populist politics of the last decade haven’t meant a universal rightward march, as so many feared. But they have meant that very few leaders anywhere have managed to build and sustain majorities that allow them to do what we used to think of simply as governing: designing new policies to improve the lives of their citizens, then implementing those changes over time. Franklin Roosevelt was still figuring out what the New Deal was supposed to be well into his second term, and Reagan’s “morning in America” was affirmed by his landslide re-election and the subsequent victory of his successor, George H. W. Bush. Even though Barack Obama won the closest thing to a true landslide in modern American history, he still needed to win again in 2012 to secure the Affordable Care Act.

But in America the window of policy opportunity now seems to shrink with each cycle. If you want government just to stand by and stand down, turnover and turmoil works fine. But if you want real social change? Even in an age of desiccated expectations, leaders have to be able to deliver something concrete if they hope to survive the rage of voters.

In France, Emmanuel Macron is coming to the end of a decade in power that began with promises to resolve the nation’s crises and divisions with a sort of technocrat’s magic wand. Nine years later, that project has failed, and Macron himself is catastrophically unpopular. One recent poll put his approval rating at 15 percent. Since dissolving Parliament in the summer of 2024, he’s been struggling to maintain a governing coalition and has barely managed to pass a budget — doing so this year without parliamentary approval in the face of two no-confidence votes.

But what’s just as striking is that the alternatives don’t seem to hold much appeal for the French, either. The leading candidate to succeed Macron is the far-right candidate Marine Le Pen. But though she has consolidated the French right and is seen abroad as a kind of unstoppable force, she remains remarkably unpopular at home, with only about a third of the country behind her and most of the voting public divided among a half-dozen candidates who have essentially no chance of winning. (In a runoff, she’s widely expected to triumph, by collecting second- and third-choice votes.) It’s enough to make the near future seem unmanageable: Close to 90 percent of the country believes it is heading in the wrong direction, but none of the leading candidates can claim the support of more than one-third of its voters.

Politics isn’t just a popularity contest but the way nations deal with structural change. And here the case of France is especially telling. The country is aging, growing slowly when it grows at all and being squeezed by social welfare obligations and ballooning debt. The average French retiree now makes more money than the average working person. And though the problem isn’t quite as stark in most other wealthy countries, it is hard to find one whose politics haven’t been distorted by what the American conservative commentator Russ Greene has called “total boomer luxury communism” — the hoarding of resources by the old and ailing.

This is especially galling to French youth, given that Macron’s governments have cut taxes on corporations and the wealthy as well as services but made no obvious improvements to their own prospects, which look relatively dim. But it is also the case that France spends more of its budget on schools than most other countries in Europe, and considerably more on health care and pensions. Most French people would tell you that the quality of all public services is in obvious decline, but fewer seem to trust that the state is capable of improving them. And while you can find prominent economists with a sunnier story to tell about the economic vitality of the continent, few voters believe them — and to the young, that relative optimism sounds like a cruel joke. Sound familiar?

It isn’t just the French who’ve been caught, viselike, between what seems unacceptable and what seems unachievable. The question is what it might take to break the vise.

Source images for illustration above: Elyxandro Cegarra/Anadolu, via Getty Images; Mélanie Salaün /Hans Lucas/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images; Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images; Manu Brabo/Getty Images; Nelson Almeida/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images; Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images; Anne-Christine Poujoulat/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images; Teresa Suarez/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images.

David Wallace-Wells is a staff writer for the magazine and the author of ‘‘The Uninhabitable Earth: Life After Warming.’’

The 2,000-Nit OLED in Apple’s New MacBook Is a Big Deal

Wired October 28, 2026

Laptops with OLED screens aren’t particularly special. They’ve been around for a decade. You can currently buy a touchscreen OLED machine for as little as $700, and even the iPad Pro has had an OLED screen since 2024.

So, why did Apple wait over a decade to release its own touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro? The simple answer for the long wait is that the company wanted to do it “the Apple way.” But in this case, “the Apple way” involves somehow cranking up the display to 2,000 nits, solving both the brightness and glare problems that OLED laptops have always suffered from.

Having seen the thing with my own eyes at a media event today in Los Angeles, I can tell you that this screen is the real deal.

Apple is using a tandem OLED panel, the same layer-stacking technology used in the OLED iPad Pro. The real innovation here, however, is that the panel has been optimized to hit a new peak brightness of 2,000 nits, and that’s a result that matters.

That big number is meaningless on its own, but here’s the context. Nits are the standard measure of screen brightness used across the consumer tech industry. A cheap OLED laptop maxes out around 300 nits. A higher-end OLED laptop might get you up to 1,000 nits of brightness—but only in brighter and more colorful High Dynamic Range content like specific streaming apps, YouTube videos, and games. In other words, the vast majority of the time you’re using an OLED, it’ll feel like a dimmer screen than normal. The iPad Pro can get up to 1,600 nits for HDR content, and 1,000 nits for the less bright, less colorful Standard Dynamic Range content. That’s closer.

But this MacBook Pro’s screen is on an entirely different level. It’s a ground-up redesign of the tandem OLED layer arrangement in the iPad Pro, even down to the manufacturing process. And the result is that it can blast your eyes with 2,000 nits of brightness in both SDR and HDR. That means whether you’re looking at some generic wallpaper, a website, or an HDR-compatible movie, you’ll feel that extra brightness. That’s why, I assume, Apple gave it the name PROLED XDR. In a world where the words “OLED” and “HDR” don’t necessarily indicate how good the experience is, more weighty jargon is needed.

As with all tech, bigger numbers don’t always add up to a noticeable difference for the user. But when it comes to HDR performance, we’ve been waiting a long time for OLED to catch up.

HDR, or High Dynamic Range, serves as a measure of color depth, brightness, and contrast—and in the past, this has always involved a trade-off. An OLED screen can turn each individual pixel any color, and it can turn off individual pixels in the display. This allows OLED to have great color control and unbeatable contrast, since when you turn a pixel off, it renders absolutely black.

But OLEDs couldn’t get super bright, and other screen tech like mini-LED could get much brighter, which is why Apple stuck with mini-LED for years, using it on the MacBook Pro and Studio Display XDR. This technology allowed Apple to have the laptops with the best HDR performance out there.

With the 2026 MacBook Pro, that compromise no longer exists. This OLED screen has both the brightness and contrast in its pocket, and you can see it.

An OLED panel has lots of more benefits over conventional backlighting beyond just contrast. Mini-LED struggles with an effect called blooming, where bright parts of images bleed light to the surrounding area, which is where lots of detail is lost in the image. OLED completely fixes that, giving each pixel a much wider range of control (up to completely turning off). As part of the Apple event I attended, we were shown a selection of HDR images with lots of contrast, a number of which had fields of darkness at the edges that made it look like the image simply disappeared into the bezel. Very pretty. We also watched a darker scene in the show Widow’s Bay in HDR, which was an excellent showcase of the range of detail this screen can show.

The new screen helps this MacBook stay exceedingly light, as well. Much of the savings in weight comes from the OLED design, since the screen uses thinner and lighter materials than screens past. Despite the computer using the same aluminum chassis as the previous MacBook Pro, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro weighs just 3 pounds, which is 12 percent lighter than before.

To put the new screen into context, we were also shown a comparison between Apple’s OLED and the OLED of a high-end competitive Windows laptop. The difference was striking, especially in off-axis viewing. At its worst, there were visible rainbow effects on the Windows machine’s screen.

There’s a catch, though. While Apple’s screen can get up to 2,000 nits, it’s normally capped at 1,000 nits. When the laptop’s built-in adaptive brightness sensor thinks you need a boost, the screen’s brightens increases up to 2,000 nits. So the brightness only hits the high end when you’re outside or working under really harsh lighting conditions. The previous-gen MacBook Pros also did this, but to a lesser degree. With this machine, you’re getting 400 more nits of SDR brightness right out of the box, with the ability to crank it up to twice as much.

Glare is another issue with conventional, low-brightness OLED laptops that the MacBook Pro improves. When deeper blacks are rendered on the screen, it often results in harsher reflections. Sometimes it can get so bad, it feels like you’re looking into a mirror. The brightness alone on the MacBook Pro goes a long way toward overpowering glare and reflections, but Apple is also using what it claims is a “state-of-the-art” anti-reflective coating. Almost every laptop screen uses some kind anti-reflective coating, so one can hope that Apple’s “state-of-the-art” coating is at least on par with those, but I can attest that this is the very best I’ve seen.

The ultimate solution to cutting glare and reflections is still the option for a nano-texture display, where the anti-reflective pattern is actually etched into the screen itself rather than layered on top. That’s available as an upgrade on both the 14-inch and 16-inch models.

The other major innovation happening with the MacBook Pro’s screen is the introduction of touch. Like OLED itself, this is a feature we’ve seen on many other laptops for well over a decade. I came in hoping Apple would swing for the fences here, but its use of touch interaction feels much more modest. (Let us quickly forget the failure of the Touch Bar from 2016.)

The implementation itself is impressive. Interacting with elements on the screen feels every bit as fluid as it does on an iPad. The screen also supports many of the familiar trackpad gestures, such as pinch to zoom or a three-fingered swipe to switch Spaces.

The most natural feeling touch optimizations have been lifted directly from iPadOS. If you tap in the top left window controls, they zoom in to let you select more precisely. You can even grab a window and flick it to the side to quickly get into Split View. My favorite optimization is the ability to tap, hold, and slide down to select an item within the Menu Bar. Very clever. And yet, I was still hoping for a stronger commitment on the software side. You can’t use an Apple Pencil on this screen, and nothing in the hardware of the MacBook Pro has been adjusted to make touching the screen feel any more ergonomic.

The bigger issue is with third-party apps, though. While touch-to-click will work on all apps automatically, it’s up to developers to do any more than that. Even the third-party apps we were shown during demos had varying degrees of touch optimization.

The 3D modeling application ZBrush was a good example. While certain aspects were touch-enabled, none of the controls or menus had the useful optimizations that Apple’s first-party apps had. Hopefully this touch option will become more widely adopted, but I can foresee a future in which these fingers-first interactions are mostly forgotten outside of occasionally scrolling down a webpage with your thumb. And let me be clear: All of this is more than what Microsoft has ever done to optimize Windows 11 for touch. (And Microsoft even has Windows 2-in-1 tablets to support!)

With the 2026 MacBook Pro, Apple is doubling down on what’s working well for it: leading the way in high-end hardware. There’s plenty more testing to do on the MacBook Pro in the coming weeks, but this OLED screen already looks like the one the entire industry will be chasing for years to come.

This Is What the GOP’s Final Midterms Push Looks Like

Wired October 28, 2026

Republicans are spending the final week ahead of the midterm elections defending historically red Senate seats that have suddenly become competitive, according to federal filings and sources familiar with the matter.

A significant focus is now on four Senate races in ​K​ansas, ​South Carolina, ​Nebraska, and even ​Mississippi, all traditionally red seats, in what’s ​an ominous development for Republicans in their effort to at least keep control of the upper chamber.

Trump operatives tell Inner Loop that they do not expect ​Democrats to win those Senate seats and that they have ​mainly directed GOP outside groups to spend there to ​​help boost incumbents that only have a narrow lead.

But ​t​he operatives also concede that they are having to divert an increasing amount of resources ​to those states—states that president Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024 and where Republicans never dreamed of having to spend tens of millions of dollars.

In total, in the penultimate week of the campaign, the Senate Republican–aligned Senate Leadership Fund spent $14 million across those four states, according to a WIRED review of federal filings. The biggest spend has been in Kansas, where SLF has abruptly dumped more than $5 million.

Trump operatives say Kansas has been a major headache since the start of October, when Trafalgar Group​, a GOP pollster, found Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton one point ahead of ​incumbent GOP senator Roger Marshall.

Marshall, a doctor, has had an unusually tough race following a slew of negative stories about how he pursued legal action against his patients with unpaid bills and how much time he spends in Florida. Some political operatives have also complained that he has not taken his race seriously, sources say.

​But the last-minute spending is also coming in places like South Carolina, where SLF spent another roughly $5 million to help incumbent Darline Graham, who has struggled to galvanize Trump's base despite having the president’s endorsement that propelled her to victory in the primary.

SLF also spent nearly $3 million in Nebraska to help Republican incumbent senator Pete Ricketts, who has been behind in some polls, and in Mississippi, the fund put just under $1 million toward Republican incumbent senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The final sprint has highlighted the fraught predicament for Republicans, who are having to patch a seemingly ever-growing number of vulnerabilities.

Trump's campaign schedule has also added several deep-red states that are flashing warning signs, in addition to the expected campaign stops in battleground states. Last week, Trump went to Kansas and South Carolina. This week, he has been in Mississippi and will return to Kansas and South Carolina, as well.

Still, several Trump operatives tell Inner Loop they have been encouraged by the fact that Democratic candidates lately have not expanded their leads in several key Senate races—a concern that has cropped up among some Senate Democratic leadership aides.

Chief among their concerns is Michigan, the best GOP pickup opportunity. Many of the most viable paths to Democrats taking the Senate majority pass through the state, but Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has suffered lingering issues with key voting blocs.

Black voters turned out in droves to help Barack Obama carry the state in 2008 and 2012, and the conventional wisdom in Washington is that El-Sayed will need similar support in order to keep the seat blue, one of the Democratic aides tells Inner Loop.

But the trouble for El-Sayed, they add, has been the decades-long animosity between Arab and Black communities in Michigan, a divide that was further strained during the primary when supporters of his challenger, Haley Stevens, ran ads featuring Barack Obama praising her earlier work during the financial crisis.

In an effort to rebuild at least part of that coalition, Obama held a joint rally with El-Sayed in Detroit over the weekend, which aides are hoping could persuade some voters. Operatives aren’t sure if it’ll be enough.

We will have to see how it pans out. See you next week, on the other side!

This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Most Servers on the Planet Are Vulnerable to This Firmware Code-Execution Flaw

Wired October 28, 2026

Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.

The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.

The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.

With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.

“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”

CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.

As the official advisory puts it:

During network boot, the PXE Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe) keeps a receive request open for ICMP error messages and copies each received message into the fixed 504-byte field Mode. IcmpError of its private context structure. The copy loop’s bounds handling is incorrect in both the IPv4 and IPv6 handlers (PxeBcIcmpErrorDpcHandle and PxeBcIcmp6ErrorDpcHandle): for a message longer than 504 bytes it still copies bytes into the field, and it advances the destination pointer by the cumulative rather than the per-fragment length, so an oversized message writes attacker-controlled bytes past the field. Nothing earlier on the receive path restricts the message length.

The malicious error can be delivered through a simple unicast sent from any network distance to a target device’s IP address, as long as it’s sent during the PXE boot sequence. An attacker can deliver a denial-of-service by causing the boot sequence to hang. When the attacker knows what the target firmware build is, it can plant a “counterfeit event” that executes the malicious code on the CPU in its UEFI firmware environment. The code runs in ring 0, a CPU’s most privileged execution level. Because exploits bypass attestation processes designed to cryptographically prove to remote servers that the hardware is secure, they present a key opportunity for elevating limited privileges.

CVE-2026-97631 joins a long list of previously discovered vulnerabilities in UEFI or code that works closely with it. The most severe of them, LogoFail, stemmed from logo images included in the UEFI of just about every hardware maker. Rendering bugs allowed attackers to subvert the chain of trust UEFI enforces and go on to install malicious components before the OS loaded or Secure Boot ran. PixieFail was a vulnerability similar to CVE-2026-97631. It, too, was the result of faulty PXE boot flaws in EDK2. Following discovery of the vulnerability, researchers embarked on multiple fuzzing projects designed to surface other critical flaws in the open source code library. It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw.

Other recently discovered UEFI flaws include:

Like CVE-2026-97631, exploitation or use of these payloads is appealing because it allows attackers to infect machines early in the boot process, before TPM and other defenses load, so they can inflict maximum damage. Given the ubiquity of CVE-2026-97631, Moore said it’s likely a “forever” bug that will live on in end-of-support systems.

There are important caveats and limitations to exploiting this latest vulnerability. As noted, some level of control over a local network is a prerequisite. That likely limits exploitation to insiders or attackers, such as nation-states or ransomware operators, who manage to gain low-level access inside a network and are looking for a way to elevate system rights. There’s no evidence yet that CVE-2026-97631 provides an initial entry point into a network. There are other hurdles to clear.

“For exploiting the vulnerability itself, an attacker needs to guess specific addresses within the target system, so it’s not something that you can throw a single exploit at any target and get RCE across a diverse range of devices, but it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those,” Jesse Michael, a principal researcher at firmware security firm Eclypsium, told Ars.

“Unlike some of the previous, high-profile vulnerabilities like BootHole, Black Lotus, and Baton Drop, this vulnerability can be fixed with a basic code fix, which will require deploying a BIOS/UEFI update, but they don’t need to deal with revocations, pk/kek/db/dbx key management updates, or making sure to update OS and provisioning media like you do with Secure Boot bypasses in the bootloader itself.”

CVE-2026-97631 doesn’t affect home and small office users, or any other users who boot their devices solely from disk drives. Instead, it applies only to organizations with machines that boot from local networks, or conceivably from Internet-connected resources. Even then, the targeted firmware must rely on EDK2, as opposed to a different reference implementation, and use the PXE functionality (which is turned on by default).

In an email, Intel said that none of its “commercial products currently under security support” are known to be affected. “Intel does not include the affected EDK2 functionality in its reference code, though it may be integrated by an OEM board vendor or system manufacturer,” the company added. It advised customers to check with their system manufacturer for specific guidance. Publicly available Intel reference code, however, makes reference to EDK2. Further, TianoCore has said that each Intel-supplied UEFI development kit “is a fully validated implementation … for a specific revision of the EDK II source.” Many other Intel documents reference EDK2 as well.

Arm, meanwhile, responded to a list of questions with: “CVE-2026-97631 is not directly applicable to Arm’s product portfolio.” Like Intel, firmware the company makes available also borrows heavily from EDK2. TianoCore has also documented Arm’s reliance on EDK2.

While it’s possible some platforms are free of EDK2 code, it’s prudent for users of all servers to investigate if CVE-2026-97631 affects them.

Questions sent to AMD, Phoenix Technologies, AMI, Microsoft, and Amazon—likely some of the other biggest organizations affected—went unanswered when this post went live. Without concrete answers to questions about the use of EDK2 by organizations like these, it’s impossible to say what or how devices are affected and what actions, if any, these organizations, or their users, should take. Representatives from the TianoCore Project also didn’t respond.

Some readers are likely to be unhappy at the lack of detail. Sometimes—particularly in cases involving botched disclosures that break embargoes months before they’re scheduled to lift—there’s no escaping the lack of actionable information in initial reporting.

Those affected should check with the maker of the firmware being used to boot their systems and ask for guidance. Beyond that, they should consider turning off network boot capabilities at least temporarily if possible. Firmware configurations should always enable security features such as TPM and Secure Boot whenever possible, although those defenses don’t protect against this particular threat. It’s also a good idea to monitor logs for signs of exploitation attempts.
